signals.title: geoToH3 error messages reference swapped argument positions in default lat_lon mode
signals.text: _Found via ClickGap automated review. Please close or comment if this is incorrect or needs adjustment._ _Retrospective finding from a historical scan of [PR #78852](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/78852) (merged 2025-04-15). Confirmed on current codebase — close with a note if already fixed._ ### Describe what's wrong When geoToH3 is called with Float32 arguments (accepted by type validator but rejected in execution), the error message references the wrong argument position and the wrong type. E.g., geoToH3(toFloat32(55.71), toFloat64(37.79), toUInt8(15)) reports 'Illegal type Float64 of argument 2' when the actual issue is Float32 at argument 1. **Root cause:** geoToH3.cpp:103-104: error for !col_lat always references arguments[1] and position 2, but in lat_lon mode col_lat comes from arguments[0] (position 1). Similarly line 113-114: error for !col_lon always references arguments[0] and position 1, but in lat_lon mode col_lon comes from arguments[1]. **Why we believe this is a bug:** geoToH3.cpp:88-97 assigns col_lat/col_lon from different argument indices based on geotoh3_argument_order setting, but geoToH3.cpp:99-115 hardcodes arguments[1]/position 2 for col_lat errors and arguments[0]/position 1 for col_lon errors, matching only the old lon_lat order. **Affected locations:** - `src/Functions/geoToH3.cpp:99` — Error message for col_lat null check references wrong argument index - `src/Functions/geoToH3.cpp:109` — Error message for col_lon null check references wrong argument index **Impact:** When a user passes Float32 to geoToH3 in default lat_lon mode, the error message points to the wrong argument (position and type), making debugging confusing. The error says the Float64 argument is bad and reports the wrong position. ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `f86671aa80af`). ### How to reproduce ```sql #!/usr/bin/env bash # Tags: no-fasttest # Test: geoToH3 error messages reference wrong argument position in default lat_lon mode CURDIR=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd) # shellcheck source=../shell_config.sh . "$CURDIR"/../shell_config.sh # In default lat_lon mode, arg1=latitude, arg2=longitude # Pass Float32 as arg1 (latitude). Error should reference argument 1. # BUG: error references argument 2 and shows Float64 type instead of Float32. ERR1=$($CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT --query "SELECT geoToH3(toFloat32(55.71), toFloat64(37.79), toUInt8(15))" 2>&1) echo "$ERR1" | grep -oP 'argument \d' | head -1 # Pass Float32 as arg2 (longitude). Error should reference argument 2. # BUG: error references argument 1 and shows Float64 type instead of Float32. ERR2=$($CLICKHOUSE_CLIENT --query "SELECT geoToH3(toFloat64(55.71), toFloat32(37.79), toUInt8(15))" 2>&1) echo "$ERR2" | grep -oP 'argument \d' | head -1 ``` ### Expected behavior ``` argument 1 argument 2 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` argument 2 argument 1 ``` ### Additional context **Open risks:** - Similar pattern may exist in other H3 functions with setting-dependent argument ordering **Suggested fix:** Make the error message indices dynamic based on geotoh3_argument_order, or use the correct argument index for each variable: for col_lat, reference the actual source index (0 in lat_lon mode, 1 in lon_lat mode), and similarly for col_lon. **Analysis details:** Confidence HIGH | Severity P3 | Testability: `STATELESS_SQL` Found during automated review of [PR #78852](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/78852). --- _ClickGapAI · Confidence: HIGH · Severity: P3 · Finding: `h_pr78852_001`_

signals.title: When a Refreshable MaterializedView fails to delete tmp tables, it keeps creating more tmp tables until the server runs out of disk
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour I created a large materialized view with 1-day refresh. The server ran out of disk space the next week. When I got the server back online, table bytes showed 1 `tmp.inner_id.123` table and 7 `_tmp_replace_xyz` tables, all for the same MV. The entry in `system.view_refreshes` showed this: ``` exception: Code: 359. DB::Exception: Table or Partition in <db.table> was not dropped. Reason: 1. Size (65.89 GB) is greater than max_[table/partition]_size_to_drop (50.00 GB) 2. File '/var/lib/clickhouse/flags/force_drop_table' intended to force DROP doesn't exist How to fix this: 1. Either increase (or set to zero) max_[table/partition]_size_to_drop in server config 2. Either pass a bigger (or set to zero) max_[table/partition]_size_to_drop through query settings 3. Either create forcing file /var/lib/clickhouse/flags/force_drop_table and make sure that ClickHouse has write permission for it. Example: sudo touch '/var/lib/clickhouse/flags/force_drop_table' && sudo chmod 666 '/var/lib/clickhouse/flags/force_drop_table'. signals.title: singleValueOrNullState / singleValueOrNullMerge lose semantic state during merge and serialization
signals.text: **Describe the unexpected behaviour** `singleValueOrNull` tracks two semantic flags in addition to the stored value: `first_value` and `is_null`. In the current implementation: - merge does not propagate `rhs.is_null` - write/read serialize only the underlying value payload That means aggregate states can change meaning in two ways: 1. a partial state that already means `result must be NULL` can merge into an empty destination and turn back into a concrete value 2. a valid single-value state can lose `first_value = false` after serialization/deserialization and then merge back as `NULL` Current code on `master`: - merge path and state fields: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/fac6aa2045d1c81e28650fdd39dcbdb477f25d28/src/AggregateFunctions/AggregateFunctionSingleValueOrNull.cpp#L26-L77 - explicit TODO about serialization losing `first_value` / `is_null`: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/fac6aa2045d1c81e28650fdd39dcbdb477f25d28/src/AggregateFunctions/AggregateFunctionSingleValueOrNull.cpp#L79-L83 **Which ClickHouse versions are affected?** Confirmed in current `master` by source review at commit `fac6aa2045d1c81e28650fdd39dcbdb477f25d28`. This appears to be longstanding. The same pattern already existed in the original implementation added on June 4, 2021: - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/289c5d3ad680c6e07ef189eed9ea30417acdac65/src/AggregateFunctions/AggregateFunctionMinMaxAny.h#L633-L668 - https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/289c5d3ad680c6e07ef189eed9ea30417acdac65/src/AggregateFunctions/AggregateFunctionMinMaxAny.h#L789-L801 So this likely affects all released versions since `singleValueOrNull` was introduced. **How to reproduce** I have not executed the SQL below locally yet; these are the minimal validation queries derived from the current implementation. 1. Merge-state loss: ```sql SELECT singleValueOrNullMerge(s) FROM ( SELECT singleValueOrNullState(number) AS s FROM numbers(2) ); ``` The inner state has already observed two distinct values, so the final result should be `NULL`. From the current merge code, it looks like the empty destination copies only the stored value from `s` and ignores `s.is_null`, so this may return the first stored value instead. 2. Serialized-state loss: ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_single_value_or_null_state; CREATE TABLE t_single_value_or_null_state ( id UInt8, s AggregateFunction(singleValueOrNull, UInt64) ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; INSERT INTO t_single_value_or_null_state SELECT 1, singleValueOrNullState(toUInt64(42)); SELECT singleValueOrNullMerge(s) FROM t_single_value_or_null_state GROUP BY id ORDER BY id; DROP TABLE t_single_value_or_null_state; ``` This should return `42`. From the current `write/read` implementation, only `data()` is persisted; `first_value` and `is_null` are dropped. After deserialization, the state appears non-empty but still has `first_value = true`, which should make the final merge return `NULL`. **Expected behavior** - A partial state that has already determined `multiple distinct values => NULL` should stay NULL when merged again. - A serialized/deserialized state should preserve `first_value` and `is_null`. - `singleValueOrNullState` followed by `singleValueOrNullMerge` should be semantically stable. **Additional context** This looks separate from the recent JSON-specific crash report / fix: - issue: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/103630 - PR: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105535 That pair is about passing `result_type` instead of `value_type` during deserialization for JSON. The issue here is broader semantic state loss in merge and serialization logic itself. The 2024 rewrite kept the same behavior: - `49d089d` Reimplement singleValueOrNull - `ff98e763` AggregateFunctionSingleValueOrNull: Prefer composition to inheritance

signals.title: `DESCRIBE` and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` report stale column types for TO-target materialized views after upstream `ALTER MODIFY COLUMN`
signals.text: When a materialized view is created with `TO target_table`, ClickHouse infers and stores the view's column types from the SELECT at creation time. If the source or target table's column types are later changed via `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN`, the view's stored types do not refresh — even though runtime data flow uses the source's and target's *current* types and works correctly. This means `DESCRIBE` and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` show types that no longer reflect runtime behavior, which makes schema-drift auditing very confusing. ### Reproduction ```sql CREATE TABLE source ( id UInt64, status Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1) ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE target ( id UInt64, status Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1), cnt UInt64 ) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree ORDER BY (id, status); CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv TO target AS SELECT id, status, count() AS cnt FROM source GROUP BY id, status; -- Initial state matches: DESCRIBE mv; -- status: Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1) -- Extend the enum in both source and target: ALTER TABLE source MODIFY COLUMN status Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1, 'C' = 2); ALTER TABLE target MODIFY COLUMN status Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1, 'C' = 2); DESCRIBE source; -- Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1, 'C' = 2) DESCRIBE target; -- Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1, 'C' = 2) -- Matview's stored type is still the original: DESCRIBE mv; -- Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1) <-- stale SHOW CREATE TABLE mv; -- column list still Enum8('A' = 0, 'B' = 1) -- Despite the stale type, runtime works: INSERT INTO source VALUES (1, 'C'); SELECT * FROM target WHERE id = 1; -- ┌─id─┬─status─┬─cnt─┐ -- │ 1 │ C │ 1 │ -- └────┴────────┴─────┘ ``` ### Expected `DESCRIBE` and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` on TO-target materialized views should report the current effective schema, refreshed when the source / target tables evolve. ### Impact Operators auditing schema drift reasonably trust `DESCRIBE` and `SHOW CREATE TABLE` to reflect what's enforced. With this behavior, you can end up convinced a matview is missing an enum value when in fact runtime is fine — or, in the reverse case, convinced everything is fine because source and target match while a stale matview type silently differs. ### Version 26.2.1.413 (ClickHouse Cloud).

signals.title: REFRESH on stopped or paused materialized view fires after START and only once even it's triggered multiple times, not out of order
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour Consider: ```sql create table src (x Int64) engine Memory; insert into src values (1); create materialized view v refresh every 1 year (x Int64) engine Memory empty as select x from src; system stop view v; system refresh view v; -- Here I'd expect the count below to be 1, but is 0. select sleep(2) format Null; select 'after refresh while stopped', count() from v; system start view v; -- The remembered refresh fires only now; wait for it. system wait view v; select 'after start', count() from v; drop table v; drop table src; ``` From documentation: "Trigger an immediate out-of-schedule refresh of a given view." Therefore I'd expect it to be triggered despite it's stopped or paused ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? v26.5.2.39-stable ### How to reproduce ```sql create table src (x Int64) engine Memory; insert into src values (1); create materialized view v refresh every 1 year (x Int64) engine Memory empty as select x from src; system stop view v; system refresh view v; -- Here I'd expect the count below to be 1, but is 0. select sleep(2) format Null; select 'after refresh while stopped', count() from v; system start view v; -- The remembered refresh fires only now; wait for it. system wait view v; select 'after start', count() from v; drop table v; drop table src; ``` ### Expected behavior `system refresh view v;` is being triggered despite view is stopped. ``` after refresh while stopped 1 after start 1 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace `system refresh view v;` is being triggered only after view is started. ``` after refresh while stopped 0 after start 1 ``` In case this is expected behavior, problem is if `system refresh view v;` is executed multiple times. Example: ``` system stop view v; system refresh view v; system refresh view v; system refresh view v; system start view v; -- The remembered refresh fires only now; wait for it. system wait view v; -- Here I'd expect the count below to be 3, but is 1. select 'after start', count() from v; ``` should return: ``` after start 3 ``` but it returns 1 (refresh is triggered only once): ``` after start 1 ``` ### Related issues and pull requests Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107476 (I would prefer to wait for this PR to be merged and then change the behavior of this in case the suggestion above is correct and reasonable.) ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: Runner-wide OOM (OOM in dmesg / Server died) on Stateless test runners, especially arm_asan_ubsan, azure
signals.text: Tracking the recurring runner-wide total-memory OOM seen on the Stateless test runners. The clickhouse-server process is killed externally by the runner (kernel OOM reaper / cgroup), not by a per-query `max_memory_usage` limit and not by a per-test bug. Requested by @alexey-milovidov in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106177#issuecomment-4697249422. ### Signature - Reported tests: `OOM in dmesg` and the downstream `Server died`. - The `OOM in dmesg` context is the kernel reaper line, with no in-process ClickHouse stack and no `max_memory_usage` exception. Example (PR #106177, sha `bcab07c64fe`, `Stateless tests (arm_asan_ubsan, azure, parallel)`): ``` [ 4715.228520] oom_reaper: reaped process 5618 (clickhouse-serv), now anon-rss:0kB, file-rss:268kB, shmem-rss:0kB ``` Still the same signature on the latest hit (PR #108103, 2026-06-26): ``` [10409.875013] oom_reaper: reaped process 5159 (clickhouse-serv), now anon-rss:0kB, file-rss:140kB, shmem-rss:0kB ``` - This is distinct from the multistage-distributed-queries heap-use-after-free (#106020, reverted by #107122), which showed a SIGSEGV / heap-use-after-free with a ClickHouse frame. There have been zero such CH-frame UAF/SEGV rows on `arm_asan_ubsan, azure` in the last 10 days, so the residual failures are the genuine external-kill host-OOM class, not that bug. ### Evidence it is runner-wide, not per-test At a single sha/run (PR #106177, `bcab07c64fe`), `OOM in dmesg` fired on 38 distinct build/test shards (amd_debug, amd_tsan, amd_msan, amd_asan_ubsan, amd_llvm_coverage, arm_binary, arm_asan_ubsan azure parallel and sequential, and others). That breadth across unrelated shards in one run indicates a host-memory squeeze on the runner box, not a per-shard regression. ### Breadth and timeline (CIDB `default.checks`) The box-wide storm in early June self-resolved. Daily OOM-kill counts on the `arm_asan_ubsan, azure` shard: - 06-09 = 13, 06-10 = 93, 06-11 = 59, 06-12 = 6, 06-13 = 1. The sharp decline tracks the #107122 revert of #106020 (merged 06-11 01:37 UTC), which ended the box-wide memory storm. Since then the class persists at a low, steady residual level (roughly 2 to 7 hits/day on `arm_asan_ubsan, azure`, mostly across unrelated PRs, occasionally master), and the all-runner breadth is now 1 to 2 shards/day rather than dozens. So this is now steady-state host-RSS pressure on these runners (heaviest on the ASan + Azure shard, which carries the most memory overhead), not an active incident. ### Representative report https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106177&sha=bcab07c64fe0b38a77582b4d8fc6ae935285d276&name_0=PR&name_1=Stateless%20tests%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%2C%20azure%2C%20parallel%29 ### Related work In-flight and recently merged memory-tracking / overcommit work that should reduce this class: - #106055 (bound untracked memory per-CPU to avoid overcommit and OOMs) — merged 2026-06-27. - #104964 (dynamically adjust memory limit based on system free/cached memory) — merged 2026-06-12. - #104965 (server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`) — open. - #104976 (speculatively reserve growth headroom on top of observed RSS) — open. Note: #107037 (flaky test 01603_read_with_backoff_bug) tracked one victim test of this class but is now closed; there is currently no open umbrella tracking issue for the runner-wide OOM class, which is why this one is filed. ### Suggested labels testing, infrastructure

signals.title: Add a TOLERANCE clause to ASOF JOIN
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Use case `ASOF JOIN` currently matches each left row with the most recent right row at or before the left timestamp, with no way to cap how far back that match may reach. We would like an optional `TOLERANCE` clause that bounds the maximum time gap between the left key and the matched right key, so that only "recent enough" matches are returned and stale rows are excluded. This is a common requirement in time-series and financial analytics (for example transaction cost analysis, quote-to-trade enrichment, and sensor/state enrichment), where a match that is technically the latest available but minutes or hours old is misleading. **Current behavior** For a trade joined to the prevailing quote: ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time ``` If the nearest preceding quote for a given trade is very old, `ASOF JOIN` still returns it. There is no built-in way to say "only match if the quote is within N units of the trade". ### Describe the solution you'd like An optional `TOLERANCE` clause on `ASOF JOIN` that accepts an interval (or numeric) value and restricts matches to those where the difference between the left and matched right key is within the given bound. Suggested syntax (open to alternatives): ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 10 SECOND ``` **Semantics**: a left row at `t.time` matches a right row at `q.time` only if both hold: - `q.time <= t.time` (existing ASOF inequality) - `t.time - q.time <= tolerance` When no right row is within tolerance, the behavior should follow the join type: `ASOF LEFT JOIN` returns the left row with NULL/default right columns, `ASOF JOIN` (inner) drops the row. ### Describe alternatives you've considered The gap can be filtered after the join: ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time WHERE t.time - q.time <= INTERVAL 1 SECOND ``` This is correct but can be slower than necessary. The join still scans backward to find a match that the `WHERE` clause then discards. With a native tolerance, the backward scan can stop as soon as a right row is older than the left row by more than the tolerance, since no earlier row can qualify. For an `ASOF LEFT JOIN`, a post-join WHERE instead removes the entire result row, breaking `LEFT JOIN` semantics. ### Additional context This capability is well established, which gives a clear reference for expected semantics.
signals.author: ayakovlev-clickhouse

signals.title: Native protocol: send String columns with a size stream
signals.text: ### Company or project name chconn ### Use case In the Native protocol, `String` columns are sent as `varint(size) + bytes` for every row. A client has to decode this row by row: read one varint, copy one value, repeat. The client also can not preallocate the buffer, because it does not know the total data size before reading all rows. For string-heavy queries this is the most expensive part of reading data in a client. I am the author of [chconn](https://github.com/vahid-sohrabloo/chconn) (Go client, native protocol) and in profiles of string-heavy SELECTs this decode loop dominates the client CPU time. On the storage side this problem is already solved. Since 25.10 there is `MergeTreeStringSerializationVersion::WITH_SIZE_STREAM` (default since 25.11): String columns in MergeTree parts are stored as a sizes substream (UInt64 per row) plus a data substream. But the Native protocol still always uses `SINGLE_STREAM`. `NativeWriter` and `NativeReader` build their `SerializationInfo` with `SerializationInfoSettings::enableAllSupportedSerializations()`, and this function keeps `string_serialization_version = SINGLE_STREAM`. The comment on this function already says: "Additional serialization versions can be added here in the future" — this proposal is exactly that. ### Describe the solution you'd like Add a new protocol revision, same pattern as `DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_V2_DYNAMIC_AND_JSON_SERIALIZATION`: ``` DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_STRING_WITH_SIZE_STREAM_SERIALIZATION = 54487 ``` When both sides are on this revision or higher: - `NativeWriter` builds the `SerializationInfo` with `string_serialization_version = WITH_SIZE_STREAM` and `propagate_types_serialization_versions_to_nested_types = true`. So all Strings use the new format, also inside `Array` / `Nullable` / `Map` / `Tuple` / `Variant` / `JSON`. This reuses the same serialization trees that MergeTree uses since 26.3, no new format code is needed. - `NativeReader` enables the same versions based on the peer revision. So the server can also accept this format on INSERT, and `clickhouse-client` supports it automatically (same code). In a Native block all substreams go into one buffer, so for a plain String column the layout is: ``` N x UInt64 sizes (little-endian) | all string data concatenated (no per-row prefixes) ``` A client on the new revision reads `8*N` bytes, sums the sizes (so it can allocate the exact buffer size), and then reads the whole data with one bulk read. No per-row parsing, no reallocation. Clients keep both decoders and select by the negotiated revision, like it already works for LowCardinality, custom serializations and Dynamic/JSON V2. Old clients and old servers are not affected at all. INSERT works in both directions: a client on the new revision must also send Strings in this format, because the server reader selects the serialization from the peer revision. So inserts get faster too, but a client has to implement both read and write. ### Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ### Additional context I made a small prototype on master (12 lines, writer side only, gated by a setting just to test) and implemented the client side in chconn. Client-side decode benchmark (same data, both formats, Go): | workload | varint | size-stream | speedup | |---|---|---|---| | 1M strings, len 20 | 35 ms, 4 allocs | 8.9 ms, 0 allocs | ~4.0x | | 1M strings, len 0-60 | 41 ms, 4 allocs | 9.3 ms, 0 allocs | ~4.4x | | 100k strings, len 200 | 7.1 ms | 3.1 ms | ~2.3x | End to end (patched master 26.7.1.1, localhost TCP, `SELECT s FROM bench_strings`, 5M rows, avg length 29.5, MergeTree, same server and table, only the wire format is different): | | wall time | rows/s | |---|---|---| | varint | 152-158 ms | ~32M | | size-stream | **39 ms** | **~128M** | I verified the results are byte-identical between both formats. One note: the new format sends more bytes for short strings (8-byte sizes instead of 1-byte varints, about +35 MB for these 5M rows) and it is still ~4x faster on localhost. With LZ4/ZSTD compression the size bytes are mostly zeros and compress very well, so on a real network it should also win. The nested types come almost for free from `propagate_types_serialization_versions_to_nested_types`, but the transport needs round-trip tests for all of them (Array, Nullable, Map, Variant, JSON...). If there is interest I can prepare a PR (writer + reader + revision constant + tests).
signals.author: vahid-sohrabloo

signals.title: Parquet fails to write Nullable(Tuple) correctly
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe the unexpected behaviour When writing a Nullable(Tuple(...)) column (including the geo aliases, Nullable(Point), Nullable(Ring) element types, Array(Nullable(Point))) to Parquet, the tuple's own null map is discarded: the schema written is a required group with nullable leaves, so Nullable(Point) comes out as Tuple(1 Nullable(Float64), 2 Nullable(Float64)). Reading the file back with the original schema fails with Code: 53 ... Requested type of column p doesn't match parquet schema: parquet type is Tuple, requested type is Nullable(Point) (TYPE_MISMATCH); reading with schema inference turns NULL row into (NULL,NULL) Parquet can express this (an optional group), and Arrow, ArrowStream, & ORC all round-trip correctly. `output_format_parquet_use_custom_encoder` 1 and 0 produce the same schema. ### How to reproduce Repro on 26.6.1.431: ``` -- clickhouse local --allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1 INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet, 'p Nullable(Point)') SELECT * FROM values('p Nullable(Point)', (1,2), (NULL)); DESCRIBE file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet); -- p Tuple(`1` Nullable(Float64), `2` Nullable(Float64)) SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet, 'p Nullable(Point)'); -- Code: 53. DB::Exception: ... parquet type is Tuple, requested type is Nullable(Point). (TYPE_MISMATCH) SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet); -- (1,2) then (NULL,NULL), NULL row lost ``` Same for `Nullable(Tuple(a UInt8, b String))` & `Array(Nullable(Point))` ### Expected behavior round trip preserves NULL ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: SYSTEM RELOAD/UNLOAD DICTIONARY ON CLUSTER ignores the initiator's current database and silently targets `default`
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse CI monitoring (@groeneai). ### Describe what's wrong `SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY <bare-name> ON CLUSTER <c>` and `SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY <bare-name> ON CLUSTER <c>` do not resolve the dictionary name against the initiator's current database before the statement is put on the DDL queue. The bare name is serialized as-is, so every worker re-resolves it against its own current database, which for a query arriving over the DDL queue is `default`. Consequence: run from database `mydb`, the command silently reloads/unloads `default.d` instead of `mydb.d`, and it returns success. If `default.d` does not exist the command is a no-op; if it does exist, an unrelated dictionary is reloaded. There is no error either way, so the operator has no signal that the wrong dictionary was touched. Filed at the request of @Manerone in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111756, which fixes part of this. See "Additional context" for what that PR covers and what remains. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Version: master `26.8.1.1` (commit `c462bd70270441b71070b4c5417a32e33cac0bab`), debug build. No non-default settings. Single node is enough. The server needs `<distributed_ddl>`, a keeper, and a cluster containing itself: ```xml <clickhouse> <distributed_ddl><path>/clickhouse/task_queue/ddl</path></distributed_ddl> <remote_servers> <one_node><shard><replica><host>127.0.0.1</host><port>9000</port></replica></shard></one_node> </remote_servers> </clickhouse> ``` ```sql CREATE DATABASE mydb; -- the dictionary the user means CREATE OR REPLACE DICTIONARY mydb.d (k UInt64, v String) PRIMARY KEY k SOURCE(NULL()) LAYOUT(FLAT()) LIFETIME(0); -- a same-named decoy in `default` CREATE OR REPLACE DICTIONARY default.d (k UInt64, v String) PRIMARY KEY k SOURCE(NULL()) LAYOUT(FLAT()) LIFETIME(0); SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY mydb.d; SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY default.d; USE mydb; SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY d ON CLUSTER one_node; SELECT database, name, status FROM system.dictionaries WHERE name = 'd' ORDER BY database; ``` ### Expected behavior `mydb.d` is `LOADED`, `default.d` stays `NOT_LOADED` -- the same target the non-`ON CLUSTER` form picks. ### Actual result ``` after ON CLUSTER default d LOADED after ON CLUSTER mydb d NOT_LOADED ``` Control, same session, same server, `ON CLUSTER` dropped: ``` after local (control) default d NOT_LOADED after local (control) mydb d LOADED ``` The statement returned success in the failing case. The entry serialized into Keeper carries the unqualified name: ``` query: SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY ON CLUSTER one_node d ``` `SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY ... ON CLUSTER` behaves the same way. ### Additional context Code path on master (`a1ae499e22944d8`): * `InterpreterSystemQuery::execute` returns inside the `if (!query.cluster.empty())` branch (`src/Interpreters/InterpreterSystemQuery.cpp:361-366`) **before** the `RELOAD_DICTIONARY` / `UNLOAD_DICTIONARY` canonicalization block at `:378-382`, so on the `ON CLUSTER` path no qualification happens at all. * The worker-side rewrite does not supply it either: `ASTSystemQuery::getRewrittenASTWithoutOnCluster` (`src/Parsers/ASTSystemQuery.h:278-281`) calls `removeOnCluster` (`src/Parsers/ASTQueryWithOnCluster.h:48-57`), which injects `params.default_database`. `DDLTask.cpp:507` sets that from `address_in_cluster.default_database`, i.e. the cluster address's `<default_database>`, not the initiator's current database. PR #111756 by @Manerone moves the qualification ahead of the `ON CLUSTER` dispatch and fixes the case above. I verified that empirically: with only its `InterpreterSystemQuery.cpp` hunk applied to `a1ae499e22944d8` (build id `a9c961304b95de468e98629a04ada7c56003c136`), an `ON CLUSTER` command issued from a node that is itself in the cluster and hosts `mydb.d` leaves `mydb.d LOADED` and `default.d NOT_LOADED`. One case is still open with that patch applied, which is why the PR was left unmerged. `ExternalDictionariesLoader::qualifyDictionaryNameWithDatabase` (`src/Interpreters/ExternalDictionariesLoader.cpp:211-232`) only fills in `.database` when the calling server can resolve the name itself (`has(resolved_name)`). So a coordinator or gateway node that enqueues the DDL without hosting the dictionary leaves the name bare and each worker falls back to `default` again. Measured on a two-node setup, both nodes running the patched binary: node A is the initiator and is **not** a member of cluster `c_workers` and hosts no dictionaries; node B is the only cluster member and hosts both `mydb.d` and `default.d`. ``` -- on node A, in database mydb: SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY d ON CLUSTER c_workers; -- returns success -- observed on node B: default d LOADED mydb d NOT_LOADED ``` Keeper entry: `query: SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY ON CLUSTER c_workers d`. The precondition is confirmed on node A: `USE mydb; SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY d` throws `Code: 36. DB::Exception: Dictionary (\`d\`) not found. (BAD_ARGUMENTS)` and `system.dictionaries` there is empty, so the `has()` check takes the leave-bare path. Fixing this seems to need the initiator's current database propagated independently of whether the initiator can resolve the dictionary locally. That has one wrinkle worth deciding explicitly: for a bare name, local execution resolves an XML dictionary ahead of a same-named dictionary in the current database, so unconditionally qualifying would change which one a bare `ON CLUSTER` name selects on workers that host an XML dictionary of that name.
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Paimon incremental read: a Keeper watermark left ahead of the warehouse (e.g. after restore) silently and permanently skips committed data
signals.text: ## Describe what's wrong A Paimon table read with incremental reads enabled (`paimon_incremental_read = 1`, which keeps a consumed-snapshot watermark in Keeper at `<paimon_keeper_path>/committed_snapshot`) can **silently and permanently skip durably-committed data** if the Keeper watermark is ever left ahead of the warehouse's latest snapshot id — for example after the Paimon warehouse is restored from an older backup, or is rolled back / truncated by another engine, while the ClickHouse Keeper cursor is not correspondingly reset. `PaimonMetadata::collectIncrementalDataFiles` resolves the resume point by comparing the Keeper watermark to the warehouse's current latest snapshot id, and treats "watermark `>=` latest" as an unconditional no-new-data case: ```cpp else if (*committed_snapshot_id >= state->snapshot_id) // PaimonMetadata.cpp:825 { LOG_DEBUG(log, "Snapshot {} already processed (committed={}), no new data", // :828 state->snapshot_id, *committed_snapshot_id); return {}; // :830 } ``` There is no read-repair and no error on this path — it returns an empty file list at `LOG_DEBUG`. So every snapshot the writer commits after the restore whose id is `<=` the stale watermark is never delivered to any consumer, with no exception and no user-visible log. Snapshots committed *above* the stale watermark resume normally, which makes the loss a silent hole rather than a total stall. The table-identity guard `validateTableIdentity` does not catch this: it re-reads schema-0 `timeMillis`, which is unchanged by a byte-copy restore, so the guard passes and the stale watermark is trusted. This is distinct from the *documented* At-Most-Once loss (`PaimonStreamState.h:35-37`), which concerns the window between advancing the watermark and finishing consumption *within a single poll*; here durably-committed data that no consumer ever received is dropped at resume time. This surface is behind the experimental setting `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine` (default off). ## Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on `26.8.1.1`; the code on current `master` is identical (`PaimonMetadata.cpp:825-830`). ## How to reproduce Requires the experimental Paimon engine and a Paimon warehouse (e.g. written with `pypaimon`), read via `PaimonLocal` with incremental reads and a Keeper cursor: 1. Create a warehouse with snapshots 1..3 (300 distinct rows) under the server's `user_files/`. Back up the warehouse directory at the snapshot-1 point. 2. `CREATE TABLE pt (...) ENGINE = PaimonLocal('<table_path>') SETTINGS paimon_incremental_read = 1, paimon_keeper_path = '/paimon/cursor', paimon_replica_name = 'r1'` with `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1`. 3. Poll `SELECT ... FROM pt` incrementally — all 300 rows are delivered and the Keeper watermark reaches 3. 4. Restore the warehouse directory from the snapshot-1 backup (schema unchanged). Have the Paimon writer append two new snapshots of new, distinct rows — these become snapshots 2 and 3 again (ids `<=` the stale watermark 3). 5. Poll again (and once more): **zero of the new rows are returned, no error is raised**, and the Keeper watermark stays 3. 6. Append one further snapshot (snapshot 4, id `>` 3): only snapshot 4's rows are returned — confirming the consumer is alive and the loss is confined to the snapshots at id `<=` the stale watermark. Controls that isolate the cause: reading the same restored-and-re-appended warehouse under a **fresh** `paimon_keeper_path` delivers all the new rows (so the warehouse content is intact and readable); and without the restore, appending snapshots above the watermark delivers normally. ## Expected behavior When the committed watermark is ahead of the warehouse's latest snapshot id (the warehouse has moved backwards relative to the cursor), ClickHouse should detect the disagreement and either fail loudly or reset the cursor to the warehouse state, rather than silently returning no data and permanently skipping every subsequent commit at id `<=` the stale watermark. ## Error message and/or stacktrace None — the defining property is that the skip is silent (only a `LOG_DEBUG` "no new data" line).
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: Paimon incremental read: the unfenced processing_lock lets a second consumer silently duplicate acknowledged rows after a session expiry
signals.text: ## Describe what's wrong The Paimon incremental-read stream state (`allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine`) coordinates competing consumers that share one `paimon_keeper_path` with an ephemeral `processing_lock` znode. That lock has **no fencing**, so if the lock is lost while a consumer is mid-read (the usual cause being a Keeper session expiry that auto-removes the holder's ephemeral node), a second consumer acquires the freed lock and re-reads the same committed snapshot range. Both consumers then deliver the same committed data — an at-least-once **duplicate of already-acknowledged rows, with no error logged anywhere**. The `processing_lock` exists precisely to make the read/commit critical section mutually exclusive, so this defeats its only purpose. The unfenced-ness is visible in three places in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/PaimonStreamState.cpp` (line numbers on `master`): 1. Acquire writes the owner's `replica_name` into the lock node but it is **never read back** anywhere — the value is dead (`acquireProcessingLock`, lines 70–90): ```cpp keeper->create(processing_lock_path, replica_name, zkutil::CreateMode::Ephemeral); ``` 2. Release is an **unconditional** `tryRemove(path, -1)` whose return code is discarded, so it deletes whatever node is at the path — including an ephemeral created by a *different* session (`removeProcessingLock`, lines 269–274): ```cpp keeper->tryRemove(processing_lock_path, -1); ``` 3. The watermark advance is a **blind** `makeSetRequest(..., -1)` in its own standalone `tryMulti` with no check op on the lock and no monotonicity guard, so it succeeds regardless of whether the caller still holds the lock or whether another consumer moved the watermark underneath it (`setCommittedSnapshot`, lines 214–238): ```cpp ops.emplace_back(zkutil::makeSetRequest(committed_path, toString(snapshot_id), -1)); ``` For contrast, the sibling `is_active` node in the *same file* is fenced correctly — it reads the node back with its `Stat` and removes it version-checked (`tryGet(is_active_path, existing_identifier, &stat)` then `tryRemove(is_active_path, stat.version)`, lines ~159 and ~165) — so applying the same discipline to `processing_lock` is clearly feasible. Note this is distinct from the documented "at-most-once" window (a *loss* on crash between watermark advance and delivery): the issue here is a **duplicate with no crash**, produced by a routine session expiry, which an at-most-once contract does not permit. ## Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes, reproduces on current `master`. The Paimon storage engine is experimental (`allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine`, default off). ## How to reproduce Two ClickHouse instances (two Keeper sessions), each with a Paimon incremental-read table over the **same** warehouse and the **same** `paimon_keeper_path`: ```sql -- on both servers CREATE TABLE c (id Int64, v String) ENGINE = PaimonLocal('/warehouse/db.db/t1') SETTINGS paimon_incremental_read = 1, paimon_keeper_path = '/paimon/stream', paimon_replica_name = 'ra'; -- 'rb' on the second server ``` 1. Commit snapshot 1 to the warehouse; consumer A drains it, so `committed_snapshot` = 1. 2. Commit snapshots 2 and 3 (ids above the watermark). 3. Consumer A starts an incremental read: it acquires `processing_lock`, reads `committed_snapshot` (still 1), and plans the read of snapshots 2–3. 4. Consumer A's Keeper session expires (network blip / GC pause / Keeper failover exceeding `session_timeout_ms`). A's ephemeral `processing_lock` is auto-removed, but A's in-flight read continues (its server process is alive; the ZooKeeper client reconnects on a fresh session). 5. Consumer B polls: it acquires the now-free `processing_lock`, reads `committed_snapshot` (still 1, because A has not advanced it yet), and delivers snapshots 2–3. 6. Consumer A finishes: its blind `setCommittedSnapshot(3)` succeeds (version `-1`), and A also delivers snapshots 2–3. Both consumers have now delivered snapshots 2–3 — the same committed rows twice, with no error. The window in step 3–4 is deterministically reproducible by pausing A's `setCommittedSnapshot` multi to Keeper and deleting the `processing_lock` znode during the pause (which is exactly what a session expiry does to the ephemeral), then letting B poll and finally releasing A. ## Expected behavior Each committed snapshot is delivered to at most one consumer. A consumer that lost its `processing_lock` (session expiry, or the node otherwise gone) must not silently commit over another consumer's progress: the watermark advance and the lock release should be fenced by lock ownership (e.g. a version/session check, as `is_active` already does) so that a stale holder fails loudly instead of duplicating acknowledged data. ## Error message and/or stacktrace None — this is the problem. No exception is thrown and nothing is logged; the duplication is silent. ## Additional context The three call sites above are all in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/PaimonStreamState.cpp`.
signals.author: zlareb1

signals.title: PK-range join sharding: pruned side yields 1 port, non-sharded fallback throws
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **`SELECT ... JOIN ...` with `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges = 1` and `join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge'` fails with `Code: 49 ... Join is supported only for pipelines with one output port, got 3 and 1. (LOGICAL_ERROR)` whenever the primary key prunes one join side to zero parts. Pre-existing on master, not introduced by this PR - found while validating the PR's claim about the join-by-shards positional-port invariant.** - **Root cause:** The `use_sharding` fallback at [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/JoinStep.cpp:153`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/0fc2db3239a1b/src/Processors/QueryPlan/JoinStep.cpp#L153) does not do what its own comment promises ("fall back to the regular join pipeline which handles different stream counts"): the `YShaped` branch it falls back to requires exactly one port per side and neither pipeline is resized, unlike the `Paste` branch in `joinPipelinesYShaped` which calls `resize(1)` first. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `optimizeJoinByShards::apply` (Optimizations/optimizeJoinByShards.cpp:311) enables layer sharding on the join and attaches per-source layers to both reads. The pruned side never builds them: `ReadFromMergeTree::initializePipeline` returns a single `NullSource` port at ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4758 when `result.parts_with_ranges` is empty, while the other side emits one port per layer. `JoinStep::updatePipeline` then sees mismatched stream counts, sets `use_sharding = false` (JoinStep.cpp:153) and calls `QueryPipelineBuilder::joinPipelinesYShaped`, which accepts only 1-vs-1 and throws at QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:374. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/JoinStep.cpp:153`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/0fc2db3239a1b/src/Processors/QueryPlan/JoinStep.cpp#L153) — use_sharding falls back to the 1-port-only YShaped join without resizing - [`src/QueryPipeline/QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:374`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/0fc2db3239a1b/src/QueryPipeline/QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp#L374) — throw site: 'Join is supported only for pipelines with one output port' - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:4758`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/0fc2db3239a1b/src/Processors/QueryPlan/ReadFromMergeTree.cpp#L4758) — pruned side emits one NullSource port instead of one port per sharded layer **Impact:** A valid query fails with a LOGICAL_ERROR (abort in debug/sanitizer builds). `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges` is off by default but is randomized on in `tests/clickhouse-test` at 30%, so any existing test that full-sorting-merge-joins two MergeTree tables where one side is pruned by the primary key can redden CI. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `0fc2db3239a1b`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/9da94266-8d1a-41af-8898-3b6ac1451724) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- Test: JOIN sharded by primary-key ranges when one side is entirely pruned by the primary key. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_04907_l; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_04907_r; CREATE TABLE t_04907_l (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 128; CREATE TABLE t_04907_r (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 128; INSERT INTO t_04907_l SELECT number FROM numbers(1000); INSERT INTO t_04907_r SELECT number FROM numbers(1000); -- The sharding applies only to reads in order, so pin `optimize_read_in_order` against the settings randomizer. SET query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges = 1, join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge', max_threads = 4, optimize_read_in_order = 1; SELECT count() FROM t_04907_l AS l JOIN (SELECT * FROM t_04907_r WHERE k > 100000) AS r ON l.k = r.k; SELECT count() FROM (SELECT * FROM t_04907_l WHERE k > 100000) AS l LEFT JOIN t_04907_r AS r ON l.k = r.k; DROP TABLE t_04907_l; DROP TABLE t_04907_r; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 0 0 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` Code: 49. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:19010. DB::Exception: Join is supported only for pipelines with one output port, got 3 and 1. (LOGICAL_ERROR) (query: SELECT count() FROM t_04907_l AS l JOIN (SELECT * FROM t_04907_r WHERE k > 100000) AS r ON l.k = r.k;) Having 1 errors! 0 tests passed. ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> In `JoinStep::updatePipeline`'s `!use_sharding` YShaped branch, resize both pipelines to a single stream before calling `joinPipelinesYShaped` (mirroring the `Paste` handling at QueryPipelineBuilder.cpp:368-372), or keep the sharded path by making the pruned side emit one empty port per layer. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - The same divergence arises from the other early return that collapses a sharded side to one port - `ReadFromMergeTree::readByLayers` returns an empty pipe when `0 == info.sum_marks` (ReadFromMergeTree.cpp:1155), which `initializePipeline` also replaces with a single `NullSource`. Same root cause, same fix. Found during automated review of [PR #114177](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114177). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114177_001` </details> cc @alexey-milovidov (from #114177) <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115352 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1724` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: allow_non_metadata_alters=0 does not block many mutation-triggering ALTERs and its documentation is unclear
signals.text: ### Company or project name EnterpriseDB ### Describe what's wrong The setting `allow_non_metadata_alters=0` is documented as a safety switch to prevent `ALTER` statements that rewrite table data. In practice it only blocks a subset of mutation-causing `ALTER` commands. Several statements that trigger mutations (background part rewrites) still succeed with the setting turned off, and the docs do not say which ones. The following statements are **not** blocked, even though they schedule mutations and rewrite parts: - `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE ... WHERE ...` - `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE WHERE ...` - `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE INDEX ...` - `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE PROJECTION ...` - `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE COLUMN ...` - `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` - `ALTER TABLE ... APPLY DELETED MASK` - `ALTER TABLE ... APPLY PATCHES` - `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN c` when `c` is an `ALIAS` (metadata-only, so arguably correct, but not documented) The setting **does** block column-payload changes (on `MergeTree` engines) e.g.: - `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN c <new_type>` when the type change rewrites data - `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN c` where `c` is a physical column (including `MATERIALIZED`) [The docs](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/settings/session-settings/allow#allow_non_metadata_alters) are very minimal: > > `allow_non_metadata_alters` > Allow to execute alters which affects not only tables metadata, but also data on disk There's no mention here of key terms like "DDL" or "mutation" that might be searched for so it's hard to find. And the description isn't specific about what it actually permits vs blocks. In reality, it only restricts a subset of mutation-causing operations, and only on `MergeTree` tables, but a user would never be able to tell that from the documentation Sidenotes: * Non-`MergeTree` engines (`Memory`, `Log`, `TinyLog`, `StripeLog`, ...) ignore the check entirely, but that's pretty reasonable as they don't really have meaningful async mutations. It's still a bit confusing as the docs don't say anything about how this does or does not affect non-mergetree tables. * Lightweight `DELETE FROM ... WHERE ...` and Lightweight `UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE ...` are also permitted when this setting is 0 to block alters; arguably these are not "mutations" or "alters" so this is fairly reasonable, but would be good to call out explicitly. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS ana_gaps; CREATE TABLE ana_gaps ( key UInt64, v_str String, v_num UInt16, v_dt DateTime, v_d Date, v_mat UInt64 MATERIALIZED key * 2, v_ali UInt64 ALIAS key * 3 ) ENGINE = MergeTree() PARTITION BY tuple() ORDER BY key SETTINGS enable_block_number_column = 1, enable_block_offset_column = 1; INSERT INTO ana_gaps (key, v_str, v_num, v_dt, v_d) VALUES (1, 'a', 1, '2020-01-01 00:00:00', '2020-01-01'); SET allow_non_metadata_alters = 0; SELECT '-- positive: DROP COLUMN (physical)'; ALTER TABLE ana_gaps DROP COLUMN v_str; -- { serverError ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN } SELECT '-- gap: ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE (explicit heavy mutation)'; ALTER TABLE ana_gaps UPDATE v_num = 42 WHERE key = 1; SELECT 'mutations:', count() FROM system.mutations WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 'ana_gaps'; SELECT '-- gap: ALTER TABLE ... DELETE (explicit heavy mutation)'; ALTER TABLE ana_gaps DELETE WHERE key = 999; SELECT 'mutations:', count() FROM system.mutations WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 'ana_gaps'; SELECT '-- gap: MATERIALIZE COLUMN (default backfill)'; SET allow_non_metadata_alters = 1; ALTER TABLE ana_gaps ADD COLUMN v_backfill UInt64 DEFAULT key + 100; SET allow_non_metadata_alters = 0; SELECT 'mutations:', count() FROM system.mutations WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 'ana_gaps'; ALTER TABLE ana_gaps MATERIALIZE COLUMN v_backfill; SELECT 'mutations:', count() FROM system.mutations WHERE database = currentDatabase() AND table = 'ana_gaps'; ``` Result of execution - the explicit mutations and the `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE COLUMN` all triggered mutations and were unexpectedly permitted to run: ``` -- positive: DROP COLUMN (physical) -- gap: ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE (explicit heavy mutation) mutations: 1 -- gap: ALTER TABLE ... DELETE (explicit heavy mutation) mutations: 2 -- gap: MATERIALIZE COLUMN (default backfill) mutations: 2 mutations: 3 ``` For details and a more complete list of statements that bypass this check, see the test case lightweight CI run I did at https://github.com/ringerc/ClickHouse-patches/pull/3 to validate these, particularly the test sql for the gaps and the test script for the engine matching: * [04869_allow_non_metadata_alters_gaps.sql ](https://github.com/ringerc/ClickHouse-patches/blob/test-allow-non-metadata-alters-gaps/tests/queries/0_stateless/04869_allow_non_metadata_alters_gaps.sql) and [04869_allow_non_metadata_alters_gaps.reference](https://github.com/ringerc/ClickHouse-patches/blob/test-allow-non-metadata-alters-gaps/tests/queries/0_stateless/04869_allow_non_metadata_alters_gaps.reference) * [04870_allow_non_metadata_alters_engines.sh](https://github.com/ringerc/ClickHouse-patches/blob/test-allow-non-metadata-alters-gaps/tests/queries/0_stateless/04870_allow_non_metadata_alters_engines.sh) and [04870_allow_non_metadata_alters_engines.reference](https://github.com/ringerc/ClickHouse-patches/blob/test-allow-non-metadata-alters-gaps/tests/queries/0_stateless/04870_allow_non_metadata_alters_engines.reference) ### Expected behavior Expected `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE`, `ALTER TABLE ... DELETE`, `ALTER TABLE ana_gaps MATERIALIZE COLUMN` etc to be blocked by `allow_non_metadata_alters` ### Error message and/or stacktrace N/A ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context The [changelog for the setting's initial introduction read](https://clickhouse.com/docs/resources/changelogs/oss/2020#new-feature-5) > Add setting allow_non_metadata_alters which restricts to execute ALTER queries which modify data on disk. Disabled be default. Closes [#11547](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/11547). [#12635](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/12635) ([alesapin](https://github.com/alesapin)). Related issues * https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/11547 * https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/12635 Related experiment in migration-blocking DDL: * https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114594

signals.title: Wrong result: optimize_trivial_count_query makes count(arrayJoin(arr)) return the table's row count instead of the number of array elements
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe what's wrong - With the default `optimize_trivial_count_query = 1`, `SELECT count(arrayJoin(arr)) FROM t` returns the number of rows in the table instead of the number of array elements. - arrayJoin is a row-multiplying operator, so the aggregate must observe the post-expansion stream. The trivial-count optimization replaces the entire table read with a stored row counter and never evaluates count's argument, so the ARRAY JOIN expansion is silently dropped. No error, no warning. - The optimization rests on the premise "the number of rows the aggregate sees equals the number of rows stored in the table." That holds for `count()`, `count(1)` and `count(non_nullable_col)`, but arrayJoin breaks it, and nothing in the guard list checks for it. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce - https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a93a2cb4-e0f1-450b-a97e-0acef509da3b ``` ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┬──────────┐ │ Query │ Result │ Correct? │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) │ 2 │ ✗ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(arrayJoin(A)) SETTINGS optimize_trivial_count_query = 0 │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ count(*) FROM (SELECT arrayJoin(A) ...) │ 5 │ ✓ │ ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────┼──────────┤ │ sum(length(A)) │ 5 │ ✓ │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┴──────────┘ ``` ### Expected behavior - The `count(arrayJoin(A))` should return the total number of array elements across all rows, equivalent to sum(length(A)). ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_ <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #115227 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1681` (included in `26.8` and later) - Backported to: `26.7.5.3`, `26.6.4.4` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Apply `SORT + LIMIT` before `ARRAY JOIN`
signals.text: ## Use case ```sql SELECT payload FROM t ARRAY JOIN arr ORDER BY ts LIMIT 10; ``` With an average array size `k`, the `ORDER BY` currently sorts `rows(t) * k` rows, although the sort key does not depend on the array at all. The same holds for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`: the truncation happens above the expansion, so the expansion is performed for rows that are immediately discarded. The plan is: ``` Limit(10) Sorting(ts, limit=10) Expression ArrayJoin(arr) ReadFromMergeTree ``` The `ARRAY JOIN` is already *below* the sort, so the fix is a reorder, not a push-down of a new step. Note that this is not about avoiding column replication — that is largely solved already. `enable_lazy_columns_replication` defaults to `true` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp:6641`), the joined element column *is* the array's nested column (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:280`, `getDataPtr`), all other columns are only index-wrapped (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:288-292`), and `transformColumnsWithSharedIndex` (`ColumnReplicated.cpp:784`) transforms the shared index once per block. What remains is that the sort itself processes `k` times more rows than it has to. ## Why the reorder is sound `ArrayJoinResultIterator::next` walks input rows in order and takes elements from the nested column in order. So every input row expands into a **contiguous run** of output rows, and the runs preserve input order. Therefore, if every input row produces at least one output row, the first `n` output rows come from the first `k <= n` input rows, and a plain row-count limit of `n` may be evaluated below the `ARRAY JOIN`. The only counterexample is an input row that produces zero output rows: an empty array under an inner `ARRAY JOIN`. `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` is immune, because `emptyArrayToSingle` in the iterator constructor already guarantees at least one element. This means **no weighted limit is needed for correctness** — an emptiness guard is enough. The same reasoning is already written down for the `arrayJoin`-in-expression form in `liftUpFunctions.cpp:96-103`, where the reorder is currently refused only when a `LIMIT` is present. ## Proposed implementation ### 1. Emptiness guard below an inner `ArrayJoinStep` Insert `Filter(length(c) > 0)`. This removes exactly the rows the `ARRAY JOIN` removes itself, so it is a valid rewrite on its own, independent of any limit — a small first commit with a trivial correctness argument. - `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` — no guard needed. - inner, aligned — `length(c1) > 0` for any one joined column; `hasEqualOffsets` (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:277`) enforces equal sizes anyway. - inner, unaligned — `greatest(length(c1), ..., length(cn)) > 0`, because `arrayResize` pads every array to the maximum size. - `Map` columns — `length(m)` is defined and is the right function here. - Constant arrays — the guard const-folds away. - Several chained `ARRAY JOIN`s — one guard per step (the multiplicities multiply). - Use `length(arr) > 0`, not `arr.size0 > 0`: `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` is a query-tree pass and cannot rewrite a filter created by the plan optimizer. The subcolumn form is only needed by the follow-up issue below. ### 2. Teach `ArrayJoinStep` that it preserves order `getTraits` sets `preserves_sorting = false` (`ArrayJoinStep.cpp:26`), so `applyOrder` drops all sortedness across the step. Contiguous runs mean order *is* preserved for every sort prefix that does not touch the joined columns, so the flat bool should become a prefix rule in `applyOrder.cpp`: keep the prefix up to the first joined column. Trap: a joined column keeps its **name** across the step — `ArrayJoinAction::prepare` replaces the column in place and only the type changes. So the rule must exclude joined columns by name; checking that a sort key is present in the input header is not sufficient. `buildSortingDAG` already performs exactly this removal (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:313-318`). ### 3. Move `Sorting` below `ArrayJoin` Swap the two steps and keep `limit = n` unchanged. This is the change that matters: an `n * k`-row top-N becomes an `n`-row top-N. - Precondition: no sort key is a joined column (by name, see above), and all sort keys are present in the step's input header. - First version: `SortingStep::Type::Full`, `!hasPartitions()`, no `limit_by` hint. - Only cross the `ArrayJoinStep` itself and `ExpressionStep`s that preserve order and cardinality (no `arrayJoin` inside). A `FilterStep` between the sort and the `ARRAY JOIN` blocks the move, since the guard cannot account for it. - Pass ordering: `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` normally lifts the intervening `Expression` above the sort first, so run after it and match a direct child. ### 4. Move `Limit` below `ArrayJoin` `ArrayJoinStep` fails the `preserves_number_of_rows` check in `tryPushDownLimit` (`limitPushDown.cpp:136`), so the case without `ORDER BY` needs an explicit branch that inserts the guard and swaps the steps. Expected payoff on its own is modest — roughly one block of expansion, because `LimitTransform` already finishes the pipeline and `ArrayJoinResultIterator` is `max_block_size`-windowed (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:222-233`). Its real value is that it makes the follow-up issue (deferring the array read) possible. There is no offset work to do: `LimitStep::getLimitForSorting` already returns `limit + offset` (`LimitStep.h:29`), and the planner sets `partial_sorting_limit = limit_length + limit_offset` (`Planner.cpp:525`). ### 5. Optional follow-up: exact weighted limit Instead of the guard, the sort could keep rows until the prefix sum of `length(arr)` reaches `n`, which prunes harder (`n / avg_size` rows instead of `n`) and needs no filter. The cost is that `limit` is a scalar threaded through `PartialSortingTransform` (the `limit - 1`-th row threshold, `PartialSortingTransform.cpp:152-160`), `MergeSorter`, the remerge heuristic `limit * 2 < sum_rows_in_blocks` (`MergeSortingTransform.cpp:210-214`), `MergedData`, and `TopKThresholdTracker`. This is a sharpening, not a prerequisite; it should be driven by performance tests. ## Read-in-order interaction `buildSortingDAG` zeroes the limit when it sees a `FilterStep` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:297-298`), so the guard blocks the read-in-order limit hint. This is not a regression: the hint is *already* zero for inner `ARRAY JOIN` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:309-310`), and `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` keeps it because it needs no guard. Recovering it for the inner case is what the weighted limit above would buy. `optimizePrimaryKeyConditionAndLimit` walks through `FilterStep`, so that path is unaffected. ## Scope limits This issue covers only the `ARRAY JOIN` clause form, that is, a real `ArrayJoinStep`. The `arrayJoin` function form lives inside `ActionsDAG` and is invisible to plan passes; extracting it into an `ArrayJoinStep` is tracked separately and would unblock roughly twenty `hasArrayJoin` bail-outs at once. ## Test plan - Correctness matrix: inner / `LEFT`, aligned / unaligned, several joined arrays, `Map`, empty arrays, all arrays empty, `Nullable`, constant arrays, `LIMIT` with `OFFSET`, `LIMIT WITH TIES` (must be refused), `LIMIT BY` between the steps, `ORDER BY` mentioning a joined column (must be refused), chained `ARRAY JOIN`s. - `EXPLAIN` plan shape tests, plus plan-serialization tests for the new step shape. - Check that `rows_before_limit_at_least` and `exact_rows_before_limit` are unchanged. - `tests/performance/` case with a large average array size and a small `LIMIT`. - Each stage behind its own setting, default off, flipped in a later commit.

signals.title: Add Decimal-returning pow(Decimal)
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse ### Use case It would be useful to provide a precision-preserving variant of `pow()` that returned a Decimal value for Decimal arguments. ### Describe the solution you'd like The current [pow function](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/functions/regular-functions/math-functions#pow) returns Float64, even when its argument is a Decimal. This leads to loss of precision. Consider this example (CH v26.7.2): ``` SELECT pow(1.2345678901234567, CAST(2, 'Decimal')) ┌─pow(1.234567⋯'Decimal'))─┐ 1. │ 1.5241578753238834 │ └──────────────────────────┘ ``` Compare to the use of numeric arguments in Postgres (which perfectly preserve precision): ``` david=# select pow(1.234567890123456789, 2::numeric); pow ---------------------- 1.524157875323883675 ``` ### Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ### Additional context ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse#339

signals.title: Uncompressed Keeper snapshots are written as 0-byte files; node cannot restart
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With `compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format=false`, every snapshot Keeper writes to a local disk is 0 bytes although it logs `Created persistent snapshot N`. On the next restart Keeper dies with `Failure to load from latest snapshot ... Cannot read all data. Bytes read: 0 ... Manual intervention is necessary for recovery. Problematic snapshot can be removed but it will lead to data loss (CORRUPTED_DATA)`.** - **Root cause:** In the non-zstd branch the file buffer is wrapped BY REFERENCE (`std::make_unique<CompressedWriteBuffer>(*writer)`), so finalizing `compressed_writer` (:903) only pushes bytes into `writer`'s in-memory buffer; `compressed_writer->sync()` (:906) is the base no-op for that class and `writer.reset()` (:910) destroys the file buffer without `finalize`/`next`, discarding everything. The zstd branch passes ownership (`wrapWriteBufferWithCompressionMethod(std::move(writer), ...)`), so finalize/sync propagate — which is why only the uncompressed path is broken. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `KeeperStateMachine::create_snapshot` -> `writeSnapshotToDisk` -> `KeeperSnapshotManager::writeSnapshotFile` (KeeperStateMachine.cpp:1027, local-disk branch) -> KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:896. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:896`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/ac58c4e749468/src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp#L896) — non-owning CompressedWriteBuffer over the file write buffer - [`src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:910`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/ac58c4e749468/src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp#L910) — writer.reset() without finalize/sync - [`src/Coordination/KeeperStateMachine.cpp:1027`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/ac58c4e749468/src/Coordination/KeeperStateMachine.cpp#L1027) — local-disk snapshots go through writeSnapshotFile **Impact:** Any Keeper/ClickHouse deployment with `compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format=false` silently writes empty snapshots. The node refuses to start after any restart and recovery requires deleting the snapshot, which ClickHouse's own message describes as data loss; a leader also has nothing usable to send to a recovering follower. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `ac58c4e749468`). ### How to reproduce ```python import pytest import helpers.keeper_utils as keeper_utils from helpers.cluster import ClickHouseCluster cluster = ClickHouseCluster(__file__) node_zstd = cluster.add_instance( "node_zstd", main_configs=["configs/keeper_zstd.xml"], stay_alive=True, with_remote_database_disk=False ) node_plain = cluster.add_instance( "node_plain", main_configs=["configs/keeper_plain.xml"], stay_alive=True, with_remote_database_disk=False ) SNAPSHOT_DIR = "/var/lib/clickhouse/coordination/snapshots" @pytest.fixture(scope="module") -- def started_cluster(): -- try: cluster.start() yield cluster -- finally: cluster.shutdown() @pytest.mark.parametrize("node_name", ["node_zstd", "node_plain"]) -- def test_snapshot_survives_restart(started_cluster, node_name): node = cluster.instances[node_name] keeper_utils.wait_until_connected(cluster, node) zk = keeper_utils.get_fake_zk(cluster, node.name) zk.create("/test_uncompressed_snapshot", b"somedata") idx = keeper_utils.send_4lw_cmd(cluster, node, cmd="csnp").strip() node.wait_for_log_line(f"Created persistent snapshot {idx} with path") sizes = node.exec_in_container(["bash", "-c", f"stat -c '%n %s' {SNAPSHOT_DIR}/snapshot_*"]).strip() print(f"{node_name} SNAPSHOT_FILES: {sizes}") node.restart_clickhouse() keeper_utils.wait_until_connected(cluster, node) zk = keeper_utils.get_fake_zk(cluster, node.name) assert zk.get("/test_uncompressed_snapshot")[0] == b"somedata" # configs/keeper_zstd.xml and configs/keeper_plain.xml are identical single-node keeper # configs (tcp_port 9181, server_id 1, local log/snapshot paths, four_letter_word_white_list *), -- # except that keeper_plain.xml adds inside <coordination_settings>: # <compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format>false</compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format> ``` ### Expected behavior ``` Both parameterizations pass: the snapshot file is non-empty for both settings and the node restarts and still serves /test_uncompressed_snapshot. ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` node_zstd SNAPSHOT_FILES: /var/lib/clickhouse/coordination/snapshots/snapshot_13_ebe6b90817820fc1.bin.zstd 440 -> PASSED node_plain SNAPSHOT_FILES: /var/lib/clickhouse/coordination/snapshots/snapshot_15_4d88ed92c255dd85.bin 0 -> FAILED (Exception: Cannot start ClickHouse, see additional info in logs) node_plain clickhouse-server.err.log: 2026.08.19 01:42:55.320161 <Error> void DB::KeeperDispatch ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Finalize and sync the underlying file buffer in the non-zstd branch, e.g. after `compressed_writer->finalize()` add `writer->finalize(); writer->sync();` (or give the LZ4 branch ownership of `writer` the way the zstd branch does). </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - The same non-owning wrap exists at KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:687 (`serializeSnapshotToBuffer`), but there the sink is `WriteBufferFromNuraftBuffer` whose `getBuffer()` finalizes, so that path is correct. Found during automated review of [PR #111715](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111715). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr111715_001` </details> cc @al13n321 @antonio2368 (from #111715)
