signals.title: [RFC] Nullable(Array) support: staged implementation
signals.text: ## Status Accepted design, staged implementation in progress. Supersedes #105192. This RFC replaces the earlier draft RFC #105192 by @zhanglistar. That document, together with the exploratory implementation in #104816, is the direct ancestor of everything below: the stream-naming approach, the framework treatment of null rows, the gating strategy and a large body of tests all originate there. #104816 was closed in favour of a staged implementation by the core team, and its code is reused with attribution (`Co-authored-by` trailers on the commits that carry it). Thanks also to @Avogar for the original blocker analysis, which shaped the design, and to @alexey-milovidov for the resolutions to it. ## Goal Allow the array value itself to be `NULL`, distinctly from an empty array: ```sql NULL::Nullable(Array(UInt32)) != []::Array(UInt32) ``` This is not the same as `Array(Nullable(T))`, which already works and makes *elements* nullable. Arrow, ORC, Parquet, Spark, Hive and JSON producers all distinguish "list field absent or NULL" from "list present but empty", and ClickHouse currently cannot represent the difference, so those reads are lossy. ## Non-goals - `Nullable(Map(...))`. `Map` is physically `Array(Tuple(keys, values))`, so it depends on this work, but it is out of scope. - Changing the rule that `Map` keys cannot be nullable. - Flipping `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()`. See below — this is a deliberate and load-bearing decision, not an omission. ## Core design **`DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable()` keeps returning `false`, permanently.** `Nullable(Array(T))` is constructible only through `makeNullableAllowingArray`, which reaches a private `DataTypeNullable` constructor via a friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. This is the single most important property of the design, and the reason is not the one an earlier revision of this document gave. It is not primarily about blast radius during the rollout. `canBeInsideNullable` is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and those places do two different jobs: 1. **Handle a `Nullable(Array)` that already exists** — serialization, subcolumn extraction, the nullable subcolumn creator, `Nested::unwrapNullableTuple`. 2. **Decide whether to *produce* a `Nullable`** — `getLeastSupertype`, `makeNullableSafe`, cast resolution. Only the second kind would behave differently if the predicate were flipped. The first kind needs explicit `Nullable(Array)` handling either way, because once the type can be created at all, this code has to cope with it. And the second kind is exactly the kind whose change is a user-visible result-type break. Measured on a current build with every gate off: ```text if(1, 1, NULL) -> Nullable(UInt8) a supertype exists if(1, tuple(1), NULL) -> Nullable(Tuple(UInt8)) a supertype exists (Tuple's predicate is true) if(1, [1], NULL) -> Variant(Array(UInt8)) no supertype, so the Variant fallback applies ``` `Variant` is the fallback used only when no common supertype exists. Flipping the predicate would give array-versus-`NULL` a supertype, so `if(1, [1], NULL)` would silently change from `Variant(Array(UInt8))` to `Nullable(Array(UInt8))` for queries people run today. **That change cannot be gated.** The `compatibility` setting is implemented by replaying old *setting values* — `SettingsChangesHistory` entries are `{setting, old value, new value, description}` — so a behaviour change is only reversible if a setting is read at the point of decision. `canBeInsideNullable()` is a property of a type object, not of a call site: a `DataTypePtr` does not know which session created it, and the predicate is consulted during background merges, metadata load and distributed query fragments, where a session setting is not a defined concept. The exploratory work tried exactly this for the `Tuple` case and had to reach for `Context::getGlobalContextInstance()`, documenting that "config changes for global context settings are applied after server restart" — global state with a restart caveat, which is not gating. So flipping the predicate would be an unconditional result-type change with no `compatibility` value and no individual setting that restores the previous behaviour. Conversely, building genuine dual behaviour would mean keeping the explicit per-site decisions described here *and* adding a second branch at each — more code than the current design, not less. `Nullable(Tuple)` is the cautionary example rather than a counter-example. Its predicate is `true`, and the consequence is observable today: ```sql SET enable_nullable_tuple_type = 0; SELECT if(0, tuple(1), NULL); -- \N, of type Nullable(Tuple(UInt8)) ``` The gate does not contain the type: with the setting explicitly disabled you still get real `Nullable(Tuple)` values, because type inference never consults it. We are deliberately more conservative in light of how much corner-case work that feature required after merge. ### What this costs `canBeInsideNullable()` now returns `false` for a type that demonstrably *is* inside `Nullable`. That is a permanent, accepted cost rather than a transitional one: - Any guard of the form `if (t->canBeInsideNullable())` reachable by a `Nullable(Array)` value must be extended with `|| isArray(t)`. We already missed one — see the known-defect section below. - `makeNullableSafe` returns its argument unchanged for `Array`, silently degrading `Nullable(Array)` to `Array` rather than throwing. There are 32 such call sites. - **Every `canBeInsideNullable` guard added anywhere in the codebase from now on is wrong for `Nullable(Array)` by default.** This is the real long-term price, and the Stage 4 audit is what bounds it. Do not attempt to "clean this up" later by flipping the predicate. There is no gated path back. Identifying every reachable instance is the **call-site audit**, delivered in Stage 4 (below). This is the audit @Avogar asked for in #104816, reframed: the question is not "are 75 files correct" but "which sites can a `Nullable(Array)` value actually reach, and which of those need to change". ### Gating A single session setting, `allow_experimental_nullable_array_type`, gates **every user-facing path that can produce the type** — not only DDL. That includes `CREATE TABLE` and `ALTER`, table-function column lists, and the functions that accept a type by name (`toNullable`, `JSONExtract`, `defaultValueOfTypeName`, `accurateCastOrDefault`, `dynamicElement`, `CAST`). Internal C++ construction is ungated. This makes the gate a single clean seam between internal machinery and external interface, which is what the staging below is built around. ## MergeTree serialization ### The collision Stream names come from `getNameForSubstreamPath`. `Nullable` appends `.null`; `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1`, …; array *elements* add no name component at all, only a nesting level. ```text Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.null c <-- collision ``` Two distinct null maps would share one file name. Shipping that would corrupt data. ### Resolution A second, *structured* naming scheme, used only for columns whose type requires it (`needsStructuredSubstreamNames`), which inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements: ```text Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))): c.null outer null map c.size0 array offsets c.array.null element null map c.array.nested element data Nullable(Array(UInt32)): c.null outer null map c.size0 array offsets c.array.nested element data Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))): c.size0 outer array offsets c.array.null inner nullable array's null map c.array.array.size0 inner array offsets c.array.array.nested.null element null map c.array.array.nested element data ``` Note that the outer null map and the array offsets keep their plain `.null` and `.size0` names; only the streams below an array element acquire the `.array` component. This is the naming the implementation actually produces, verified by driving real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than by reasoning about substream paths — see the correction note at the end of this issue. Every currently-legal type keeps byte-identical legacy names, so existing parts remain readable with no migration and no format version bump. Selection is **per column, from the type as stored in the part**, on both read and write, so a single query can span old and new parts, and unaffected columns inside a part that contains a structured column keep their legacy names. `columns_substreams.txt` records the actual on-disk substream names for Compact parts and is the source of truth on read. Not in `serialization.json`, which describes serialization kinds and statistics rather than physical file names. Not a global part format version bump, since the change is column-scoped and must coexist with legacy names in the same part. ### Requirements this must meet These are the acceptance criteria for Stage 2, and they are stronger than what #104816 demonstrated: 1. **No legacy stream name changes for any currently-legal type** — proven over a corpus, not sampled. The proof is that the structured scheme is never *selected* for such a type, neither by the type nor by any path enumerated for it: the legacy naming code is then the only code that runs, and it is not modified. 2. **Collision-free names for arbitrary nesting** of `Array`, `Nullable`, `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant`, `Dynamic` and `Object`, including substream cache keys and prefix/suffix substreams. 3. **A single source of truth for names.** #104816 duplicated the substream-to-name switch, and `Object`/JSON substream types are added to `master` continuously, so a duplicate will drift. 4. **The column type is required, and losing it must not fail silently.** *(Revised — see the correction log.)* This was originally stated as "one naming oracle, or a proven equivalence between two". That is not achievable: the path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The same path requires different names for different types, so no path-only oracle exists and the two arms are not competing answers to one question — the path-based arm covers `Dynamic`/`Object` columns whose static type does not reveal the runtime variant. The hazard is therefore not disagreement between arms but a caller that supplies no type at all: it silently receives legacy names for a structured column. What is required instead: - where the substream path *proves* a type was needed, resolving a name without one raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than returning a name no writer produced; - the divergent case above is pinned by a test, so the reason the type is required is documented where a reader will look; - a test asserts the guard never fires for any currently-legal type; - **every MergeTree caller passes the column type** — an explicit obligation for Stage 3, verified there rather than assumed. ## Subcolumns The outer null map must propagate into subcolumns: ```sql SELECT a.null FROM t; -- UInt8 SELECT a.size0 FROM t; -- Nullable(UInt64), not UInt64 ``` `NullableSubcolumnCreator` handles this. Note that bare `Array(T).null` must stay an invalid Dynamic subcolumn path: the null map belongs to the `Nullable` wrapper, not to the array, so `getSubcolumn(42::Dynamic, 'Array(UInt64).null')` must keep failing rather than returning an all-ones map. ## Function execution framework `defaultImplementationForNulls` unwraps nullable arguments, runs the function on the nested columns and patches the result. When the result type cannot be `Nullable` — historically true for `Array` — it substitutes defaults for null rows. Left alone, this silently turns a `NULL` array into `[]` for roughly 70 unmigrated array functions. The contract: - For an array-returning function with a `Nullable(Array)` argument, the result type becomes `Nullable(Array(...))`. - Array arguments are normalised to empty at null rows before the call, so functions that have not been individually migrated still see well-formed offsets. - The row null map is the OR of the input null maps, and is re-applied to the result. - A function may opt in to producing the nullable result itself via `preserveNullableArrayResultForDefaultNulls`, for cases like `arrayElementOrNull` where the function's own null semantics must win. This is deliberately narrower than #105192 proposed. That draft sketched four separate framework capabilities; one opt-in virtual plus automatic normalisation turned out to be sufficient, and the smaller surface is easier to reason about. **Ordering constraint:** the framework must land before the gate opens. Otherwise the type is storable but silently lossy through most functions, which is worse than not having it. ## Semantics | Expression | `NULL::Nullable(Array(T))` | `[]::Array(T)` | `[x]::Array(T)` | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `isNull(a)` | `1` | `0` | `0` | | `length(a)` | `NULL` | `0` | `1` | | `empty(a)` | `NULL` | `1` | `0` | | `a.size0` | `NULL` | `0` | `1` | | `arrayElement(a, 1)` | `NULL` | default | `x` | | `arrayElementOrNull(a, 1)` | `NULL` | `NULL` | `x` | | `arrayMap(f, a)` | `NULL` | `[]` | `[f(x)]` | | `arrayFilter(f, a)` | `NULL` | `[]` | filtered | Questions #105192 left open, now resolved: - **`arrayJoin` / `ARRAY JOIN` over `Nullable(Array)` is explicitly unsupported** and throws `TYPE_MISMATCH`. Row-cardinality semantics for a NULL array have no obviously correct answer, and silently treating it as `[]` would defeat the purpose of the type. Revisitable later; not blocking. - **Aggregate functions treat a NULL array as any other NULL value.** Aggregates that skip nulls skip null arrays; those that collect values may collect them where the result type can represent them. This falls out of the existing `Null` combinator rather than needing per-function work. - **Formats never infer the type by default.** Inference is behind its own separate setting, `schema_inference_allow_nullable_array_type`. ## Staged implementation One pull request per stage, each targeting `master`, merged before the next opens. | # | Stage | Content | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Type and column foundation | `makeNullableAllowingArray`, private constructor, `ColumnNullable` exception. `DataTypeFactory` still rejects the type string, so the type is constructible from C++ only and unreachable from any query. | | 2 | Serialization and substream naming | Structured naming, cache keys, deserialization order, plus the four requirements above. Still unreachable from SQL. | | 3 | MergeTree wiring, gate opens | Typed stream names, wide and compact readers and writers, `columns_substreams.txt`, merges, mutations, `ALTER`. `DataTypeFactory` starts accepting the type string, and `validateDataType` / `InterpreterCreateQuery` begin enforcing the gate: the factory is permissive and the entry points are restrictive. Paths not yet migrated throw `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. | | 4 | Function framework and audit | The framework contract above, the full call-site audit, and the `unwrapNullableTuple` fix. | | 5 | Array functions and aggregates | Migration by category; `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` throws replaced with real behaviour. | | 6 | Remaining creation paths | The functions that take a type by name — `toNullable`, `JSONExtract`, `defaultValueOfTypeName`, `accurateCastOrDefault`, `dynamicElement`, `CAST` — each gated. User documentation. | | 7 | Formats, explicit schema only | Arrow, Arrow IPC, ORC, Parquet, MsgPack, BSON, Native, plus the `Native` format specification. | | 8 | Schema inference | Behind `schema_inference_allow_nullable_array_type`, including schema-cache keys. | | 9 | Stabilisation | Fuzzing, performance and storage overhead, beta decision. | Stages 1 and 2 are verifiable by unit tests only, since the type cannot be named in a query. That is deliberate: it makes "internal machinery only" a checked property rather than an intention, and Stage 3 flipping it becomes a visible change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. Stage 3 introduces the gate rather than Stage 6 so that Stages 4 to 9 are testable with ordinary stateless tests. Between Stages 3 and 5 the type is reachable only with the experimental setting explicitly enabled, and any path not yet migrated **throws** rather than returning a wrong answer. Substituting `[]` for `NULL` in the interim was considered and rejected: it would ship exactly the defect this feature exists to remove. ## Known defect inherited from the exploratory work `Nested::unwrapNullableTuple` substitutes defaults for an `Array` field of a `Nullable(Tuple(...))`, so a NULL struct's list field becomes `[]`. It is reached from the ORC, Arrow and Arrow IPC readers when a nullable struct sits inside a list. Reproducer, against an Arrow file holding `Array(Nullable(Tuple(x Array(Int32))))` whose second element is `NULL`: ```sql SET allow_experimental_nullable_array_type = 1; SELECT a FROM file('nt.arrow', Arrow, 'a Array(Tuple(x Nullable(Array(Int32))))'); -- [([1,2]),([])] -- expected [([1,2]),(NULL)] ``` The requested type *is* honoured (`toTypeName` reports `Nullable(Array(Int32))`) but the value comes back as `[]` with `isNull() = 0`. Cause: the branch tests `elem_type->canBeInsideNullable()`, which is `false` for `Array` by design, so the default-substitution path is taken before the hinted type is applied. Fixed in Stage 4. This is not a regression — with the gate disabled the same hint is rejected outright — but it is an instance of the exact conflation the feature exists to remove, occurring inside the feature. It was found by chasing a single `canBeInsideNullable` call site, which is the argument for completing the audit before the gate widens. ## Testing matrix - **Types:** `Nullable(Array(T))`, `Nullable(Array(Nullable(T)))`, `Array(Nullable(Array(T)))`, multidimensional, inside `Tuple`, `Map`, `Variant`, `Dynamic`, `Object`, `Nested`. - **Storage:** wide and compact parts, old-part reads, merges, mutations, projections, materialised views, `ALTER`, `columns_substreams.txt` integrity. - **Subcolumns:** `.null`, `.size0`, nested `sizeN`, tuple subcolumns inside arrays. - **Functions:** every array function by category; `if`, `multiIf`, `CAST`, `accurateCastOrNull`, `IN`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, `ORDER BY`. - **Aggregates:** `groupArray`, `groupUniqArray`, `arrayReduce`, combinators, state serialization. - **Formats:** `Native`, `Values`, `JSONEachRow`, CSV, TSV, Arrow, ArrowStream, ORC, Parquet, MsgPack, BSON. - **Fuzzing:** AST fuzzer, function stress, serialization round-trip. ## Related - Supersedes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 - Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 ## Correction log **2026-08-19, stream names.** The stream-name example in *MergeTree serialization → Resolution* originally showed `c.array.size0` for the array offsets and `c.array` for the element data. Both were wrong. They were carried over from #105192 and the exploratory implementation's own documentation, and had never been checked against the code. The cause is worth recording, because it also invalidated the exploratory work's unit tests for this area. The naming decision for a stream depends on what precedes the final substream in its `SubstreamPath` — in particular on whether a null map precedes it. `SerializationNullable::enumerateStreams` emits the null-map substream, then **pops it** before recursing into the nested type, so the path seen while naming the array's own streams contains no null map. A hand-built path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs in production; the real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and it takes a different branch. Expectations written against hand-built paths were therefore self-consistent and simultaneously wrong about two of the four streams. Combined with a shell test whose `Before drop:` listing was never actually emitted, the on-disk naming for this feature had no accurate test and no accurate documentation. The fix on our side is to derive every naming expectation from a real `enumerateStreams` walk, and to state the acceptance criteria as properties over a corpus of types rather than as spot checks on constructed paths: - the structured scheme is never selected for any type that is legal today, which is what makes "no existing stream name changes" a proof rather than a sample; - a caller that has the column type and one that does not must produce identical names for a legal type; - all stream names of a type containing `Nullable(Array)` are distinct, at arbitrary nesting depth. **2026-08-19, criterion 4.** Restated. The original wording asked for a single naming oracle or a proven equivalence between two, which is not achievable — the naming of a stream genuinely depends on the column type and not only on the substream path. The revised criterion and its rationale are in *Requirements this must meet* above; the reasoning and what replaced it are in the Stages 1–2 comment on this issue. **2026-08-20, the rationale for `canBeInsideNullable`.** The *Core design* section originally justified keeping the predicate `false` as a blast-radius decision: 105 call sites, too many to audit safely. That reasoning is real but weak, and it would expire once the feature reached GA, inviting a future contributor to flip the predicate as cleanup. The section now gives the argument that actually holds. The call sites split into those that must handle an existing `Nullable(Array)` (unchanged by a flip) and those that decide whether to create one (changed by a flip) — and the second group is precisely where a flip becomes a user-visible result-type change, from `Variant(Array(T))` to `Nullable(Array(T))`, that the `compatibility` mechanism cannot express, because that mechanism replays setting values and a type-level predicate cannot read a setting. The consequence is that the decision is permanent, and that the explicit opt-in call sites are the correct long-term shape rather than debt to be repaid.

signals.title: Text index written by 26.6 is unreadable by older replicas in the same cluster — breaks rolling upgrades
signals.text: ### Company or project name Nebius ### Describe what's wrong Since 26.6, ClickHouse writes the `text` skip index with sparse index version 1, which no earlier version can read. An older replica that receives such a part through normal replication fails every query that uses the index: ``` Code: 246. DB::Exception: Unsupported version of sparse index (1): While reading part all_0_0_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CORRUPTED_DATA) ``` **This is not a downgrade problem.** It breaks the upgrade itself. During a rolling restart of a replicated cluster, an already-upgraded replica writes parts with a v1 text index, replication delivers them to replicas that have not been restarted yet, and those replicas start failing reads — while both versions are running normally and no data directory has been touched. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Three files and six commands. This runs **one ReplicatedMergeTree cluster with both versions live at the same time** — the state a rolling upgrade passes through. Nothing is downgraded and no data directory is moved. ```bash mkdir ch-textindex && cd ch-textindex cat > keeper.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <listen_host>0.0.0.0</listen_host> <keeper_server> <tcp_port>9181</tcp_port> <server_id>1</server_id> <log_storage_path>/var/lib/clickhouse-keeper/log</log_storage_path> <snapshot_storage_path>/var/lib/clickhouse-keeper/snapshots</snapshot_storage_path> <raft_configuration> <server><id>1</id><hostname>keeper</hostname><port>9234</port></server> </raft_configuration> </keeper_server> </clickhouse> EOF cat > repl.xml <<'EOF' <clickhouse> <zookeeper><node><host>keeper</host><port>9181</port></node></zookeeper> <macros> <shard>1</shard> <replica from_env="REPLICA"/> </macros> </clickhouse> EOF cat > docker-compose.yml <<'EOF' services: keeper: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper:26.6.2.160 volumes: [./keeper.xml:/etc/clickhouse-keeper/keeper_config.xml:ro] old: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.3.10.60 environment: {REPLICA: old} volumes: [./repl.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/repl.xml:ro] new: image: clickhouse/clickhouse-server:26.6.2.160 environment: {REPLICA: new} volumes: [./repl.xml:/etc/clickhouse-server/config.d/repl.xml:ro] EOF docker compose up -d for r in old new; do until docker compose exec -T $r clickhouse-client -q "SELECT 1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 1; done; done # 1. the same replicated table on both replicas for r in old new; do docker compose exec -T $r clickhouse-client -q " CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, s String, INDEX idx s TYPE text(tokenizer = array)) ENGINE = ReplicatedMergeTree('/clickhouse/tables/1/t', '{replica}') ORDER BY id"; done # 2. write on the already-upgraded replica, let replication carry the part over docker compose exec -T new clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, hex(number) FROM numbers(20000)" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SYSTEM SYNC REPLICA t" # 3. the old replica only fetched that part, it never wrote one docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SYSTEM FLUSH LOGS" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SELECT DISTINCT event_type FROM system.part_log WHERE table = 't'" # 4. the same query on each replica docker compose exec -T new clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = '3039'" docker compose exec -T old clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t WHERE s = '3039'" docker compose down -v ``` Output of the last three steps: ``` DownloadPart <- step 3: fetched, not written locally 1 <- step 4 on the new replica Code: 246. DB::Exception: Unsupported version of sparse index (1): While reading part all_0_0_0: While executing MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder). (CORRUPTED_DATA) <- step 4 on the old replica ``` No special settings are needed — the optimizer chooses the index on its own, which is how we hit it in production. `hasToken(s, '3039')` fails identically. `SELECT count() FROM t` still works, so only queries that touch the index break. [ch-textindex-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31214857/ch-textindex-repro.zip) ### Expected behavior Either of: 1. A reader that meets a sparse index version it does not understand skips the index and reads the granules, instead of failing the query. Skip indexes are an optimisation; an unreadable one should not be fatal. 2. Failing that, the format bump is called out as backward-incompatible in the changelog with a "drop the text index before upgrading" note, as was done for the 25.12 v3 change in #91518. Currently it is neither: the query fails, and the 26.6 changelog does not mention it. Related: #91518 introduced the sparse-index version header in 25.12 and *was* flagged backward-incompatible. #111550 (open) received review feedback describing this same hazard for a later layout change — *"older binaries misparse new ones, so rolling upgrades/downgrades ... have no safe migration path"* — recommending a versioned reader that migrates or throws an explicit rebuild-required error. The 26.6 bump shipped without either. ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests A search for the error text (`"Unsupported version of sparse index"`, `"version of sparse index"`) returns no existing report. - **#91518** — *Inverted Text Index v3* (merged, 25.12). Introduced the version header for the text index sparse index. It was explicitly flagged backward-incompatible, with a changelog note telling users to drop the index before upgrading and rebuild it. The 26.6 bump changes the same field with no equivalent note. - **#111550** — *Text index: introduce new storage layout for positions* (open). Review feedback on it describes this exact hazard for a later layout change: *"older binaries misparse new ones, so rolling upgrades/downgrades on tables that already use `support_phrase_search` have no safe migration path"*, and recommends giving the layout a new persisted version while keeping a reader that either migrates or throws an explicit rebuild-required error. That is the same remedy this issue asks for. - **#103398** — *Upgrade from 25.x to 26.x ends with CORRUPTED_DATA* (closed). The same failure shape in a different subsystem: rolling upgrade of a replicated cluster, error 246, `Unknown version of serialization infos (1). Should be less or equal than 0`. It was resolved by manual intervention (`SYSTEM RESTORE REPLICA`) rather than by making the reader tolerant, so the pattern of a version field that older binaries reject outright is recurring. - **#94494** — *Fix text index mrk file incompatibility* (merged 26.1, backported 25.12.4.32). A different text index format problem (`.mrk` with non-adaptive `index_granularity`, triggered by merges). Listed to distinguish it: it is not this bug. - **#84606** — *Text index: remove multi format versions handling* (merged, July 2025, not-for-changelog). Consolidated `Format::v2` into `v1` and removed multi-version handling. Predates the version header, so it is not the cause, but it is context for how format-version tolerance in this index has been treated. ### Additional context **Workaround** On the not-yet-upgraded replicas, `SETTINGS use_skip_indexes = 0` makes the query succeed; `ALTER TABLE ... DROP INDEX` also works. Both give up the index for the duration. - Reproduced on `clickhouse/clickhouse-server` and `clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper` docker images, linux/aarch64. - Single shard, two replicas, one keeper. Nothing else required.

signals.title: Re-attached partition carrying a since-dropped column permanently wedges the mutation queue (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER); KILL MUTATION does not recover
signals.text: **Company or project name** ClickHouse **Describe what's wrong** `ATTACH PARTITION` silently accepts detached parts that still contain a column which was dropped from the table while the partition was detached. The re-attached part reads fine (`SELECT` works, the extra on-disk column is ignored) and merges normalize it fine, but every subsequent mutation touching that part permanently fails with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` (Code 47), wedging the table's mutation queue. The failure is not recoverable the way the error message suggests: `KILL MUTATION` on the failing mutation does not help, because the poisoned state is the part, not the mutation — the next mutation on the table fails identically. The only ways out are `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on the affected partition (a merge rewrites the part and drops the phantom column) or dropping the partition. On a partition with no insert traffic, background merges never pick up a single part, so the queue stays wedged indefinitely; any client using `mutations_sync >= 1` gets `Code: 341 UNFINISHED`. The sequence is a plausible maintenance pattern: detach old data, clean up the schema, re-attach the old data later. **Does it reproduce on the most recent release?** Yes **How to reproduce** * Which ClickHouse server versions are incompatible: reproduces on 26.8.1.1068 (official master build) and on 26.3.2.3 (official build) — long-standing, not a recent regression; the error text differs by analyzer generation, the wedge is the same. * Queries to run that lead to an unexpected result: ```sql CREATE TABLE r (id UInt64, val UInt64, p UInt8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY p ORDER BY id; ALTER TABLE r ADD COLUMN c UInt32; INSERT INTO r SELECT number, number, 1, 42 FROM numbers(100); ALTER TABLE r DETACH PARTITION 1; ALTER TABLE r DROP COLUMN c; -- no attached part has c, drop is metadata-only ALTER TABLE r ATTACH PARTITION 1; -- part comes back still carrying column c on disk SELECT count() FROM r; -- 100, reads are fine ALTER TABLE r DELETE WHERE id = 5 SETTINGS mutations_sync = 2; -- wedges ``` Then observe: ```sql SELECT mutation_id, is_done, latest_fail_reason FROM system.mutations WHERE table = 'r'; ``` The mutation never completes. `KILL MUTATION WHERE mutation_id = 'mutation_4.txt'` followed by another `ALTER TABLE r DELETE ...` fails with the same error on the same part, so the suggested recovery in the error message does not work. `OPTIMIZE TABLE r FINAL` rewrites the part and un-wedges the queue. **Expected behavior** Mutations should treat a physical column that is absent from the table metadata the same way reads and merges already do — ignore it and drop it on rewrite. Alternatively, if a part carrying a since-dropped column is not supposed to be attachable, `ATTACH PARTITION` should reject it loudly instead of accepting a part that poisons every later mutation. **Error message and/or stacktrace** On 26.8 (new analyzer wording): ``` Code: 341. DB::Exception: Exception happened during execution of mutation 'mutation_4.txt' with part '1_3_3_0' reason: 'Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression identifier `c` in scope c, p, val, id, c, p, val, id. Maybe you meant: ['p']. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER)'. This error maybe retryable or not. In case of unretryable error, mutation can be killed with KILL MUTATION query ``` On 26.3 (old wording, same wedge): ``` Code: 47. DB::Exception: Missing columns: 'c' while processing: 'c, p, val, id, c, id, val, p', required columns: 'c' 'p' 'val' 'id', maybe you meant: 'p', 'val' or 'id'. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` **Additional context** Found while running a concurrent DDL + mutation + partition-churn workload: with `DETACH`/`ATTACH PARTITION` and `ADD`/`DROP COLUMN` interleaved, the wedge appears within seconds and every queued `ALTER ... UPDATE`/`DELETE` on the table inherits the failure until a merge happens to rewrite the poisoned part.

signals.title: Fuzzy search with mergeTreeTextIndex usage
signals.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Use case Is it possible to use mergeTreeTextIndex with editDistanceUTF8 I need to find a word with a typo in my table. I create a text index and use mergeTreeTextIndex for editDistanceUTF8 as a dictionary of available words ### Describe the solution you'd like For example: ```sql DROP TABLE IF EXISTS pruning_demo; CREATE TABLE pruning_demo ( product_id UInt32, product_text_garner String DEFAULT '', INDEX idx_words product_text_garner TYPE text( tokenizer = icu('en'), preprocessor = normalizeUTF8NFKCCasefold(product_text_garner), postprocessor = stem(product_text_garner, 'en') ) ) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY product_id; INSERT INTO pruning_demo (product_id, product_text_garner) VALUES (1, 'I work with ClickHouse'), (2, 'I WORK with databases'), (3, 'She is working today'), (4, 'This is homework'), (5, 'The workshop is closed'), (6, 'Work should be found'), (7, 'WORKING'), (8, 'workshop'), (9, 'homework'), (10, 'No matching value'), (11, 'Work should not be found'), (12, 'Should work be found?'); EXPLAIN indexes = 1 SELECT product_id FROM pruning_demo WHERE hasAllTokens(product_text_garner, 'WORK') ORDER BY product_id; WITH normalizeUTF8NFKCCasefold('wark') AS search_word, ( SELECT groupUniqArray(token) FROM mergeTreeTextIndex( currentDatabase(), 'pruning_demo', 'idx_words' ) WHERE editDistanceUTF8(token, search_word) <= 1 ) AS fuzzy_tokens SELECT product_id, product_text_garner, fuzzy_tokens, search_word FROM pruning_demo WHERE hasAnyTokens(product_text_garner, fuzzy_tokens) ORDER BY product_id; ``` ### Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` accepted with session `allow_statistics = 1` but executed with the server default — permanently stuck mutation when the profile disables statistics
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` is **validated with the submitting session's `allow_statistics` value, but executed with the server-default value**. When a server profile sets `allow_statistics = 0` and a session enables it per-query (`SETTINGS allow_statistics = 1` — the same session-level opt-in that `ADD STATISTICS` honors), the mutation is accepted and then fails forever in the background: - `mutations_sync = 1` returns `Code: 341 UNFINISHED` wrapping `Code: 80. DB::Exception: Alter table with statistics is disabled. Turn on allow_statistics.`; - without `mutations_sync` the statement returns success and the mutation sits in `system.mutations` with `is_done = 0`, retrying the same failure indefinitely, wedging the table's mutation queue until a manual `KILL MUTATION`. The behavior is also internally inconsistent: - `ADD STATISTICS` under the same session opt-in succeeds (metadata change honors the session value); - background **merges materialize the declared statistics regardless of the gate** (measured: `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on the same server writes the `TDigest` statistics while the explicit mutation verb is refused). So the only affected path is the explicit `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` mutation, and it fails at execution time after passing validation at submission time. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — master 26.8.1.1673 (official build). ### How to reproduce Server profile disables statistics (`users.xml`): ```xml <clickhouse> <profiles><default><allow_statistics>0</allow_statistics></default></profiles> </clickhouse> ``` Then: ```sql CREATE TABLE gt (k UInt64, a Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO gt SELECT number, number FROM numbers(100); ALTER TABLE gt ADD STATISTICS a TYPE tdigest SETTINGS allow_statistics = 1; -- OK ALTER TABLE gt MATERIALIZE STATISTICS a SETTINGS allow_statistics = 1, mutations_sync = 1; -- Code: 341. DB::Exception: Exception happened during execution of mutation 'mutation_2.txt' -- with part 'all_1_1_0' reason: 'Code: 80. DB::Exception: Alter table with statistics is -- disabled. Turn on allow_statistics. (INCORRECT_QUERY)' SELECT mutation_id, is_done, latest_fail_reason FROM system.mutations WHERE table = 'gt'; -- mutation_2.txt 0 Code: 80. DB::Exception: Alter table with statistics is disabled. ... -- (retries forever; KILL MUTATION is the only way out) ``` Required settings: only the profile-level `allow_statistics = 0` plus the session-level `= 1`; everything else is defaults. ### Expected behavior Either of: - validate at submission and reject the `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` immediately when the effective execution context will refuse it (fail fast, no stuck mutation), or - execute the mutation under the value the submitting session was authorized with (the way merges already materialize declared statistics irrespective of the gate). A statement that is accepted but can never complete, and that blocks the table's mutation queue until a manual `KILL MUTATION`, is the worst of both. ### Additional context Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signals.title: Keeper: parent `Stat` fields `cversion` and `pzxid` differ from ZooKeeper
signals.text: ### Company or project name gmonit.ru ### Describe what's wrong Two fields of a parent node's `Stat` behave differently in ClickHouse Keeper than in ZooKeeper, and the two differences go in opposite directions: * **`cversion` changes more often than in ZooKeeper** — Keeper bumps a parent's `cversion` on every `setData` of a direct child. * **`pzxid` changes less often than in ZooKeeper** — Keeper does not update a parent's `pzxid` when a child is removed. **What I'm asking:** whether both are intentional. I don't have an opinion on which behaviour is correct and I'm not proposing a change — the rest of this issue is just the evidence. The two concrete questions are at the bottom. Measured with the same Java client (3.9.5) against Keeper 26.8.1.1431 and 26.3.9.8, and against `zookeeper:3.9` as a reference. Both Keeper versions behave identically. Operations on a **direct child** of the observed parent: | Operation on child | ZK `cversion` | Keeper `cversion` | ZK `pzxid` | Keeper `pzxid` | |--------------------------|---------------|-------------------|------------|----------------| | `create` | +1 | +1 | bumped | bumped | | `delete` | +1 | +1 | bumped | **not bumped** | | `setData` | unchanged | **+1** | unchanged | unchanged | | anything on a grandchild | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | `numChildren` matches ZooKeeper in all cases. On Keeper I also checked `setACL` on a child (leaves the parent untouched) and an ephemeral child expiring with its session (`cversion` +1, `pzxid` not bumped); I did not run those two against ZooKeeper, so they are out of the comparison. The difference is confined to the stat: the parent's `cversion` bump does not fire a child watch, so `NodeChildrenChanged` is not emitted on `setData` of a child. ### Where this comes from **`cversion`** — the `Set` handler increments the parent's counter after updating the node itself: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L882-L890 ZooKeeper stores the *number of creates* and converts it to the *number of changes* when the stat is handed to a client, so deletes are accounted for without a second counter and `setData` cannot contribute: https://github.com/apache/zookeeper/blob/7af463e0fd5097930f52864911b224d8b9e6a485/zookeeper-server/src/main/java/org/apache/zookeeper/server/DataNode.java#L155-L164 ```java // when we do the Cversion we need to translate from the count of the creates // to the count of the changes (v3 semantics) // for every create there is a delete except for the children still present to.setCversion(stat.getCversion() * 2 - numChildren); ``` **`pzxid`** — in the `Remove` handler the update is guarded by `restored_from_zookeeper_log`, so it happens only while replaying a log imported from ZooKeeper, not on ordinary deletes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L534-L536 ZooKeeper updates it on every delete (`DataTree.deleteNode`). ### Why the combination matters Taken together, no single field answers ZooKeeper's "did the child set change?" question on Keeper: `cversion` reports changes that did not touch the child set, `pzxid` misses removals, and `numChildren` cannot see one child being replaced by another. Only the pair `(pzxid, numChildren)` is equivalent. ClickHouse itself reads `cversion` with ZooKeeper semantics in three places, which is expected since the same code also runs against real ZooKeeper: * [`DatabaseReplicated.cpp#L454`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Databases/DatabaseReplicated.cpp#L454) and [`#L476`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Databases/DatabaseReplicated.cpp#L476) — reads the replica list, re-reads the stat of `/replicas`, and retries if `cversion` changed, throwing `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED: Cannot get consistent cluster snapshot` after `max_retries = 10`. On Keeper a `setData` on any `/replicas/<host>` node counts as a change even though the set of replicas did not change. * [`ClusterDiscovery.cpp#L319`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Interpreters/ClusterDiscovery.cpp#L319) — uses `cversion` as the version of the shard list. * [`NamedCollectionsMetadataStorage.cpp#L274`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Common/NamedCollections/NamedCollectionsMetadataStorage.cpp#L274) — detects that the collection list changed. I have not seen a failure from any of these; they are listed because they show the direction of the effect — extra work rather than missed updates. ### Migrating from ZooKeeper 1. **Client code.** Code that reads `cversion` to mean "children were added or removed" becomes more sensitive on Keeper; code that reads `pzxid` for the same purpose becomes less sensitive and misses deletions without any error. 2. **Snapshot conversion.** `clickhouse-keeper-converter` reads `cversion` from the ZooKeeper snapshot as-is ([`ZooKeeperDataReader.cpp#L132`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/ZooKeeperDataReader.cpp#L132)), but a ZooKeeper snapshot stores the internal value (the create count), not what clients were served. For a node that had children deleted, `cversion` therefore drops after conversion relative to what ZooKeeper reported. The same field seeds the sequential counter later in the same loop ([L146](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/ZooKeeperDataReader.cpp#L146)), so the two uses are coupled. The txn-log half of the conversion works on the stored counter rather than the served one. `Remove` increments `cversion` unconditionally ([L593](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L593)), including while replaying a `DeleteTxn`, whereas ZooKeeper leaves the stored counter untouched on a delete — the +1 a client sees there is produced by the `2C − N` translation at read time. In practice the drift is bounded: a replayed `CreateTxn` carries `parent_cversion` and the Create handler snaps to it ([L356-L359](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L356-L359)), so only deletes after a parent's last create leave a lasting difference. <details> <summary>Why the existing tests do not surface the difference</summary> * [`test_keeper_back_to_back/test.py#L173`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_back_to_back/test.py#L173) — `assert_eq_stats` does compare `cversion` between real ZooKeeper and Keeper, and [`test_stats`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_back_to_back/test.py#L182) does call `set`. But `set` is applied to the node whose stat is then compared, so the *parent* (`/`) is never inspected and the difference falls outside the assertion. * [`test_keeper_session/test.py#L286`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_session/test.py#L286) — `test_create2_tree_parent_stats` only creates children, so `setData` on a child is never exercised; it also asserts the parent's `cversion` with `>=` rather than `==` ([L308](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_session/test.py#L308)), so it would not fail even if it were. * [`test_keeper_zookeeper_converter/test.py#L292`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_zookeeper_converter/test.py#L292) — compares `cversion` after conversion. The pre-snapshot deletions in these tests are all of children of `/`, and `compare_states` skips `/` and `/zookeeper` by design ([L350](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_zookeeper_converter/test.py#L350), commented "both paths have strange stats"). For the nodes whose stats are compared no children had been deleted, so `2C − N` reduces to `C` and the conversion difference is invisible. * [`test_keeper_znode_time/test.py#L51`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_znode_time/test.py#L51) also asserts `cversion` equality, but between two Keeper nodes rather than against ZooKeeper, so it cannot catch this either. * There are no unit tests covering `cversion` in `src/Coordination/tests/`. </details> ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on 26.8.1.1431 and on 26.3.9.8. ### How to reproduce Create a parent, then create / modify / delete children under it, reading the parent's stat after each step. Any ZooKeeper client will do. **`cversion`.** Create one child, then write to it five times — Keeper: ``` after create /s1/a cversion=1 pzxid=41508 numChildren=1 after 5x setData /s1/a cversion=6 pzxid=41508 numChildren=1 ``` `zookeeper:3.9`, the same first two steps, then continued through a grandchild and the deletes: ``` create /t1/a cversion=1 pzxid=9 numChildren=1 5x setData /t1/a cversion=1 pzxid=9 numChildren=1 create grandchild /t1/a/deep cversion=1 pzxid=9 numChildren=1 delete grandchild and /t1/a cversion=2 pzxid=17 numChildren=0 ``` (The last step deletes two nodes but `cversion` moves by one, since only `/t1/a` is a direct child of the observed parent.) **`pzxid`.** Create two children, write to one, delete both — Keeper: ``` baseline cversion=0 pzxid=41646 numChildren=0 create a cversion=1 pzxid=41647 numChildren=1 create b cversion=2 pzxid=41648 numChildren=2 setData a cversion=3 pzxid=41648 numChildren=2 delete a cversion=4 pzxid=41648 numChildren=1 delete b cversion=5 pzxid=41648 numChildren=0 ``` `pzxid` stops moving after the last `create`, while in the ZooKeeper run above it advances from 9 to 17 on the deletes. ### Expected behavior Two questions, per the note at the top: * Is the `Set` handler incrementing the parent's `cversion` deliberate? The same increment is present in v22.3 ([`KeeperStorage.cpp#L613`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/v22.3.20.29-lts/src/Coordination/KeeperStorage.cpp#L613), inside `KeeperStorageSetRequestProcessor`) and survived the later storage refactorings, and the in-process `TestKeeper` used by ClickHouse's own tests does the same thing ([`TestKeeper.cpp#L554`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Common/ZooKeeper/TestKeeper.cpp#L554)), so it doesn't look accidental. * Is the `restored_from_zookeeper_log` guard on the `pzxid` update in `Remove` intentional? If both are intentional, documenting them alongside the other known ZooKeeper compatibility gaps (#59489) would help — `cversion` on Keeper answers a different question than on ZooKeeper ("did anything about my direct children change, including their data"), and that is useful to know either way. If they are not, one thing worth weighing first: `cversion` participates in the node digest, digests travel in the Raft log, and a mismatch is fatal (`std::terminate` in `assertDigest`), so changing the computed value needs care across a rolling upgrade of a live quorum, not just a `KEEPER_CURRENT_DIGEST_VERSION` bump. ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_

signals.title: Keeper: PERSISTENT_RECURSIVE watch events carry the watch path instead of the path of the changed node
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong Persistent recursive watches (`addWatch`, opcode 106, `AddWatchMode.PERSISTENT_RECURSIVE`) were added to Keeper in #88813, as part of the ZooKeeper parity ticket #59489. They fire, they are removed by `removeWatches`, they are restored by `setWatches2` after a reconnect, and the event **type** matches ZooKeeper. The event **path** does not: Keeper sends the path the watch was registered on, not the path of the node that actually changed. The path is the only place that information could live, so the event carries no indication of *what* changed. That is not something a client can work around — the information never reaches it. The visible consequence is that Apache Curator's `CuratorCache` — the standard "keep a subtree in memory" recipe from `curator-recipes`, and the recommended replacement for the deprecated `TreeCache` — silently builds an incorrect cache on Keeper. No exception, no `ConnectionLoss`, no log line: the cache simply holds contents that do not match the server. Non-recursive `PERSISTENT` watches are not affected by this, since their events refer to the watched node itself by definition. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes. Checked on `clickhouse/clickhouse-keeper` 26.3.9.8 and on 26.8.1, with identical results — i.e. this is not a regression in a recent build, it is how the feature has behaved since it landed. The reference runs use `zookeeper:3.9` on `localhost:2181` with the same client code; Keeper is on `localhost:9181`. Client side: ZooKeeper Java client 3.9.5, Curator 5.9.0. ### How to reproduce **1. Raw client — the bug itself.** ```java ZooKeeper zk = new ZooKeeper("localhost:9181", 15000, e -> {}); // 2181 for the ZooKeeper reference run zk.create("/w", new byte[0], OPEN_ACL_UNSAFE, CreateMode.PERSISTENT); zk.addWatch("/w", e -> System.out.println(e.getType() + " " + e.getPath()), AddWatchMode.PERSISTENT_RECURSIVE); zk.create("/w/sub", new byte[0], OPEN_ACL_UNSAFE, CreateMode.PERSISTENT); zk.create("/w/sub/leaf", "v1".getBytes(), OPEN_ACL_UNSAFE, CreateMode.PERSISTENT); zk.setData("/w/sub/leaf", "v2".getBytes(), -1); Thread.sleep(2000); ``` | Operation | ZooKeeper 3.9 | Keeper | |-----------------------|-------------------------------|----------------------| | `create /w/sub` | `NodeCreated /w/sub` | `NodeCreated /w` | | `create /w/sub/leaf` | `NodeCreated /w/sub/leaf` | `NodeCreated /w` | | `setData /w/sub/leaf` | `NodeDataChanged /w/sub/leaf` | `NodeDataChanged /w` | The type survives, the address is lost. Deletions behave the same way; we measured that case through Curator rather than the raw client (see below), where the delivered path is again the watch root. A side effect of the same behaviour: `PERSISTENT` and `PERSISTENT_RECURSIVE` watches on the same path become indistinguishable on the client, because the event arrives with that path in both cases and the client's `ZKWatchManager` hands it to both watchers. **2. `CuratorCache` on top of it — the impact.** ```java CuratorFramework client = CuratorFrameworkFactory.newClient("localhost:9181", new RetryNTimes(3, 1000)); client.start(); client.blockUntilConnected(); client.create().creatingParentsIfNeeded().forPath("/cc/b", "v1".getBytes()); CuratorCache cache = CuratorCache.build(client, "/cc"); cache.listenable().addListener((type, oldNode, node) -> System.out.println(type + " " + (node != null ? node.getPath() : oldNode.getPath()))); cache.start(); Thread.sleep(1000); client.create().forPath("/cc/b/g", "v1".getBytes()); // ZooKeeper: NODE_CREATED /cc/b/g; Keeper: nothing Thread.sleep(1000); client.delete().forPath("/cc/b"); // ZooKeeper: NODE_DELETED /cc/b; Keeper: NODE_DELETED /cc Thread.sleep(1000); cache.stream().forEach(d -> System.out.println("cached: " + d.getPath())); cache.close(); client.close(); ``` Resulting cache contents, `/cc` and `/cc/b` created before the cache starts: | Operation | ZooKeeper 3.9 | Keeper + `CuratorCache` | |------------------------|-----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------| | create direct child | correct | correct | | `setData` on the child | correct | correct | | create grandchild | correct | no cache events at all; the node never appears in the cache | | delete the child | `NODE_DELETED /cc/b` | `NODE_DELETED /cc` — `/cc` drops out of the cache and the deleted `/cc/b` stays in it | ("correct" here means the final cache contents; we did not diff the full event stream for those two rows.) The mechanism is visible in `CuratorCacheImpl`: ```java // NOTE: Persistent/Recursive watchers never trigger NodeChildrenChanged switch (event.getType()) { case NodeDataChanged: case NodeCreated: { nodeChanged(event.getPath()); // <- path taken from the event ``` `nodeChanged` / `removeStorage` are called with the path the event carried, i.e. with the watch root, so the recipe re-reads — or evicts — the wrong node. The delete row is the worst of the four: the cache both loses an entry that still exists on the server and keeps an entry that no longer does. ### Why the first two rows still work They work by accident, not because the path happens to be right there. `CuratorCacheImpl.checkChildrenChanged` compares the parent's `cversion` and skips the children walk when it has not moved. In Keeper the parent's `cversion` is *also* incremented on `setData` of a direct child (an extra `++new_parent_stats.cversion` in the `Set` handler in `src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp`, present since v22.3 — #115457). So `nodeChanged("/cc")` re-reads `/cc`, the `cversion` differs, the walk over `/cc`'s children runs and happens to repair the cache. Creating a grandchild does not touch `/cc`'s `cversion` at all — neither in Keeper nor in ZooKeeper — so `checkChildrenChanged` returns immediately, nothing is re-read, and row 3 fails. That `cversion` divergence is a separate issue — #115457 — and is mentioned here only because it explains why the breakage looks partial instead of total. ### Where it comes from `KeeperStorage::processWatchesImpl`, `src/Coordination/KeeperStorage.cpp`: ```cpp std::string_view current_path = path; while (true) { auto watch_it = persistent_recursive_watches.find(current_path); if (watch_it != persistent_recursive_watches.end()) { ... watch_list_response->path = current_path; // <- the ancestor the watch is registered on ... } if (current_path == "/") break; current_path = Coordination::parentNodePath(current_path); } ``` The loop walks up the ancestors looking for registered recursive watches, and puts `current_path` — the current candidate of that walk, i.e. the registration path — into the response. The path of the node that actually changed is right there in the `path` argument and is simply not used. This also explains why the non-recursive modes are unaffected: `processWatchesImplBase` sets `watch_response->path = std::string{path}`, and the list watches deliberately report the parent, which is what `NodeChildrenChanged` means in ZooKeeper. ### Expected behavior `NodeCreated` / `NodeDataChanged` / `NodeDeleted` delivered through a `PERSISTENT_RECURSIVE` watch should carry the path of the node that changed, as ZooKeeper does. The current behaviour reduces a recursive watch to "something under this subtree changed", which is enough as a coarse invalidation trigger, but not enough for any recipe that expects ZooKeeper semantics — and `CuratorCache` is such a recipe. ### Workaround (not verified by us) Make Curator fall back to the older `TreeCache`-based implementation, which is built on one-shot watches and therefore does not depend on the recursive-watch path at all: ```java CuratorFramework client = CuratorFrameworkFactory.builder() .connectString("localhost:9181") .retryPolicy(new RetryNTimes(3, 1000)) .zookeeperCompatibility(ZookeeperCompatibility.builder() .hasPersistentWatchers(false) .build()) .build(); CuratorCache cache = CuratorCache.bridgeBuilder(client, "/cc").build(); ``` `bridgeBuilder` is the part that matters: plain `CuratorCache.build()` always returns `CuratorCacheImpl` and never consults the compatibility settings. There is also a blunter switch — the JVM system property `-Dcurator-cache-bridge-force-tree-cache=true`. Note that `hasPersistentWatchers(false)` is client-wide: it also disables persistent watches for everything else in the process that relies on them, not just for this cache. We have not run either variant against Keeper yet, so treat it as a lead rather than a confirmed fix. ### Related - #59489 — ZooKeeper parity - #88813 — the PR that added `addWatch` / `removeWatches` / `setWatches` - #92480 — persistent watches were not removed on session close (fixed) - #115457 — the parent's `cversion` is bumped on `setData` of a child

signals.title: RESTORE DATABASE ... AS ... corrupts/crashes views using FROM table AS alias FINAL,  other_table
signals.text: ### Company or project name Critical Manufacturing S.A. ### Describe what's wrong Restoring a database backup under a different name (`RESTORE DATABASE src AS dst FROM ...`) mishandles views whose `SELECT` uses a table alias immediately followed by `FINAL` in a multi-table (comma-joined) `FROM t1 AS a FINAL, t2 AS b`. This is valid, documented syntax (["When a table has an alias, FINAL must come after the alias, not before it"](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/statements/select/from#final-modifier)), and views are created and queried correctly before any rename-restore. Depending on the query's complexity, this produces one of two failures only when the database is renamed during restore: 1. Silent alias drop (minimal repro below): the restored view's stored definition loses the alias(es) entirely, silently corrupting the view — it then fails when queried. 2. Hard crash (seen on a more complex, real production view with CTEs/multiple joins — full trace below): the restore itself fails with a `SYNTAX_ERROR` while ClickHouse tries to re-resolve the qualified table name for the rename. No issue occurs if the database is restored under its original name (no `AS `) or if the `CREATE VIEW` is executed directly (not via backup/restore) — pointing at the backup-restore-time table-name rewrite (`DB::BackupMetadataFinder::findTableInBackupImpl`) as the common cause, not the general SQL parser. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Tested and reproducible in these versions: - 25.3.6.56 - 26.3.9.8 - **26.3.19.3** ``` CREATE DATABASE testdb; USE testdb; CREATE TABLE t1 (id UInt32, val String) ENGINE = ReplacingMergeTree ORDER BY id; CREATE TABLE t2 (id UInt32, label String) ENGINE = Memory; INSERT INTO t1 VALUES (1, 'a'); INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (1, 'x'); CREATE VIEW v1 AS SELECT a.id, b.label FROM t1 AS a FINAL, t2 AS b WHERE a.id = b.id; -- Works fine so far: SELECT * FROM v1; BACKUP DATABASE testdb TO Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); --Restoring under a DIFFERENT name silently drops both aliases from the view definition: RESTORE DATABASE testdb AS restoredtestdb FROM Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); USE restoredtestdb; SHOW CREATE VIEW v1; -- Actual: -- FROM restoredtestdb.t1 -- FINAL, -- restoredtestdb.t2 -- WHERE a.id = b.id -- (aliases `a` and `b` are gone, but the WHERE clause still references them) SELECT * FROM v1; -- Code: 47. DB::Exception: Unknown expression identifier `a.id` in scope -- SELECT a.id, b.label FROM restoredtestdb.t1 FINAL, restoredtestdb.t2 WHERE a.id = b.id. -- Maybe you meant: ['t1.id']. (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) -- Restoring under the ORIGINAL name works correctly (no alias loss): DROP DATABASE testdb; RESTORE DATABASE testdb FROM Disk('backups', 'repro_backup'); USE testdb; SHOW CREATE VIEW v1; -- Actual: -- FROM testdb.t1 AS a -- FINAL, -- restoredtestdb.t2 AS b -- WHERE a.id = b.id -- (aliases `a` and `b` are present) SELECT * FROM v1; ``` ### Expected behavior Aliases are kept when restoring with a rename. Fix expected for 26.3 LTS. ### Error message and/or stacktrace Complete statements and error messages present as comments in the reproduction example. ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: Deriving deterministic conditions from conditions involving the current time for the query condition cache
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe the situation When a user writes ``` time >= now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY ``` it cannot be used for the query condition cache. But if we add a redundant condition: ``` time >= now() - INTERVAL 10 DAY AND time >= '2026-08-09' -- this is rounded down to the previous day ``` The condition can be used until the end of day. By persisting conditions with coarsened boundaries, we can balance between cache usefulness and invalidation. For example, the rounding can be up/down to the grid with the size of the interval multiplied by some configured constant (e.g., 1.0) and some maximum (e.g., 1 day). ### Which ClickHouse versions are affected? . ### How to reproduce . ### Expected performance _No response_ ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signals.title: Parts written by an INSERT concurrent with DROP PROJECTION keep the dropped projection; after any mutation CHECK TABLE permanently fails with UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong An `INSERT` that is still running when `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PROJECTION` commits keeps using its metadata snapshot from query start, so the parts it writes after the drop still materialize the dropped projection (`.proj` directory on disk and an entry in the part's `checksums.txt`). Nothing ever reconciles those parts: the drop's cleanup mutation was created before their block numbers, so it never rewrites them, and every later ordinary mutation hardlinks the orphaned `.proj` directory into the new mutated part. Beyond the false alarm, merges are blocked wherever affected and clean parts coexist in one partition: merge assignment refuses ranges whose parts have differing projection sets, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` and `OPTIMIZE ... PARTITION` permanently fail with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE` (`Parts have different projection sets: {} in '...'`), and the partition can never merge down. In that mixed state nothing non-destructive heals it: `DETACH PARTITION` + `ATTACH PARTITION` re-attaches the part still carrying the orphaned `.proj` (renumbered, still failing `CHECK`), `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR PROJECTION <dropped name> IN PARTITION` completes without removing the directories, and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. `OPTIMIZE FINAL` heals only the uniform case where every part in the partition carries the same orphaned projection set (they merge together and the merge drops the unknown projection). The lasting symptom appears as soon as any mutation rewrites such a part: `CHECK TABLE` permanently fails for the mutated part with `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` (`Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj`), although every data file is intact and all rows are readable. The un-mutated ancestor part passes `CHECK TABLE` (it is covered by the unknown-projection tolerance), so the table degrades from "checks clean" to "permanently reports broken parts" at the first mutation, which for an operator is a corruption alarm that never clears. On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the background part-check thread (`ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix`) logs the same `Part has broken projections` for the part, on every replica that has it. The unknown-projection tolerance in `checkDataPart` (added for parts that legitimately carry a projection dropped while they were detached) removes the unknown `.proj` entries from the in-memory checksums and sets `is_broken_projection` with a comment saying the caller can then handle it gracefully — but the entries are not erased from `projections_on_disk`, so the `require_checksums && !projections_on_disk.empty()` branch right below throws `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` anyway (`src/Storages/MergeTree/checkDataPart.cpp`, "Found unexpected projection directories"). A mutated part takes the `require_checksums` path, which is why the throw fires exactly for the mutation descendants. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes. Reproduces on 26.8.1.1708 (official master build) and on 26.4.1.1, so it is long-standing, and on both `MergeTree` and `ReplicatedMergeTree` (2-replica cluster: `CHECK TABLE` returns 0 on both replicas). ### How to reproduce Against any running server (the race window is the INSERT's runtime, ~5 s here, so the interleaving is reliable): ```bash clickhouse-client -q "CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id" clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t ADD PROJECTION p1 (SELECT part, sum(val) GROUP BY part)" # slow INSERT: the metadata snapshot is taken at query start clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, sleepEachRow(0.05)*0 + number, 0 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS max_block_size=10, min_insert_block_size_rows=10, max_insert_threads=1" & sleep 1.5 # DROP PROJECTION commits while the INSERT is still running clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t DROP PROJECTION p1" wait # any ordinary mutation over the affected parts clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t UPDATE val = val + 1 WHERE id < 50 SETTINGS mutations_sync=2" clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t" # 100 - data is fine clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=1" # 0 clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=0" | grep $'\t0\t' ``` The same end state is reached with asynchronous mutations (`mutations_sync=0`); the synchronous form above is only for determinism. In this repro all parts of the partition carry the orphaned projection, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL` merges them and heals the check. When the partition mixes affected and clean parts (one more concurrent INSERT after the drop is enough), `OPTIMIZE` fails with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE: Parts have different projection sets` and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. It survives server restarts. ### Expected behavior Either the INSERT does not materialize a projection that was dropped before its parts were committed, or parts that legitimately carry a since-dropped projection keep passing `CHECK TABLE` after mutations, matching the graceful-handling intent already present in `checkDataPart` for the un-mutated case. A part whose data files are all intact must not be reported broken forever, and its presence must not permanently block merge assignment in its partition. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0_8_8_0_12 0 Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) (version 26.8.1.1708 (official build)) ``` On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the same error surfaces through the background part check: ``` Part `0_7_7_0_11` has broken projections. It will be ignored. Broken projections info: Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) 5. DB::checkDataPart(...) 7. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartImpl(String const&, bool) 8. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix(String const&, std::optional<long>*, bool) 9. DB::StorageReplicatedMergeTree::checkDataNext(std::shared_ptr<DB::IStorage::DataValidationTasksBase>&) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct from #100413: that issue covers a fetch-side flavor where `checksums.txt` references a `.proj` directory that was never transferred (`NO_FILE_IN_DATA_PART`). Here no detach, attach or fetch is involved — an `INSERT` racing `DROP PROJECTION` plus one mutation is enough, and the direction is inverted: the `.proj` directory exists on disk but is unknown to the table metadata.
