signals.title: [RFC] Text index: columnar front coding and `dictionary_block_encoding` parameter
signals.text: This RFC proposes two changes to the text index dictionary: 1. A new parameter `dictionary_block_encoding`, which names the token layout of a dictionary block. It replaces the boolean `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression`. 2. A new layout `columnar_frontcoding`. It stores the same data as front coding, but keeps the per-token integers in two bit-packed columns. It is smaller and decodes faster. The two are independent. The parameter is useful on its own, and the layout could ship under the old boolean. Together they also leave room for further layouts later. ## Background The text index dictionary lives in `.dct`. It is split into blocks of `dictionary_block_size` tokens (512 by default). Tokens inside a block are sorted. Two facts about `.dct` shape this proposal. - **It is already compressed.** Each dictionary block starts a new compressed block, so a lookup decompresses only one block. The codec comes from `default_compression_codec`, then the server `<compression>` config, then the built-in `LZ4`. Nobody has to ask for it. - **The format is self-describing.** Each block starts with a `tokens_format` varint. `deserializeTokens` reads it and picks the decoder. So one table can hold parts with different formats, and a merge can read them all. Today the index parameter `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression` picks between two formats: `0` for raw tokens, `1` for front coding. Front coding is a *token encoding*. It runs before the codec, not instead of it. With default settings the dictionary is front coded, then `LZ4` compressed. ## Motivation Front coding stores two varints per token: the length of the prefix shared with the previous token, and the length of the suffix. The suffix bytes follow. This costs space. A prefix length needs about 5 bits, but a varint spends 8. Tokens are sorted, so suffixes are short, often one or two bytes. The two varints can be bigger than the data they describe. This costs decode time too. `deserializeTokensFrontCoding` does two dependent varint reads per token inside the reconstruction loop. The loop also calls `resize_exact`, because the total size is not known in advance. Both costs grow when tokens are short. With `ngrams(6)`, sorted tokens share 5 characters with the previous token, so the suffix is one byte. The varints are twice the payload. ## New parameter: `dictionary_block_encoding` The current parameter is a boolean, so it cannot name a third layout. Replace it with names: | `dictionary_block_encoding` | `tokens_format` | Meaning | |-------------------------|-----------------|---------| | `none` | `0` | Raw tokens | | `frontcoding` | `1` | Front coding, today's default | | `columnar_frontcoding` | `2` | New layout, below | A matching setting `text_index_dictionary_block_encoding` sets the table default, like the other `text_index_*` settings. The index argument wins over the table setting. `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression` stays accepted. See Compatibility. ## New layout: `columnar_frontcoding` Keep front coding, but move the two integers out of the byte stream. A block stores all prefix lengths, then all suffix lengths, then all suffix bytes. Current layout (`tokens_format = 1`): ``` varint tokens_format varint num_tokens varint first_token_size bytes first_token varint prefix_length \ varint suffix_size | repeated per token bytes suffix / ``` Proposed layout (`tokens_format = 2`): ``` varint tokens_format varint num_tokens varint first_token_size bytes first_token varint prefix_length_width -- bits per value, 0 if all values are 0 varint suffix_size_width -- bits per value bits prefix_length[n-1] -- bit-packed column bits suffix_size[n-1] -- bit-packed column bytes all suffixes ``` The token infos after the tokens do not change. ### Example Four sorted tokens: `token1`, `token10`, `token11`, `token2`. | Token | Prefix length | Suffix | |-----------|---------------|--------| | `token1` | - | - | | `token10` | 6 | `0` | | `token11` | 6 | `1` | | `token2` | 5 | `2` | Today, interleaved: ``` 6 "token1" | 6 1 "0" | 6 1 "1" | 5 1 "2" ``` Proposed, three regions: ``` 6 "token1" | widths: 3 1 | prefix: 6 6 5 | suffix: 1 1 1 | bytes: "0" "1" "2" ``` The prefix column needs 3 bits per value, because the largest value is 6. The suffix column needs 1 bit. So one token costs 4 bits instead of two varints. For a full block of 512 tokens: | Layout | Bytes for the integers | |--------|------------------------| | Front coding | 512 × 2 varints ≈ 1024 | | Columnar front coding | 512 × 4 bits + 2 width bytes ≈ 258 | ### Why it decodes faster - Each column holds one kind of value, so a per-block bit width beats a varint per value. - Both columns are unpacked in bulk first. The reconstruction loop then does two `memcpy` per token and no varint decoding. - The total size is known before reconstruction starts, so the output column is sized once. ## Measurements Background merges were stopped, so all configurations get the same part layout. Sizes are summed over active parts only. Decode is a full dictionary scan with `use_text_index_dictionary_cache = 0`, minimum of 7 runs. Parts are unmerged and each holds its own dictionary, so read the ratios, not the absolute numbers. Token layout alone, with `default_compression_codec = 'NONE'`: | Dataset | `frontcoding` | `columnar_frontcoding` | Size | Decode | |---------|---------------|------------------------|------|--------| | `text_log`, 50M rows, `splitByNonAlpha` | 119.3 MB / 262 ms | 111.4 MB / 250 ms | **−6.7%** | **−4.6%** | | hackernews, 8M rows, `splitByNonAlpha` | 135.8 MB / 391 ms | 128.6 MB / 373 ms | **−5.3%** | **−4.6%** | | `text_log`, 10M rows, `ngrams(5)` | 54.2 MB / 138 ms | 48.7 MB / 133 ms | **−10.2%** | **−3.6%** | | `text_log`, 10M rows, `ngrams(6)` | 142.2 MB / 380 ms | 124.0 MB / 363 ms | **−12.8%** | **−4.5%** | The size gain grows as tokens get shorter, as the layout predicts. The decode gain is about 4.5% everywhere. With the inherited codec on top, which is what would ship: | Configuration | `.dct` | Decode | |---------------|--------|--------| | `frontcoding` + `LZ4`, today | 107.2 MB | 312 ms | | `columnar_frontcoding` + `LZ4` | 103.4 MB (**−3.5%**) | 292 ms (**−6.4%**) | **The size gain depends on the data once a codec runs on top.** Bit-packing removes redundancy the codec used to find: a varint column repeats a lot, a bit-packed column does not. On a synthetic dictionary of `token0 … token99999`, `columnar_frontcoding` + `LZ4` was **0.25% larger**. On `text_log` it was 3.5% smaller. The decode gain does not depend on the codec. Write cost is not measurable. Build time is dominated by tokenization and posting lists. It varied by about 1% with no ordering that followed the layout. ## Configuration ```sql -- per index INDEX idx doc TYPE text(tokenizer = 'splitByNonAlpha', dictionary_block_encoding = 'columnar_frontcoding') -- per table, for text indexes that do not set the argument SETTINGS text_index_dictionary_block_encoding = 'columnar_frontcoding' ``` The table setting applies to new parts only. Existing parts keep their layout. To see what a part uses: ```sql SELECT DISTINCT part_name, dictionary_compression FROM mergeTreeTextIndex(currentDatabase(), tab, idx); ``` `dictionary_compression` gains a `columnar_front_coded` value, next to `raw` and `front_coded`. The numeric enum values do not change. ## Compatibility ### The old parameter keeps working `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression` is stored in the `CREATE TABLE` text of existing tables. ATTACH parses index arguments again, and an unknown argument throws `Unexpected text index arguments`. Removing it would stop those tables from starting. So it stays as a deprecated alias: | Deprecated | New equivalent | |------------|----------------| | `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression = 0` | `dictionary_block_encoding = 'none'` | | `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression = 1` | `dictionary_block_encoding = 'frontcoding'` | `0` must mean "raw tokens that still inherit the part codec". That is what `none` means here. Mapping `0` to "raw tokens, no compression" would make every affected dictionary larger after an upgrade. Precedence: - Both arguments in one index definition: error. They set the same thing. ```sql -- error INDEX idx doc TYPE text(tokenizer = 'splitByNonAlpha', dictionary_block_encoding = 'frontcoding', dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression = 1) ``` - Both settings on one table: `text_index_dictionary_block_encoding` wins if set explicitly, otherwise the old setting is used. Settings come from several config layers, so both being set is not always a mistake. - An index argument always wins over a table setting. ### Reading old parts Nothing to do. Each block stores its own `tokens_format`. ### Old servers reading new parts This is the only real risk. A server that does not know `tokens_format = 2` fails with `CORRUPTED_DATA: Unknown tokens serialization format (2)`. It affects a downgrade after an upgrade, and a mixed-version cluster where an old replica fetches a new part. Being self-describing does not help, because the reader has never heard of the format. Plan: 1. Add the parameter with default `frontcoding`, so nothing changes on upgrade. 2. Change the default to `columnar_frontcoding` in a later release. Record it in `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` so `compatibility` restores the old value, and add a changelog note about downgrades. ### Merges A merge reads source parts with different layouts and writes the output in the currently configured layout. This works because the format is per block. The merge path must resolve the layout the same way the insert path does. Otherwise a merge can silently rewrite `columnar_frontcoding` back to `frontcoding`, and no error is raised. So a test should assert the layout of the merged part, not only the query results. ## Follow-up Front coding has one more cost. A token can only be decoded after the token before it. So to read one token, the whole block must be decoded. Example: `hasToken(doc, 'clickhouse')` needs one dictionary block. That block holds 512 tokens. All 512 are decoded. Then a binary search picks the one token that was needed. Restart points would fix this. Every 32 tokens, store the full token instead of a prefix length. A lookup then decodes 32 tokens instead of 512. The measurements above do not show this. They are full dictionary scans, which decode every token anyway. A point lookup should gain much more than 4.5%. Restart points would also help SIMD. Today each token waits for the token before it, so the decode loop cannot be vectorized.

signals.title: CSVWithNames and CSVWithNamesAndTypes Incorrectly exports NULL Tuple as single column but defines multiple columns
signals.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse/pg_chdb ### Describe what's wrong In 26.7 (but not 26.5), exporting values for a `Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))` column breaks the value up into multiple columns, but when the value is `NULL`, only one of the columns is populated. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Using `clickhouse client --allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1`: ``` CREATE TABLE boxes ( id Int32 PRIMARY KEY, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point)) ); INSERT INTO boxes VALUES (1, NULL); INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('/tmp/geos-tmp.csv', 'CSVWithNames', 'id Int32, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))') SELECT * FROM boxes SETTINGS allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert=1 SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/geos-tmp.csv', 'CSVWithNames', 'id Int32, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))') SETTINGS allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert=1 ``` ### Expected behavior As seen in 26.5: ``` ┌─id─┬─box──┐ 1. │ 1 │ ᴺᵁᴸᴸ │ └────┴──────┘ ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace In 26.7: ``` Received exception: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '\n': (at row 1) : Row 1: Column 0, name: id, type: Int32, parsed text: "1" Column 1, name: <SKIPPED COLUMN>, type: Nothing, parsed text: "<BACKSLASH>N" ERROR: Line feed found where delimiter (,) is expected. It's like your file has less columns than expected. And if your file has the right number of columns, maybe it has unescaped quotes in values. : (in file/uri /tmp/geos-tmp.csv): While executing ParallelParsingBlockInputFormat: While executing File. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context The content of `gens-tmp.csv` on 26.5 is: ```csv "id","box" 1,\N ``` But on 26.7 it's: ```csv "id","box.high.1","box.high.2","box.low.1","box.low.2" 1,\N ``` Not sure why the tuple was converted to multiple columns on export, but `NULL` is not properly mapped to that pattern.

signals.title: Shipped sort gate ignores WITH FILL: ORDER BY ... WITH FILL throws NOT_IMPLEMENTED
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1`, any `SELECT ... ORDER BY <col> WITH FILL` fails with `Code: 48. DB::Exception: WITH FILL is not supported in serialized sort description: While executing Remote. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED)`. The same query on the same binary returns rows with `parallel_replicas_plan_based = 0` (classic parallel replicas) and with `enable_parallel_replicas = 0`.** - **Root cause:** `sortingCanBeShipped` delegates the shippability decision to `SortingStep::isSerializable()` (SortingStep.h:160-163), which inspects only the sort TYPE and `scatter_partitions` - never the sort DESCRIPTION. A `WITH FILL` sort is `Type::Full` with `scatter_partitions == 0`, so it passes the gate although `serializeSortDescription` hard-rejects it. `subtreeIsShippable(parent_node)` cannot catch it either: the unserializable `FillingStep` sits ABOVE the sorting node, outside the checked subtree. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** applyParallelReplicas.cpp:307 accepts the lift when `sortingCanBeShipped` (:377-379) is true -> the sort is cloned into the fragment at :320 -> the fragment is serialized for the replicas -> `SortingStep::serialize` (SortingStep.cpp:730) calls `serializeSortDescription`, which throws for any element with `with_fill` (SortDescription.cpp:310-311). **Affected locations:** - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp:379`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp#L379) — sortingCanBeShipped - gate that lets a WITH FILL sort into the shipped fragment - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp:320`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/Optimizations/applyParallelReplicas.cpp#L320) — partial_sorting_node.step = sorting_step->clone() - puts the WITH FILL sort description into the fragment - [`src/Processors/QueryPlan/SortingStep.h:160`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Processors/QueryPlan/SortingStep.h#L160) — isSerializable() checks only type and scatter_partitions, not the sort description - [`src/Core/SortDescription.cpp:310`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/a4efc96a3f8ce/src/Core/SortDescription.cpp#L310) — serializeSortDescription throws NOT_IMPLEMENTED for desc.with_fill **Impact:** Every `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL` query (with or without LIMIT, with or without INTERPOLATE, with `parallel_replicas_local_plan` 0 or 1) is rejected outright once `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled. `WITH FILL` is a common gap-filling idiom for time-series dashboards, so enabling the setting breaks those queries wholesale. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `a4efc96a3f8ce`). ### How to reproduce ```sql -- Test: ORDER BY ... WITH FILL under plan-based parallel replicas returns the same rows as local execution. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_pr_with_fill; CREATE TABLE t_pr_with_fill (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY a; INSERT INTO t_pr_with_fill SELECT number * 4 FROM numbers(5); SET enable_analyzer = 1; SET enable_parallel_replicas = 1; SET parallel_replicas_for_non_replicated_merge_tree = 1; SET max_parallel_replicas = 3; SET cluster_for_parallel_replicas = 'test_cluster_one_shard_three_replicas_localhost'; SET parallel_replicas_local_plan = 1; SET parallel_replicas_plan_based = 1; -- CI randomizes automatic_parallel_replicas_mode; pin the manual mode so the split engages. SET automatic_parallel_replicas_mode = 0; SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2 SETTINGS enable_parallel_replicas = 0; SELECT '---'; SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2; DROP TABLE t_pr_with_fill; ``` ### Expected behavior ``` 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 --- 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0 2 4 6 8 10 12 14 16 --- Code: 48. DB::Exception: Received from localhost:19020. DB::Exception: WITH FILL is not supported in serialized sort description: While executing Remote. (NOT_IMPLEMENTED) (query 14, line 20) (in query: SELECT a FROM t_pr_with_fill ORDER BY a WITH FILL STEP 2;) ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Reject a sort whose description carries `WITH FILL` before shipping it. Narrow fix: add `&& std::none_of(desc.begin(), desc.end(), [](const auto & c) { return c.with_fill; })` to `sortingCanBeShipped`. Broader fix (also covers `tryMakeDistributedSorting` and any future consumer): make `SortingStep::isSerializable()` return false when any element of `result_description`/`prefix_description` has `with_fill`, mirroring the check `serializeSortDescription` already enforces. Trade-off: the broader fix costs read-in-order for WITH FILL queries under plan-based parallel replicas - the same state as before this PR. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - A window pre-sort WITHOUT `PARTITION BY` (`OVER (ORDER BY a)`) is also newly shipped by this rule and is not covered by 04909 (which only tests the excluded partitioned case). It planned cleanly in EXPLAIN here, but could not be executed locally. Found during automated review of [PR #114315](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114315). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114315_001` </details> cc @devcrafter @nickitat (from #114315)

signals.title: Lossy-codec rejection skips partition-key columns; pruning drops matching rows
signals.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With a lossy codec (`SZ3`) on a column used in the partition key, the same predicate returns fewer rows when partition/part pruning is used than when the rows are scanned: `SELECT count() FROM t WHERE i >= 300 AND i < 400` returns 91 while `SELECT countIf(i >= 300 AND i < 400) FROM t` over the same table returns 92. 6 of 1000 rows sit in a partition that contradicts their own read-back value.** - **Root cause:** The new check's column set is the sorting key only, although the failure mode it guards against (a value derived from the pre-compression block being stored separately from the lossily-compressed data) applies identically to the partition key, whose value and minmax index are also derived pre-compression. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `MergeTreeData::checkProperties` ([`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1033`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1033)) iterates only `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey()`. `getColumnsRequiredForPartitionKey()` ([`src/Storages/StorageInMemoryMetadata.h:247`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/StorageInMemoryMetadata.h#L247)) is never consulted, so `PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)` with `i CODEC(SZ3(...))` is accepted. The partition value and the part-level `minmax_i.idx` are computed by the writer from the pre-compression block, while the data stream is written lossily - so `KeyCondition` prunes on values the part no longer contains. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1033`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1033) — new lossy-codec check iterates only getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey() - [`src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp:1052`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/6c8e5b1397b5f/src/Storages/MergeTree/MergeTreeData.cpp#L1052) — throw BAD_ARGUMENTS; the message names only the sorting key **Impact:** Silent wrong results: a query whose predicate touches the partition-key column returns fewer rows than the same predicate evaluated over a full scan, and rows are stored in a partition their own value contradicts (so `DROP PARTITION`, `_partition_id` filters and partition-wise merges all act on the wrong rows). No error is raised at any point. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `6c8e5b1397b5f`). ### How to reproduce [▶ Run on ClickHouse Fiddle](https://fiddle.clickhouse.com/a4e07fd3-1f5d-45c5-a666-4202ab5427be) <details> <summary>Reproducer</summary> ```sql -- no-fasttest: needs sz3 library -- no-random-settings, no-random-merge-tree-settings: SZ3 is lossy and its output depends on how the data -- is split into compressed blocks -- A lossy codec on a column of the partition key: the partition value and the part minmax index are -- computed before compression, so they contradict the values that are read back. DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; SET allow_experimental_codecs = 1; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; CREATE TABLE t_lossy_partition_key (k Int64, i Float64 CODEC(SZ3('ALGO_INTERP_LORENZO', 'REL', 0.01))) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k PARTITION BY intDiv(toInt64(i), 100); INSERT INTO t_lossy_partition_key SELECT number, number * 1.1 FROM numbers(1000); SELECT countIf(toString(intDiv(toInt64(i), 100)) != _partition_id) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; SELECT count() FROM t_lossy_partition_key WHERE intDiv(toInt64(i), 100) = 3; SELECT countIf(intDiv(toInt64(i), 100) = 3) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; SELECT count() FROM t_lossy_partition_key WHERE i >= 300 AND i < 400; SELECT countIf(i >= 300 AND i < 400) FROM t_lossy_partition_key; DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t_lossy_partition_key; ``` </details> ### Expected behavior ``` 0 91 91 91 91 ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 6 91 92 91 92 ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Extend the loop's column set to the partition key: iterate over the union of `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey()` and `new_metadata.getColumnsRequiredForPartitionKey()`, and generalise the message to name the key that the column belongs to. Alternatively, restrict the PR title/changelog to the sorting key and file the partition-key hole separately. </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - Secondary skip indexes on a lossy column are the same shape of hazard (index built pre-compression); three probe shapes failed to produce a divergence because the codec error stayed inside the granule range, so this is unproven rather than ruled out. Found during automated review of [PR #114531](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114531). Severity P2 · Finding `h_pr114531_001` </details> cc @groeneai @rschu1ze (from #114531)

signals.title: Allow interactive queries finish in the background
signals.text: **Use case** A user can run an interactive session with long-running INSERT SELECT. If the session is interrupted, the query is typically canceled (after an exception about connection loss in an attempt to send progress or read a network packet from a user). But it is sad if the query was running for a long time. **Describe the solution you'd like** If a query is not expected to return any result to the user (such as SELECT) and does not require any data from the user (such as INSERT without SELECT), we can catch exceptions related to a network connection with the user, stop sending the progress packets and waiting for the incoming packets (such as cancellation), and continue normally. The user can reconnect and then observe the progress in `SHOW PROCESSLIST`. **Additional context** The current behavior (query termination on connection loss) is also good. The behavior should be controllable by a setting. <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #112816 - Merged into: `26.8.1.1697` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.text: How to reproduce: ```sql WITH RECURSIVE subquery1 AS ( SELECT 1 AS x UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 AS level FROM subquery1 WHERE x < 5 ), subquery2 AS ( SELECT 1 AS id FROM subquery1 ), subquery3 AS ( SELECT id FROM subquery2 UNION ALL SELECT cc.id FROM subquery3 AS cc INNER JOIN subquery2 AS oe ON cc.id = oe.id UNION ALL SELECT cc.id FROM subquery3 AS cc ) SELECT * FROM subquery3 FORMAT Null ``` Exception: ``` Received exception: Code: 49. DB::Exception: UNION query subquery1 AS (SELECT 1 AS x UNION ALL SELECT x + 1 AS level FROM subquery1 WHERE x < 5) is not recursive: While executing RecursiveCTESource. (LOGICAL_ERROR) ```

signals.title: Introduce `system.iceberg_files` table
signals.text: ### Background Currently ClickHouse provides `system.iceberg_history` (src/Storages/System) for snapshot history and `system.iceberg_metadata_log` for low-level debug logging of metadata parsing. However, there is no structured, queryable view of the data files that make up an Iceberg table's current snapshot. Spark exposes `table.files / table.data_files` (https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-queries/#files) metadata tables that allow users to inspect the table's physical layout. This is valuable for: - Diagnosing performance issues (e.g. too many small files, skewed partitions) - Understanding table structure without external tooling - Monitoring partition-level file/row counts `system.iceberg_metadata_log` contains similar information but as raw JSON/Avro blobs, is per-query (not a stable view of the table state), and requires explicit opt-in via `iceberg_metadata_log_level`. ### Implementation notes Proposed schema ``` database String table String snapshot_id Int64 content Enum8('DATA' = 0, 'POSITION_DELETE' = 1, 'EQUALITY_DELETE' = 2) file_path String file_format String record_count Int64 file_size_in_bytes Int64 partition String schema_id Int32 sequence_number Int64 sort_order_id Nullable(Int32) null_value_counts Map(Int32, Int64) column_sizes Map(Int32, Int64) value_counts Map(Int32, Int64) equality_ids Nullable(Array(Int32)) ``` - Follow the existing `StorageSystemIcebergHistory` pattern: iterate all Iceberg tables, read metadata, fill columns. - Most fields already exist in `ManifestFileEntry`. Two fields — `record_count` and `file_size_in_bytes` are present in the Avro manifest schema (field-ids 103 and 104) but currently not stored in ManifestFileEntry and need to be added. - The partition column should contain a human-readable serialization of `ManifestFileEntry::partition_key_value`. Example ```sql CREATE TABLE iceberg_db.events ( event_date Date, user_id UInt64, event_type String ) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://s3:9000/warehouse/events', ...) PARTITION BY event_date SETTINGS iceberg_format_version = 2; After a simple insert: INSERT INTO iceberg_db.events VALUES ('2025-01-01', 1, 'click'), ('2025-01-01', 2, 'view'), ('2025-01-02', 3, 'click'); SELECT database, table, content, file_path, file_format, record_count, file_size_in_bytes, partition, sequence_number FROM system.iceberg_files WHERE database = 'iceberg_db' AND table = 'events'; ┌─database───┬─table──┬─content─┬─file_path──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─file_format─┬─record_count─┬─file_size_in_bytes─┬─partition──────┬─sequence_number─┐ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-01/00000-0-....-00001.parquet │ PARQUET │ 2 │ 847 │ {2025-01-01} │ 1 │ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-02/00000-0-....-00002.parquet │ PARQUET │ 1 │ 631 │ {2025-01-02} │ 1 │ └────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────┘ After a second insert (two snapshots, three data files): INSERT INTO iceberg_db.events VALUES ('2025-01-01', 4, 'purchase'); ┌─database───┬─table──┬─content─┬─file_path──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─file_format─┬─record_count─┬─file_size_in_bytes─┬─partition──────┬─sequence_number─┐ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-01/00000-0-....-00001.parquet │ PARQUET │ 2 │ 847 │ {2025-01-01} │ 1 │ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-02/00000-0-....-00002.parquet │ PARQUET │ 1 │ 631 │ {2025-01-02} │ 1 │ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-01/00000-1-....-00001.parquet │ PARQUET │ 1 │ 620 │ {2025-01-01} │ 2 │ └────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────┘ ``` <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #104415 - Merged into: `26.6.1.614` (included in `26.6` and later) - Backported to: `26.5.8.4` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Release pull request for branch 26.3
signals.text: This PullRequest is a part of ClickHouse release cycle. It is used by CI system only. Do not perform any changes with it. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > Touches query analyzer/optimizers and network I/O/SSL code paths, plus introduces new distroless Docker images/entrypoint logic; regressions could affect query semantics/perf or connectivity. Broad dependency/build/CI updates increase integration risk despite many changes being incremental. > > **Overview** > **Adds distroless Docker images for `clickhouse-server` and `clickhouse-keeper`** and introduces a new compiled `clickhouse docker-init` program to replace shell-based entrypoints, including initdb script execution and user/db bootstrapping. > > **Improves robustness and compatibility across runtime/query execution:** fixes partial-write handling in Poco stream buffers and HTTP chunked writes, tightens `Content-Length` enforcement, and surfaces SSL read/write/handshake timeouts as `TimeoutException`s. Extends analyzer optimizations (notably rewriting `Map` key lookups to dynamic key subcolumns in filters) and adds plumbing for `MATERIALIZED` CTE metadata through the query tree/identifier resolution. > > **Refines optimizations and correctness checks:** makes quantile fusion stable with duplicate levels, hardens inverse dictionary lookup rewrites with semantic-safety guards and set overflow settings, and fixes several aggregate-function edge cases (self add/sub in BSI, safer `quantileTiming` deserialization, legacy null-adapter handling for `sumCount`, correct signedness in LLVM codegen). > > **Updates CI/build and dependencies:** switches stateless tests to Node 20 + npm `azurite`, adds distroless to docker build matrix/tests, disables backport-branch automerge, and bumps/adjusts bundled deps and build flags (e.g., OpenSSL `3.5.6`, xz updates, jemalloc LTO disable). Documentation is updated for `MATERIALIZED` CTEs, Map bucketed serialization, and related notes. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit c04e83b7958da5876b5f8e4b66344cad2ef6a0ff. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY -->

signals.title: Add `user_files_policy` server setting for custom disks in user_files directory
signals.text: Add a new `user_files_policy` server configuration parameter, similar to `tmp_policy`, that allows user files to reside on custom storage volumes, including S3-backed disks. When configured, the policy's volume (which must have exactly one volume) provides the disks for user file storage. All file operations (`file()` table function, `StorageFile`, dictionaries, `DatabaseFilesystem`, etc.) now route through the `IDisk` interface when a volume is configured, enabling S3 and other remote storage backends. Key changes: - `user_files_policy` setting in `ServerSettings` with XML config example - `Context` stores `VolumePtr` and exposes `getUserFilesVolume`, `getUserFilesPaths`, `setUserFilesPolicy` - `StorageFile` supports disk-based glob matching via `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingOnDisk`, disk-based reads via `disk->readFile`, and disk-based writes via `disk->writeFile` - `FunctionFile` reads through disk I/O when volume is configured - All 13 callers of `getUserFilesPath` updated for multi-path validation - Helper overloads `pathStartsWith(path, vector)` and `fileOrSymlinkPathStartsWith(path, vector)` added - Integration test with local multi-disk and S3 (`s3_plain`) scenarios ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `user_files_policy` server setting to store `user_files` on a custom disk, including S3-backed disks. This allows customers to have a "scratch area" for files in ClickHouse Cloud, shared among all replicas. Note: keeping as a draft, because the code is not generalized enough. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Introduces a new storage-policy-backed path for `user_files` and rewires many read/write and path-validation code paths (including remote disks), which could affect file access semantics and security boundaries if edge cases are missed. > > **Overview** > Adds a new server setting `user_files_policy` that binds the `user_files` directory to a storage policy (enforced to *exactly one volume with one disk*) and stores the resolved `VolumePtr` in `Context`, with server startup applying it via `setUserFilesPolicy`. > > Updates user-files consumers to become disk-aware when a policy is configured: `file()`/`StorageFile` switch to `IDisk`-based globbing, reads, writes, schema inference and truncation (plus new helpers like `splitUserFilesAbsolutePath`, `userFilesPathExists`, and symlink-escape checks), while features that require local POSIX paths (`ATTACH ... signals.title: Add assertions in IColumn::mutate to verify deep unique ownership of sub-columns
signals.text: Investigation for https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/99920 This is a draft PR with diagnostic assertions to help find a COW violation bug where columns stored in `HashJoin` have their `allocatedBytes()` change because internal sub-columns are modified by someone who treats immutable columns as mutable. ## What was found The bug manifests as `data->allocated_size != debug_allocated_size` exception in debug builds. Investigation narrowed it down to: 1. **Removing the single-chunk optimization** in `Squashing.cpp:70-72` fixes the bug — this optimization passes chunks through without `IColumn::mutate`, so columns remain shared with Memory engine blocks 2. The **modification happens between** `addBlockToJoin` calls — during pipeline processing of the next chunk 3. The mutation is a **reallocation** (reserve/grow), not a data write — `protect()` (mprotect) doesn't catch it 4. The assertions in this PR (`IColumn::mutate` deep ownership check) **do NOT fire** — meaning the mutation happens outside the `IColumn::mutate` path entirely. Someone treats an immutable column as mutable without going through `mutate`. ## Reproducer The test `04049_fix_hashjoin_shared_column_allocated_size` reproduces the exception in debug builds. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100185&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/100185](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F100185+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Disable read-in-order when primary key selectivity is poor
signals.text: When the WHERE clause cannot use the primary key effectively (e.g., `LIKE '%...'`), the `optimize_read_in_order` optimization kills parallelism: each part is read by a single stream instead of many. This can make `ORDER BY` queries 4x slower than the same query without `ORDER BY`. Example on a 2.5B row table with `ORDER BY path` and `WHERE path LIKE '%stderr.log'`: - Without ORDER BY: ~9.5s - With ORDER BY (read-in-order): ~40s - With `optimize_read_in_order = 0`: ~9.6s The fix adds a runtime check in `ReadFromMergeTree::spreadMarkRanges`: if the primary key index selected more than a configurable fraction of all granules and there is no LIMIT, we fall back to parallel reading with per-stream `PartialSortingTransform` + `MergeSortingTransform`, so the output is still sorted as the `SortingStep` above expects. New setting `read_in_order_max_primary_key_ratio` controls the threshold. The default is 1.0, which preserves the previous behavior (never disable read-in-order based on primary key selectivity): the heuristic is opt-in until the default threshold is tuned against the performance report. Set it below 1.0 (e.g. 0.5) to enable the guard. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add a new setting `read_in_order_max_primary_key_ratio` that can disable the read-in-order optimization when the primary key selectivity is poor (more than the given fraction of granules selected), falling back to parallel reading with sorting. This avoids severe parallelism loss for queries like `SELECT ... WHERE path LIKE '%...' ORDER BY path`. The default 1.0 preserves the previous behavior; set a lower value (e.g. 0.5) to enable the heuristic. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) New setting `read_in_order_max_primary_key_ratio` (Float, default 1.0): maximum ratio of selected to total primary key granules for `optimize_read_in_order` to stay enabled. When the ratio exceeds this value, read-in-order is disabled in favor of parallel reading with per-stream sorting. The default 1.0 preserves the old behavior. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=100377&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/100377](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F100377+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Parallelize read-in-order from a single part with PrefetchingConcatProcessor
signals.text: When a single MergeTree part is split into multiple streams for read-in-order, use the new `PrefetchingConcatProcessor` instead of relying on the downstream `MergingSortedTransform`. The key difference: - `MergingSortedTransform` marks all inputs as needed but only consumes from one stream at a time (for non-overlapping ranges), and each port can only buffer 1 block — so after initial prefetch, reading becomes sequential. - `PrefetchingConcatProcessor` marks all inputs as needed AND pulls data from non-current inputs into internal buffers, keeping upstream sources busy. It outputs data in strict input order (concatenation), which is correct because ranges from a single part are non-overlapping and pre-sorted. This avoids both the merge comparison overhead and the sort overhead, while enabling true parallel IO and filtering across range groups. Benchmark on 100M rows (4 threads, single part, poor PK selectivity): - Single-thread read-in-order: 1.57s - Parallel + sort (no read-in-order): 1.27s - PrefetchingConcat: 0.61s (2.6x faster) ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve the performance of queries that are reading in the order of the primary key. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Changes read-in-order execution and introduces a new buffering processor in the query pipeline; incorrect gating or backpressure/buffering behavior could impact result ordering or memory usage in some MergeTree reads. > > **Overview** > **Adds `PrefetchingConcatProcessor`**: a new concat-like processor that keeps *all* inputs marked needed and buffers per-input chunks (bounded by `max_buffered_chunks`) to prefetch non-current streams while still outputting streams strictly in order. > > **Wires it into MergeTree read-in-order**: `ReadFromMergeTree` now conditionally replaces `MergingSortedTransform` with `PrefetchingConcatProcessor` when reading in ascending order from a *single part* split into multiple streams and only when there is filtering work (`PREWHERE` or row-level filter); it also adds `prefer_multiple_streams`/`setPreferMultipleStreams()` so aggregation-/distinct-in-order paths can opt out to avoid collapsing parallel streams. > > **Tests/bench coverage updated**: adds a new stateless test asserting `PrefetchingConcat` appears only for single-part reads and preserves sort order, adjusts an existing buffering test to force multi-part behavior, and adds a performance scenario guarding against regressions for filter-less `ORDER BY` reads. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit c0ba40d2f630976681024d2ac941261c4abdbe57. signals.title: Add leader election for non-replicated MergeTree on shared storage
signals.text: Add leader election for non-replicated MergeTree tables on shared object storage (currently `S3`; `Azure` is implemented but not yet enabled, pending test coverage), enabling active/standby failover without external coordination (no Keeper). Uses conditional writes (`If-Match` / `If-None-Match`) on object storage to maintain a lease file with JSON content `{"version":1,"leader_id":"...","timestamp":...}`. The leader renews its lease periodically; followers monitor and claim leadership when the lease expires. New MergeTree settings: - `leader_election` (Bool, default false) — enable leader election - `leader_election_heartbeat_interval` (Seconds, default 10) — lease renewal interval - `leader_election_session_timeout` (Seconds, default 30) — lease expiry threshold; must be at least 3x the heartbeat interval When not the leader, inserts, merges, and DDL are blocked; background data processing is skipped. Mutations are unsupported on the currently enabled `S3` `plain_rewritable` metadata layout, including on the leader. Participating nodes should keep their clocks synchronized (NTP) to within `leader_election_session_timeout`; the conditional-write protocol always prevents split-brain, but excessive clock skew can cause leadership churn. Closes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/91613 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `leader_election` setting for non-replicated MergeTree tables on shared object storage, enabling active/standby failover using conditional writes without external coordination. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Three new MergeTree-level settings are added: - `leader_election` (Bool) — When enabled on a non-replicated MergeTree table stored on an `S3` object storage disk (`Azure` is implemented but rejected at table creation until it has test coverage), multiple ClickHouse instances sharing the same data path will elect a single leader. Only the leader performs writes and merges. Followers act as read-only replicas and automatically claim leadership when the current leader's lease expires. Mutations are unsupported on the currently enabled `S3` `plain_rewritable` metadata layout, including on the leader. - `leader_election_heartbeat_interval` (Seconds, default 10) — How often the leader renews its lease and followers check for an expired lease. - `leader_election_session_timeout` (Seconds, default 30) — How long a lease remains valid without renewal. Must be at least 3x `leader_election_heartbeat_interval`. Example, using the same UUID and shared `S3` storage policy on each node: ```sql CREATE TABLE shared_table UUID '12345678-abcd-abcd-abcd-123456789abc' (x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x SETTINGS storage_policy = 's3', leader_election = true, leader_election_heartbeat_interval = 10, leader_election_session_timeout = 30; -- On every follower, attach the same table definition with the same UUID. ATTACH TABLE shared_table UUID '12345678-abcd-abcd-abcd-123456789abc' (x UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY x SETTINGS storage_policy = 's3', leader_election = true, leader_election_heartbeat_interval = 10, leader_election_session_timeout = 30; ``` <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **High Risk** > High risk because it introduces new leader-election coordination and modifies core `MergeTree` write/DDL/drop and catalog cleanup paths; bugs could cause write unavailability or accidental deletion/incorrect visibility on shared storage. > > **Overview** > Adds a **Beta** `leader_election` mode for non-replicated `MergeTree` tables on shared S3/Azure, using a conditional-write lease file to ensure only one instance performs inserts/merges/mutations while followers remain read-only and can take over on failure. > > Introduces new MergeTree settings (`leader_election`, `leader_election_heartbeat_interval`, `leader_election_session_timeout`) with validation, new `MergeTreeLeaderElection*` metrics/events, and follower part-refresh + leader takeover sync to load new parts and advance block counters before enabling writes. > > Hardens destructive operations for shared-storage tables: blocks most `ALTER`/partition-mutation operations and `RENAME` under leader election, gates background processing on leadership, and updates drop/cleanup logic (`dropSkipsDataDirectoryCleanup`, `DatabaseCatalog`/`StorageTableProxy` fail-closed behavior) to avoid recursive deletion or hangs when tables are shared or cannot be materialized. Adds documentation and integration/stateless tests covering failover, metrics, validation, and rejection cases. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 78c1252915ba512bebf94a147932158e1bacecf0. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY --> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101039&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101039](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101039+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support `SIMILAR TO` pattern matching predicate
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support `SIMILAR TO` pattern matching predicate ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ x ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. At a minimum, the following information should be added (but add more as needed). - Motivation: Why is this function, table engine, etc. useful to ClickHouse users? - Parameters: If the feature being added takes arguments, options or is influenced by settings, please list them below with a brief explanation. - Example use: A query or command. --> - Motivation: SQL standard has SIMILAR TO predicate that combines SQL LIKE wildcards (%, _) with regular expression metacharacters `|, *, +, ?, [...], {m,n}, (...)`. Note that excluded are `^, $, .`. It is supported by PostgreSQL and others. See the [PostgreSQL documentation on pattern matching](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-matching.html#FUNCTIONS-SIMILARTO-REGEXP) for reference. I also added: negation and substring pattern shortcut. Syntax highlighting is also hooked in to highlight the metacharacters. - Parameters: None. - Example use: ```sql SELECT similarTo('ClickHouse', 'Cl_ck[hH]ouse'); -- Returns: 1 SELECT 'ClickHouse' NOT SIMILAR TO 'Cl%ck[0-9]ouse'; -- Returns: 1 ``` - Corner cases - Character class inside bracket expression. - Bracket expressions don't nest. So `[[:a]]` is invalid, but up to RE2 to process. Addresses https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/99608. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Adds new SQL operator/function surface area and a new pattern-to-regexp translator, which can affect query parsing and string filtering semantics; risk is moderate due to edge cases in escaping/bracket handling and regex compilation paths. > > **Overview** > Adds SQL-standard `SIMILAR TO` pattern matching (and `NOT SIMILAR TO`) implemented via new `similarToPatternToRegexp()` conversion and new `similarTo`/`notSimilarTo` functions wired into `MatchImpl`/`Regexps::createRegexp`. > > Extends the parser to recognize and pretty-print `SIMILAR TO` / `NOT SIMILAR TO`, updates CNF NOT-pushing inversions, and adds syntax-highlighting support for SIMILAR TO metacharacters. > > Updates call sites to the new `Regexps::createRegexp<like, similar_to, ...>` template signature and expands query fuzzer swap sets plus a new stateless test suite covering SIMILAR TO behavior and corner cases. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit e17d9fd7d3d079c5528a281d7a9af6781ecff4dd. signals.title: Respect max_http_get_redirects setting in HTTPDictionarySource
signals.text: ### What this PR does `HTTPDictionarySource` did not call `withRedirects` on its HTTP request builder, so HTTP dictionary sources rejected every redirect with `TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` even when `max_http_get_redirects` was set to a non-zero value. This made it impossible to create dictionaries from HTTP(S) URLs that redirect (e.g. pre-signed object-storage URLs), while the `url` table function and other HTTP sources already follow redirects. This adds `.withRedirects(context->getSettingsRef()[Setting::max_http_get_redirects])` to all four request paths (`loadAll`, `loadUpdatedAll`, `loadIds`, `loadKeys`), matching the pattern already used in `StorageURL`. The `max_http_get_redirects` value is taken from the dictionary's `SETTINGS` clause; the default of `0` keeps the previous (redirect-rejecting) behavior, so this is not backward incompatible. A new stateless test `04498_http_dictionary_max_redirects` starts a local HTTP server that issues a `302` redirect and verifies that the dictionary refuses to follow it when `max_http_get_redirects = 0` (`TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS`) and loads successfully when redirects are allowed. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/90521 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes): HTTP dictionary sources (`SOURCE(HTTP(...))`) now respect the `max_http_get_redirects` setting, so dictionaries can be created from URLs that redirect. signals.title: Auto-escape XML special characters in from_env config substitutions
signals.text: ### What this PR does When direct config values loaded via `from_env` contain XML special characters (`&`, `<`, `>`), the `ConfigProcessor` failed with `SAXParseException` because the raw value was concatenated directly into an XML string. Direct values are now escaped before being embedded into the XML DOM, so an environment variable can hold any XML-1.0-legal value — including one that looks like an XML fragment (taken as literal text) and one that contains the `]]>` sequence the XML grammar forbids in character data. Existing `<include from_env="..."/>` substitutions continue to interpret their value as an XML subtree. Upgrade note: a direct `from_env` value that was XML-entity-encoded for the old XML parser (for example `a&b`) now resolves to its exact literal bytes and must be set raw (`a&b`) instead. This migration is documented and covered by an integration regression. The contents of a ZooKeeper node referenced via `from_zk` may be a whole subtree. A value beginning with `<` is parsed as an XML fragment (both for a structural `<include>` and for a leaf substitution), which is kept for backward compatibility because earlier versions always interpreted a `from_zk` value as XML. An explicit `<include from_zk="..." yaml="true"/>` parses a non-`<` value as a YAML subtree. Without `yaml="true"`, the value remains literal text, so `<include>` is also the generic "replace this element with the node contents" form and may carry a leaf value such as a secret. Whitespace surrounding that `<include>` becomes part of the leaf value, so direct leaf substitutions such as `<password from_zk="..."/>` or `<some_setting from_zk="..."/>` are recommended when exact bytes matter. Those direct leaf substitutions keep a non-`<` value as literal text using its exact original bytes, so existing *plain-text* scalar substitutions and secrets keep working unchanged on upgrade. There is one deliberate behavior change on upgrade: a leaf value that was XML-entity-encoded to satisfy the old parser (which reparsed every `from_zk` value as XML and rejected a raw `&`, `<` or `>` as not well-formed) is now kept as its exact original bytes. A value stored as `a&b` used to decode to `a&b`, but now resolves to the literal `a&b`; such values must be stored raw (`a&b`) instead. This is documented in `docs/concepts/features/configuration/server-config/configuration-files.mdx` and covered by an integration regression. Upgrade note: the same literal-text behavior applies to direct ordinary-element `from_env` substitutions such as `<profiles from_env="..."/>`. Existing XML-subtree imports in that form must migrate to `<profiles><include from_env="..."/></profiles>`; this is documented and covered by an integration regression. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78835 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry: Fixed direct config substitutions via `from_env` failing when XML-1.0-legal values contain XML special characters like `&`, `<`, `>`, or the `]]>` sequence; existing `<include from_env="..."/>` XML-subtree substitutions are unchanged. An explicit `<include from_zk="..." yaml="true"/>` substitution can read a YAML subtree wherever the generic `<include>` form is used, including inside a leaf element, so it must not be used for a literal secret or setting. Without the explicit `yaml="true"` attribute, a non-`<` value is literal text, but direct non-`<` leaf `from_zk` substitutions are recommended for exact-byte secrets/settings, because surrounding whitespace of an `<include>` becomes part of a leaf value. Values beginning with `<` continue to be interpreted as XML fragments for backward compatibility. Upgrade note: a direct `from_env` value or a non-`<` leaf `from_zk` value that was previously XML-entity-encoded (for example `a&b`) now resolves to its exact literal bytes and must be stored raw (`a&b`) instead. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101773&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101773](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101773+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support specifying or auto-assigning Parquet field_ids for output columns
signals.text: ### What this PR does Two related knobs for writing Parquet files with column `field_id` metadata — needed for Apache Iceberg compatibility, which identifies columns by `field_id` rather than by name. Both knobs can be used independently or together. #### 1. Explicit per-column overrides New setting `output_format_parquet_column_field_ids : Map(String, Int32)`. ```sql SET output_format_parquet_column_field_ids = '{"col_a": 10, "col_b": 20, "col_c": 30}'; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('data.parquet') SELECT 1::UInt32 AS col_a, 'x'::String AS col_b, 42::Int64 AS col_c; ``` Each output column gets the id specified in the map. The map must cover every output column (unless auto-assign below is enabled to fill the gaps), and ids must be unique; violations raise `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with specific messages. #### 2. Auto-assign (Iceberg writer convention) New setting `output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids : Bool`, default `false`. When enabled, every output column is assigned a unique sequential `field_id` starting at `1`, matching the convention used by Apache Iceberg writers. ```sql SET output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids = 1; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('iceberg.parquet') SELECT 1 AS a, 'x' AS b, 42 AS c; -- a -> 1, b -> 2, c -> 3 ``` #### 3. Mixed mode The two settings compose: override-map entries win for the columns they mention; auto-assign fills the remaining columns with the smallest unused positive ids. ```sql SET output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids = 1, output_format_parquet_column_field_ids = '{"b": 1}'; INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('mixed.parquet') SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS b, 3 AS c; -- b -> 1 (override), a -> 2, c -> 3 (auto-assign skipping 1) ``` ### Implementation - `src/Core/FormatFactorySettings.h` — declare both settings. - `src/Formats/FormatSettings.h` — carry a `std::vector<std::pair<String, Int32>>` of overrides and the `auto_assign_field_ids` bool; no string parsing on the hot path. - `src/Formats/FormatFactory.cpp` — convert the `Map` setting into the pair vector, with structural validation (tuple shape, string keys, integer values in `Int32` range). - `src/Processors/Formats/Impl/ParquetBlockOutputFormat.cpp` — `buildColumnFieldIds()` resolves overrides against the actual output header, auto-assigns unused ids if the flag is on, and rejects unknown columns, duplicate ids, and non-covering overrides. ### Test `tests/queries/0_stateless/04321_parquet_column_field_ids.sh` writes Parquet files with `clickhouse-local`, reads the `field_id` metadata back with `pyarrow`, and covers: - Explicit per-column overrides. - Auto-assign only. - Mixed override + auto-assign. - Writing with neither setting (no `field_id`s, unchanged behavior). - Nested types: auto-assign and dotted-path overrides for `Array.element`, `Tuple` subfields, and `Map.key`/`Map.value`. - Geo columns written as WKB under GeoParquet (the `Point`/`Array`/`Tuple` shape collapses to a single top-level field). - Error cases: unknown column, non-covering map (top-level and nested), duplicate id, non-integer value, negative id, and a dotted top-level name colliding with a nested path (in both auto-assign and override modes). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58753 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry: Added `output_format_parquet_column_field_ids` (`Map(String, Int32)`) to set explicit Parquet `field_id` overrides per column and `output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids` (`Bool`) to auto-assign sequential `field_id`s to every output column, matching the Apache Iceberg writer convention. The two settings can be combined. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches the Parquet write path and schema generation to emit `field_id` metadata, which could affect interoperability and schema expectations; defaults are preserved unless new settings are enabled. > > **Overview** > Adds two new Parquet output settings to control column `field_id` metadata for Iceberg compatibility: `output_format_parquet_column_field_ids` (explicit per-column overrides) and `output_format_parquet_auto_assign_field_ids` (sequential auto-assignment starting at 1). > > `FormatFactory` now parses/validates the `Map` setting into typed overrides up-front, while `ParquetBlockOutputFormat` resolves the final `field_id` mapping (including error checks for unknown columns, duplicates, negative ids, and incomplete coverage when auto-assign is off) and explicitly rejects using these settings when a datalake writer provides its own column-id mapping. > > Documentation and a new stateless test are added to verify correct `field_id` emission via `pyarrow` and expected failure modes. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit ce5f371493174b5b0ee58307dfc05f5df32af0b2. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY --> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101783&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101783](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101783+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Ask for continuation in single-line mode when query is incomplete
signals.text: ### What this PR does In single-line interactive mode, pressing Enter on an incomplete query (one where the parser reaches the end of input still expecting more tokens) no longer sends it and shows a syntax error. Instead, a newline is inserted into the same edit buffer, exactly like pressing Alt+Enter, so the whole query stays under a single prompt and the arrow keys can navigate and edit across all of its lines. A trailing `;` still forces submission (for example, to deliberately submit an incomplete query and see its syntax error). This replaces the earlier approach that printed a separate `:-] ` continuation prompt and read additional lines, which prevented cross-line editing and could split pasted queries. The completeness check is now passed to `ReplxxLineReader` as a callback and consulted from the `commit_action` bound to Enter. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/64886 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): In single-line interactive mode, `clickhouse-client` now keeps an incomplete query under a single prompt and lets you continue it on the next line (like pressing Alt+Enter) instead of sending it immediately. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (not required for this change) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101785&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101785](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101785+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: feat(promql): Parse Prometheus Query API POST bodies as urlencoded form
signals.text: The Prometheus Query API (`QueryAPIImpl`) read parameters only from `HTMLForm(settings, request)`, which parses the URL query string. For POST requests with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, the PromQL `query` and range parameters live in the body, so they were empty and clients such as `prometheus/client_golang` saw failed or empty evaluations. `QueryAPIImpl` now uses `HTMLForm(settings, request, *request.getStream())` for POST and PUT so the body is merged with any query string (same behavior as `HTMLForm::load`). `RemoteWriteImpl` and `RemoteReadImpl` keep the default path so the raw body stream is not consumed before protobuf handling. Added `tests/integration/test_prometheus_protocols/test_query_api_post_body.py` comparing GET and POST for instant and range queries. Using the [prometheus/compliance](https://github.com/prometheus/compliance) PromQL harness, the reported pass count rose from **4 / 539 (~0.7%)** to **205 / 539 (~38%)** in one full run—about **+37 percentage points** and **~51×** more passing queries versus that baseline, consistent with POST clients no longer sending an empty `query` from the server’s perspective. Fixes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/93191. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix Prometheus Query API ignoring POST form bodies <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.4.1.813` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Not a fix: "Not-ready Set" exception when buildOrderedSetInplace fails
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924 `FutureSetFromSubquery::buildOrderedSetInplace` (the speculative set build run during primary key analysis for `IN` subqueries) used to consume the subquery `source` plan up front. If the in-place build then failed silently (e.g. due to subquery timeout with `timeout_overflow_mode = 'break'`, where the executor stops without throwing and without setting `is_created`), the set remained permanently unbuilt and `FunctionIn` threw "Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument". The core fix — running the in-place pipeline against a clone of the source plan so that `DelayedCreatingSetsStep::makePlansForSets` can still build the set after a silent failure — has meanwhile been merged in #107924, which falls back to the original destructive build when the source plan contains a step that does not implement `IQueryPlanStep::clone`. After merging master, this PR carries the remaining hardening on top of #107924: - `clone` implementations for eleven more query-plan steps: `JoinStep`, `FillingStep`, `ExtractColumnsStep`, `FractionalLimitStep`, `FractionalOffsetStep`, `MergingAggregatedStep`, `NegativeLimitStep`, `NegativeLimitByStep`, `NegativeOffsetStep`, `StreamInQueryResultCacheStep`, `ReadFromQueryResultCacheStep`. `IN` subqueries whose plans contain these steps (e.g. `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL`, joins planned as `JoinStep`, subqueries going through the query result cache) previously took the destructive fallback, where a silent in-place failure still reproduces the "Not-ready Set" exception; with clone support they take the non-destructive path and recover. - `JoinStep::clone` covers only the join algorithms whose `IJoin` implementation supports cloning: `HashJoin`, `ConcurrentHashJoin`, `ConstantJoin` and `FullSortingMergeJoin`. `JoinSwitcher` (`join_algorithm = 'auto'`), `SpillingHashJoin`, `MergeJoin` / `PartialMergeJoin` and `GraceHashJoin` keep the pre-existing destructive fallback: `IJoin::isCloneSupported` also gates `optimizeJoin`, `convertOuterJoinToInnerJoin` and `QueryPipelineBuilder`, so widening it would silently enable join swapping and outer-to-inner conversion for never-validated stateful spilling algorithms. This limitation is documented at the throw site, and `04649_not_ready_set_with_non_clonable_join_algorithms` pins that those algorithms still produce correct results (the `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` stays internal). - `FilledJoinStep` (`StorageJoin` and dictionary joins) and `JoinStepLogicalLookup` (direct key-value joins) intentionally remain non-clonable as well: they wrap live storage-backed join state with no safe copy semantics (`IJoin::clone` constructs an empty join rather than copying the filled state). The constraint is documented at both classes. - Copying a `QueryResultCacheWriter` (which is what `StreamInQueryResultCacheStep::clone` does) now carries over both the original's `query_start_time` and its `skip_insert` decision. On the successful in-place build path the copy is the only writer that is ever finalized, so otherwise `query_cache_min_query_duration` would be measured from the clone point and an already cache-resident key would be buffered into a throwaway buffer instead of being skipped. Pinned by `04652_query_result_cache_subquery_clone_min_query_duration` and `04653_query_result_cache_subquery_clone_skip_insert`. - `QueryPlan::clone` now preserves `max_threads` and `concurrency_control`, so a pipeline built from a cloned plan runs under the same resource contract as the original instead of defaulting to `max_threads == 0` with concurrency control disabled. - The Planner no longer plants query result cache steps into a *logical* plan. A logical plan is not executed where it is built: it is serialized and shipped to another node (parallel replicas with `serialize_query_plan = 1`, see `createRemotePlanForParallelReplicas`), while `StreamInQueryResultCacheStep` and `ReadFromQueryResultCacheStep` hold node-local state (a `QueryResultCacheWriter`, or the cached chunks) that has no serialized representation. Before this, `query_cache_for_subqueries = 1` together with parallel replicas and `serialize_query_plan = 1` failed the whole query with `Method serialize is not implemented for StreamInQueryResultCache`. The cache is still populated and read by the plan the initiator executes itself. - Regression tests using the `prepared_sets_build_ordered_set_inplace_fail` failpoint: `04095_global_not_in_parallel_replicas` (the original parallel-replicas reproducer), `04492_not_ready_set_with_fill_subquery` (a `WITH FILL` subquery source plan), `04550_not_ready_set_with_join_subquery`, `04648_not_ready_set_with_query_result_cache_subquery` (both the cache write and the cache read path) and `04649_not_ready_set_with_non_clonable_join_algorithms`. The original failure was observed in the [Stress test (amd_tsan)](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=d0432097aed783bd35054dce2edcefe0c4e5122c&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29) on master, where `considerEnablingParallelReplicas` triggers `selectRangesToRead`, which calls `buildOrderedSetInplace` for primary key analysis. Note on the changelog category: the "Not-ready Set" exception is a `LOGICAL_ERROR`, so reproducing it on the unfixed build aborts the server on the sanitizer builds that the per-arch Bugfix validation jobs run on, and the validation harness deliberately treats a mid-run server death as inconclusive rather than as a reproduced bug. Automated bugfix validation is therefore structurally impossible for this fix, and the user-visible bug fix for the common plan shapes already shipped with #107924; the remaining hardening here is classified as an Improvement. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Extend the non-destructive speculative in-place set build for `IN` subqueries (introduced in [#107924](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107924)) to more query-plan shapes: `clone` is implemented for eleven more query-plan steps, including clone-supported joins via `JoinStep`, `ORDER BY ... WITH FILL` via `FillingStep`, and the query result cache steps. Such subqueries now preserve the original source plan and can recover from a silent in-place build failure instead of throwing "Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument". A cloned query plan now preserves `max_threads` and `concurrency_control` of the original plan. Also fixed `Method serialize is not implemented for StreamInQueryResultCache` when `query_cache_for_subqueries = 1` is used together with parallel replicas and `serialize_query_plan = 1`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=102192&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/102192](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F102192+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add tests for best-effort parsing of microsecond and nanosecond Unix timestamps
signals.text: Support for 16-digit (microsecond) and 19-digit (nanosecond) Unix timestamps in the best-effort parser landed in `master` with https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105233, so only test coverage is left here: microsecond and nanosecond cases in `01281_parseDateTime64BestEffort`, including reading them at a lower requested scale, and a new test pinning `toDateTime64` to the same result under `cast_string_to_date_time_mode = 'basic'` and `'best_effort'`.
