signals.title: Lazy materialization for reading local Parquet files (`file` / `File`)
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110970 Follow-up to the lazy materialization for object storage (#110970), as discussed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110970#issuecomment-5247858385: implement it for plain local Parquet files read through `StorageFile` — the `file` table function and the `File` table engine. For `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` queries, the columns that are not needed for sorting and filtering are read only for the `n` rows that survive the `LIMIT`. The format side (row-selective Parquet reads via `FormatFilterInfo::rows_to_read`) and the plan split (`JoinLazyColumnsStep`, `LazyMaterializingTransform`) from #110970 are reused as-is; this PR adds the `StorageFile` counterpart of the two branches: - The main pass appends a `__global_row_index` column (file index in a per-query `LazyFileRegistry` + physical row numbers from `ChunkInfoRowNumbers`) in `StorageFileSource::generate`. - The lazy branch (`LazilyReadFromFile` → `LazyReadFromFileSource` → `StorageFileLazyRowsSource`) reopens only the surviving files (at most `LIMIT n` of them) with a per-file set of rows to read and `parquet.preserve_order`. - The storage-agnostic column-split logic of `ReadFromObjectStorageStep::keepOnlyRequiredColumnsAndCreateLazyReadStep` (which columns can be deferred: `DEFAULT` expression dependencies, PREWHERE inputs, hive partition and virtual columns) is extracted into the shared `splitLazilyReadColumnsFromFormatInfo` and reused by both storages. **Generation safety.** POSIX has no conditional read, so the reread cannot be pinned the way `If-Match` pins it on S3. Instead the reread fails close with the new `FILE_CHANGED_DURING_READ` error when the file's generation token — sub-second mtime + inode + size, reusing `computeFileCacheVersionToken` from the query condition cache integration — no longer matches the one captured when the main pass opened the file. The token is validated at file registration time in the main pass, and both before and right after the reopen in the lazy pass. Replace-by-rename (the common atomic-update pattern) is always caught since it changes the inode; an in-place rewrite is caught up to the filesystem timestamp tick (and already tears a single-pass read today). **Gates** (`ReadFromFile::canUseLazyMaterialization`): Parquet format only, no file descriptor reads (stdin cannot be reopened), no archive entries, no `distributed_processing`, no `--rename_files_after_processing`, uncompressed files only. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization_for_file` (enabled by default), on top of `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization`. **Bug fix for #110970 shared via the helper:** deferring a requested subcolumn (e.g. of a `JSON` column) left the lazy branch's format header empty and the query failed with `Not found column or subcolumn ... in block`, because the format header contains the parent column of a requested subcolumn while the split filtered it by subcolumn names. The split now maps requested columns to their storage-level names — the parent of a deferred subcolumn moves to the lazy branch, and stays in the main branch as well when a sort key still needs another subcolumn of it. Covered for both storages by the new tests. On a 1 GB local Parquet file (2M rows × 105 columns equivalent shape: two 300-byte strings), `SELECT * ... ORDER BY k DESC LIMIT 5` runs 3× faster (0.15 s vs 0.45 s, page-cache warm), with results verified identical with the optimization on and off. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Lazy materialization for `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` queries (#110970) now also applies to local Parquet files read with the `file` table function and the `File` table engine: the columns that are not needed for sorting and filtering are read only for the `n` rows that survive the `LIMIT`. The second read of a surviving file fails close with the new `FILE_CHANGED_DURING_READ` error if the file was modified between the two passes. Controlled by the new setting `query_plan_optimize_lazy_materialization_for_file` (enabled by default). Also fixes lazy materialization for object storage failing with `Not found column or subcolumn ... in block` when a requested subcolumn (e.g. of a `JSON` column) is deferred. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114262&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114262](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114262+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix a Keeper server never joining the cluster when background snapshot IO is enabled
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/NuRaft/pull/123 ## Problem With `nuraft_use_bg_thread_for_snapshot_io` enabled, a Keeper server added to the cluster never joins. The leader's catch-up loop waits indefinitely for a response that cannot arrive, so the configuration change is never committed. The setting is off by default, which is why this has gone unnoticed. ## Root cause `sync_log_to_new_srv` builds one of two requests for the joining server — a snapshot request when the peer is below the retained log, or a log-pack `sync_log_request` otherwise — and then dispatches on the snapshot IO mode: ```cpp if (!params->use_bg_thread_for_snapshot_io_) { srv_to_join_->send_req(srv_to_join_, req, ex_resp_handler_); } else { snapshot_io_mgr::instance().invoke(); } ``` Only the *snapshot* branch hands its work to the IO thread. Nothing ever enqueues a log pack with `snapshot_io_mgr` — `create_sync_snapshot_req` is its only producer — so with background snapshot IO on, invoking the thread does not send the log-pack request. It is dropped. Observed on the unfixed build as the new server absent from the cluster configuration and stuck at log index 1 while the leader was at 12. ## Solution Dispatch on what was actually built rather than on the IO mode. The snapshot branch leaves the request null exactly when it has queued the work with the IO thread; in every other case — including the log-pack branch in *both* IO modes — there is a request and it must be sent. Covered by `log_sync_with_async_snapshot_io_test` in NuRaft's `learner_new_joiner_test`, verified to fail against the exact pre-patch code while the four existing tests in that binary keep passing. NuRaft pull request #123 is merged, and the submodule now points at NuRaft's merge commit `2fcee8a` rather than the branch, so the Keeper integration tests, `nightly_keeper` and Jepsen exercise the merged code here. Relative to `master`'s previous pin `dd3d098`, the only NuRaft change this brings in is that fix. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix a Keeper server never joining the cluster when `nuraft_use_bg_thread_for_snapshot_io` is enabled: the log batch sent to a joining server was silently dropped, so the membership change never completed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114275&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114275](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114275+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1659` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Fix inconsistent results with filter push-down over `ANY INNER JOIN`
signals.text: `ANY INNER JOIN` returns an arbitrary match per left row, so filtering the right table before the join can change which row is matched: a predicate that would have rejected the original match may accept the replacement, thus resulting in outputs inconsistent with evaluating the join and the filter in order, observable within one query as the added test shows. Block push-down of such predicates to the right side only. The left side is preserved and its rows are probed independently, so dropping some of them cannot change the match taken for the others. Predicates over the equi-join keys are still pushed to both sides, since every row of a match set shares the key value. 01655_plan_optimizations test changes only in the operand order of an equi-key push-down: those conjuncts now reach the right stream through the equivalent-columns path rather than the direct one. Fixes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/79189 ### Changelog category: - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry: Fix inconsistent results when a filter on a non-key column of the right table was pushed down below an ANY INNER JOIN. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114313&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114313](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114313+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1708` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Apply read in order with ORDER BY for plan-based parallel replicas
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114723 Plan-based parallel replicas (`parallel_replicas_plan_based`) splits the plan at the reading step into a `UNION` of a local read and a fragment shipped to the replicas. The split marker was lifted through `Expression`/`Filter`/`Aggregating`/`Union`/`Join`, but not through `SortingStep`, so for a plain `ORDER BY` the sort stayed on the initiator above the union and neither the local half nor the shipped fragment contained a `Sorting` above the read. `ReadFromMergeTree::requestReadingInOrder` was therefore never called on either side and both announced `CoordinationMode::Default`: results were correct, but the read-in-order optimization was lost compared to classic parallel replicas, which uses `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` for the same query. The split now lifts through `SortingStep` the same way it already does through `AggregatingStep`: a full sort is cloned into the fragment and the initiator keeps a `MergingSorted` sort above the union. Each side then re-derives read-in-order from the same sort description and they agree on `WithOrder` / `ReverseOrder` - `ReverseOrder` was not reachable under plan-based parallel replicas before. Since `SortingStep::serialize` drops the limit, a top-N is restated as an explicit `LimitStep` inside the fragment, as `tryMakeDistributedSorting` already does; it is skipped when an enclosing `LIMIT` has `alwaysReadTillEnd`, so `exact_rows_before_limit` stays exact. This also fixes a pre-existing failure on the same path: `tryOptimizeTopK` injects an internal `__topKFilter` function that is not registered in `FunctionFactory`. It was suppressed for `make_distributed_plan` but not for plan-based parallel replicas, so `SELECT ... ORDER BY <non-primary-key> LIMIT n` failed on the replica with `Unknown function __topKFilter`. A read that carries Top-K is now excluded from the shipped fragment (`mergeTreeReadCanBeShipped`), so such a query stays local and keeps its Top-K filtering instead of being distributed. Suppressing Top-K up front instead was rejected: enabling `parallel_replicas_plan_based` does not by itself mean the plan gets shipped, so that would silently lose Top-K for queries that end up running locally anyway. Verified locally against a three-replica cluster: `ReadType: InOrder` / `InReverseOrder` and `ReadPoolParallelReplicasInOrder` are reached, the coordinator logs `WithOrder` and `ReverseOrder`, and results stay identical to non-parallel execution for `ORDER BY` with `LIMIT`, deep `OFFSET`, filters, `WITH TIES`, `LIMIT BY`, `exact_rows_before_limit` and a full-sorting merge join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Apply the read-in-order optimization to `ORDER BY` queries when `parallel_replicas_plan_based` is enabled: the sort is now shipped to the replicas and merged on the initiator, so each replica reads in the sorting key order. Also fixes `Unknown function __topKFilter` for `ORDER BY` on a non-primary-key column with this setting enabled. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114315&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114315](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114315+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1688` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signals.title: Bound size_decompressed in the compressed frame header
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108096 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The uncompressed size in a compressed block header is now limited to 1 GiB, like the compressed size next to it. Previously a block could declare 4 GiB and the reader would reserve that much memory before decoding failed. Compressed write buffers keep both sizes within the limit, emitting several blocks where they previously emitted one larger one. ### Description **The problem.** A compressed block header holds two sizes: compressed and uncompressed. The reader checks the compressed one against a 1 GiB limit, does not check the uncompressed one at all, and then allocates that many bytes before decoding. A peer claiming 4 GiB makes the reader ask for 4 GiB. Impact is low, since the allocation is virtual and decoding fails right after, but the checksum is no substitute: it is an unkeyed hash over bytes the same peer sent. **Why one `if` is not enough.** ClickHouse can write blocks above 1 GiB today, because `max_compress_block_size` and `compressor --block-size` are unclamped, so a read-side check alone would make ClickHouse unable to read its own data. Writers need capping too. **The change.** 1. Writers cap their buffer so both header fields fit. The uncompressed size is the buffer fill level, so capping the buffer caps the field. The compressed size can be larger (`NONE` stores the body as-is, LZ4 expands incompressible input), so the cap also subtracts the codec's worst-case expansion. 2. The reader rejects an uncompressed size above 1 GiB while parsing the header, before allocating. Where the codec stores its body as-is, it also checks the body length matches. 3. Readers of data written before this cap opt out with one call. That accounts for 14 of the 23 files, mechanical except `CHECK TABLE`, which opts out per file class so it accepts whatever a read accepts. All 20 sites were traced to their writer. Two gaps remain, with the reader bound as the backstop: the cap cannot shrink a block when a codec's reported expansion overflows 32 bits, and `compressor -d` opts out. Test `04848_compressed_decompressed_size_bound` builds headers above and below the bound, and checks ClickHouse still reads what it writes. Related: #108096 (touches its initializer list), #113877 (mine, adjacent codec arithmetic).

signals.title: Do not treat an existing object as proof that a multipart upload completed
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114348 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113994 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed silent data loss when writing to a fixed S3 key that already holds an object, for example `INSERT INTO FUNCTION s3(...)` with `s3_truncate_on_insert = 1`. If the multipart upload was aborted between create and complete, for example by an `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle rule, `CompleteMultipartUpload` correctly returned `NoSuchUpload`, but the error was rewritten to success whenever any object existed at the key, so the INSERT was acknowledged while none of its rows were stored and the previous object kept being served. The error is now only absorbed when the object at the key is the one the upload would have produced. Closes #114348. ### Description Requested by @ zlareb1 in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114348#issuecomment-5255487765. `Client::CompleteMultipartUpload` absorbs `NoSuchUpload` if a `HeadObject` finds any object at the key. That check is from #56475, whose premise is a completion that succeeded and whose response was lost - i.e. the completion was replayed *and* the object is this upload's. Key existence tests neither, so a genuinely aborted upload against a key holding an unrelated object also passes, and the INSERT is acknowledged with none of its rows stored. `NO_SUCH_UPLOAD` is unretryable and excluded from `isTransientCompleteMultipartUploadError`, so this rewrite is the only thing between the abort and a silent success. MergeTree over S3 is unaffected: it writes random unique keys. The rewrite now requires the object to carry the ETag implied by the request's own part list, `md5(concat(binary md5 of each part))-<N>`. No extra request, no new state, and both callers (`WriteBufferFromS3`, `copyS3File`) are fixed at once. It fails closed: when the ETag does not match or is not derivable - SSE-KMS, a non-default checksum algorithm, S3 Express, a provider that computes it differently - the original error is returned, so a replay that used to be absorbed now errors. A failed INSERT is recoverable; a silently discarded one is not. A matching ETag proves the payload, not the create-time attributes: a completion may also carry `If-Match` / `If-None-Match`, and `CreateMultipartUpload` may carry metadata or a storage class, which this layer cannot observe. That residual is pre-existing, strictly less reachable here, and unset on the in-tree S3 multipart paths. #113994 addresses it in `WriteBufferFromS3`, which knows the writer identity. A new integration test fails on master (INSERT acknowledged, old object survives) and passes here, with a no-fault control. Two unit tests keep #56475 honest: a matching object is absorbed, a foreign one errors. cc @ scanhex12 @ kssenii @ CheSema <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114375&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114375](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114375+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add SHARED REGEXP path placement policy to JSON
signals.text: Adds `SHARED REGEXP 'pattern'` to `JSON` type declarations so matching root-relative flattened paths are always stored in shared data instead of competing for dedicated dynamic-path subcolumns. This is useful for high-cardinality path families whose promotion would displace more useful paths. Matching is partial by default, like `SKIP REGEXP`. Set the persisted `JSON` type parameter `shared_regexp_use_partial_match=0` to require full-string matching. Typed paths take precedence over `SHARED REGEXP`; `SKIP` and `SKIP REGEXP` continue to discard matching data. Rules are evaluated against the complete path from the original `JSON` root, including derived sub-objects. The rules are compiled once into an immutable `RE2` matcher, with bounded rule count and pattern sizes. A single rule uses direct `RE2` matching and multiple rules use `RE2::Set`. `JSON` columns without rules keep a null matcher, their existing binary type encoding, and their existing row-placement path. Metadata snapshots are copied lazily only when retained placement provenance actually changes a type. Placement provenance is stored in part column metadata and retained by default through horizontal and vertical merges, wide and compact mutations, column renames, lightweight-update patch materialization, and `Array`/`Nullable`/`Tuple`/`Map` wrappers. Removing a rule therefore does not unexpectedly promote already-shared paths during a later rewrite. Set the `MergeTree` table setting `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` to opt into reconsidering those paths. Policy-only metadata changes inside `Variant` are documented as unsupported. The `Native` binary type encoding uses `JSON` encoding version 1 only when a policy is present; ordinary `JSON` types remain byte-identical version 0. The canonical `JSON` documentation and `Native` format specification are updated accordingly. Testing includes 18 focused unit tests and 9 stateless scenarios covering syntax, partial/full matching, root-relative sub-objects, all supported wrappers, flattened `Native` and `RowBinary` paths, horizontal/vertical merges, compact/wide mutations, renames, statistics, and both lightweight-patch application paths. An 88.6 MB real Elasticsearch `indices_stats` document produced 143,555 flattened paths; all 143,290 paths targeted by `^indices[.]` remained in shared data and none became dynamic. A one-run end-to-end smoke comparison was 1.66 s without the policy and 1.69 s with it, with a 0.055% max-RSS difference; these small differences are noise-level, not a statistical benchmark. **Scope note:** `SKIP`/`SKIP REGEXP` already applied inconsistently between array-shaped and object-shaped occurrences of the same path on `master`, independent of `SHARED REGEXP` (a path skipped when the value at that path is an object could still surface when the value is an array of objects). This PR's fix for `SKIP REGEXP` on dynamically inferred nested objects closes one instance of that inconsistency; the underlying array-vs-object gap predates this PR and is not otherwise addressed here. **Scope note:** for a value dynamically inferred as its own nested `JSON` object (an inconsistent-shape array/object under a dynamic path), a policy-only `ALTER` followed by a plain read correctly picks up the new `SHARED REGEXP`/`SKIP REGEXP` rules for that nested object. A `allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion=1` merge or mutation that rewrites such a part afterward does not: it reconstructs the nested object's dynamic-path structure from cached per-column type state that a policy change doesn't refresh, so paths inside it can still be placed according to the rule in effect when the object was first materialized. This is opt-in (`allow_json_shared_data_paths_repromotion` defaults to off) and not fixed by this PR. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `SHARED REGEXP` rules to the `JSON` data type to keep matching paths in shared data, with configurable full-string matching and explicit control over re-promoting paths after rules are removed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114414&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114414](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114414+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Split the new-release-branch and patch release flows into separate jobs
signals.text: Follow-up to #113834 addressing https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113834#discussion_r3757704220: the single `release_job.py` entangled `create_new_release`, `is_branch_release`, and `release_type == "patch"` across one step sequence. The "new" (cut a release branch) and "patch" flows share almost nothing, so they are fully separated — into two job files **and** two dispatch workflows. - `ci/jobs/release_branch_job.py` + `ci/workflows/create_release_branch.py` (`CreateReleaseBranch`) — the "new" flow only: fetch history, configure git auth, prepare, push tag, push the new branch, open the master version-bump PR, merge. Its only inputs are `ref` and `dry-run`; it has no `release_type` branching, no `create_new_release`, no `only-repo`/`only-docker`, and no Docker/R2/GPG setup — so its credential cleanup only removes the env script. - `ci/jobs/release_job.py` + `ci/workflows/create_release.py` (`CreateRelease`) — the "patch" flow only. The `type` input is gone and every previous `release_type == "patch"` guard is now unconditional; `auto_releases.yml` no longer passes `type: patch` (it only ever released patches). `create_release.py` loses its argparse CLI: both orchestrators (and the tests) call its release actions as functions directly (`prepare_release_info`, `push_release_tag`, ..., `merge_prs`, `post_status`). The two job files drop argparse too — their parameters only ever arrive as workflow inputs, read via praktika `Info`. `update_contributors` uses `os.path.relpath` so the embedded "autogenerated by" path no longer requires the module to live under cwd. `create_release.yml` / `create_release_branch.yml` were regenerated via `praktika yaml`. Validated with workflow dry-runs: the new-branch flow is green end-to-end; the patch flow reaches the inherently non-hermetic package download (S3 404 for a synthetic version, same as before the refactor). Stacked on #113834 (based on its branch, not `master`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113834 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signals.title: Fix wrong results of the partial aggregation strategy in distributed query plans
signals.text: The partial+merge aggregation strategy of `make_distributed_plan` rewrites a final aggregation into a partial `AggregatingStep` plus a memory-efficient `MergingAggregatedStep`. The memory-efficient merge consumes each input as a stream of two-level buckets in ascending order, but the rewrite kept `should_produce_results_in_order_of_bucket_number = false` on the partial step, so its multi-stream output was combined into the single exchange stream in arbitrary order. When a bucket arrived after the merge had already emitted it, the merge emitted it a second time: duplicated `GROUP BY` keys with split aggregate states (for ClickBench Q08, a wrong `COUNT(DISTINCT UserID)`). The fix, one commit each: - Make the row count estimation look through `LogicalExchangeStep`. The `#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD` guard around it was needed when the exchange steps existed only in the private repo; since they are in the public repo, the guard only made every aggregation over a distributed read fall back to the Shuffle strategy in non-cloud builds (and masked this bug there). - Validate the bucket delivery order in `GroupingAggregatedTransform`: an unannounced late bucket now fails with a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception instead of silently duplicating groups. - Wait for delayed buckets in `GroupingAggregatedTransform` when the consumer needs the output in bucket order, and release the announcements of finished inputs. Covered by a gtest. - Build the partial step with `should_produce_results_in_order_of_bucket_number = true` when the merge is memory-efficient (`AggregatingStep::cloneAsPartial`). The partial aggregation then produces a single bucket-ordered stream per worker, the same contract the classic distributed path establishes on shards. Covered by a stateless test that reproduces the duplicated keys on the code without the fix (about 80% of single runs, 8 repetitions, 50k rows, ~0.5s). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix duplicated `GROUP BY` keys in the partial aggregation strategy of `make_distributed_plan`, and allow this strategy for aggregations over a distributed read. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114523&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114523](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114523+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Deduplicate the final DISTINCT in parallel
signals.text: The final `DISTINCT` merged all of its input streams into one and deduplicated them on a single thread, so `SELECT DISTINCT` did not scale with `max_threads` while the equivalent `GROUP BY` did - aggregation parallelizes its merge over two-level hash tables, `DISTINCT` had nothing of the sort. This repartitions the input streams by the hash of the `DISTINCT` columns instead of merging them: equal values then land in the same stream, so every stream can be deduplicated on its own, and what is left to merge is already deduplicated. The repartitioning uses `scatterByPartition`, which `SortingStep` and `ShuffleSendStep` already use. Whether the order of the step's output is free to change is only known where the sorting properties are, so the decision is taken in `applyOrder`. The new setting `allow_parallel_distinct`, enabled by default, controls it. It is not applied when: - the input is already globally sorted, because then `DISTINCT` keeps the order of its input and the repartitioning would break it; - there is a `LIMIT`, because the transform stops early anyway and the single stream keeps `LIMIT` returning the first values of the input rather than an arbitrary subset; - the streams are already disjoint - `allow_distinct_partitions_independently` covers that case and skips the merge entirely. `max_rows_in_distinct` and `max_bytes_in_distinct` keep their global meaning: the streams hold disjoint parts of one `DISTINCT` set, so the transforms add up the sizes of their sets in a shared counter and check the limits against the total. Enforcing them in the single final transform instead would have disabled the optimization for everyone who sets them - including all of CI, where the test profile sets both to `10G`. Every input chunk is split across all partitions, so the number of partitions is capped rather than following `max_threads`. On `SELECT DISTINCT number FROM numbers_mt(4e7)` the total CPU time the scatter adds grows by 8% at 4 partitions, 20% at 16 and 96% at 96; without the cap that turned into a wall-clock regression at high `max_threads`. Wall clock, minimum of 3 runs, aarch64: | workload | `max_threads` | before | after | speedup | |---|---|---|---|---| | 20M distinct `UInt64`, `MergeTree` | 4 | 0.442 s | 0.205 s | 2.16x | | | 16 | 0.458 s | 0.148 s | 3.09x | | | 96 | 0.502 s | 0.165 s | 3.04x | | 40M distinct `UInt64`, `numbers_mt` | 4 | 0.965 s | 0.545 s | 1.77x | | | 16 | 0.929 s | 0.360 s | 2.58x | | | 96 | 0.886 s | 0.299 s | 2.96x | | 8M distinct `String`, `numbers_mt` | 4 | 0.515 s | 0.288 s | 1.79x | | | 16 | 0.517 s | 0.093 s | 5.56x | | | 96 | 0.518 s | 0.083 s | 6.24x | The measurements were taken on a busy machine, hence the minimum of several runs; the existing `distinct_in_order`, `distinct_high_cardinality` and `sorted_distinct` performance tests cover these shapes, so the performance comparison job is the authoritative check. `DISTINCT` without `ORDER BY` has no defined row order, and the repartitioning changes the order it happens to produce. Two existing tests relied on it: `04109_sort_propagation_apply_order` asserts that per-stream sortedness reaches `DISTINCT`, so it pins the setting off, and `00585_union_all_subquery_aggregation_column_removal` gets the explicit `ORDER BY` it was missing. Other tests that depend on the incidental order of a `DISTINCT` may surface in CI and should be fixed the same way. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114532 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/48988 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Evaluate the final `DISTINCT` on several threads by repartitioning its input by the hash of the `DISTINCT` columns, instead of merging everything into a single stream and deduplicating it on one thread. Up to 6x faster on high-cardinality `DISTINCT`. Controlled by the new setting `allow_parallel_distinct`, enabled by default. Note that this changes the order in which a `DISTINCT` without `ORDER BY` returns rows, which was never defined. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114550&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114550](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114550+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix stale MATERIALIZED column values read through a chain while a mutation is pending
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/100613 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/50237 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99281 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103182 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115371 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115372 **Scope changed.** The staging half of this pull request — recomputing a chain of `MATERIALIZED` columns one dependency level at a time during a mutation — landed on master in the meantime via #103182, which also generalizes it to `APPLY PATCHES`, so all of it was dropped here. What remains is the read path, which master still gets wrong: the read set is closed in `AlterConversions`, and `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` keeps a single line of change, resolving `MATERIALIZED` defaults against the whole table instead of the read task's columns. The two defects that belong to the staging path are split out into #115371 and #115372. ## Problem With a mutation still pending, reading a `MATERIALIZED` column that reaches the updated column only through another `MATERIALIZED` column returns the stale on-disk value, while reading the whole chain returns the recomputed one: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x Int32, y Int32, m1 Int32 MATERIALIZED x + 1, m2 Int32 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1, m3 Int32 MATERIALIZED m2 + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO t (x, y) VALUES (10, 0); SYSTEM STOP MERGES t; SET alter_sync = 0, mutations_sync = 0, apply_mutations_on_fly = 1; ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 20 WHERE 1; -- stays pending ``` ``` SELECT m2 FROM t; -- 12 (stale; must be 22) SELECT m3 FROM t; -- 13 (stale; must be 23) SELECT x, m1, m2, m3 FROM t; -- 20 21 22 23 (correct) ``` - The result of a query depends on which columns it selects, so the same value read two ways disagrees. - The same happens for a `MATERIALIZED` column defined over a subcolumn (`m1 MATERIALIZED t.a + 1` with a pending `UPDATE t = ...`): `SELECT m1` returns the stale value unless the query happens to select `t` as well. - Selecting a `MATERIALIZED` column together with a column the mutation updates fails outright with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` whenever the first one's dependencies are not in the select list, even when that column has nothing to do with the mutation. - Once the mutation finishes, the values are correct — only the pending window is affected. ## Root cause Reading with `apply_mutations_on_fly` builds the pending commands into the read pipeline. `AlterConversions::addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized` decides which extra columns must be read so that the `MATERIALIZED` columns being selected can be recomputed, and it only looked one hop deep: ```cpp for (const auto & column_name : read_columns_set) if (default is MATERIALIZED) for (const auto & dependency : TreeRewriter(context).analyze(expression, source_columns)->requiredSourceColumns()) if (all_updated_columns.contains(dependency)) required_source_columns.insert(dependency); ``` For `m2 MATERIALIZED m1 + 1` the only dependency is `m1`, which is not in `all_updated_columns`, so nothing is added, `filterMutationCommands` drops the `UPDATE x` command as irrelevant to the read set, and `m2` is returned from disk. Two further details of the same analysis: - the default expression is not normalized with `replaceSubcolumnsToGetSubcolumnFunctionInQuery`, so `m MATERIALIZED t.a` is seen to depend on `t.a` rather than on `t`, and a pending `UPDATE t` is filtered out (or the analysis fails with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` when the subcolumn does not resolve against `source_columns`); - a `MATERIALIZED` column whose expression reads an `EPHEMERAL` column can never be recomputed outside `INSERT`, so analysing it against physical columns must be avoided rather than attempted. ## Solution Two sites, because the read set has two consumers that must agree. ### `AlterConversions::addColumnsRequiredForMaterialized` — close the read set 1. **Transitive closure.** A breadth-first walk seeded with the read columns replaces the single pass, so the `MATERIALIZED` columns in between are read too and the interpreter recomputes the whole chain instead of `filterMutationCommands` dropping the `UPDATE` as irrelevant. 2. **Only a column that is recalculated pulls in dependencies, and it pulls in all of them.** The walk asks of the column it visits whether the interpreter recalculates it, and if so takes its whole expression, because the stage that rewrites it evaluates that expression against the block — including the part reading a column no mutation touches (`c MATERIALIZED m1 + y`, where `y` is untouched). A column that keeps its stored value contributes nothing, so an unrelated chain is neither read nor keeps a command the query does not need alive. 3. **Subcolumn rewrite.** Dependencies are analysed after `replaceSubcolumnsToGetSubcolumnFunctionInQuery`, matching what `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` does before analysing the same expression. Without it `m MATERIALIZED t.a + 1` is seen to depend on `t.a` while `all_updated_columns` holds `t`; the names do not match and a pending `UPDATE t` is filtered out. This is a one-hop defect, independent of the chain. 4. **`EPHEMERAL` columns added to the analysis source list.** `getAllPhysical` excludes them, so analysing `me MATERIALIZED x + e` threw `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` inside this function. Measured on master, `SELECT me` with any pending `UPDATE` fails this way. Also a one-hop defect, and analysing every hop of a chain would have multiplied its reach. 5. **`can_recalculate` mirrors the interpreter's policy.** `MutationsInterpreter` never recomputes a `MATERIALIZED` column that reads an `EPHEMERAL` one, so such a column is not treated as recalculable here either. The read set must not promise a recomputation the interpreter refuses. 6. **Memoised lookups.** `getMutationSteps` runs per read task per part, so each default expression is analysed at most once per call and each reachability question answered at most once. ### `MutationsInterpreter::prepare` — resolve defaults against the whole table `available_columns` was serving two different roles: which `MATERIALIZED` columns need recalculating, and which columns their expressions may be resolved against. For a plain `UPDATE` the two coincide. A table carrying a `MATERIALIZED` column the mutation does not affect breaks the coincidence — its dependencies are legitimately outside the read set — and the analysis failed with `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, taking the query with it: ```sql CREATE TABLE t (x Int32, y Int32, m Int32 MATERIALIZED x + 1, n Int32 MATERIALIZED y + 1) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); ALTER TABLE t UPDATE x = 20 WHERE 1; -- stays pending SELECT m, n FROM t; -- Missing columns: 'y' while processing: 'y + 1' SELECT x, n FROM t; -- the same, and this one fails on master too ``` Deciding whether a column has to be recalculated must not require reading what it reads, so the default expressions are now resolved against every column of the table. For a materialising mutation this changes nothing, since `available_columns` already covers the part; only an on-fly read has a narrow list. ### Coverage Regression test `04869_materialized_chain_on_fly_read` covers six cases, each measured individually against master `5bd006cd298`: - the plain chain read tail-only — returns the stale value; - the chain read next to the updated column, without the intermediate hop — throws `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`, because the surviving command makes the interpreter analyse a default whose dependency is not in the read set; - one command assigning two columns, with the query reading the other assignment target — throws for the same reason, after the command is narrowed and loses the assignment the chain depends on; - a pending `DELETE` that keeps a command alive while the set of updated columns stays empty — returns the stale value, since the analysis is skipped entirely; - columns the mutation does not affect, read on their own and next to the updated column, and a recalculated column reading an untouched one — stale value or `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` depending on the select list; - the subcolumn default and the `EPHEMERAL`-derived column — stale value and `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` respectively. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed reading a table while a mutation is in progress: a `MATERIALIZED` column could return a stale value, and selecting one together with an updated column could fail with an error. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114561&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114561](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114561+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Mongo queries: keep whole documents in a JSON column
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58394 Adds two ways to run MongoDB queries against ClickHouse: - a **wire protocol endpoint** (`mongo_port`), so MongoDB drivers and tools such as `pymongo` and `mongosh` can connect to ClickHouse as if it were a MongoDB server; - a **query dialect** (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`), so MongoDB shell syntax can be sent over the usual ClickHouse interfaces. This continues @scanhex12's https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493 - it holds all of its commits - and changes how a collection is stored, which is what the review of that pull request asked for (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/68493#discussion_r3771132310): a collection the endpoint creates keeps whole documents in one `JSON` column rather than a column inferred per field of the first document. ```sql CREATE TABLE db.users (`_id` String, `json` JSON) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY `_id` ``` The document goes into the `JSON` column, whose paths are its fields, and its object id into the `_id` column, which is the primary key. A document may then hold a field that no document before it had, may leave out a field another one has, and `$exists` answers what it means. A table that was created in ClickHouse keeps its own columns, and a field of a query names the column of the same name there, so an application can also be pointed at a table that already holds the data. A read of the documents as they are stored selects them next to the types of their paths, so a date reads back as a BSON date and an integer as an `int32`/`int64` of its width. The integration tests of `test_mongo_protocol` say what each shape answers now - a collection of documents where that is what is tested, a table created in ClickHouse where the test is about a column - and 75/75 of them pass. **This is a draft** because a few things of a document collection are an explicit error rather than an answer: an `update` of it, an index over a path, the `mongo` dialect over it, the element-wise match of an array by equality or `$in`, `$unwind` of a path, and the accumulators that read a number. They are the next commits; every one of them is listed in `docs/en/interfaces/mongo.md` and pinned by a test in the meantime. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a MongoDB-compatible wire protocol endpoint (the `mongo_port` server setting) and a MongoDB query dialect (`SET dialect = 'mongo'`) for basic collection operations. A collection the endpoint creates keeps whole documents in a `JSON` column. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114577&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114577](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114577+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: diff-review skill second edition
signals.text: Reworks the `diff-review` skill in `.claude/skills/diff-review` — the local in-browser diff review that Claude Code serves before a commit or a PR. Heads-up: I tailored this to how *I* like to review, so please treat it as a suggestion rather than a standard. Check the branch out, run it on one of your own diffs, and keep it only if you find it helpful. What changed: - **Multi-round review.** Sending a round no longer ends the review: the server stays up, the agent works on the comments it was handed while you keep reading, and each comment turns green in the page as it gets addressed. - **Comments are durable state.** They are written to the `--out` file as you type, so they survive a server restart or a page reload, and after the agent's fixes move the code they are relocated by their anchor line instead of pointing at the wrong place. Resolutions, replies and dismissals are part of that state. - **Explicit review range.** `--staged`, `--head <sha>` and `--committed` alongside `--base`, so a review of recorded work never picks up local edits; the header always states which range is on screen. - **Navigation.** Directory tree with per-file status, `+a −d` counts and open-comment badges, a path filter, an all-files page, whole-file mode with expandable folded regions, a Comments pane listing open and already-addressed comments, draggable sidebar and split, keyboard shortcuts with a `?` overlay, and light / dark / system themes. - **Tests.** `ui.html` is split into ES modules under `ui/`, covered by `ui_test.mjs`, and `persist_test.mjs` exercises the whole persistence round-trip against real servers on a throwaway repository. - Vendored `@pierre/diffs` bumped from 1.2.12 to 1.3.5. Local agent tooling only — nothing in the server, the build or the tests. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114615&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114615](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114615+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix DPsub join reordering silently dropping single-table ON-clause filters
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111898 The `dpsub` join-order algorithm silently dropped single-table filter and constant predicates that live in a `JOIN ... ON` clause (e.g. `t1.value = 'x'`), returning extra rows. `greedy` uses a different placement path and was unaffected. The predicates are placed in `collectJoinEdgesMask`. Two placement conditions there each silently dropped such a predicate: - `two_relations` required the whole join step to be exactly two relations, so the predicate was dropped whenever its relation was introduced against an already-multi-relation subplan (e.g. `t1` at the top of `t1 JOIN (t2 JOIN t3)`). - `fromLeft() || fromRight() || fromNone()` dropped the predicate for any single-table filter on a relation whose id is >= 2, because `fromLeft`/`fromRight` test relation ids 0 and 1 specifically (they describe the two inputs of a binary join step, not "references a single relation"). The predicate is now attached at the join that introduces its relation (the split whose one side is exactly that relation), and pure constants at the earliest two-relation join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `dpsub` join-order optimization (`query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm = 'dpsub'`) silently dropping single-table filter conditions from a `JOIN ... ON` clause, which could return extra rows. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114629&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114629](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114629+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Revert "Revert "NATS: add inline credentials setting""
signals.text: Reverts https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178, restoring the `nats_credentials` setting of the `NATS` table engine (originally added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733), and fixes the reason of the original revert: the possibility of referencing arbitrary server paths through `nats_credential_file`. `nats_credential_file` is a path on the server filesystem: the server opens it with its own privileges, and during authentication the credentials are sent to `nats_url`, which comes from the same query. So a path taken from SQL lets anyone who can define a `NATS` source probe the local filesystem (the error text distinguishes a missing file, a permission error, and a file without a seed), and exfiltrate files the server can read to a NATS server they control (the part of the file before the seed line is sent verbatim in the `CONNECT` frame's `jwt` field). See the analysis in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733#discussion_r3750203599. This hole predates #110733 (`nats_credential_file` exists since 24.2), but with the inline `nats_credentials` setting restored, the path form is no longer needed in SQL at all. The restriction, modelled on `StorageMySQL::getSSLParams` (`e700bbec4c84c585`): `nats_credential_file` is accepted only from a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. Every SQL spelling — the `SETTINGS` clause, an engine-argument override `NATS(collection, nats_credential_file = ...)`, or a named collection created by `CREATE NAMED COLLECTION` — throws `BAD_ARGUMENTS` with a message directing to `nats_credentials`. It is rejected on provenance, whether the query assigned the key at all, rather than on the resulting value, so an override with the empty string cannot silently drop the credentials the operator configured. Loading from previously-validated metadata (server startup, force-restore, and short-syntax `ATTACH`) is exempt via `isLoadingFromExistingMetadata`, so existing tables keep working after an upgrade; a user-issued full `ATTACH TABLE` query is still checked. `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY SETTING` is not a bypass: the `NATS` engine does not support settings alter. Replacing a configured path with inline `nats_credentials` from the query remains allowed — the path itself is not used then — as long as the named collection permits it. Because the contents are the only spelling a query has, `nats_credentials` inherits the override permission of the path key it replaces, the same way `ssl_ca_pem` does for `ssl_ca` in `findOverrideForbiddingKey`: credentials the operator pinned with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">` cannot be replaced through the contents form either, in either spelling, while the contents form stays usable when `allow_named_collection_override_by_default` is disabled (it is not a new key, it replaces one the collection defines). The `SETTINGS` clause is applied on top of the collection values without passing through the named-collection override check, so `resolveCredentialSource` enforces the same permission for both spellings. An empty `nats_credentials` is refused as well: it can only drop the credentials a collection carries, in either form, never replace them with other ones. Tests: a new stateless test `04891_nats_credential_file_path_restriction` covers all rejected SQL spellings and the accepted configuration-file sources, using `NATS` named collections added to the stateless-test server configuration (`tests/config/config.d/named_collection.xml`, with `nats_url = '127.0.0.1:1'`, so passing the validation surfaces as `CANNOT_CONNECT_NATS`) — one with a plain `nats_credential_file`, one where it is locked with `overridable="false"`, and one without credentials at all; `04665_nats_credentials_named_collection` is updated — the `nats_credential_file` query-override direction is now rejected. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110733 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114178 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/85213 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Backward Incompatible Change ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `NATS` table engine accepts credentials inline in the new `nats_credentials` setting (the same payload as a `.creds` file), and no longer accepts `nats_credential_file` from SQL: the path is a reference to a file on the server filesystem, which the server opens with its own privileges, so it can only be specified in a named collection defined in the server configuration file, or as `nats.credential_file` in the server configuration itself. A query may replace such a configured path with inline `nats_credentials`, unless the operator pinned it with `<nats_credential_file overridable="false">`. Tables created before this restriction keep working after an upgrade. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114644&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114644](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114644+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Speed up `IN (subquery)` set building by pre-deduplicating each `MergeTree` partition independently
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108326 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105126 The set for `IN (subquery)` is built by a single `CreatingSetsTransform`: all streams of the subquery are merged into one and every row is hashed serially, no matter how many threads read the data. If the partition expression of the subquery's table is a function of the subquery's output columns (the set is keyed on all of them), the reading will now emit each partition through a single port and each stream is deduplicated independently before the filling transform. Because a key then lives in exactly one stream, per-stream deduplication is complete, and the single filling transform only hashes unique rows — the serial part of the build shrinks from all rows to distinct rows, and the deduplication itself runs in parallel. ```sql CREATE TABLE t (a UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple() PARTITION BY a % 8; INSERT INTO t SELECT number % 1000000 FROM numbers(100000000); OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL; EXPLAIN PIPELINE SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t) SETTINGS allow_creating_set_partitions_independently = 1, max_threads = 8; ``` ```response (CreatingSets) DelayedPorts 9 → 8 (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (Aggregating) Resize 1 → 8 AggregatingTransform (Expression) ExpressionTransform (Filter) FilterTransform (ReadFromSystemNumbers) NumbersRange 0 → 1 (CreatingSet) CreatingSetsTransform <- the single filling transform now hashes ~1M unique rows instead of 100M Resize 8 → 1 DistinctTransform × 8 <- new: parallel pre-deduplication on partition-disjoint streams (Expression) ExpressionTransform × 8 (ReadFromMergeTree) MergeTreeSelect(pool: ReadPoolInOrder, algorithm: InOrder) × 8 0 → 1 <- per-partition reading (8 partitions → 8 streams) ``` On the table above (100M rows, 1M distinct keys, 8 balanced partitions; 64-core machine, average of 3 runs after 2 warm-ups): | query | off | on | speedup | |------------------------------------------------------------|--------|--------|---------| | `SELECT count() FROM numbers(10) WHERE number IN (SELECT a FROM t)` | 0.643s | 0.113s | 5.7× | ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up set building for `IN (subquery)` on partitioned `MergeTree` tables by keeping each partition's rows within a single stream and deduplicating each stream independently, so the single set-filling transform — previously hashing every row serially — only sees unique rows. This applies when the partition expression is a deterministic function of the subquery's output columns. The optimization is not applied when the largest partition holds more than twice the rows of the average partition; the new setting `force_creating_set_partitions_independently` (disabled by default) bypasses this check. Controlled by the new setting `allow_creating_set_partitions_independently` (enabled by default). --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114645&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114645](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114645+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)]

signals.title: Record TopK-filtered granules in the query condition cache
signals.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Granules fully filtered by the dynamic threshold of an `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (TopK) read are now recorded in the query condition cache, so repeat runs of such queries skip them at the mark-selection stage instead of re-reading and re-filtering most of the table. On the ClickBench Q24/Q26 shapes (`SELECT SearchPhrase FROM hits WHERE SearchPhrase <> '' ORDER BY EventTime LIMIT 10`), a warm run drops from ~95M rows / ~12000 granules read to ~1.3M rows / ~160 granules, and from ~15–30 ms to ~8 ms on a 96-core machine. The `ORDER BY ... LIMIT n` (TopK) optimization pushes a dynamic `__topKFilter` threshold into the `MergeTree` read as a PREWHERE, dropping rows that cannot beat the running top-N. But the granules it emptied were never recorded in the query condition cache: the PREWHERE write path in `MergeTreeSelectProcessor::read` rejects non-deterministic conditions, and `__topKFilter` is one. Only the downstream WHERE `FilterTransform` wrote entries, at whole-chunk granularity, which learns almost nothing (a single surviving row voids the attribution of the whole chunk) — measured on hits, warm runs still selected 11766 of 12348 granules and re-read ~95M of 100M rows. The original out-of-tree build of this optimization (PR #81944, commit `2e2f594308f4` plus the follow-up making the TopN dynamic filters deterministic and reusable for the cache) recorded them and skipped ~98% of granules on warm runs — that is the 2–3x Q24/Q26 gap measured in issue #114639. Recording these granules is sound: for a fixed plan and data, the running threshold only tightens, so a granule none of whose rows survive the filter contains no row that could reach the final top-N, regardless of the threshold trajectory. The entries are keyed with the TopK plan salt (`TopKFilterInfo::condition_hash`: sort column, type, `LIMIT`, direction, `NULLS` direction, collation locale, number of sort columns, and the part-set snapshot), mirroring what the WHERE write path already does since #104478/#110507 — only the same TopK plan over the same part set ever reuses them. Changes: - `isDeterministicAllowingTopKFilter` (two identical static copies in `updateQueryConditionCache.cpp` and `ReadFromMergeTree.cpp`) moved into `VirtualColumnUtils`. - The TopK salt is plumbed to the reader via `MergeTreeReaderSettings::query_condition_cache_top_k_salt`. - The PREWHERE write path accepts a `__topKFilter`-bearing condition when the salt is present, folding the salt into the cache key. Any other non-deterministic condition is still never cached. - The PREWHERE consult path (`filterPartsByQueryConditionCache`) applies the salt exactly when the PREWHERE contains `__topKFilter`, so the keys match the write side; deterministic user PREWHERE conditions keep using plain, unsalted entries shared with non-TopK queries. - `04217_query_condition_cache_topk` and `04242_query_condition_cache_topk_collate` pin exact cache entry counts, which double (each TopK plan now writes a WHERE entry and a PREWHERE entry per part). - New test `04891_query_condition_cache_topk_prewhere_granules` isolates the PREWHERE write path with a WHERE-less TopK query (on current master such a query writes no cache entries at all), asserts that the ASC and DESC plans do not share granule decisions, and that a warm run selects fewer marks. - New performance test `topk_query_condition_cache.xml` with the ClickBench Q24/Q26 shapes over `hits_100m_single`. Measured on the 100M-row single-part ClickBench `hits` (96-core aarch64, hot, interleaved runs): warm Q24/Q26 at 0.007–0.009 s, on par with the original bench-opt build (0.009–0.011 s), against 0.015–0.03 s for current master; warm runs read 159 of 12348 granules against master's 11766. A first run with an empty cache shows no measurable overhead (0.016–0.019 s with the mechanism on and off). Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114639 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110507 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114659&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114659](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114659+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not hold the DDL guard during TRUNCATE
signals.text: `TRUNCATE TABLE` held the table's DDL guard while removing data, and truncate can wait for running merges or for other replicas to process `DROP_RANGE`. Any DDL on that name — including background threads that need it — was blocked for that whole time. Release the guard before `IStorage::truncate` for databases with UUIDs, matching `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`, which never took it. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TRUNCATE TABLE` no longer blocks concurrent `DROP`, `RENAME` and other DDL queries on the same table while the data is being removed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114672&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114672](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114672+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114679&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114679](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114679+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support aggregate functions in the trivial GROUP BY LIMIT optimization
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114637 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (`optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`, default `true`) now also fires for projections **with aggregate functions**, e.g. ClickBench Q17 (`SELECT UserID, SearchPhrase, COUNT(*) FROM hits GROUP BY UserID, SearchPhrase LIMIT 10`), while keeping the aggregate values of the returned keys **exact**. **Why it was restricted.** The settings-based rewrite (`max_rows_to_group_by = n + offset` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`) enforces the cutoff per aggregation stream: a key kept by one stream and rejected by another loses the other stream's rows and comes out of the merge with an undercounted value. Returning an unspecified subset of the groups is fine for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`; returning wrong values is not. **How it works now (shared kept keys, zero hot-path cost).** The streams aggregate completely normally until the first one exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys (the pre-existing per-block `checkLimits`). That stream publishes a frozen seed of exactly `n + offset` kept keys with empty aggregate states (`ManyAggregatedData::SharedKeptKeys`); every stream then rebuilds its hash table to exactly that key set — keeping the states it accumulated for the kept keys, dropping the rest — and continues on the pre-existing `no_more_keys` path against a table of `n + offset` keys. Streams that finished consuming before the freeze are rebuilt by the last stream before the merge. Every row before the freeze is aggregated normally and every later row of a kept key finds its key in the rebuilt table, so the merged values are exact; the dropped keys are absent from every rebuilt table and never reach the result. The rebuild reuses the existing two-stage machinery (`convertToChunks(final = false)` + `mergeOnBlock`), so the hot aggregation loops in `Aggregator.cpp` are untouched. **Where it fires.** The cutoff is detected in the planner and enabled only when the node performs the complete aggregation itself (first and second stage): partial states sent to a remote initiator would be merged with other nodes' states, whose kept keys differ, and the values would be undercounted again — across nodes instead of across threads. On the shards of distributed queries and on the replicas of parallel-replicas reading it stays off. The settings-based rewrite of `OptimizeTrivialGroupByLimitPass` remains for aggregate-free projections (it is sound cross-shard). For the 8/16-bit key methods (fixed hash maps bounded by the key space) the cutoff stays inert and the aggregation is complete and exact. External aggregation is disabled when the cutoff is armed (spilled buckets would bypass the restriction); memory stays bounded by roughly `n + offset` keys plus one block of keys per stream. **Guards for wrong results of the existing optimization.** The shape check (shared between the pass and the planner, `getTrivialGroupByLimit`) now also rejects `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions and `arrayJoin` in the projection. These consume or filter the groups after the aggregation, and all four cases were verified to return wrong results on master with the default settings (e.g. `SELECT DISTINCT intDiv(k, 25000) FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 3` returned 1 row instead of 3; `SELECT count() OVER () FROM t GROUP BY k LIMIT 5` returned ~100 instead of 100000). Test `04837` pins all four in both the top-level (pass) and subquery (planner) forms. The guards are also submitted separately as the minimal backportable bug fix https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114695 (issue https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114693); whichever merges second needs a trivial conflict resolution. **Measured** on a 96-core aarch64 box, `SELECT number % 100000000 AS k, count() FROM numbers_mt(200000000) GROUP BY k LIMIT 10`: 0.06–0.13 s with the optimization vs 0.37–0.94 s without (interleaved hot runs on a shared machine). The values of the returned keys match the full aggregation exactly (verified by the `04836` join-against-truth tests for `UInt64`/`String`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable`/two-key shapes, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`max`/`uniqExact`, with `OFFSET`, under single-stream and 16-stream execution, from aggregate projections, and over `remote()`). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The trivial `GROUP BY ... LIMIT n` optimization (setting `optimize_trivial_group_by_limit_query`) now also applies to queries with aggregate functions in the projection, such as ClickBench Q17: once any aggregation thread exceeds `n + offset` distinct keys, all threads are restricted to a single shared set of kept keys, so the hash tables stay small while the aggregate values of the returned keys remain exact (about 2x on ClickBench Q17). Additionally, the optimization no longer fires for queries with `DISTINCT`, `QUALIFY`, window functions, or `arrayJoin` in the projection, where it could return wrong results. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114690&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114690](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114690+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: CI: run the full test suite only when review threads are resolved
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114724 This change limits the PR CI pipeline to builds and preliminary checks while review threads are unresolved, and records the gate in `Review Threads` and `Mergeable Check` statuses. The gate re-evaluates at workflow completion and after changes to the `ignore-unresolved-threads` label. GitHub Actions has no supported review-thread event, so thread changes after a completed workflow require a manual CI re-run; the documentation states that limitation. A failed pre-hook marker write leaves filtering disabled, so the full suite runs. The final review-thread marker preserves whether a limited pipeline needs replay even when another post-hook fails.
