signals.title: Aggregation pushdown below JOIN in the Cascades optimizer
signals.text: ## Motivation Queries like `SELECT count() FROM t1 LEFT JOIN t2 ON t1.key = t2.key GROUP BY t1.key` aggregate after the join, although most of the aggregation work can be done on one join input before the join. When the pushed side has few distinct group keys, aggregating first shrinks the join input dramatically. This is the classic *eager aggregation* transformation (Yan & Larson, VLDB 1995). It is not always a win — with nearly-unique group keys the extra aggregation is pure overhead — so it is implemented as a cost-based alternative in the Cascades optimizer: the memo keeps both plans and the cost model picks. ## What is implemented A new transformation rule `AggregationPushdown` with two variants: - **Partial pushdown**: a partial aggregation (`final = false`) below one join input, and a `MergingAggregated` step above the join. The pushed side's group keys are extended with every column of that side referenced by the join condition and residual filter, which makes all rows within a partial group indistinguishable to the join — the join then filters or duplicates whole groups uniformly, and merging `m` duplicated copies of a state equals processing the underlying rows `m` times. This is semantically exact, including for `ALL` joins with fan-out, and requires no uniqueness knowledge. - **Full pushdown**: when every `GROUP BY` key belongs to the pushed side, the join-condition columns are a subset of the `GROUP BY` keys, and the strictness rules out duplication (`ANY`/`SEMI`/`ANTI` with the join kind matching the pushed side), the aggregation stays final below the join and no merge is needed. When legal, it strictly dominates the partial variant and is emitted instead of it. The legality matrix was derived from the hash-join implementation and independently re-verified during review. Notably, `ANY INNER JOIN` is excluded from the matrix entirely: it emits at most one row per join *key* (`setUsedOnce`), not per probe row, so pushing aggregation below it would change results. The correctness test contains a tripwire scenario against future wrong enablement. Safety rules encoded in the rule (each bails out and leaves the classic plan): the pushed side must never be null/default-extended by the join (an unmatched preserved row would otherwise carry an empty aggregate state and silently contribute nothing); global aggregation (`GROUP BY ()`) is excluded (an empty join output must still produce one row); all aggregate arguments must resolve to the pushed side; `join_use_nulls`/`USING` type-changing joins, grouping sets, `overflow_row`, `max_rows_to_group_by`, in-order aggregation, and name collisions between the two sides are all rejected. Supporting changes: - `MergingAggregatedStep` gets an opt-in `allowInputWithoutAggregatedChunkInfo` mode (join output chunks carry no `AggregatedChunkInfo`, and special column representations must be materialized before merging). The `only_merge` aggregator consumes keys and states positionally, so the rebuilt join projects keys first, then state columns. - **Wire format**: the new mode is serialized as flag bit 64 of `MergingAggregatedStep`, gated behind query plan serialization version 9 (bumped from 8). On a mixed-version cluster the plan fails at plan time with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` (naming `SET cascades_aggregation_pushdown = 0` as the escape hatch) instead of a remote runtime error. Note that the version bump also excludes version-8 replicas from parallel-replicas distributed plans, per the documented design of `DBMS_QUERY_PLAN_SERIALIZATION_VERSION`. - `AggregatingStep::rebaseOntoInput` re-bases an aggregation onto a new input with a different key set; new memo helpers build the three-level (partial) and two-level (full) alternatives. The rule is gated by the new `EXPERIMENTAL` setting `cascades_aggregation_pushdown` (default on) and takes effect only together with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` and `make_distributed_plan = 1`. ## Testing - `04926_cascades_aggregation_pushdown`: EXPLAIN plan shapes for both variants and both sides, stat-hint steering in both directions, guard negatives (`FULL`, `ASOF`, `INNER ANY`, `join_use_nulls`, grouping sets, global aggregation, mixed-side aggregate arguments), executed queries with hand-verified values (including fan-out multiplicity and mixed equi+residual conditions), and a 3-join task-budget sanity check. - `04927_cascades_aggregation_pushdown_correctness`: 22+ scenarios, each executed with the optimizer on and off with identical results (fan-out duplication, unmatched rows, multi-key and expression join keys, residual conditions, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`avg`/`uniqExact`/`countIf`, keys from both sides, `SEMI`/`ANTI`/`ANY`, keys-only `GROUP BY`, empty inputs, full-pushdown cases), plus plan-shape canaries proving the pushed plans actually fire for the test's tables. - The full `*cascades*` and `*merging_aggregated*` stateless test sets pass locally on a test-config server. One pre-existing test (`04330_cascades_activation_gating`) pins the new setting off in one case whose own assertion (about subplan broadcasting) would otherwise be made vacuous by the new, cheaper plan. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added aggregation pushdown below `JOIN` (eager aggregation) to the experimental Cascades optimizer as a cost-based alternative: a partial aggregation is performed on one join input before the join and merged above it, or, when the join provably neither duplicates nor null-extends the aggregated side and the join keys are a subset of the `GROUP BY` keys, the aggregation is pushed below the join entirely. Controlled by the new setting `cascades_aggregation_pushdown` (enabled by default; takes effect only with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` and `make_distributed_plan = 1`). --- 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115354&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115354](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115354+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: The `_database` and `_table` virtual columns of a `Merge` table carry the matched child's name again
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113735 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/84139 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/63665 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/102471 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107418 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113242 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `WHERE _table = ...` or `WHERE _database = ...` filter over a `Merge` table silently returning no rows when the matched child reads through another table, for example a `Distributed`, a nested `Merge`, or a `Buffer` child. The `_database` and `_table` virtual columns of a `Merge` table now always carry the name of the matched child, as they did before 25.7, not the name of the table the child delegates its read to. ### Description `ReadFromMerge::getSelectedTables` prunes the children of a `Merge` table by evaluating a filter on `_database`/`_table` against each child's own name, but the values in the rows were stamped by whatever storage eventually read them - for a `Distributed` child, the remote table on the shards. The two sides contradicted each other, and every query where both fire silently returned wrong results: a filter naming the child returned no rows (pruning kept the child, but no row carried its name), and a filter naming the remote table returned rows only at processing stages where the pruning happened not to fire. ```sql CREATE TABLE t_leaf (s String) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY s; CREATE TABLE t_dist AS t_leaf ENGINE = Distributed(test_cluster_two_shards_localhost, currentDatabase(), t_leaf); CREATE TABLE m (s String) ENGINE = Merge(currentDatabase(), '^t_dist$'); SELECT count() FROM m WHERE _table = 't_dist'; -- 0 on master, all rows with this fix ``` **History.** Before #63665 (25.7), the `Merge` engine substituted the child's own name for `_table`/`_database` itself (`WITH '<child>' AS _table` per child), so the values and the pruning agreed. #63665 gave every table its own `_table` virtual column, which disabled that gated substitution: the reader deep down stamps the name, and for a delegating child that is a different table. #102471 then removed the dead substitution machinery, and #107418 pinned the new values with a regression test - while the pruning kept matching child names all along. **The fix** makes the `Merge` engine produce these columns itself again, unconditionally: references to them are replaced with a constant carrying the child's name right in the child query tree (so expressions computed on the shards see it too; the analyzer path pins the action name via `__actionName`, the old interpreter path uses the `WITH` substitution), and at `FetchColumns` the constant columns are added to the child plan, inserted at the positions the columns have in the requested header, because a child whose execution names differ from the common header (a `Distributed` child) is matched by position in `convertAndFilterSourceStream`. **This is a deliberate semantic choice, and the alternative is #113735.** Only one of the two semantics can be consistent with pruning: the pruning can only ever match the child's name, since the `Merge` table cannot know which table a child delegates to without classifying every child. #113735 keeps the underlying-table values and therefore has to prove, per storage class and recursively through `Buffer`/`Alias`/proxy wrappers, whether a child stamps its own name - with a fail-closed carve-out for streaming engines. Under child-name semantics all of that machinery is unnecessary, streaming children keep being pruned exactly as before, and the docs' claim that "the `_table` column acts as an index" is actually true. The cost: `_table` through `Merge` over `Distributed` reads `t_dist`, not `t_leaf`; each nesting level of `Merge` reports its own child. Tests `00717` (whose leaf-name expectations were rewritten in #63665 itself), `03094`, `04338`, `04367`, `03031` and `01902` are updated accordingly; the new test `05019_merge_virtual_columns_delegating_children` covers the pruning and the values over `Distributed`, nested `Merge` and `Buffer` children, with both analyzers. This also unblocks #113242, whose only functional CI failure was `00717_merge_and_distributed` newly reaching the pruning defect at `FetchColumns`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115356&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115356](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115356+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix `clickhouse-local` printing TSV instead of PrettyCompact in interactive mode
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/105249 Interactive `clickhouse-local` on master renders query results as `TSV` instead of the terminal default `PrettyCompact`. `applyCmdOptions` seeds the `default_format` setting on `global_context` as the fallback format of the sessions of the embedded protocol listeners (`SYSTEM START LISTEN`), where it must match a real `clickhouse-server` (`TabSeparated`). `client_context` is copied from `global_context` and inherits the seed, and the per-query output-format resolution introduced in #105249 treats a non-empty `default_format` setting as the fallback format, so the seed overrode the interactive display default. (#105249 guarded `--vertical` against exactly this failure mode, but the plain interactive default slipped through: it is the one case where `is_default_format` stays true.) The fix clears the seeded value on `client_context`, in `makeFormatOptionsPrivateToTheClient`, which already handles the mirror image of this problem for the `format` / `input_format` / `output_format` settings. This client renders results from its own `ClientBase::default_output_format`, so the seed is not needed there. Explicit choices keep working: an explicit `--default_format` on the command line is left in place (guarded by `cmd_settings->isChanged`), and a later `SET default_format = ...` or an in-query `SETTINGS` clause lands on `client_context` after the clearing. The served sessions still get the fallback through `global_context`. Verified against the master CI binary (26.8.1.1658, where the regression reproduces): emulating the fix by forcing an empty `default_format` on the client restores `PrettyCompact`, while `SET default_format = 'JSONEachRow'` and `SETTINGS default_format = 'CSV'` continue to be honored. The added `04927_local_interactive_default_format.expect` test fails on current master and passes with the fix emulated; the listener-side default is already covered by `04501_local_http_default_format.expect`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a regression on master (not present in any release): interactive `clickhouse-local` rendered query results as `TSV` instead of `PrettyCompact`. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115360&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115360](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115360+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Perf: Optimize PromQL and for exact groups
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL `and` expressions with an exact group key skip redundant matching stages. ## What changed - add a fast path for the PromQL set operator `and` - use it when both inputs already match on the original `group` column - join the unique left and right `VECTOR_GRID` inputs directly - keep the left-hand values and filter them by right-side sample presence - keep `on(...)`, non-empty `ignoring(...)`, `on()`, and other transformed matching keys on the existing general path - add exact-output coverage for grouped `and` expressions - cover empty `ignoring()` when both inputs already have exact groups - add a performance fixture with an exact-group query and an `and on(instance)` control ## Why this is safe `VECTOR_GRID` guarantees one row per `group`. The fast path is enabled only when the matching rules leave the original `group` column unchanged on both sides, so the join key is already unique and exact. The exact-group path removes the right-side per-group count aggregation and the transformed-key join. It returns the left value only when the corresponding right value is present, which is the existing `and` masking behavior. `on(...)`, non-empty `ignoring(...)`, and other cases that transform the matching key keep the current general lowering. Empty `ignoring()` is treated like default matching when both inputs already have exact groups. ## Benchmark Ran `tests/performance/promql_set_operators_and.xml` on Apple Silicon with the Release build from this PR. - 8,000 series - 4,000 matching groups - 300 samples per series - 7 measured runs per query on each of two local server instances The table shows the average of the two per-server medians. Both queries are equivalent for this fixture. The default query uses the new exact-group fast path. The `and on(instance)` query keeps the existing generic implementation. | Query | Median | | --- | ---: | | exact-group `and` | 130.2 ms | | equivalent `and on(instance)` query | 139.8 ms | The exact-group query took 130.2 ms versus 139.8 ms for the existing implementation, which is 6.9% faster in this test. ## Tests - add grouped exact-output coverage for `and` - add exact-output coverage for empty `ignoring()` - keep the existing ungrouped and transformed-key `and` coverage - compile the changed translation unit with the ClickHouse warning set and `-Werror` Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115219 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115374&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115374](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115374+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Bound the shutdown wait for cancelled backups and restores
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115105 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): With `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores = 0`, a `BACKUP` or `RESTORE` whose I/O did not return kept the server from terminating on a single `SIGTERM`, because shutdown waited for it to reach a final status with no timeout. That wait is now bounded by `shutdown_wait_unfinished`, and new backups and restores are refused once shutdown has begun. ### Description Related: #115105 Reported by @ PedroTadim, who [asked me to take it](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115105#issuecomment-5326577830). The issue stays open. **Cause.** Shutdown waits with `status_changed.wait` - no timeout, predicate on the operation status only, so it lasts as long as the operation. `cancelAll` does not help: cancellation is polled per file (`checkTimeLimit()` before `writeFile`), and within a file `BackupImpl` uses the `copyData` overload with no cancellation hook, so a thread parked in a read never sees it. **Change**, all inside the `shutdown_wait_backups_and_restores = 0` branch of `Server.cpp`: refuse new operations, bound the wait at `shutdown_wait_unfinished`, and on non-convergence feed the forced exit that already handles `!joined_refresh_tasks`. That exit is `_exit`, so the unbounded `thread_pools->wait()` in `BackupsWorker::shutdown()` is never reached rather than bounded. `addInfo` refuses after its dedup early-return: `UNFINISHED` for internal operations (retriable in `DDLWorker`), `QUERY_WAS_CANCELLED` otherwise. **Not fixed here.** The default `= 1` branch is untouched, so the hang is still reachable with stock settings: that setting is documented as waiting for backups to *finish*, so capping it changes the guarantee and is your call. Also unchanged: the per-file cancellation granularity, and `BackupsWorker::shutdown()` reached without this guard (failed startup script), where bounding its status waits just moves the block to the pool join. An abandoned backup keeps its `CREATING_BACKUP` row and can leave partial files. **Validation.** The new tests wedge a backup with the existing `backup_pause_on_start` failpoint, which parks the thread upstream of both `checkTimeLimit()` polls, so the operation never sees its own cancellation. The oracle is whether `stop_clickhouse()` escalated to `SIGKILL`, not elapsed time and not a log line (`_exit` discards the async log queue). One arm requires self-exit and fails on master; a second raises the setting to 600 and requires the server to keep waiting, so a hardcoded deadline fails it. 50/50 stable; sibling shutdown and on-cluster cancel tests pass. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115377&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115377](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115377+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
signals.author: groeneai

signals.title: Add a notebook mode to the Web UI
signals.text: Adds a notebook mode to the Web SQL UI (`/play`): a tab can become an ordered sequence of cells, each either a query with its own result or a block of Markdown text — the shape of document Jupyter, Observable, Hex and Deepnote use, and for the same purpose: keeping a chain of queries, and the reasoning between them, on one page. ## How it works A tab starts as a single query cell and looks exactly as it always has — no headers, no cell chrome, no notebook. Once a query has produced a result, a large muted `[+]` appears under it and expands into the two kinds of cell that can be added, query or text. Adding the second cell is what turns notebook mode on, and it is per tab: one tab can be a notebook while another stays a plain single-query editor, and each tab remembers its own notebook across reloads. From two cells on, each cell gets a header with its position and kind (`1. Query`, `2. Text`) and the editing actions: run, edit, insert a cell before, move up/down, delete. There is still exactly one query editor on the page — the full one, with its highlighting backdrop, autocompletion and query-parameter inputs. In notebook mode it is docked into whichever query cell is active, and shown only while it has the focus; as soon as focus leaves, that cell collapses to its query on a single line, syntax highlighted, whitespace runs reduced to one space, fading out on the right. The Run / progress / copy / download row docks under the query being edited, between it and its result, and appears and disappears with the editor. Results are more compact: a smaller font with the cell padding scaled to match, and a table of at most a quarter of the viewport that is its own scroll container on both axes, so its (thin) scrollbars sit at its own edges and a long or wide result neither pushes the notebook down the page nor widens it. Results and Markdown editors can be resized by dragging their bottom edge, as the query editor already could. A text cell shows its Markdown source with the markers highlighted while it is being edited, and the rendered result once editing finishes. Raw HTML is escaped and link targets are restricted to `http`, `https`, `mailto` and relative URLs. ## Implementation The query text, parameters and result snapshot moved from the tab to a cell. `tab.query` / `tab.result` / `tab.resultEl` and the rest are now accessors onto the cell the editor is docked in, so the editor, history, URL and persistence code is unchanged and always means "the cell in front of the user". A run captures its own cell, so moving on to another cell mid-run does not redirect the response. The Logs/Metrics view and the resource meters follow the cell whose result they describe. The whole notebook is persisted in IndexedDB alongside the rest of the workspace, and history entries record the cell they belong to so Back/Forward cannot push one cell's query into another. A tab holding a single cell renders exactly as before — verified by screenshot diff against `master`: 51 pixels differ, all on one row, all by 1 in a single channel. ## Testing Driven in headless Chrome against a local server: cell creation and deletion, moving and inserting cells, collapsing and expanding, per-tab independence, tab duplicate/close with a docked editor, query parameters inside a cell, per-cell errors, reload restore from IndexedDB, "Run all" inside a cell, the Logs and Metrics views per cell, column and result resizing, the theme switch and download menu inside the docked Run row, Markdown rendering and backdrop alignment, and light and dark themes. Two pre-existing issues were fixed along the way: the download drop-down positioned itself without accounting for `#main`'s scroll offset, and the `#run` submit button needed `form="controls"` once it could be moved out of the form's subtree. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a notebook mode to the Web UI (`/play`). After a query is run, a `[+]` button under the result adds further cells, each either a query with its own result or a block of Markdown text, turning the tab into a notebook in the style of Jupyter or Observable. Cells can be run, reordered, inserted and deleted individually; the query editor collapses to a single line when it is not focused, results are bounded and scroll inside themselves, and the whole notebook is restored on reload. Notebook mode is per tab, so a tab that has only one cell looks and behaves exactly as before. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115378&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115378](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115378+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add a `bucketed` schema for `system.metric_log`: a single Map column with Enum keys and 128 buckets
signals.text: Adds a new `schema_type` option `bucketed` for `system.metric_log` (the default `wide` and the `transposed` schemas are unchanged): ```xml <metric_log> <schema_type>bucketed</schema_type> </metric_log> ``` With this schema, all profile events and current metrics are stored in a single `metrics` column of type `Map(Enum16(...), Int64)`, where the `Enum16` value is the global metric index and zero values are not stored (a lookup of a missing key in a `Map` returns `0`). The default table definition uses the bucketed `Map` serialization with a constant number of 128 buckets: ``` SETTINGS map_serialization_version = 'with_buckets', map_serialization_version_for_zero_level_parts = 'basic', max_buckets_in_map = 128, map_buckets_strategy = 'constant', map_buckets_min_avg_size = 0 ``` Parts created by inserts keep the basic serialization to avoid creating many small files on every flush; merged parts are always split into 128 buckets. Every metric is also exposed through an `ALIAS` column, e.g. `ProfileEvent_Query UInt64 ALIAS metrics['ProfileEvent_Query']`, so all queries, dashboards, and tests written for the `wide` schema continue to work. Reading a single metric goes through the `Map` key subcolumn (`metrics.key_ProfileEvent_Query`), which reads only the bucket containing the key: in a local test it reads ~100 times less data than reading the whole map (616 vs 60716 bytes on the same rows). Supporting changes: - `arrayElement` on a `Map` with `Enum` keys now accepts the string name of the enum value (`m['name']`): the index is cast to the key type, so an unknown name throws the `UNKNOWN_ELEMENT_OF_ENUM` exception, while a name that is in the `Enum` but absent from the map returns the default value. This previously threw `ILLEGAL_TYPE_OF_ARGUMENT`. - The rewrite of `m['key']` to a key subcolumn in `FunctionToSubcolumnsPass` now supports `Enum`-keyed maps indexed by the name of the enum value, so both the aliases and ad-hoc queries prune buckets. - System logs can declare additional default engine settings via `getDefaultEngineSettings`, merged with the `settings` from the server configuration when no custom `engine` is specified. - An unknown `metric_log.schema_type` value is now rejected with an error instead of silently disabling the table. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add a new `bucketed` schema type for `system.metric_log`, which stores all metrics in a single `Map(Enum16(...), Int64)` column using the bucketed `Map` serialization with 128 buckets, plus a per-metric `ALIAS` column for compatibility: the table consists of a few columns instead of thousands, zero values are not stored, and reading a single metric reads only one of the 128 buckets. In addition, a `Map` with `Enum` keys can now be indexed by the string name of the enum value, e.g. `map['name']`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115380&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115380](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115380+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Query cache on disk, backed by the filesystem cache
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115361 The query cache can now additionally store its entries on disk, backed by a preconfigured filesystem cache (an entry of the `filesystem_caches` section of the server configuration), selected per query with the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`. Compared to the in-memory query cache, this gives the entries more space, makes them survive server restarts, and (with a distributed filesystem cache) provides a way to share them between servers. Design, following the RFC in the issue: - The entries are ordinary filesystem cache entries, indistinguishable from other data in the same filesystem cache: they are not held from deletion, they are evicted by the same rules, and there are no specific limits on their total size or number other than the limits of the filesystem cache itself. The keys are hashed with a salt so that they cannot intersect with other keys in the filesystem cache. - No extra in-memory state is kept: all metadata needed to validate an entry (TTL, user id, roles, the shared flag) is serialized into the entry itself, followed by the result payload in `Native` format, compressed with the codec from the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_codec` (default `ZSTD(3)`; reading is independent of the setting because the compressed frames are self-describing). - The on-disk cache works independently of the in-memory cache and can separately be enabled for reads and/or writes with the new settings `enable_reads_from_query_cache_on_disk` and `enable_writes_to_query_cache_on_disk` (both `true` by default, activated by setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`). If both caches are enabled for reads, the lookup is attempted first from memory and only on a miss from disk. If both caches are enabled for writes, the result is written to both. A result served from memory is not written to disk. - A stale (expired TTL), partially evicted, corrupt, or inaccessible (another user's non-shared) entry is treated as a cache miss; stale entries are overwritten on the next write. - Introspection of the on-disk entries in `system.query_cache` is out of scope, per the issue. New profile events: `QueryCacheOnDiskHits`, `QueryCacheOnDiskMisses`, `QueryCacheOnDiskReadBytes`, `QueryCacheOnDiskWrittenBytes`. Tests: `05019_query_cache_on_disk_local` proves persistence across process restarts (separate `clickhouse-local` invocations sharing one filesystem cache directory, including a cached non-deterministic result, TTL expiry, and disabled reads); `05020_query_cache_on_disk` covers the server path with user isolation, sharing via `query_cache_share_between_users`, and error cases (unknown cache name, invalid codec). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The query cache can now store its entries on disk, backed by a preconfigured filesystem cache: this gives the entries more space, makes them survive server restarts, and (with a distributed filesystem cache) provides a way to share them between servers. Select the filesystem cache with the new setting `query_cache_on_disk_cache_name`; see also the new settings `query_cache_on_disk_codec`, `enable_writes_to_query_cache_on_disk`, and `enable_reads_from_query_cache_on_disk`. Closes [#115361](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115361). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115382&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115382](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115382+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add the experimental Trino SQL dialect
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `trino` value of the `dialect` setting (gated by `allow_experimental_trino_dialect`): queries written in Trino SQL are translated to ClickHouse SQL, including Trino-specific syntax (`ARRAY[...]` literals, `TRY_CAST`, `UNNEST`, `ROW` constructors and types, `VALUES` tables, `OFFSET` before `LIMIT`, `FETCH`) and a mapping of several hundred Trino function names and argument conventions to their ClickHouse equivalents. Since Trino SQL is close to ClickHouse SQL (which already parses `AT TIME ZONE`, `FILTER (WHERE ...)`, `IS DISTINCT FROM`, `DATE`/`TIMESTAMP` literals, `GROUPING SETS`, `NULLS FIRST/LAST`, `WITH RECURSIVE`, ...), the dialect is not a separate grammar. It works in three stages in `src/Parsers/Trino/`: 1. **Token-level syntax translation** (`TrinoSyntaxTranslator`): `ARRAY[1, 2]` -> `[1, 2]`, `TRY_CAST(x AS t)` -> `accurateCastOrNull(x, 't')`, `ROW(...)` -> `tuple(...)` / `Tuple(...)`, `UNNEST` in `FROM` -> `ARRAY JOIN` (`LEFT JOIN UNNEST ... ON TRUE` -> `LEFT ARRAY JOIN`, `WITH ORDINALITY` -> `arrayEnumerate`, maps -> `mapKeys`/`mapValues`), `(VALUES ...)` -> a subquery over `SQLStandardValues`, `OFFSET n LIMIT m` -> `LIMIT m OFFSET n`, `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY/WITH TIES` -> `LIMIT`, `TIMESTAMP(p) [WITH TIME ZONE]` type -> `DateTime64(p)`, lambdas are parenthesized (the ClickHouse parser cannot parse a lambda after a literal argument), and backslashes in string literals are escaped (in Trino a backslash is a regular character). 2. **The standard ClickHouse parser** parses the result. If nothing needed translation, the original buffer is parsed directly, and `INSERT` statements with inline data (`VALUES`/`FORMAT`) are always delegated as-is so that the zero-copy data pointers stay valid. 3. **AST-level function mapping** (`TrinoFunctionMapper`): ~100 renames plus ~50 structural rewriters built from a review of all ~340 functions in the Trino documentation. This includes argument reordering for every higher-order function (Trino passes lambdas last, ClickHouse first: `transform(arr, f)` -> `arrayMap(f, arr)`), parametric-aggregate conversion (`approx_percentile(x, p)` -> `quantileTDigest(p)(x)`, `listagg(x, sep)` -> `groupConcat(sep)(x)`), and — most importantly — the names that resolve in ClickHouse with **different semantics** and would silently return wrong results if passed through: `to_unixtime` (an alias of `parseDateTime` in ClickHouse), `date_diff` (boundary crossings vs complete units -> `age`), `week` (non-ISO mode 0 -> `toISOWeek`), `from_unixtime(u, x)` (format string vs time zone), `rand`/`random` -> `randCanonical`, `transform`, `repeat`, `histogram`, `map(karr, varr)` -> `mapFromArrays`, `format` -> `printf`, and the varchar family (`length`, `substr`, `upper`, `lower`, `strpos`, `lpad`, ...) which is code-point-based in Trino and byte-based in ClickHouse (-> `...UTF8` variants). The feature gate follows the `polyglot` pattern: `SET` queries are handled before the gate inside the parser, so a misconfigured profile can always be recovered with `SET dialect = 'clickhouse'`. ClickHouse functions whose names do not collide with Trino names remain accessible from the dialect. Unsupported constructs (`TABLESAMPLE`, `TRY(...)`, comparator `array_sort`, ...) throw explicit `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`/`BAD_ARGUMENTS` errors instead of misbehaving, and semantics that cannot be fixed by translation at the query level (integer division `/`, `round` banker's rounding on Float, `greatest`/`least` NULL handling) are documented. The translation is observable with `EXPLAIN SYNTAX`. Note: `polyglot_dialect = 'trino'` already exists via the `polyglot` transpiler, but it performs no function mapping and passes `ARRAY[...]` through untranslated; this first-class dialect provides a much more complete translation. `BETWEEN SYMMETRIC` is translated to `BETWEEN least(a, b) AND greatest(a, b)`, and the Trino `JSON` type family is mapped to the ClickHouse `JSON` type, accepting that only objects are supported: `JSON '...'` literals and `json_parse` become casts to `JSON`, `json_format` becomes `toJSONString`, and `json_extract`, `json_extract_scalar`, `json_value`, `json_query`, `json_exists`, `json_size`, `json_array_contains` and `is_json_scalar` are translated to the ClickHouse JSON functions (the string-based JSONPath functions do not accept the `JSON` type, so casts flowing directly into them are unwrapped back to the JSON text; non-object documents are rejected when materialized as `JSON` values). Validation: the translation was exercised against four corpora derived from Trino's own tests and documentation: - **732 self-contained query/expected pairs** extracted from Trino's functional tests (`core/trino-main/src/test/java/io/trino/sql/query/Test*.java`): 206 produce identical results; of the rest, ~270 need ClickHouse engine features (`LATERAL` joins alone gate 139, plus correlated-subquery decorrelation shapes and non-integer window frame offsets) and the remainder are unsupported constructs or documented semantic differences. 75 order-deterministic pairs are committed as `05021_trino_conformance` (following the KQL conformance-test precedent), and three more conformance tests pin the adopted corpora: `05022_trino_conformance_presto_scalar` (1054 Presto scalar-function assertions), `05023_trino_conformance_tempto` (119 Tempto product-test queries running against their fixture tables inlined into the test), and `05024_trino_conformance_impala` (44 generic-SQL Impala expressions) — every adopted query verified to produce the documented result and to be stable under randomized time zones, thread counts and block sizes. - **43 convention-based Tempto product tests** (`testing/trino-product-tests` at tag 455, `.sql`/`.result` pairs): 30 of the 34 runnable ones match (using the fixed 25-row `nation`/5-row `region` TPC-H tables). - **294 `SELECT`-with-expected-result examples** from the official function documentation: 142 match. - The **22 TPC-H queries in Trino dialect** from `testing/trino-benchmark-queries`: all parse and translate. - **1689 scalar-function assertions** scraped from `prestodb/presto` unit tests (`assertFunction("expr", TYPE, value)` style) plus the **130 Tempto product tests Presto kept after the fork**, executed against real TPC-H sf0.01 data and the `datatype`/`workers` fixture tables: 1059 and 91 match respectively (most of the rest use Presto-only functions that do not exist in current Trino). The 43 Trino-era Tempto tests reach 38/43 with the data available. - **146 expression tests** from `apache/impala` as a generic-SQL cross-check (Impala is a different dialect; 44 match, and the divergences are Impala-specific by design — e.g. Impala's `LIKE` treats a backslash as an escape character while Trino treats it literally). These corpora drove another round of semantic fixes: outer joins produce NULLs (`join_use_nulls`), `sum`/`avg`/`min`/`max` over an empty set return NULL (`-OrNull` variants), `count` returns a signed bigint, `greatest`/`least` propagate NULL arguments, LIKE backslash literalness, minute-precision `TIMESTAMP` literals, `reduce` output lambdas, `bit_count` arbitrary widths, `width_bucket` over an array of bounds, and `json_array_get`. Of the 294 examples, 142 produce results matching the documentation (plus a few that differ only by printing the current time or the session time zone); most of the rest use deliberately unsupported constructs (SQL:2016 `MATCH`/`UNIQUE` predicates, `U&'...'` literals, functions with no ClickHouse counterpart, non-object `JSON` documents per the design above). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115383&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115383](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115383+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not let an alias give `randConstant` a second value in one query
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112938 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `randConstant` returning two different values in one query when its calls carry different aliases. `randConstant` is documented to hold a single value for the whole query, and `SELECT randConstant() = randConstant()` already returned `1`, but adding aliases as in `SELECT randConstant() AS a, randConstant() AS b` produced two unrelated values. ### Description ```sql SELECT randConstant() = randConstant() -- 1 SELECT a = b FROM (SELECT randConstant() AS a, randConstant() AS b) -- 0 <-- wrong ``` `randConstant` is documented to return "a single random value that remains constant across all rows in the current query execution", and its argument is documented as existing only "to prevent common subexpression elimination when the same function call is used multiple times in a query". So two bare calls must agree, and asking for a second value is spelled `randConstant(1), randConstant(2)`. `RandomConstantOverloadResolver::buildImpl` draws a new value on every call, so identical calls have to share one built `FunctionBase` to fold to one constant. `resolveFunction` arranges that with `functions_cache`, keyed by `getTreeHash`. That hash covers the alias, so the two aliased calls missed each other in the cache, each folded to its own literal, and no later common subexpression elimination could bring them back together — by then they were two different literals. With `enable_analyzer = 0` the same query returns `1`, so this is analyzer-only. The key now ignores aliases. An alias renames an expression and never changes the value the `FunctionBase` captures, so aliased calls share what bare calls share. What separates two calls is still their arguments, which the hash covers. The change is narrower than the cache's reach suggests. Only a function folded through its own `FunctionBase` can be split this way; anything evaluated per row, such as `rand` or `generateUUIDv4`, is deduplicated later by ordinary common subexpression elimination, which already ignored aliases — `SELECT rand() AS a, rand() AS b, a = b` reads `1` on `master` today. To bound it rather than argue it, I swept all 57 zero-argument non-deterministic functions, comparing each one aliased and bare, before and after: `randConstant` is the only function whose result changes, from `0` to `1`, and no bare result moves at all. Test `05023` fails on exactly its four aliased rows without the change. Its five controls — the bare comparison, the distinct-argument row (four arguments rather than two, so it cannot flake on a value collision), the across-rows row, and the `now` and `rand` rows — pass either way. Verified by building and running against the branch build: `05023` plus the five existing tests that read `randConstant` (`03611`, `01418`, `00912`, `04327` across shards, `03047` under mutations) all pass. The 382-test `analyzer` family was run on both arms of an exact A/B on the same tree — the one-line change reverted, rebuilt, rerun — and the two arms are identical: 352 pass and the same 18 fail on both, all of them for missing fixtures in my local server rather than for this change. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115384&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115384](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115384+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Sync `BackupImpl` lock-file handling and the Cloud-only resume state
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/69709 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/clickhouse-private/pull/69709 This is the public side of the private pull request above, and most of it is that sync. The shared files both touch -- `BackupImpl.h`, `BackupImpl.cpp`, `BackupFactory.h` -- are identical here and there, down to the blank lines, so `Check public build` can overlay the private ones unchanged and later syncs have nothing to reconcile in them. What stays private is where continuing an interrupted backup is implemented, because nothing outside ClickHouse Cloud resumes one. The part that changes this build is the lock-file handling. `open` removes a lock it created when the verification that follows throws. Otherwise the lock outlives the failed attempt and fences the destination against every later one, which cannot match it either: a retry picks a fresh backup UUID, so the orphaned lock belongs to nobody, and every later `BACKUP` to that destination fails until someone deletes the file by hand. `removeLockFile` now reports whether the destination still holds the lock. `checkLockFile(false)` is false both for a foreign lock and for one it could not read, so a caller could not tell "not ours" from "unknown" while the lock was still there; `tryRemoveAllFiles` reports that as a failure rather than claiming the destination is clean. `createLockFile` asks for the lock with `writeFileIfNotExists` and, when that fails, compares what is there against what it would have written: its own contents mean a concurrent backup, a completed `.backup` means the backup already exists, and a lock that has since disappeared rethrows the original failure rather than guessing. `writeFileIfNotExists` is only exclusive where the storage can be -- `S3` and `Azure` implement it, every other writer falls back to an ordinary write -- so on those other destinations it is the comparison, not the create, that detects a concurrent backup. The rest is behind `CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD` and compiles to nothing here: `CreateParams` carries the resume parameters, `open` hands them to a `BackupResumer` this build does not have, and the places that read them are the ownership check before anything becomes visible, the timestamp a continuation republishes, the lock a continuation is allowed to find, and the manifest it does not write again. `BackupImpl` keeps one member for the last of those, `metadata_already_published`; the parameters themselves stay out, along with everything that acts on them. So this build behaves as it did: it writes its own timestamp and always publishes metadata. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `BACKUP` no longer leaves a lock file behind in its destination when the attempt that created it fails before writing anything. No later backup could match such a lock, so every retry to the same destination failed until the file was deleted by hand. Backups to `S3` and `Azure` destinations now also create the lock exclusively, and a lock that belongs to another backup is reported as a concurrent backup rather than as whatever error the storage returned. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115387&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115387](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115387+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Self-contained binary: embedded CA certificates; DNS without resolv.conf and hosts in musl builds
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/musl/pull/6 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The ClickHouse binary is now self-contained and works in a container image built `FROM scratch` with no additional files when built with musl. CA certificates (the Chromium root store, taken from the gRPC submodule) are embedded into the binary and used as a fallback when no CA certificates are found on the filesystem. In musl builds, when `/etc/resolv.conf` does not exist, DNS falls back to well-known public resolvers instead of the unreachable localhost, and `localhost` resolves to loopback per RFC 6761 even without `/etc/hosts`. ### Description The goal is a self-contained binary: a musl build should run in a container image built `FROM scratch` (or as the init process of a minimal system) without any files in the image — no CA certificates, no `/etc/resolv.conf`, no `/etc/hosts`, no `/etc/passwd`. Only the kernel interfaces (`/proc` and the standard minimal `/dev` that every container gets) are expected. **Embedded CA certificates** (all builds, not only musl). Every TLS context is created by `Poco::Net::Context::init`, which loads default CA certificates from `SSL_CERT_FILE`/`SSL_CERT_DIR`, `/etc/ssl`, and a list of well-known distribution locations, and previously threw `Cannot load default CA certificates` when none were found — so in a bare container, the TLS listeners did not start and every HTTPS request (S3, Azure, `url`, dictionaries, secure ZooKeeper, `remoteSecure`) failed at context creation. Now the root store maintained in the gRPC submodule (`contrib/grpc/etc/roots.pem`, the Chromium root store, 115 roots) is embedded with C23 `#embed` and added to the trust store only when the filesystem yields nothing. Certificates found on the filesystem always take precedence, and the embedded ones are not loaded at all in that case. An existing but *empty* certificate directory (e.g. an `/etc/ssl/certs` left behind by a removed `ca-certificates` package) also engages the fallback, since a directory without hash-named files can never yield a certificate at verification time; previously it silently produced an empty trust store that failed at handshake time. The embedded certificates are visible in `system.certificates` with `path = '(embedded)'`, and the feature can be disabled with `-DENABLE_EMBEDDED_CA_CERTIFICATES=0`. **DNS without `/etc/resolv.conf`** (musl builds). musl is built from sources from the ClickHouse fork, so the fallback lives there (https://github.com/ClickHouse/musl/pull/6) and covers every consumer of `getaddrinfo` in the binary at once — Poco, NuRaft asio, and the client libraries in contrib. When the file does not exist, the resolver uses `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8`, `2606:4700:4700::1111` instead of the upstream fallback of `127.0.0.1`, which cannot answer in such an environment. A `resolv.conf` that exists but configures no nameservers — or exists but is unreadable — keeps the upstream localhost fallback, since it expresses an intentional local configuration. **`localhost` without `/etc/hosts`** (musl builds, same fork PR). `localhost` and any name under `.localhost` resolve to the loopback addresses per RFC 6761 when the hosts file yields nothing for them, and are never sent to DNS resolvers — matching c-ares and systemd-resolved. Without this, the public-resolver fallback above would leak `localhost` queries to the network. An `/etc/hosts` entry still takes precedence. Also fixed along the way: - The aarch64 openldap configuration lacked the musl guard for `bits/types.h` that the x86_64 one received when musl started to be built from sources (CI only has an x86_64 musl build), so aarch64 musl builds did not compile. - The server failed at startup with `FAILED_TO_GETPWUID` when there is no `/etc/passwd` and the effective user does not match the data owner, while merely trying to render the name for the diagnostic message; it now uses the numeric id, the same as for a null `getpwuid_r` result. Also fixed `getUserName` writing into unused string capacity. ### Verification Everything was verified on an aarch64 musl build (`cmake/linux/toolchain-aarch64-musl.cmake`) running in a chroot containing only the binary, `/proc`, and `/dev`: - `clickhouse local --query "SELECT count() > 0 FROM url('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/master/README.md', LineAsString)"` returns `1` — DNS through the embedded fallback resolvers plus TLS against the embedded root store, with no `/etc` at all. The same works with an existing but empty `/etc/ssl/certs`. - `strace` confirms `localhost` lookups produce zero DNS packets while resolving to `127.0.0.1`/`::1`, and that DNS queries go to the fallback resolvers. - `clickhouse server` starts (`Ready for connections`) and `clickhouse client` connects and executes queries inside the same bare chroot. The new integration test `test_embedded_ca_certificates` covers the certificate fallback in CI: it removes every certificate location from the container (and separately re-creates an empty `/etc/ssl/certs`), restarts the server, and checks that HTTPS still works and that `system.certificates` shows the embedded roots. The DNS part cannot be covered by CI tests, because the test builds link glibc; it is covered by the manual verification above. Not covered (possible follow-ups): client libraries in contrib that load CA certificates through their own code paths (librdkafka for Kafka broker TLS, NATS, MongoDB, MySQL and PostgreSQL clients, LDAP) — all of them have explicit CA configuration options; and glibc builds still need the resolver libraries and `resolv.conf` from the OS, as before. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115389&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115389](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115389+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Avoid overflow in the `uniq` aggregate function at cardinalities above ten billion
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/6078 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112052 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `uniq` aggregate function returned garbage (e.g. `18446743978444128518`) for cardinalities above roughly thirty billion, because its state kept only 32 bits of each hash and the correction formula overflowed. The state now keeps full 64-bit hashes (state version `1`): `SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(100000000000)` returns `100288510111` (+0.29%), and the estimate stays accurate up to trillions. States written by older versions remain readable, and distributed queries in mixed-version clusters keep working: the state version on the wire is derived from the negotiated protocol revision, and merging with a state that carries only 32 bits of hash information degrades the calculation to the legacy accuracy, since the discarded bits cannot be recovered. --- ### The bug The `uniq` state (`UniquesHashSet`, a BJKST-style adaptive sampling set) truncated all hashes to 32 bits. Beyond a few billion distinct values, all `2^32` hash buckets fill up, and the collision-correction formula computes `round(2^32 * (log(2^32) - log(2^32 - res)))` with `res >= 2^32` — `log` of a non-positive number, and the cast of the resulting infinity/NaN to an integer is undefined behavior that produced the values reported in the issue. ### The fix The state now keeps the full 64-bit hash. The 32-bit hash used before was exactly the low half of the 64-bit hash that is now kept, which makes the two formats compatible in one direction: truncation reproduces the legacy state *bit for bit*, while the reverse is information-theoretically impossible (the discarded 32 bits of the hashes of the already-absorbed elements cannot be recovered — any scheme that "upgrades" a 32-bit state produces phantom duplicates and estimates off by up to 2x at moderate cardinalities). Hence the compatibility model: - **State version `1`** stores 8-byte hash values behind a flags byte; version `0` keeps the legacy layout. The versioning scheme follows the recent `quantileDeterministic` one (#112052) exactly: the default version stays `0` so that unversioned types in persisted data keep the byte layout they always had; a fresh state spells version `1` out in its type name (`AggregateFunction(1, uniq, UInt64)`); a fresh `CREATE TABLE` gets the version pinned at DDL time; on the `Native` wire the version is derived from the negotiated revision (new constant `DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_UNIQ_STATE_VERSION_1 = 54493`). - **Serialization for an old peer** (or into a version-`0` column) truncates the hashes — an old server receives exactly the state it would have computed itself. - **A state read from version-`0` data** is kept in a "compat" mode (a 32-bit hash `h` is stored in the 64-bit cell as `(h << 32) | h`, which preserves both the placement and the thinning bits of the legacy implementation with no separate code path for lookups). Merging a 64-bit state with a compat state downgrades the former by truncation, so mixing old and new states gives exactly the legacy result rather than a subtly wrong one. - The legacy estimate formula is clamped, so a saturated version-`0` state now returns the saturation limit (about `9.5e10`) instead of the garbage value. ### Results ``` SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(50000000000) -- 50068359760 (+0.14%), was 18446743978444128518 SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(100000000000) -- 100288510111 (+0.29%), was 18446743978444128518 SELECT uniq(number) FROM numbers_mt(1000000000000) -- 1010107886346 (+1.0%) ``` Cross-version compatibility was verified against a real 26.7 server: an old state read by the new server, a new state read by the old server (both through raw column transfer and through partial-aggregation states of a two-shard `remote`), all produce exactly the estimate the old server computes natively (`1001943` for `numbers(1000000)`), while the new server alone gives the 64-bit estimate (`1002018`). ### Two latent bugs of #112052 fixed on the way Both were exposed by the new `uniq` version but reproduce with `quantileDeterministic` on current master: - `ColumnBLOB::toBLOB` (parallel block marshalling) serialized the payload with the state version resolved from the local type, while `NativeWriter::write` announces the version derived from the negotiated revision, so the receiver lost sync inside the blob: `SELECT medianDeterministic(n, n) FROM remote('127.0.0.{1,2}', default, t) GROUP BY n % 2 SETTINGS enable_parallel_blocks_marshalling = 1, prefer_localhost_replica = 0` failed with `Skip degree in quantileDeterministic state is 120` (an exception, in a release build). - A view of a `ColumnAggregateFunction` (the result of a sort, filter, or index operation) and a plain copy of it dropped the state version, so `SELECT arraySlice(groupArray(x), 1, 1) FROM (SELECT medianDeterministicState(number, number) AS x FROM numbers(10) GROUP BY number ORDER BY number)` failed with `Cannot read all data`. ### Cost The stored hashes are twice as large: a saturated state takes 1 MiB in memory and 512 KiB serialized (was 512 KiB / 256 KiB), and the per-element serialized size of `uniqState` columns doubles. Group-heavy queries with mid-sized groups are moderately slower due to the doubled memory traffic of the state's hash table (roughly 10-20% on `SELECT uniq(number) ... GROUP BY number % N` microbenchmarks under load; a single large state is not slower). This is the price of the information that the fix fundamentally requires; `uniq` remains much faster than `uniqExact` and `uniqCombined`. ### Tests - A `gtest` for `UniquesHashSet` covering the estimator at a simulated cardinality of `10^11` (the overflow scenario), the saturation clamp of the legacy formula, round trips of both formats, cross-format merges and deduplication, and rejection of corrupt states. - `05023_uniq_state_version_64bit_hashes`: version pinning, wire round trips of both versions, cross-version deduplication, exactness below the sampling threshold. - `05024_aggregate_state_version_parallel_marshalling` and `05025_aggregate_state_version_in_column_views` for the two bugs above, covering both `uniq` and `quantileDeterministic`. - Reference updates for tests that print `uniq` estimates over more than 65536 distinct values, state type names, or raw state bytes. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115393&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115393](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115393+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Complete ZooKeeper finalization before logging exceptions
signals.text: ZooKeeper session finalization can wait on send and receive threads while completing outstanding requests. Rendering exception stack traces on those threads can delay their exit and, in turn, delay cleanup. Capture exceptions during send, receive, and callback cleanup. Log them only after the request queue is finished and all pending callbacks have run. This keeps diagnostic work out of the session-finalization path. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix ### Changelog entry: Fix a case where expensive ZooKeeper exception logging could delay session finalization and leave pending requests unresolved. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115396&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115396](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115396+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Enforce settings constraints on nested SETTINGS and SET name = DEFAULT
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109473 Two code paths mutated session or query settings without calling `checkSettingsConstraints`, so an authenticated user could override a setting an administrator had locked with `CONST`, `readonly`, `MIN`/`MAX`, or a feature tier. Where those constraints are the tenant-isolation boundary, this breaks multi-tenant isolation. ### A nested `SETTINGS` clause was applied unchecked `QueryTreeBuilder::buildSelectExpression` applied a `SELECT` node's `SETTINGS` clause to the per-node context copy with no constraint check. A clause on an outer query is validated by `InterpreterSetQuery::applySettingsFromQuery`, but a clause inside a subquery, a CTE, or a view's inner query reached only the analyzer. The Planner then read the mutated context, so with `additional_table_filters` - a documented row-level isolation mechanism - the user read other tenants' rows: ```sql -- rejected SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}; -- accepted before this change, returning every tenant's rows SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}); ``` There were no `checkSettingsConstraints` call sites anywhere in `src/Analyzer`, `src/Planner` or `src/Processors`. The legacy interpreter has always checked the same clause in `InterpreterSelectQuery`, so the analyzer becoming the default silently dropped the check. ### `SET name = DEFAULT` was applied unchecked The parser stores `SET k = v` in `ASTSetQuery::changes` and `SET k = DEFAULT` in `ASTSetQuery::default_settings`, and only the former was validated before `Context::resetSettingsToDefaultValue` applied the compiled-in default. So `SET readonly = DEFAULT` cleared a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile and re-enabled `INSERT`, `CREATE` and `DROP`, and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` cleared a resource cap. The same gap existed in the Arrow Flight `SetSessionOptions` reset branch, whose value-assignment branch already checked. ### A `profile` change was not checked against the constraints it installs A `SET` statement was validated as a whole before it ran, but a `profile` change among its settings replaces the constraint set halfway through it. So a single statement overrode the very constraint that the profile it names installs, while the same settings applied as two separate statements were rejected: ```sql -- rejected SET profile = 'p'; SET max_execution_time = 999; -- accepted before this change, for a profile p with max_execution_time = 10 CONST SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = 999; SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = DEFAULT; ``` ### The fix A new `SettingsConstraints::checkCanReset` validates a reset request, reached through `Context::checkSettingsConstraintsForDefaults` from both `InterpreterSetQuery` entry points, the Arrow Flight reset branch, and the analyzer: * For a built-in setting the compiled-in default is checked as the new value, via the new `Settings::getDefaultValue`, so min/max, `CONST`, tier and source restrictions all apply. Resetting a setting that already holds its default stays allowed, including under `readonly = 1`, because the constraint checker skips a change equal to the current value. * A custom setting has no compiled-in default - resetting it erases it - so only its writability is checked. This matters: erasing a `CONST` custom setting that a row policy reads through `getSetting` is exactly how the reported isolation boundary was broken. `buildSelectExpression` also no longer ignores a nested `SETTINGS name = DEFAULT`, which was previously a silent no-op; it is now checked and applied as a reset. It is applied to the subquery's context only and is not recorded on the `QueryNode`, so it stays invisible to the consumers that read a subquery's settings off the query tree - as it was when the clause was dropped outright. That limitation is documented at the call site and tracked in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115415. For the `profile` case, `InterpreterSetQuery` now checks the rest of the statement against the constraints the profile installs. That requires the profile to have been applied first, so the checking runs on a scratch copy of the context and nothing is applied to the real one until all of it passes: a rejected statement leaves the session alone rather than applying the profile and dropping its own tail. The changes are then applied in one call with the original list, so the order in which they take effect - and therefore which assignment wins - is unchanged. ### Behaviour change A `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view - the default for `CREATE VIEW` - whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails. This restores the behaviour of the legacy interpreter, which has always checked that clause. An administrator can keep such a view working with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER`, because `getSQLSecurityOverriddenContext` switches to the definer, whose constraints then apply. Note the limit of that workaround: it copies the invoker's changed setting *values* while switching the user, so a `CONST`/`MIN`/`MAX` constraint does not travel and the view works, but a `readonly = 1` value does travel and the inner clause is rejected even under `DEFINER`. A `readonly` user reading a view whose inner query sets a setting therefore has no workaround other than removing the clause from the view. ### Testing `05019_settings_constraints_reset_and_nested` covers, in a `CONST`-constrained session: a rejected `SET x = DEFAULT`; a no-op reset of an already-default setting still being allowed; a `CONST` custom setting resisting erasure; a nested `SETTINGS` clause rejected in a subquery, in a CTE, and in the `= DEFAULT` form; an unconstrained nested clause still working; and a `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` view still reading while its `INVOKER` equivalent is rejected. It also pins down that a `SETTINGS` clause written after a nested `UNION` or `INTERSECT` is rejected: the parser attaches such a clause to one of the member `SELECT`s rather than to the compound query, so it is covered by the same check, whichever member it lands on. `05021_settings_constraints_set_profile_in_same_query` covers the `profile` case: an explicit value and a reset after the `profile` change both rejected against the profile's constraints, the profile left unapplied by a rejected statement, an assignment before the `profile` change still allowed, the profile's constraints in force afterwards, and an unconstrained setting after the change still applying. `05020_settings_constraints_readonly_user` covers a user under a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile: `SET readonly = DEFAULT` and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` both rejected, the session still readonly afterwards, and a nested `SETTINGS` clause unable to lift the user's row filter. One existing test needed a fix. `04102_hash_join_stress_test` used `SETTINGS max_joined_block_rows = 100` inside a subquery; the setting is called `max_joined_block_size_rows`. The misspelling went unnoticed because `Settings` accepts custom settings, so `Settings::set` stores an unrecognised name instead of rejecting it, and the `SQL_`/`custom_` prefix validation lives in `AccessControl::checkSettingNameIsAllowed`, reached only from `SettingsConstraints::checkImpl`. The same clause on a top-level query has always been rejected with `UNKNOWN_SETTING`; only the nested form escaped. The name is now spelled correctly. The Arrow Flight reset branch is not covered by a test: there is no functional-test harness for the Arrow Flight server, and the change there is the same three lines as its sibling value-assignment branch. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a settings-constraint bypass. A `SETTINGS` clause inside a subquery, a CTE or a view's inner query, `SET <name> = DEFAULT`, and a setting assigned or reset after a `profile` change in the same `SET` statement, now all enforce settings constraints, so none of them can be used to leave readonly mode or to override a `CONST`, `MIN` or `MAX` constraint. Note that a `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails, matching the behaviour of the old analyzer; use `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for such a view. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115397&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115397](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115397+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Bound the Cascades cluster node count by the distributed-read bucket limit
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): A very large `distributed_plan_workers_num` no longer makes the server abort with a `std::length_error` when the experimental `make_distributed_plan` and `enable_cascades_optimizer` are enabled. Such a node count is now rejected with `INVALID_SETTING_VALUE`. ### Description Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109770 That PR capped the sibling setting the same way. Found by `AST fuzzer (arm_asan_ubsan)`: [CI report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=105987&sha=58887a838b23240918d8f9e717a4bed777136134&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) (unrelated carrier PR). Reproduces deterministically: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t SETTINGS enable_cascades_optimizer = 1, make_distributed_plan = 1, distributed_plan_execute_locally = 1, distributed_plan_workers_num = 9223372036854775807; -- std::length_error in sliceMarksAcrossBuckets; the server dies in a debug build ``` `buildContext` resolves `cluster_node_count` from the internal query parameter, from `distributed_plan_workers_num`, or from the configured worker cluster, checking only for zero. The `ParallelRead` rule passes it through as the read's bucket count, and `sliceMarksAcrossBuckets` sizes a vector to it as its first statement, before the 256 ceiling already threaded in is consulted. `buildContext` now also rejects a resolved count above `max_distributed_read_buckets`, beside the existing zero check. Bounding the resolved value covers all three sources of the count and every consumer of it: the read buckets, the layer budget `FINAL` derives from them, and the exchange fan-out sized from the count. Not inside `sliceMarksAcrossBuckets`, which `FINAL` legitimately calls with `target_buckets * 16`-derived counts before grouping the layers into at most 256 tasks. Behaviour change: a count above 256 that did not reach the plain slicer (`257`, a `FINAL` read, or a worker cluster above 256 replicas) is planned today and is now refused. Such a plan reads serially but can still scatter to that many exchange destinations, which is the memory cost this same ceiling already bounds for the sibling settings. @ davenger, say so if you would rather bound the setting itself (a worker lease count) or clamp. `04320_distributed_plan_read_rejects.sql` gains seven arms: both sources of the count, both read paths, and three positive controls (256 accepted on the plain and `FINAL` paths, plus a rule-based query with a huge `workers_num` untouched). It fails on unpatched master with `server died`, and passed 50/50 runs with the fix. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115398&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115398](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115398+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support bearer-token authentication in BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP (attempt 2)
signals.text: Recreated from #110313 with the same changes. `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP` had no way to authenticate with a bearer token: callers spliced an `Authorization: Bearer` entry into the header list themselves and had to remember not to pass HTTP Basic credentials at the same time, because both occupy the same header. `create` now takes the credential directly, in three overloads: Basic credentials, a bearer token, or both — with a non-empty token taking precedence, so the either/or rule lives in one place instead of in every caller. `create` also appends the bearer header to a local copy of the header list rather than mutating the builder, so a builder can be reused without carrying over a stale token. Every bearer-token call site of the class is migrated to the new overloads: - `HTTPBasedCatalogUtils` and `UnityCatalog`: built the header by hand and passed never-used HTTP Basic credentials alongside; now call `create` with the token. - `RestCatalog`, `OneLakeCatalog`, `BigLakeCatalog`: `getAuthHeaders` now returns an `AuthHeaders` (a bearer token plus extra headers). The bearer goes to `create`; only genuine extra headers (a user-supplied `auth_header`, `x-goog-user-project`, `User-Agent`) stay in the header list. `OneLakeCatalog`'s pre-obtained token also moved from a spliced header to the bearer. - `PaimonRestCatalog`: the `bearer` token provider (the `dlf` request-signing branch keeps its own signed headers). Out of scope — different transport (plain Poco requests or S3-client headers), not `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP`: `OpenAIProvider`, `CloudJWTProvider`, ArrowFlight `AuthMiddleware`, GCS `diskSettings`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110313&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110313](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110313+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1702` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->
