signals.title: Fix has()/indexOf() zero-pad inconsistency for Array(FixedString)
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115311 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `has`/`indexOf` giving different results for `Array(FixedString)` depending on whether the array is a constant or a materialized column. Example: `has([toFixedString('V0', 3)], toFixedString('V0', 4))` was returning `0`, but the same check on a materialized array, or a plain `equals()`, returns `1`. Now both paths zero-pad `FixedString` values of different width the same way, so results are consistent. --- ### Problem `has`/`indexOf` on a constant array goes through `executeConst()` in `src/Functions/array/arrayIndex.h`. This function converts the array to `Array` (basically `std::vector<Field>`) and compares elements using `accurateEquals(Field, Field)`. The issue is `Field` does not have a separate type for `FixedString` -- it just becomes `Field::Types::String`. So once a `FixedString` value is put into a `Field`, there is no way to tell it apart from a normal `String`. And `accurateEquals` for `String` vs `String` is just plain `std::string` comparison, exact length only. No zero-padding. But the non-constant path (materialized array) works directly on `IColumn`/`ColumnFixedString`, and there zero-padding is applied correctly (same as `equals()` does, via `memcmpSmallLikeZeroPaddedAllowOverflow15`). So constant and non-constant paths give different answers for the same input. ### Fix Added a small helper `Impl::arrayIndexFieldsEqual()` in `arrayIndex.h`. It does zero-pad comparison for `Field`-level strings, but only if we already know from the *declared types* (before converting to `Field`) that one side is `FixedString`. This flag is computed once in `executeConst()` and passed down. Important: plain `String` vs `String` should NOT be zero-padded, that would be wrong behavior for normal strings. So the fix only kicks in when a `FixedString` type is actually involved. Note: `indexOfAssumeSorted` has a similar looking issue in its own binary search code (`Main::lowerBound`), but that function assumes the array is already sorted by the caller, which is a different contract, so not touching it here. Keeping this PR scoped to what the issue actually reports. ### Testing - Used a live tracer to confirm the actual code path changed, not just the output. After the fix, `accurateEquals` is not called anymore for the `FixedString` width-mismatch case (goes into new zero-pad branch instead). For plain `String` vs `String` (`has(['ab'], 'abc')`) it still calls `accurateEquals` like before -- so no unintended behavior change there. - Ran a matrix of 1791 generated cases covering different width/content combinations plus explicit `String`/`String` negative controls. Checked 4 things per case: constant result vs `materialize()`d result, constant result vs `arrayExists(x -> x = value, arr)` as ground truth, `indexOf` constant vs materialized, and `has` vs `indexOf` self-consistency. All 1791 cases passed, 0 mismatches. - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/04926_array_has_index_of_fixed_string_zero_pad.sql` covering the issue's repro, materialized/constant combinations in both directions, the `FixedString` vs `String` needle case, same-width negative controls, and `String`/`String` negative controls. Please review, happy to make changes if needed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115401&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115401](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115401+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Wait for the worker cleanup before force-killing the test workers
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113393 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description No related open issue; found while investigating `Stress test (*)` jobs failing with only ` script exit code: 1`. `do_run_tests` stops a run by SIGTERMing each worker and waiting `join(timeout=10)` before SIGKILLing it. That worker's SIGTERM path reaches `kill_process_group`, which on a sanitizer build sleeps **60** seconds, so every worker got 10 seconds for a 60 second cleanup and died inside that sleep. Two consequences. The sanitizer report is truncated, which is what the grace in `1a76ce9b81ce3fc` exists to collect. And `p.kill()` reaches only the worker, not the test's process group, whose PGID file is already unlinked, so the test's `bash` and `clickhouse-client` survive. When the stress harness's random query killer terminates that leaked client, the orphaned `bash` writes `Terminated` into the log file descriptor it inherited, after the parent moved on. If that lands while the job packages the logs, `tar` reports `file changed as we read it` and exits 1, and the job dies *before* the hung check. The wait is now derived from the delays that cleanup sleeps for, so the two cannot drift apart again, and `ddc6bcfbd68a761`'s escalation is unchanged: SIGTERM, bounded wait, SIGKILL, bounded wait. The sanitizer grace is one monotonic deadline shared by all workers, since they clean up concurrently, but no single wait drops below the previous 10 seconds. It is a ceiling, not a sleep, so a prompt worker is not delayed. Worst case is the grace plus 10 seconds a worker. Bounded to those sleeps, so not a guarantee: the stacktrace collection after them is not counted, uninterruptible sleep outlives any budget, and under `spawn` (`aarch` check names) there is no cleanup. A unit test pinning the budget to that delay was removed on review request, so the mechanism now rests on the CI runs that exercise the stop path. <details> <summary>Affected runs, validation, and interaction with #113393</summary> All four are sanitizer lanes over three weeks, `base_ref=master`. In each the worker log stops after the `SANITIZED`-gated print, never reaching the `Killing process group` after the sleep, and the archived log is 11 bytes short. Release and debug lanes, which skip that sleep, show none. - [`57ffb33`, PR 111575, `arm_asan_ubsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111575&sha=57ffb330ff3e3da66a99a2c8dfa6f4a49ffddc27&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29) - [`5639d68`, PR 107736, `arm_tsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=107736&sha=5639d68fe32623687d7dba60a6f72a58ffd1603b&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_tsan%29) - [`542bb86`, PR 112951, `arm_msan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112951&sha=542bb86022afb31800274d59fcd836d8c7dfc159&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_msan%29) - [`6e15957`, PR 114695, `amd_asan_ubsan`](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114695&sha=6e159579fc017f42673653cf0db45fc03ac9090d&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_asan_ubsan%29) Before the test was removed, eleven mutations each reddened it distinctly (flat 10 seconds, no `kill()` escalation, an unbounded wait, a sleep instead of a ceiling, a per-worker budget, either delay dropped from the sum, the floor removed, a wall-clock deadline, the call site reverted). End to end with real processes, the pre-change shape leaks the worker's `bash` and writes those 11 bytes 3/3; this change eliminates it 3/3. #113393 (mine, open) extracts this same sequence into `quiesce_workers_and_reap()` and keeps `p.join(timeout=10)` verbatim, relocating this defect without fixing it. They are complementary (that one reaps orphaned groups, this one stops creating them) but conflict textually. I can rebase onto it or fold this in there. </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115403&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115403](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115403+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.text: Support distributed `GROUPING SETS` aggregation in the Cascades optimizer. Follow-up to https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114950, which added it to the rule-based distributed planner; with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` such an aggregation stayed on a single node. - `TwoStageAggregationTransformation` accepts grouping-set aggregations: every worker builds partial states for every grouping set over its share of the data, and one node merges them per set. signals.title: TimeSeries: optional TTL'd recent samples table preferred by PromQL for short time ranges
signals.text: On a large `TimeSeries` table the most frequent queries — alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards — pay primary-key analysis over the whole multi-billion-row samples table and read one full granule per series: on a 71.4B-sample corpus a bare instant selector takes 0.85 s cold to return a few hundred points. When the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a fourth target table (`RECENT SAMPLES`) mimicking the samples table, plus an inner materialized view `.inner_id.recentsamplesmv.<uuid>` copying `id`, `timestamp`, `value` into it on every insert. The recent table adds `PARTITION BY` from `recent_samples_partition_by` (default `toDate(timestamp)`), `TTL toDateTime(timestamp) + toIntervalSecond(<ttl>)` with `ttl_only_drop_parts = 1`, and `recent_samples_index_granularity` (default 8192). PromQL selector reads (`prometheusQuery`, `prometheusQueryRange`, the HTTP API, remote read) prefer it whenever the selector's whole range fits in the TTL window (`min_time >= now() - TTL`) — safe because `ttl_only_drop_parts` drops a part only when all its rows have expired. The preference can be disabled with the new query setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. Off by default; not supported in `Replicated` databases yet (the inner materialized view would get a different UUID on every replica). Measured on a 71.4B-sample / 30-day / 413k-series corpus (40 PromQL queries, cold geomean vs the same binary without the feature): rules 5x (bare selector 0.85 s → 0.03 s, alert 1.9 s → 0.20 s), 30m dashboards 3.5-4.3x, 6h 1.4x, 24h 1.1x, overall 1.6-1.7x; results value-identical to 1e-15. A TTL of ~3 days is the sweet spot: it covers the intraday horizon including `offset 24h` panels at +10% disk, and avoids the regression seen with a 10d TTL, where 7d-range queries switch to the recent table and get 15% slower than on the single sorted part. Hourly partitioning is a wash overall and multiplies part count 24x, so day partitioning is the default. The cost is ingest: a fresh remote-write load of 1.3B samples slows from 324 s to 455-475 s (−30% throughput) — hence opt-in; a dedicated batched sink instead of the generic materialized-view chain is a possible follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TimeSeries` tables can now keep a "recent samples" table: when the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a TTL'd copy of the samples table (partitioned by `recent_samples_partition_by`, by day by default) fed by an inner materialized view, and PromQL queries whose time range fits in the TTL window automatically read from it, making alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards several times faster on large tables. The preference can be disabled with the new query-level setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115441&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115441](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115441+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Undo non-transactional removal marks when `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit` fails
signals.text: `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit` marks covered parts as removed before the `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE` that moves them to `Outdated`, because that marking can fail: a concurrent transaction may hold the removal lock, and storing `txn_version.txt` can fail on I/O. For a non-transactional commit nothing undid the marks that had already been written (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97211 fixed only the dangling lock part, not the marks), so those parts stayed `Active` with `removal_tid = Tx::NonTransactionalTID` and `removal_csn = Tx::NonTransactionalCSN`. After https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/92141 the lock is released inline and that lock cleanup became obsolete, yet the vector https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97211 introduced to collect the parts was still filled and never read. Such a part is inconsistent in several ways: * it is invisible to every transactional read while non-transactional reads still return its rows; * `TRUNCATE` skips it silently from then on; * `canBeRemoved` short-circuits to true for a non-transactional removal, so the part may be deleted as soon as anything moves it to `Outdated`, ignoring `old_parts_lifetime`; * if the part carries `txn_version.txt`, i.e. it was created or removed by a transaction, the inconsistency is persisted, survives a restart, and the part is then loaded as removed. The failure is reachable because `MergeTreeTransaction::rollback` restores the parts of a rolled-back removal to `Active` and only resets and unlocks their removal TID in a second loop, without holding the parts lock in between. A non-transactional `TRUNCATE` or `DROP PARTITION` covering such a part gets `SERIALIZATION_ERROR` in the middle of the loop, after earlier parts have already been marked. Track the covered parts that were marked and reset `removal_tid` and `removal_csn` for them if the loop throws. Only the non-transactional branch needs this: for transactions `MergeTreeTransaction::rollback` already resets and unlocks. The undo is best effort — every failure is logged per part, and the number of parts left inconsistent is appended to the propagated exception together with a pointer to `system.parts`. The second commit removes the `getActivePartsToReplace` call that was repeated inside `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE`. The parts lock is held for the whole of `commit`, and parts in `precommitted_parts` never cover each other, so the values computed before the scope stay valid and are now reused. That also removes a termination path, since `getActivePartsToReplace` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` for intersecting or duplicate parts and any exception inside `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE` reaches `std::terminate`. Two failpoints and two tests cover the two ways the marking loop can fail: `04838_truncate_and_drop_part_transaction_rollback_race` freezes a transaction rollback between restoring the parts and unlocking their removal TID, then checks that a concurrent `TRUNCATE` fails with `SERIALIZATION_ERROR` and leaves no part marked as removed; `04839_fail_to_remove_covered_part_in_the_middle_of_the_list` injects a failure after the first covered part of a merge has been marked. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a case where a failed non-transactional `TRUNCATE`, `DROP PARTITION` or merge left covered parts `Active` but marked as removed. Such parts were invisible to transactional reads while non-transactional reads still returned their rows, were silently skipped by later `TRUNCATE` queries, could be deleted ignoring `old_parts_lifetime`, and for parts carrying `txn_version.txt` the inconsistency survived a restart. This was only reachable when transaction were enabled. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/96023 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97211 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/92141 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115442&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115442](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115442+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix serialize_query_plan=1 requiring shard tables to exist on the initiator
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111893 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `serialize_query_plan = 1` failing with `UNKNOWN_DATABASE`/`UNKNOWN_TABLE` when a shard's table doesn't need to exist in the initiator's own catalog -- e.g. `remote('host:port', 'db', 'table')` where `db` only exists on the remote target, or a `Distributed` table relying on a per-shard `default_database` in the cluster config. Both cases now work the same under `serialize_query_plan = 0` and `= 1`. --- ### Problem `serialize_query_plan = 1` builds each shard's query plan on the initiator (to serialize and ship it), instead of shipping query text for the shard to resolve itself. `createLocalPlan` did this by constructing a fresh `InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer` from the raw query AST, which requires every referenced table to resolve in the initiator's own `DatabaseCatalog`. Two real cases where that's not true: 1. `remote('host:port', 'db', 'table')` where `db` only exists on the remote target, not the initiator. 2. A `Distributed` table declared with an empty database, relying on a per-shard `<default_database>` in the cluster config to fill it in at query time -- each shard's actual database (e.g. `shard_1`) may not exist on the initiator either. ### Fix `SelectStreamFactory::createForShardImpl` already receives an already-resolved `query_tree` (from the outer/initiator-level analysis) that it never threaded into `createLocalPlan`. Added an optional `query_tree` parameter; when present, `createLocalPlan` constructs `InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer` from the tree directly (no query tree passes applied) instead of re-resolving from the AST, avoiding local catalog lookup entirely for case 1. For case 2, the reused tree carries the empty-database placeholder baked into its `StorageDummy` from before any per-shard information was available. Added `fillInDefaultDatabaseForEmptyDatabaseTables`, which walks the tree and rebuilds a corrected `StorageDummy` using the shard's `default_database` -- the same pattern `replaceStorageInQueryTree` already uses elsewhere, but correcting the database on an existing table node instead of substituting a whole new storage. Also had to guard the existing `Context::setCurrentDatabase(default_database)` call (which asserts the database exists in the initiator's own catalog) to only run on the AST-based fallback path -- it was firing unconditionally and rejecting valid per-shard databases before the tree-based path even got a chance to run. ### Testing - Verified live against two real, separate ClickHouse server processes on different ports (not a self-referencing single-node trick) for case 1, and a genuine 2-shard cluster (real `shard_0`/`shard_1` databases on two separate server processes) for case 2. Both `serialize_query_plan = 0` and `= 1` now return byte-identical row content. - Confirmed no regression against a normal `Distributed` table with a real, fully-declared database. - Confirmed an unrelated fix in the same general code area (`ActionsDAG::serialize`-adjacent, from a separate PR) still works correctly after this change. - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/04928_serialize_query_plan_per_shard_default_database.sql` covering case 2, using the stock `test_cluster_two_shards_different_databases` cluster already defined in the test config. - Case 1 needs a genuinely separate server process (a different catalog), which the single-server `0_stateless` harness can't express -- not covered by an automated test in this PR, verified manually instead as described above. Happy to add an integration test if that's preferred. Please review, happy to make changes if needed.

signals.title: Iceberg: refresh the trusted table UUID on a reused metadata object
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115124 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99981 `Iceberg` metadata file *content* is cached in `IcebergMetadataFilesCache` under a key that includes the table's `table-uuid`. The UUID is in that key precisely to tell apart two different tables that occupy the same storage path at different times. It was captured once, when the `IcebergMetadata` object was first opened, and never refreshed: `IcebergMetadata::supportsUpdate` returns `true` while there was no `IDataLakeMetadata::update` override, so `DataLakeConfiguration::update` called the base no-op and the persistent components were never rebuilt. As a result the UUID failed in exactly the case it exists for. If an external writer drops and recreates the table at the same root with a new `table-uuid` and restarts the metadata numbering, a reused `IcebergMetadata` object probes the old key and is served the **previous** table's `metadata.json`, i.e. the previous schema and snapshot. ### The change The trusted UUID now lives in `Iceberg::TrustedTableUuid`, a `SharedMutex`-guarded cell shared by every copy of `PersistentTableComponents` describing the same table, so that struct's "thread-safe or immutable" contract still holds and a refresh is observed by all copies. All read and write call sites go through the new `PersistentTableComponents::getTableUuid` accessor. `IcebergMetadata::update` selects the current metadata file and, when the selected version does **not** strictly advance past the last validated one, re-reads that file's own `table-uuid` bypassing the UUID-keyed content cache. An Iceberg writer appending new metadata files advances the version strictly, so the extra read is skipped on the ordinary path and the cache behaves as before; a table recreated in place restarts the numbering and is caught. When the UUID does change, the latest-version cells under the previous UUID and under the table path are dropped — the content cells keyed by the previous UUID become unreachable once the trusted UUID moves, so ordinary eviction is enough for those. ### Trade-offs, stated explicitly - **A legitimate writer can move the version non-monotonically.** `iceberg_recent_metadata_file_by_last_updated_ms_field` selects by `last-updated-ms` and can pick a lower version, and snapshot expiry or rollback tooling can too. The gate is conservative in the safe direction: those cases only pay one extra uncached `metadata.json` read and still return correct data. - **A replacement can advance the version.** If a recreated table's writer happens to start at a version higher than the last validated one, the gate does not fire and the stale key is still used. Closing that would require revalidating on every `update`, which disables the metadata content cache on essentially every read. This is a bounded improvement, not a complete guarantee. - **Cost for a table whose version does not advance.** One extra uncached `metadata.json` `GET` per `update`. With the default `iceberg_metadata_staleness_ms = 0` the `metadata/` directory is listed on every query anyway, so this is a small marginal cost on top of work already being done. - `format_version` and `table_location` are still the values observed when the table was opened, and are not refreshed by `update`. That was already true before this change. ### Testing - `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/tests/gtest_iceberg_trusted_table_uuid.cpp` pins the revalidation gate and the thread-safe accessor. Built and run locally: 6/6 pass, and the 142 tests matching `*Iceberg*:*DataLake*:*ObjectStorage*` still pass. - `tests/integration/test_storage_iceberg_no_spark/test_table_replaced_in_place.py` reproduces the reported behaviour end to end: it warms the content cache, relocates a second, independently created Iceberg table's metadata onto the first table's root (leaving the first incarnation's data files in place, so a stale read returns the previous rows rather than raising), and asserts the new rows are returned. It also asserts the same with `use_iceberg_metadata_files_cache = 0` as a control. **This integration test has not been executed.** The development environment here has no ClickHouse server binary for Linux and cannot run the integration harness, so the test is unverified and relies on CI. The gtest results above were produced locally on a Debug macOS build. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Iceberg` tables serving a previous table's metadata from `IcebergMetadataFilesCache` when an external writer dropped and recreated the table at the same storage path. The `table-uuid` used as the metadata cache key is now refreshed instead of being pinned to the value observed when the table was opened.

signals.title: Nullable(Array) stages 1-2: type foundation and collision-free substream names
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115394 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 Stages 1 and 2 of the staged `Nullable(Array(T))` implementation described in the RFC, ClickHouse/ClickHouse#115394. Internal machinery only: **the type is still unreachable from any query**, and there is no user-visible change. `DataTypeFactory` continues to reject the string `Nullable(Array(UInt8))`, so this cannot be reached through DDL, a table function's column list, or any function that takes a type by name. That boundary is itself pinned by a test, so opening it in a later stage is a deliberate change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. The two stages ship together because Stage 1 alone has no production caller — `makeNullableAllowingArray` would land exercised only by unit tests. Stage 2 is the first thing that uses it. They are separate commits. ### Stage 1: the type-level foundation `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable` keeps returning `false`, permanently. That predicate is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and each encodes an assumption about which types can be wrapped. Leaving its meaning untouched means no existing code path can begin producing `Nullable(Array(...))` on its own; only code that explicitly opts in can. `makeNullableAllowingArray` is that opt-in and it is the only door — the constructor it uses is private, reachable through a single friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. The cost is that `canBeInsideNullable` now answers `false` for a type that can in fact sit inside `Nullable`. Two consequences are pinned by tests so they are deliberate rather than discovered later: `makeNullable` rejects an array, and `makeNullableSafe` silently returns the array unwrapped instead of throwing. The second is how a `Nullable(Array)` could be quietly degraded to `Array`; the sites where that matters are audited in a later stage. ### Stage 2: collision-free substream names `Nullable` appends `.null` to a stream name and `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1` and so on, while array *elements* contribute no component at all. A `Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))` column would write two different null maps to the same file. A second, structured naming scheme inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements, and is selected per column from the type as stored in the part: ```text Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.nested Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.null c.array.nested Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))) -> c.size0 c.array.null c.array.array.size0 c.array.array.nested.null c.array.array.nested Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c (unchanged) ``` Types legal today keep byte-identical names, so existing parts stay readable with no migration and no format version bump. ### Testing Expectations are derived from real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than hand-built substream paths. That distinction turned out to matter: `SerializationNullable` emits its null-map substream and pops it before recursing, so a path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs. The real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and the naming code branches on whether a null map precedes the final substream. Expectations written against constructed paths can be entirely self-consistent and still disagree with what is written to disk. The criteria are stated as properties over a corpus rather than as spot checks: - **No existing stream name changes.** Asserted as a proof rather than a sample: for 28 currently-legal types the structured scheme is never selected, neither by type nor by any enumerated path. If it is never reached then the legacy naming code is the only code that runs, and this change does not modify it. - **Typed and untyped callers agree** for every legal type, so a column cannot be written under one set of names and read under another. - **All names distinct** for thirteen shapes placing `Nullable(Array)` inside arrays, tuples, maps and variants — including their substream cache keys and their prefix/suffix substreams. - **Subcolumn reads resolve to files the writer produced.** 31 unit tests across the three suites; the full `unit_tests_dbms` suite is green at 22732 passed, 0 failed. ### Two things worth a reviewer's attention **The substream-to-name mapping existed in three places** — `getNameForSubstreamPath`, a full copy, and a partial per-element copy — and the full copy had already drifted: it was missing `MapBucketIndexes`, so a bucketed `Map` holding a `Nullable(Array)` would have lost that name component and could have written two streams under one file name. Both copies are gone, replaced by `ISerialization::getLegacyNameForSubstreamPath`. **The naming scheme cannot be decided from the substream path alone.** The path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The column type is load-bearing, and a caller that does not supply one cannot be answered correctly. Where the path proves a type was needed — `NullableElements` above an array substream can only come from a `Nullable` directly over an `Array` — resolving a name without one now raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than quietly returning a legacy name no writer produced. A test asserts this guard never fires for any currently-legal type. Ensuring every MergeTree caller passes the type is an explicit obligation for the next stage. ### Attribution The design and a substantial amount of the code originate in ClickHouse/ClickHouse#104816 by @zhanglistar, which was closed in favour of this staged implementation. Both commits carry a `Co-authored-by` trailer. The blocker analysis that shaped the design is @Avogar's, and the resolutions to it are @alexey-milovidov's. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115464&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115464](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115464+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Add only the required right keys when a join has several disjuncts
signals.text: A join with several disjuncts (`... ON a = b OR c = d`) added every right key column to its result, whether or not the query asked for it. With one disjunct the keys are split out of `sample_block_with_columns_to_add` and put back only where the query needs them, restored from the left key column - the same value, under an equality. With several disjuncts that restoration is invalid: a row matched through another clause has a right key of its own. That is a reason to *read* a key when it is asked for, not a reason to *add* it when it is not - and the plan drops those columns immediately after the join with a `ColumnPermuteTransform`. So keep the keys the query asks for and add nothing else. `TableJoin::requiredRightKeys` already tracks them and the planner fills it in `setUsedColumns`; without the analyzer nothing fills it, so there every key is kept, exactly as before. `right_table_keys` stays whole either way, so the stored right blocks - and a mixed `ON` condition evaluated against them - are untouched. For `SELECT count() FROM l ALL LEFT JOIN r ON l.a = r.a OR l.b = r.b` the join used to emit `__table2.a` and `__table2.b` for every result row, and the permutation threw them away; now it emits neither. It is not measurable on a 20M x 5M join (892 vs 903 ms with four disjuncts), so this is worth having for the work it removes and for what it unblocks, not as a speedup - no performance test is added for that reason. What it unblocks: the key-only join hash tables of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115301 are chosen for `LEFT SEMI` only when the join produces no right value at all, which with several disjuncts could never be true. `LEFT ANTI` already qualifies there; `LEFT SEMI` starts to once this lands. A new test covers what the pruning must not change: with `ON a = a OR b = b` a row matched through the second clause has an unrelated right `a`, and that value still has to reach the result whenever it is selected - across `ALL`/`ANY`/`SEMI`/`ANTI` and `LEFT`/`INNER`/`RIGHT`/`FULL`, with a non-joined right row, a residual condition, and `join_use_nulls`. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115301 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115465&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115465](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115465+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Do not strip injective functions that hide argument nullability inside uniq
signals.text: `optimize_injective_functions_inside_uniq` stripped any injective function from a `uniq*` argument, on the grounds that an injective function preserves the number of distinct values. That holds for the values, but not for the rows the aggregate sees: `AggregateFunctionFactory::get` wraps `uniq*` in the `Null` combinator when an argument is `Nullable`, and that combinator skips the rows where the argument is NULL. An injective function whose result type cannot be `Nullable` hides the nullability of its argument, so removing it turns "count every row" into "skip the NULL rows": ```sql SELECT uniqExact(tuple(x)) FROM values('x Nullable(Int32)', 1, 2, NULL); -- 2 before this change; 3 with the optimization disabled, and 3 now ``` The pass now keeps a function whenever removing it would change the argument's nullability. The affected functions are `tuple`, `bitmaskToArray` and `bitPositionsToArray` (the injective ones whose result type cannot be `Nullable`, so `makeNullableSafe` leaves it off); the affected aggregates are `uniq`, `uniqExact`, `uniqHLL12` and `uniqTheta`. `uniqCombined` and `uniqCombined64` were already protected, because the `Null` combinator changes their result type to `Nullable(UInt64)` and the pass rejects that. This also removes a discrepancy the same rewrite caused between expressions that differ only in being constant-foldable, reported in the issue: `countDistinct(tuple(NULL))` is folded into a `ConstantNode` and so escaped the pass, while `countDistinct(tuple(arrayJoin([NULL])))` did not. All the variants return 1 now. With `enable_analyzer = 0` the same rewrite runs in `TreeOptimizer` before types are resolved, so the nullability cannot be checked there and the old results stand; the test is tagged `no-old-analyzer`. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114784 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `uniq`, `uniqExact`, `uniqHLL12` and `uniqTheta` returning a wrong result for an argument wrapped in an injective function that hides nullability, such as `uniqExact(tuple(x))` over a `Nullable` column. The `optimize_injective_functions_inside_uniq` optimization removed the wrapping function, after which NULL rows were skipped instead of counted. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115466&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115466](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115466+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix UniqueKeyProbeTest.NewestLiveWinsOverOlder aborting unit_tests_dbms in Debug builds
signals.text:
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115405 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106422 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114469 ## The problem `UniqueKeyProbeSimple::probeBatch` validates the "a live key lives in <= 1 part" invariant when `probe_validates_single_live_part` is on: rather than early-skipping a key once it resolves live, debug builds probe every part for every key and throw `LOGICAL_ERROR` on a second live hit. `UniqueKeyProbeTest.NewestLiveWinsOverOlder` sets up key `5` as live in **two** parts, which is precisely the state that invariant forbids. In release builds the early-skip fires and the second live hit is never observed, so the test passes. In Debug builds it is observed, and the `LOGICAL_ERROR` aborts the whole `unit_tests_dbms` process — so every test registered after it silently never runs. ## Why CI never saw it `unit_tests_dbms` is only built and run in the ASan+UBSan, TSan, MSan and LLVM-coverage flavors. All four configure with `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=None`, which the top-level `CMakeLists.txt` rewrites to `RelWithDebInfo`, so `NDEBUG` is defined and the check is compiled out. The two Debug flavors (`amd_debug`, `arm_debug`) do compile the unit tests but publish only the `clickhouse` binary — no job consumes a Debug `unit_tests_dbms`. The abort is therefore reachable only from a local Debug build. ## Which side is wrong The invariant. It was added as review fix M8 in `89bcecefacd`, at the reviewer's request on https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106422, with the stated rationale that "a row should be present only in a single part of the snapshot". It is backed by the guard layer that keeps data in a state where it holds: merges disabled, and mutations, `ALTER ... PARTITION`, projections, TTL and lightweight updates all rejected on `UNIQUE KEY` tables. `MergeTreeData::supportsLightweightUpdate` rejects lightweight updates specifically because they would "produce duplicate live keys". The test predates the gate (both were written in the same PR, six weeks apart) and was never updated. Note also that once the invariant holds, traversal order is not observable at all — with at most one live occurrence the result is that row regardless of walk order, so "newest live wins over older live" can only be demonstrated by violating the invariant. That is why the fixture had to build forbidden state. ## The change Test-only; the production gate is left exactly as is. - `NewestLiveWinsOverOlderDead` replaces `NewestLiveWinsOverOlder`, marking the older occurrence bitmap-dead. It preserves the original intent — the newest live row wins, an older part must not override it — while respecting the invariant. It also pins something the old test did not: the Debug walk continues after a key resolves, and a later dead hit must not downgrade the resolved `FOUND_LIVE` to `FOUND_ALL_DEAD`. - `UniqueKeyProbeDeathTest.DuplicateLiveKeyAcrossPartsIsRejected` adds coverage for the invariant check itself. The `LOGICAL_ERROR` aborts rather than propagating, so it cannot be caught with `EXPECT_THROW`; it is a death test, mirroring `ColumnArrayDeathTest.NonMonotonicOffsetsAreRejected` (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114469), which fixed the same class of problem. It is guarded on `#ifndef NDEBUG` to match the gate rather than `DEBUG_OR_SANITIZER_BUILD`, since the throw only happens when the gate is on. The death test attaches a stderr channel to the root logger from inside the `EXPECT_DEATH` statement: `abortOnFailedAssertion` reports through `Poco::Logger::root` and `LOG_IMPL` drops the record when no channel is attached, so this guarantees the matcher has the message to match. Keeping it inside the statement means it runs only in the death-test child — the parent process takes the overseer role and skips the statement — so no global logger state leaks into subsequent tests. ## Caveats Not compile-verified locally: this environment has all 141 submodules uninitialized and no ccache/ninja, so building `unit_tests_dbms` was not feasible. The `amd_tidy` and `arm_tidy` jobs do configure with `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug`, `ENABLE_TESTS=1` and an explicit `-UNDEBUG`, so CI does compile the `#ifndef NDEBUG` branch even though no job runs it. The reduction's control flow was verified separately by transcribing the `probeBatch` loop into a standalone program and compiling it with and without `NDEBUG` — the old fixture throws under `-UNDEBUG` and returns row 9 under `-DNDEBUG`, the new one returns row 9 in both, and no neighbouring test in the file changes behaviour. Because the new death test is `#ifndef NDEBUG`, it will not run in any current CI job — the same gap that hides the original bug. That is expected: the check it covers does not exist in the builds CI runs the unit suite with. ## Open question for the reviewers @Michicosun — the gate uses `#ifndef NDEBUG`, while the abort it depends on keys on `DEBUG_OR_SANITIZER_BUILD`. Was "in debug builds" in the original review comment meant to include sanitizer builds? Widening the gate would give the invariant real unit-test CI coverage, but it has to happen after this fix, since today it would turn the abort into red ASan/TSan/MSan builds. Happy to follow up with that change if it is wanted. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ...

signals.title: Perf: Optimize PromQL unless for exact groups
signals.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL `unless` expressions with an exact group key skip redundant matching stages. ## What changed - add an **exact-group fast path** for the PromQL set operator `unless` - use it when both inputs already dropped `__name__`, there is no `on(...)`, and `ignoring()` is empty or absent - join the unique left and right `VECTOR_GRID` inputs directly on `group` - remove the RHS `GROUP BY`, `countForEach`, and transformed `join_group` work from this path - preserve the full LHS array when the RHS group is missing - preserve each LHS sample when the matching RHS sample is NULL - keep `on(...)`, `on()`, non-empty `ignoring(...)`, and other transformed matching keys on the existing general path ## Why this is safe `VECTOR_GRID` guarantees one row per `group`. The fast path is enabled only when the matching rules leave the original `group` column unchanged on both sides, so the join key is already unique and exact. The RHS projection adds a literal group-present marker. This keeps a missing RHS row distinct from a real RHS row whose values are NULL at some timestamps. The exact path then applies the same element-wise `unless` behavior as the existing lowering. The generic path is unchanged for matching rules that transform or collapse the group key. Empty `ignoring()` is treated like default matching when both inputs already have exact groups. ## Benchmark fixture `tests/performance/promql_set_operators_unless.xml` uses the same workload as the related set-operator benchmarks: - 8,000 series - 4,000 matching groups - 300 samples per series - exact-group `unless` compared with an equivalent `unless on(instance)` control The default query uses the new fast path. signals.title: Add with_source parameter to the JSON type storing the JSON text in the __source sub-column
signals.text: ## Motivation Reading a whole `JSON` value as a `String` (`toString(json)`, or just selecting the column in a text format) is expensive: it reads every sub-column of the JSON column — all typed paths, all dynamic paths and the shared data structure — and constructs the JSON object back for every row. Applications that store JSON documents and ship them back verbatim pay this on every query. ## What was added The `JSON` type accepts a new parameter `with_source`. A column declared as `JSON(with_source=1)` additionally stores the JSON text of each row in a separate `String` sub-column `__source`: ```sql CREATE TABLE test (json JSON(with_source=1)) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY tuple(); INSERT INTO test VALUES ('{"b" : "Hello", "a" : 42}'); SELECT json, json.__source FROM test; ``` ``` ┌─json─────────────────┬─json.__source─────────────┐ │ {"a":42,"b":"Hello"} │ {"b" : "Hello", "a" : 42} │ └──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┘ ``` Reading `json.__source` reads a single sub-column. The new setting `output_format_json_type_use_source` makes text output of such a column write the stored text instead of constructing it from the object (it saves the construction, not the reading of the column). The text is stored exactly as it was inserted. Where the original text is not available it is created from the object itself, so the sub-column always contains valid JSON: values restored from an aggregation or `JOIN` key, binary input without the JSON text (structured `RowBinary`), nested `JSON(with_source=1)` type hints (only the top level column gets the original text), and results of functions creating JSON objects such as `mergedJSONPatch`. `__source` is reserved in such types: a top level JSON key with this name is rejected during parsing, and the name cannot be used as a type hint or in the `SKIP` section. Nested keys with this name are fine. Adding or removing the parameter with `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN` always rewrites the data. The stored text is not a part of the value: it doesn't participate in comparison, so two values with the same content but different formatting stay equal and are grouped together. ## Implementation notes - The text is stored in a separate `String` column inside `ColumnObject` and serialized into its own named `ObjectSource` sub-stream, so `json.__source` is a static sub-column resolved the same way a named tuple element is. The sub-stream exists in all `Object` serialization versions except `STRING`, where the JSON text is the payload itself, and no `Object` serialization version was bumped. - In binary type encoding the JSON type version is bumped to `1`, and version `1` is written only for types that actually have `with_source=1`, so encodings of all other types stay byte-identical and readable by older servers. - `ColumnObject` keeps its type to create the text when the original is not available; the serialization for it is built lazily on first use, so nothing is built for columns that never need it. - The aggregation key representation (`serializeValueIntoArena`) deliberately stays canonical, i.e. it doesn't include the text; otherwise values differing only in formatting would form different `GROUP BY` groups while comparison says they are equal. ## Limitations - Text created from the object is written without the settings used during parsing, so with `json_type_escape_dots_in_keys` enabled keys with dots appear in it escaped (`{"a%2Eb" : 42}`). - `Native` in JSON-as-string mode transmits the constructed text unless `output_format_json_type_use_source` is set. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added the `with_source` parameter to the `JSON` data type. A column declared as `JSON(with_source=1)` additionally stores the JSON text of each row in the reserved `__source` `String` sub-column, so reading the whole value as a string is a single sub-column read instead of reading every path and constructing the JSON back. The new setting `output_format_json_type_use_source` makes text output of such columns write the stored text. The text is kept as it was inserted; where the original text is not available (for example for values restored from an aggregation key) it is created from the object, so the sub-column always contains valid JSON. A top level JSON key named `__source` is not allowed in such types. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115477&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115477](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115477+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Make submodule cache upload write-once to fix ETag download race
signals.text: Makes the submodule cache upload write-once to fix an S3 ETag download race. The submodule cache object is content-addressed by the submodule SHAs, so it never legitimately changes. Previously `_prepare_submodule_cache` uploaded it with an unconditional overwrite after a racy `head_object` existence check. Two workflow runs that both observed a cache miss could overwrite the same key while another job was downloading it. Because boto3's `download_file` validates ETag consistency across its ranged `GET`s, the reader aborted with: ``` ERROR: Failed to download S3 object [.../submodules/<hash>.tar.zst]: Contents of stored object "..." in bucket "..." did not match expected ETag. WARNING: Submodule cache download failed, will clone from GitHub ``` That failed the cache restore and forced a fallback GitHub clone, which could itself fail and fail the whole build (e.g. the `Checkout Submodules` stage). The fix switches the upload to a write-once conditional create via `S3.put(..., if_none_matched=True)` (`aws s3api put-object --if-none-match "*"`). The object becomes immutable, so a downloader can never observe an ETag flip mid-transfer. On a lost race the put returns `False` (`PreconditionFailed`) — the other writer already populated the object, which is treated as success rather than an error. The existing `head_object` fast-path and the reader-side ETag fallback are kept as defense in depth. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115478&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115478](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115478+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Modularize the adaptive aggregation, weigh its thaw by staged bytes, and add the freeze-bytes and bucket-top-K settings
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111459 Restructuring of the adaptive aggregation, plus one behavioral improvement the new structure enabled and two new settings. ### Refactoring (no behavior change) - **The block-to-staged-chunk conversion is a separate component**: `StagedChunkBuilder` in `AdaptiveAggregationStaging.{h,cpp}` owns the recorded misses, the counting sort into bucket slices, the count dedup, and the seal coalescing, and emits through an `IStagedChunkSink`. The builder knows nothing about the aggregator, so a future consumer of bucket-grouped records (e.g. a grace-style join) can reuse the representation without pulling in the aggregation machinery. - **Staged chunks travel as pipeline data instead of side-channel state**: each producing `AggregatingTransform` emits sealed chunks through its output port, and a new `AdaptiveAggregationMergeTransform` (its own processor files) absorbs them as the backlogs' only writer, uses the closed producer ports as the finish barrier, and assembles the merge. The flow is now visible in `EXPLAIN PIPELINE` and pinned by a test. - **The drain side mirrors the build side**: `StagedChunkDrainer` (merge-time and pressure-time consumption, bucket retirement) consumes chunks through a `StagedSliceApplier` — a narrow inline contract (create states, apply instructions to a contiguous slice) that is the drain's entire dependency on the aggregator. - **The adaptation decisions are rule objects that own their state and constants**: `LearningState::decide` (freeze / give-up), `FrozenState::recordProbeSample` (probe bypass), `ThawSampler` (the global thaw). `Aggregator::executeOnBlock` shrinks to phase hooks; adding an adaptation no longer grows the kernels. - **One entity per file**: `AdaptiveAggregationSession.{h,cpp}`, `AdaptiveAggregationProducer.h`, `AdaptiveAggregationDrain.{h,cpp}`, the processor files, and an updated architecture comment describing the pipeline topology. ### Behavioral change: the thaw verdict is weighted by bytes The thaw previously fired on the staged stream's repeat factor alone (> 12). That misses streams that repeat keys only a few times but drag wide payloads with every staged record. The verdict is now *wasted staged bytes per distinct key*: `(repeat factor − 1) × bytes per record > 300` — a key's first record is the price of storing-it-once; every repeat is bytes the baseline would have absorbed as an in-place update. Near-unique streams measure ~0 by construction and cannot fire; light count records tolerate high repeats; heavy-column streams stand down early in proportion to the damage. Renamed the verdict vocabulary accordingly (`adaptive_staging_wasteful`, `WastefulStagedStream`). Measured on `hits` (100M) (off → on, 16/64 threads): - `SELECT URL, min(Title) GROUP BY URL` (90-byte string key): 0.83×/0.73× → **0.99×/1.01×** - `SELECT UserID, min(URL) GROUP BY UserID` (heavy argument, +121% peak RSS before): 0.83×/0.59× → **0.97×/1.00×**, peak RSS 14.5 → 6.3 GB (matching the ordinary path) ### New settings - **`adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold_bytes`** (default 4 MiB): the byte twin of the key-count freeze threshold — a thread's local table freezes at whichever bound is reached first. Measured as the local table's own allocated bytes (hash-table buffer plus arenas), checked between blocks like the baseline's conversion thresholds; deliberately not the query-wide tracked memory, which would freeze all the locals off each other's growth. At the default it is a guardrail: calibration on the heaviest shapes shows ordinary tables keep freezing by key count (e.g. `WatchID, min(URL)`: 14 of 16 locals unchanged, two freeze earlier by bytes, at 15582 and 8192 keys), and a full ClickBench `GROUP BY` sweep of default vs `0` is noise (geomeans 1.001 / 1.007 at 16 / 64 threads). - **`query_plan_aggregation_bucket_top_k`** (default true): a dedicated toggle for the bucket top-K conversion. The contract is worded generally (`ORDER BY` over the aggregation's outputs with `LIMIT n`, gated on provable exactness) so the planned generalization beyond the lone `count()` and a single sort column extends the rule, not the setting. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The adaptive `GROUP BY` aggregation (`enable_adaptive_aggregator`) now measures whether deferring rare keys pays off and returns to the ordinary algorithm when their keys or aggregate arguments are too wide to copy profitably, so aggregations over heavy string columns (e.g. `min(URL)` per user) run at the ordinary algorithm's speed and memory. Adds `adaptive_aggregator_freeze_threshold_bytes` to bound each thread's frozen table in bytes (whichever of it and the key-count threshold is reached first freezes the table), and `query_plan_aggregation_bucket_top_k` to toggle the top-N aggregation optimization. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115480&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115480](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115480+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Use the primary key index for first-tuple-element conditions and `pointInEllipses`
signals.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54805 Follow-up to #112956, which taught `KeyCondition` to use the primary key index for `pointInPolygon(coord, [...])` with a `Point` key column. This PR closes the remaining gaps of the same shape: 1. **Conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column** (`coord.1 < 100`, `tupleElement(coord, 1) = 5`, or access by element name for named tuples) now use the primary key index. Tuple values are ordered lexicographically, so the first element is a non-strictly monotonic function of the tuple; it is analyzed through the regular monotonic-functions chain (`FunctionFirstTupleElementOfKey`), so composed chains such as `coord.1 + 1 <= N` and `NOT` also work. Other elements are not monotonic w.r.t. the tuple order and remain unanalyzed. 2. **`pointInEllipses(x, y, x0, y0, a, b, ...)`** over key columns now uses the primary key (and minmax) index. The analysis stores the union bounding box of the ellipses as a rectangle ring and reuses the existing `pointInPolygon` evaluation unchanged, in both the regular and the lightweight analysis paths. The box follows the function's exact semantics: an ellipse with a non-positive or `NaN` parameter matches no point (the function's own bounding-box check never passes for it); if all ellipses are empty, the condition folds to `ALWAYS_FALSE`; a non-finite box declines the analysis. The atom only ever reports `{maybe, maybe}` or `{no match, maybe}`, so `NOT pointInEllipses` stays correct. 3. **`pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), ...)` and `pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, ...)`** — the point written as the two elements of one tuple-typed key column — resolve to the single-key-column form from #112956, deriving the point's bounding box from the range of the tuple key column. Previously this natural rewrite silently disabled the index. ```sql CREATE TABLE points (coord Point) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY coord; INSERT INTO points SELECT (number, number) FROM numbers(100000); SELECT count() FROM points WHERE coord.1 <= 25000; -- Before: 100000 rows read (full scan). After: 26/100 granules. SELECT count() FROM points WHERE pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, 0., 0., 5000., 5000.); -- Before: full scan. After: 6/100 granules. ``` Note: the reference outputs of the two new tests were computed analytically (counts from the data distribution, granule counts from `index_granularity = 1000`); if CI reports a formatting difference in the `EXPLAIN` lines, I will update the references from the CI output. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Use the primary key index for conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `coord.1 < 100` for a table ordered by a `Point` column), for `pointInEllipses` over key columns, and for `pointInPolygon`/`pointInEllipses` with the point written as the two elements of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), [...])`). Follow-up to [#112956](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115482&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115482](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115482+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Resolve the default time zone from an absolute `TZ` path outside `TZDIR`
signals.text: If `TZ` contains an absolute path or is not set and the requested file is not inside the `TZDIR` directory, try to resolve the time zone id as the longest suffix recognized by the embedded time zone database. If the parent dir of the found suffix is `right`, the file is rejected as we assume that it contains leap seconds and such files are not supported. `glibc` ignores `TZDIR` when `TZ` is an absolute path, so this behavior is more aligned with `glibc` than failing to resolve at all. If we fail to resolve the time zone id, the reported error message now also contains the time zone database directory that was used. The embedded database is used as the oracle rather than `TZDIR` to avoid dependency on `TZDIR` if `TZ` contains an absolute path. It also doesn't need filesystem access and yields ids that `DateLUTImpl` is able to load. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/86495 ### Out of scope A `TZ` value that cannot be resolved still throws while initializing the `DateLUT` singleton, which terminates the process at startup. Matching `glibc` more closely would mean degrading to UTC with a clear warning for the operator; that is a separate behavioural change. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The default time zone is now also determined when the `TZ` environment variable holds an absolute path to a time zone file located outside the time zone database directory (`TZDIR`). The time zone id is now recovered from the longest suffix of the path that names a time zone in the embedded time zone database. Files under a `right/` directory are rejected explicitly, since they are assumed to be encoded with leap seconds, which are not supported. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115483&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115483](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115483+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Stop resolving the UTC time zone in `TimezoneMixin`
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> While profiling `clickhouse local --query "SELECT 1"` it turned out that almost all of the run happens before the query: the query itself took 1ms of a 45ms run. This is one of the sources of that startup work, split out of #112496. `TimezoneMixin` resolved the UTC time zone in its constructor, in addition to the named or default one. Building a `DateLUTImpl` walks ~146k days through cctz, about 70M instructions, and `DataTypeDateTime` / `DataTypeDateTime64` get constructed just to name a column type — for example when building the schemas of the system tables — without ever touching UTC. Only the serializations need UTC, for ISO output and for the `best_effort` parsers, so `SerializationDateTime`, `SerializationDateTime64` and the `DateTime` / `DateTime64` nodes of `JSONExtractTree` declare their own `utc_time_zone` member instead. The cost is then paid once per formatter rather than once per named type. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Naming a `DateTime` or `DateTime64` type no longer builds a UTC time zone lookup table that nothing reads, which makes constructing these types — and therefore starting up `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` — faster. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115488&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115488](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115488+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Resolve the client hostname in `ClientInfo` on demand
signals.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> Split out of #112496. `ClientInfo::fillOSUserHostNameAndVersionInfo` resolved the local FQDN through `getFQDNOrHostName`, a blocking `getaddrinfo` that also dlopens the NSS modules. Every `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` invocation paid for it even when nothing ever asked for the name, and a resolver that is slow or unreachable sat on the startup path with no short timeout. `getClientHostName` resolves it on first use instead, and `getFQDNOrHostName` caches process-wide, so the readers — `system.processes`, `query_log`, `session_log` and the TCP handshake — see the same value as before. When the name arrives from a peer in `ClientInfo::read` it describes that peer rather than us, so it is kept as received and never re-resolved locally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The client hostname is now resolved when it is first reported instead of on every `clickhouse client` and `clickhouse local` invocation. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115491&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115491](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115491+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Support safe type conversions in correlated subquery equivalence substitution
signals.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113407 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101863 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Correlated subqueries with an equality on columns that differ only in nullability (e.g. `Int64` vs `Nullable(Int64)` under `data_type_default_nullable = 1`, as in TPC-DS Q35), or on native-number columns having a least common type (e.g. `Int32` vs `Int64`), are now decorrelated via equivalent-expression substitution instead of falling back to a CROSS JOIN with a post-join filter, avoiding severe memory growth on such queries. Closes #113407. --- ## Motivation The equivalent-expression substitution in `PlannerCorrelatedSubqueries` recorded an equivalence only when both sides of the correlated `equals` had exactly the same type. A correlated `EXISTS` whose join condition compares `Int64` with `Nullable(Int64)` therefore decorrelated through the CROSS JOIN fallback; at TPC-DS SF100 (Q35 with `data_type_default_nullable = 1`) the cross-joined intermediate grew without bound (35+ GiB and climbing before being killed, versus 1.72 s / 1.70 GiB with aligned column types). ## Approach The exact-type guard was load-bearing: correlated columns are `PLACEHOLDER` nodes typed with the outer column's type, and every decorrelated DAG declares that type for its inputs, so a substituted column of a different runtime type is a logical error during execution. The substitution therefore cannot simply alias a column of another type, nor cast to the common supertype — it must produce exactly the placeholder's type. Equivalence classes now track `(column name, type)` pairs. The recording guard admits, besides equal types, two verified-safe families: - nullability-only differences (any base type) — the equality predicate rejects `NULL`s; - native-number pairs with a least supertype — for them `equals` is mathematically exact (`9007199254740993 :: Int64 = 9007199254740992.0 :: Float64` is `0`), the supertype exists only when every type embeds losslessly, and `accurateCastOrNull` is exactness-checking, so value equivalence is transitive across a class. At substitution the chosen equivalent column is converted to exactly the correlated type: `toNullable` / lossless `CAST` when widening, `assumeNotNull` / `accurateCastOrNull` when narrowing. For the narrowing conversions a `FilterStep` is inserted below the renaming that drops rows whose value is `NULL` or does not convert exactly — such rows can never satisfy the recorded equality (a top-level AND-conjunct of an ancestor filter), and dropping them before `assumeNotNull` is required so that its arbitrary result for non-converting values cannot leak into aggregation keys (the aggregation decorrelation appends correlated identifiers as group keys). Pairs whose comparison semantics are not consistent with `CAST` keep the previous CROSS JOIN fallback: `Decimal` vs `Float` (comparison converts to `Float` and is inexact), `String` vs `FixedString` (comparison ignores padding), and supertype-less numeric pairs such as `Int64` vs `UInt64` or `Int64` vs `Float64`. ## Verification - The issue's reproducer plans with zero `cross` nodes and returns the same result as the fallback. - New stateless test `05023_correlated_subquery_equivalence_type_conversion` (12 cases: both nullability directions, widening/narrowing/sideways/float numerics with adversarial boundary values, scalar-subquery aggregation with an outer `0` vs inner `NULL`, guarded fallbacks) passed 6/6 runs under harness setting randomization. - A cross-check over 16 type pairs compared `EXISTS` / `NOT EXISTS` / scalar `count()` results between substitution and the CROSS JOIN fallback on value pools with boundary values (`2^31±1`, `2^32±1`, `2^53`, `2^53+1`, non-integer floats) and `NULL`s — identical everywhere, and plan probes confirmed the substitution fires exactly for the admitted pairs. - The existing `correlated` stateless subset passes (3 environment-only failures in the local scratch setup: MinIO, test cluster, writable access storage). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115493&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115493](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115493+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signals.title: Fix geoToH3 accepting float types it cannot execute
signals.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101813 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/101813 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `geoToH3` declared that it accepts any float type but only executes `Float64`, so a `Float32` or `BFloat16` coordinate was rejected late with a message naming the wrong argument position and the wrong type. Such arguments are now rejected during analysis with the correct position and type. Closes #101813. ### Description `geoToH3` validated its coordinates with `isFloat` (`Float32 | Float64 | BFloat16`) while `executeImpl` binds them with `checkAndGetColumn<ColumnFloat64>`. A `Float32` argument therefore passed analysis and failed in a runtime check whose argument index is hardcoded for the legacy `geotoh3_argument_order = 'lon_lat'`. Under the default `lat_lon` both the reported position and type were wrong, and because the type was read off that hardcoded index the message named the other, valid argument: ``` SELECT geoToH3(toFloat32(55.71), toFloat64(37.79), toUInt8(15)); -- was (44): Illegal type Float64 of argument 2 of function geoToH3. Must be Float64. -- now (43): ... as 1st argument 'latitude' ... Expected: Float64, got: Float32 ``` I narrowed both coordinate descriptors to exact `Float64` in both order branches, restoring the check this function had before 5340c88271a4f4f. `validateFunctionArguments` is already order-aware, so position, argument name and both types are now correct in all four slots; `lon_lat` reported the right position before and still does. No query that runs today stops running, since no `Float32` or `BFloat16` call to `geoToH3` succeeds, so no `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` entry applies. Rejection does move into analysis, so a stored `MATERIALIZED geoToH3(f32, f64, 15)` is now refused during DDL validation rather than at insert time. Such a column could never be computed, so this surfaces an already-broken definition earlier. The two runtime index expressions are corrected as defence in depth; narrowing makes them unreachable, so I claim no test coverage for that half. `s2CapUnion` has the same mismatch but a fixed argument order, so its indices are correct. The new shell test asserts position, argument name and both types for each coordinate slot under both setting values, plus `BFloat16` and a `Float64` case that must still succeed. A `serverError` annotation would check only the code, which passes unfixed. Verified red without the change and green with it over 50 randomized runs. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115503&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115503](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115503+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115503&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115503](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115503+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115227 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description Related: #115227 The test added by #115227 used `unnest`, a case-insensitive alias of `arrayJoin` registered only since `8601d0ff817f` (2026-05-16), after the 25.8 and 26.3 branch points. Both backports to those branches fail the test with `Code: 46 ... Function with name 'unnest' does not exist`, while the `src/Planner` fix itself cherry-picks cleanly. It is worse than one red arm: all 19 statements of the main block are in a single client call, so the abort at statement 2 skipped statements 3-19, including all four `EXPLAIN` plan assertions. On those branches the test verified nothing. This drops the two `unnest` arms from 04743 and relocates the alias coverage into `04241_alias_unnest`, which is absent from exactly the branches that lack the alias. Nothing is weakened: `FunctionNode::resolveAsFunction` stores the canonical name, so at the guard (`hasFunctionNode(aggregates.front(), "arrayJoin")`) the two arms were indistinguishable - measured, the surviving 20 reference lines are byte-identical with and without them. `04241` gains a MergeTree trivial-count arm with an `= 0` control that reddens on its own fixture when the guard is deleted. Validated on the backports' own CI binaries (release branch plus the guard), both directions on the same binary: fails on 25.8/26.3 before, byte-equal to the reference after, with the 17 skipped assertions now executing and agreeing. 26.5/26.6/26.7 stay byte-equal. On master both tests pass `clickhouse-test`, 200/200 randomized and non-randomized, and deleting the guard reddens 7 of 04743's assertions. This does not turn the already-open backports green: each is built from the parent's frozen merge commit and #115227 is labelled `pr-backports-created`, so it is not re-processed. It fixes the file for any re-created backport and for future PRs touching it.
