signal.title: Add `user_files_policy` server setting for custom disks in user_files directory
signal.text: Add a new `user_files_policy` server configuration parameter, similar to `tmp_policy`, that allows user files to reside on custom storage volumes, including S3-backed disks. When configured, the policy's volume (which must have exactly one volume) provides the disks for user file storage. All file operations (`file()` table function, `StorageFile`, dictionaries, `DatabaseFilesystem`, etc.) now route through the `IDisk` interface when a volume is configured, enabling S3 and other remote storage backends. Key changes: - `user_files_policy` setting in `ServerSettings` with XML config example - `Context` stores `VolumePtr` and exposes `getUserFilesVolume`, `getUserFilesPaths`, `setUserFilesPolicy` - `StorageFile` supports disk-based glob matching via `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingOnDisk`, disk-based reads via `disk->readFile`, and disk-based writes via `disk->writeFile` - `FunctionFile` reads through disk I/O when volume is configured - All 13 callers of `getUserFilesPath` updated for multi-path validation - Helper overloads `pathStartsWith(path, vector)` and `fileOrSymlinkPathStartsWith(path, vector)` added - Integration test with local multi-disk and S3 (`s3_plain`) scenarios ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `user_files_policy` server setting to store `user_files` on a custom disk, including S3-backed disks. This allows customers to have a "scratch area" for files in ClickHouse Cloud, shared among all replicas. Note: keeping as a draft, because the code is not generalized enough. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Introduces a new storage-policy-backed path for `user_files` and rewires many read/write and path-validation code paths (including remote disks), which could affect file access semantics and security boundaries if edge cases are missed. > > **Overview** > Adds a new server setting `user_files_policy` that binds the `user_files` directory to a storage policy (enforced to *exactly one volume with one disk*) and stores the resolved `VolumePtr` in `Context`, with server startup applying it via `setUserFilesPolicy`. > > Updates user-files consumers to become disk-aware when a policy is configured: `file()`/`StorageFile` switch to `IDisk`-based globbing, reads, writes, schema inference and truncation (plus new helpers like `splitUserFilesAbsolutePath`, `userFilesPathExists`, and symlink-escape checks), while features that require local POSIX paths (`ATTACH ... FROM`, SQLite, `filesystem` table function, static HTTP `file://`, FileLog, several dictionary sources, error logger, etc.) now explicitly reject remote `user_files_policy` disks. > > Adds integration coverage for local-disk and `s3_plain` configurations, including globbing, absolute paths, traversal/symlink-escape hardening, write/append/truncate behavior, schema inference, and expected rejections (e.g. partitioned inserts under `user_files_policy`). > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 04b03ad8df769f756aa699f0eb7eb7fff624da1b. signal.title: Native Google Cloud Storage integration (google-cloud-cpp)
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental native Google Cloud Storage integration built on the Google Cloud C++ SDK (`google-cloud-cpp`, the GCS JSON API), as an alternative to the existing S3-compatibility path. Enable it with the new `use_native_gcs` setting for the `gcs` table function and dynamic `disk(...)` definitions, or configure a MergeTree storage disk with `object_storage_type: gcs`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes Documented in `docs/reference/functions/table-functions/gcs.mdx` (new "Native GCS integration" section). --- ## Description ClickHouse currently talks to GCS **only through its S3-compatible XML API** (the AWS SDK against a `storage.googleapis.com` endpoint, plus a cluster of GCS quirk-toggles in the S3 client). This PR adds a first-class native backend on top of the already-vendored `google-cloud-cpp` storage client. **Opt-in, non-breaking.** The `gcs()` table function and dynamic disks select the native backend only with the new experimental `use_native_gcs` setting (default `false`); otherwise they retain S3 compatibility and HMAC keys. `ENGINE = GCS` remains on the existing compatibility path. ### What's added - `ObjectStorageType::GCS` + `GCSObjectStorage : IObjectStorage` (`src/Disks/DiskObjectStorage/ObjectStorages/GCS/`), with `ReadBufferFromGCS`/`WriteBufferFromGCS` over the SDK's `ObjectReadStream`/`ObjectWriteStream` (ranged seeks, resumable uploads), native listing, `RewriteObject`-based copy, `DeleteObject`, `GetObjectMetadata`. - Registered as the `gcs` object-storage type + a `gcs` disk-type alias, so MergeTree data can live natively on GCS (`type: object_storage, object_storage_type: gcs`). - `StorageGCSConfiguration` (reuses `StorageS3Configuration`'s argument parsing) and a `TableFunctionGCS` selector that picks native vs S3-compat by the `use_native_gcs` setting. - Auth mirrors the compat surface on the native side: Application Default Credentials, service-account JSON, the `google_adc_*` OAuth refresh-token flow (reusing `IO/GCPOAuth`), anonymous / `NOSIGN`, and a REST endpoint override for the GCS emulator. - `USE_GOOGLE_CLOUD` is now exposed in `system.build_options`. ### Testing - Every changed/new translation unit compiles against the real headers and the vendored SDK (`USE_GOOGLE_CLOUD=1`, `USE_AWS_S3=1`). - Unit test for endpoint parsing (`gtest_gcs_endpoint`). - Stateless test for the setting wiring (`04502_use_native_gcs_setting`). - Integration test `test_native_gcs` runs against a `fake-gcs-server` emulator (a new `with_gcs` helper in `cluster.py`): `gcs()` INSERT/SELECT + glob with `use_native_gcs=1`, and a MergeTree-on-GCS-disk round trip. Note: `fake-gcs-server` speaks the GCS API (unlike minio, which is S3-only). The module is skipped on builds without the SDK. ### Known follow-ups - `GCSObjectStorage::iterate()` currently materializes the full listing (a lazy paginating iterator like S3's is a future optimization). - The `google_adc_*` refresh-token access token is minted eagerly (no auto-refresh yet for long-lived disks). - `readSmallObjectAndGetObjectMetadata` uses the base default (relevant only for a future native Iceberg-over-GCS path, which is not wired here). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109455&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109455](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109455+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Follow-ups for CREATE HANDLER: parse limits of the stored query, docs, refactoring
signal.text: Follow-ups from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 (`CREATE HANDLER`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106231 **Requested in review of #106231:** - The two predicates over `IAST::QueryKind` that describe the `readonly` mode - whether a query of that kind is rejected under it, and whether `readonly = 2` still lets it produce side effects - moved out of `SQLDefinedHandlerFromAST` into `Interpreters/QueryKindUnderReadonly.h`; `queryKindRequiresMutatingMethod` is renamed to `isQueryKindRejectedUnderReadonly` after the property it reports. The handler code keeps the statement-level refinements and the HTTP-method fences. - `currentHandler` and `currentRequestURL` were registered with `IntroducedIn` 26.6 (the development version when they were written); they are released in 26.8. **The one unresolved review finding:** a request could still lower the parse limits of a handler's query. `HTTPHandler::processQuery` relaxed `max_parser_depth` / `max_parser_backtracks` *before* applying the settings the request supplies, and a request names settings freely - so `GET /h?max_parser_depth=1` put the caller's value back and broke a handler the server itself had accepted. The relaxation now happens after the request settings. `max_query_size` had the same hole and did not even need a hostile request: a stored query longer than its default value is creatable and reloadable (both parse without a size limit) but failed on every invocation; it is now raised to fit the query text - not disabled, because `executeQuery` also uses `max_query_size` to decide how much of the request stream to read ahead in search of the query text, where `0` would make it read a single byte. New tests `04897_handler_request_parser_limits` and `04898_handler_large_query_invocation`, both verified to fail without the fix. **Documentation:** the `CREATE HANDLER` page was written into `docs/en/sql-reference/statements/create/handler.md` - a path in the legacy Docusaurus tree that `9440ca729a3` had already removed - so the only documentation of `CREATE HANDLER` / `ALTER HANDLER` / `DROP HANDLER` was published nowhere. It moves to `docs/reference/statements/create/handler.mdx`, with the frontmatter and internal links converted to that tree's conventions and the page registered in `docs/reference/navigation.json`. `docs/en/operations/system-tables/handlers.md` was a leftover copy of the generated `docs/reference/system-tables/handlers.mdx` whose hand-written `SHOW HANDLERS` / secret-masking paragraph had been lost; that paragraph is restored and the legacy copy deleted. The statement is now cross-referenced from the HTTP interface page, the `DROP` page and the `ALTER` overview, and the anchored (`RE2::FullMatch`) semantics of `URL REGEXP` are documented. Verified locally: all 30 SQL-defined-handler stateless tests pass against a server built from this branch (the 31st match of the `handler` filter, `03354_tcp_handler_async_insert_bug`, is unrelated and needs a writable `/var/lib/clickhouse/user_files`), and `04844_handler_deep_query_invocation` still passes without the fix, confirming it covered only the session-level limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed HTTP handler invocation so request-level `max_parser_depth`, `max_parser_backtracks`, and `max_query_size` no longer break stored handler queries, and published the `CREATE HANDLER`, `ALTER HANDLER`, and `DROP HANDLER` documentation. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114883&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114883](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114883+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Precompute hashes and prefetch for fixed-size-keys aggregation methods
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104475 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/81944 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): For the `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256` family of aggregation methods (several fixed-size keys packed into one integer), precompute the per-row canonical hashes in one pass over the batch-packed keys and reuse them to software-prefetch the target bucket and to skip rehashing the key in `emplace`. Previously the look-ahead prefetch computed every key and its hash twice per row. --- This extends the precomputed-hash + prefetch mechanism that #104475 introduced for the `prealloc_serialized` family to `HashMethodKeysFixed` (multi-key `GROUP BY` over numeric columns, e.g. ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q32). When the whole block of keys is batch-packed upfront (`prepared_keys`), the per-row canonical hashes are computed in one pass on the first `emplace`/`find` call and reused both for the look-ahead prefetch and for the insert itself, replacing the generic look-ahead in `Aggregator::executeImplBatch` that builds every key holder and hashes it a second time per row. Details: - The runtime gates mirror `prealloc_serialized`: batch-packed keys available, `enable_software_prefetch_in_aggregation`, and the `min_bytes_for_prefetch` hash-table size threshold (checked lazily on the first call, when `Data` is known). Nullable and low-cardinality variants never use `prepared_keys` and are excluded at compile time. - A new concept `HasPrefetchByHashMemberFunc` compiles the path out for tables without hash-addressed buckets (`FixedHashTable` behind `keys16`). Set, JOIN and `arrayUniq`-style callers of `HashMethodKeysFixed` pass no settings context, so nothing changes for them. - `HashMethodSerializedContext` carried only the settings and is now the shared `HashMethodSettingsContext`, also used by `HashMethodKeysFixed::createContext`. - `HashTable::isEmptyCell` (the `findKey` short-circuit for precomputed hashes, used in the `no_more_keys` mode) is made zero-key-aware: the zero key is stored outside the buffer, so an empty cell at the key's place proves nothing when the zero key is present. The existing user (`prealloc_serialized`) never produces empty keys, so this was latent; an all-zeros fixed key is common (the ClickBench `hits` table has a `SearchEngineID = 0, ClientIP = 0` group). Correctness was verified against an unpatched build of the same commit on the full ClickBench `hits` dataset (identical single part, 99,997,497 rows): full-result checksums for `keys32`/`keys64`/`keys128`/`keys256`, nullable keys and `prealloc_serialized`; the all-zero key group; the `no_more_keys` path (`max_rows_to_group_by` with `group_by_overflow_mode = 'any'`); and external aggregation (spill + merge). All results are identical. An honest note on measured impact, from the investigation written up in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114638#issuecomment-5285053418: in a local interleaved A/B on a (noisy, shared) 96-core aarch64 box, this change measures neutral on ClickBench Q30/Q31/Q35 — the generic look-ahead prefetch already covered these methods, so the remaining saving is one packed-key load plus one CRC per row. The issue's local reproduction numbers for these queries turned out to be dominated by an unrelated effect (the memory-based `max_threads` cap from #100383, which the pre-#100383 baseline build does not have — details in the issue). The perf tests that exercise these exact shapes (`tests/performance/clickbench.xml` Q30/Q31/Q32, `group_by_fixed_keys.xml`, `hash_table_sizes_stats.xml`) should be the arbiter on dedicated hardware. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114679&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114679](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114679+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Resume a NATS JetStream subscription after a reconnect
signal.text: A `NATS` table reading from a JetStream stream can stop consuming for good after the NATS server restarts, while still looking subscribed and healthy. An asynchronous JetStream pull subscription asks for more messages only when one is delivered, and when the NATS client reconnects it re-sends the `SUB` line but not the pull request the broker was holding. A broker that goes away without answering that request - a hard kill, a network partition, or a graceful restart that lands in the milliseconds between a re-subscribe and its request being parked - leaves the table subscribed and permanently silent. That is what `test_nats_restore_failed_connection_without_losses_on_write` hits when the consumer is still behind at the moment the broker is stopped: all 100000 rows were published and acknowledged into the stream, but the ones not yet delivered are never fetched again, so the view stays short of them and the test fails with `ClickHouse lost some messages: 92807`. It fails this way on about 0.2% of runs since the NATS tests came back on 2026-07-30, and at the same rate before and after #112828 recovered the closed-subscription case on 2026-08-13 (88 of 46693 runs before, 27 of 15428 after), which is what points at the window that fix leaves open. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=c260929910ea94be9a359bb69bf5e33d7b3a40e4&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28arm_binary%2C%20distributed%20plan%2C%204%2F4%29 Recovery so far keyed only on a subscription the NATS client had closed, which is what a graceful shutdown produces by answering the outstanding pull request. This reports a reconnect as well, by comparing the reconnect count the client keeps for the connection against the one taken when we subscribed, and re-subscribes through the same path. Only JetStream consumers do this: a core NATS subscription really is restored by the `SUB` line, and re-subscribing it would drop buffered messages nothing redelivers. The recovery is applied both by the background streaming task and by an in-flight direct `SELECT`, whose source retains its consumer until the query finishes. The window this closes is the residual documented in #112828, so `_restart_nats` no longer retries until a restart lands outside it, and a new test reaches that state deterministically with `SIGKILL`, which answers nothing and so leaves no closed subscription to fall back on. Verified locally with a release build, running the module through `ci.praktika`: - new test with the fix: passed twice (65 s, 146 s); - new test with `src/Storages/NATS` reverted to `master` and everything else unchanged: `AssertionError: consumption did not resume, view holds 10 of 20 keys` - the messages published after the restart never arrive; - the five existing restart tests plus `test_nats_restore_failed_connection_without_losses_on_write`, all six passed with the fix. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112828 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `NATS` engine table reading from a JetStream stream (`nats_stream`) silently stopping to consume messages after the NATS server restarted or the connection was re-established. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115343&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115343](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115343+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Resolve the client hostname in `ClientInfo` on demand
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112496 --> Split out of #112496. `ClientInfo::fillOSUserHostNameAndVersionInfo` resolved the local FQDN through `getFQDNOrHostName`, a blocking `getaddrinfo` that also dlopens the NSS modules. Every `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` invocation paid for it even when nothing ever asked for the name, and a resolver that is slow or unreachable sat on the startup path with no short timeout. `getClientHostName` resolves it on first use instead, and `getFQDNOrHostName` caches process-wide, so the readers — `system.processes`, `query_log`, `session_log` and the TCP handshake — see the same value as before. When the name arrives from a peer in `ClientInfo::read` it describes that peer rather than us, so it is kept as received and never re-resolved locally. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The client hostname is now resolved when it is first reported instead of on every `clickhouse client` and `clickhouse local` invocation. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115491&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115491](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115491+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject truncated/incomplete AI text function responses
signal.text: The AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) could silently return a truncated answer. When a provider stops early — most commonly by hitting the `max_tokens` limit — it reports this in the response, but the shared base class `FunctionBaseAI` never inspected the signal and returned whatever partial text came back. For example, `aiGenerate('Write three sentences about the ocean.', map(..., 'max_tokens', '5'))` returned the fragment `The ocean covers more than` with no error. This change normalizes each provider's native stop reason (OpenAI `finish_reason`, Anthropic `stop_reason`) into a canonical `FinishReason` enum, so the base class can make a single completeness decision without knowing the provider dialect: - `Truncated` (token/context limit) → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_TRUNCATED`. - `ContentFilter` (OpenAI `content_filter`, Anthropic `refusal`) and `ToolCall` → throws `AI_PROVIDER_RESPONSE_INCOMPLETE`. - `Complete` (natural end, or a caller stop sequence such as Anthropic `stop_sequence`) and `Unknown` (unrecognized reason) are accepted, so benign non-`stop` reasons are not misclassified as truncation. The rejection is thrown inside the existing per-row `try`, so it is non-retriable (retrying would hit the same limit) and honors `ai_function_throw_on_error`: with `1` the exception propagates; with `0` the row becomes the column default. `aiEmbed` is unaffected (embeddings have no finish reason). Integration tests in `test_ai_functions` cover truncation (throw + graceful), content-filter, an accepted unknown reason, and the Anthropic `stop_sequence` (must not throw) and `max_tokens` (must throw) cases. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): AI text functions (`aiGenerate`, `aiClassify`, `aiExtract`, `aiTranslate`) now reject truncated or otherwise incomplete provider responses (e.g. when the model hits the `max_tokens` limit) instead of silently returning partial output. Behavior follows the `ai_function_throw_on_error` setting. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111830&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111830](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111830+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not attach a cache writer to a detached file segment
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110029 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Cache file segment is in detached state`) when reading through the filesystem cache with the experimental `use_reader_executor` setting. The regression was introduced by #110029 and is not in any release, so no backport is owed. ### Description Related: #110029 **The problem.** `BuzzHouse` aborts the server with `Cache file segment is in detached state, operation not allowed`, on two unrelated PRs, first seen 8h41m after #110029 merged. CIDB STID `4043-43b7`, [report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113382&sha=97396ecebc7bcb7ee4d4921c71d1cfdd071a2895&name_0=PR&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28arm_asan_ubsan%29). **Root cause.** `FileCache::getOrSet` can hand back a synthetic `DETACHED` placeholder rather than a real segment: `getImpl` fabricates one when the covering segment is being evicted or removed, and another when the range exceeds `bypass_cache_threshold`. Such a placeholder is outside the cache metadata, holds no bytes, and the downloader role cannot be acquired on it. `DiskCacheProvider::resolve` classified it as a *writable* miss, because `segmentCommittedEnd` falls back to the write offset, which for a placeholder equals the segment start. It attached a `DiskCacheWriter`, and `ReaderExecutor::readThroughCaches` then called `claimLeadRole` on it, whose `getOrSetDownloader` hit `assertNotDetachedUnlocked`: a `LOGICAL_ERROR`, aborting the server in debug and sanitizer builds. **The change.** `resolve` now emits a writer-less miss for a detached segment, so those bytes are read from source and nothing is cached. The legacy paths already do this: `CachedOnDiskReadBufferFromFile` dispatches `State::DETACHED` to a cache bypass before acquiring any role, and `CachedOnDiskWriteBufferFromFile` skips write-through caching on `isDetached()`. `claimLeadRole` was the only one of the five non-test `getOrSetDownloader` callers reachable with a detached segment; the assertion is a correct caller contract and stays. **Reachability.** `src/IO/DiskCacheProvider.cpp` exists on no active release branch (25.8, 26.3-26.7), and #110029 is an ancestor of none of them, so no released version can reach this. `use_reader_executor` is experimental and off by default; the abort affects the `BuzzHouse` checks, which randomize it as a session setting, plus anyone opting into the experimental path. **Validation.** Deterministic, no fuzzer needed: the test arms the existing failpoint `file_cache_simulate_evicting_segment`, which makes every segment the cache reports a placeholder. Without the fix the server dies with the CI stack; with it the test passes, 50/50 randomized. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115070&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115070](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115070+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115017 (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch) Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101757 --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115017 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/101757 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix the histogram metric `keeper_read_wait_for_write_time_milliseconds` and the OpenTelemetry span `keeper.read.wait_for_write` always reading zero and never being emitted when `use_new_dispatcher` is enabled, which is the default. Both are now recorded for read requests that wait for an in-flight write, as they were before the new request dispatcher. ### Description Requested by @ al13n321 on #115017: record the histogram and the span for late and intermediate reads in the commit callback. `KeeperRequestDispatcherOld` initializes the `ReadWaitForWrite` span when it parks a read and finalizes it when the write commits. The new dispatcher replaced that queue with two carriers in `InFlightBatch`, `intermediate_reads` (parked mid-batch) and `late_reads` (parked after the last request), and instrumented neither. The wait still happens; only its measurement was lost. This initializes at both park sites and finalizes both carriers in `onCommit`. `maybeFinalize` observes the histogram before checking for a span, so one pair feeds both surfaces. `dropInFlightRequests` is deliberately not finalized: those reads never saw their write complete, so timing them would mix stream-recreation timeouts into a latency metric, and `Old` does not finalize its error path either. A test arm pins it. The initialize in `LateReads::add` runs under the lock `add` already holds, before the read is visible to `onCommit`, and adds no lock, atomic or ordering edge. `onCommit` finalizes only the first group it takes per batch: the write is applied before the commit callback runs, so a read attached while that batch's reads are already draining waited for those reads, not for the write. A test arm pins this by adding a read from inside the drain. No setting, ordering or state transition changed. Validated on an embedded-keeper server: before, the histogram stays at 0 and the span is absent while sibling keeper spans are recorded; after, the count advances and the span carries the attributes `Old` emits. Two test gaps. Parking cannot be forced deterministically from a client, so the integration test keeps its assertion tolerating the span's absence rather than gaining a flaky one. No unit test reaches the `dispatchThread` initialize, which needs a started raft stream; the server run above covers it. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115252&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115252](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115252+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Enforce settings constraints on nested SETTINGS and SET name = DEFAULT
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109473 Two code paths mutated session or query settings without calling `checkSettingsConstraints`, so an authenticated user could override a setting an administrator had locked with `CONST`, `readonly`, `MIN`/`MAX`, or a feature tier. Where those constraints are the tenant-isolation boundary, this breaks multi-tenant isolation. ### A nested `SETTINGS` clause was applied unchecked `QueryTreeBuilder::buildSelectExpression` applied a `SELECT` node's `SETTINGS` clause to the per-node context copy with no constraint check. A clause on an outer query is validated by `InterpreterSetQuery::applySettingsFromQuery`, but a clause inside a subquery, a CTE, or a view's inner query reached only the analyzer. The Planner then read the mutated context, so with `additional_table_filters` - a documented row-level isolation mechanism - the user read other tenants' rows: ```sql -- rejected SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}; -- accepted before this change, returning every tenant's rows SELECT * FROM (SELECT * FROM default.t_mt SETTINGS additional_table_filters = {'default.t_mt':'1'}); ``` There were no `checkSettingsConstraints` call sites anywhere in `src/Analyzer`, `src/Planner` or `src/Processors`. The legacy interpreter has always checked the same clause in `InterpreterSelectQuery`, so the analyzer becoming the default silently dropped the check. ### `SET name = DEFAULT` was applied unchecked The parser stores `SET k = v` in `ASTSetQuery::changes` and `SET k = DEFAULT` in `ASTSetQuery::default_settings`, and only the former was validated before `Context::resetSettingsToDefaultValue` applied the compiled-in default. So `SET readonly = DEFAULT` cleared a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile and re-enabled `INSERT`, `CREATE` and `DROP`, and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` cleared a resource cap. The same gap existed in the Arrow Flight `SetSessionOptions` reset branch, whose value-assignment branch already checked. ### A `profile` change was not checked against the constraints it installs A `SET` statement was validated as a whole before it ran, but a `profile` change among its settings replaces the constraint set halfway through it. So a single statement overrode the very constraint that the profile it names installs, while the same settings applied as two separate statements were rejected: ```sql -- rejected SET profile = 'p'; SET max_execution_time = 999; -- accepted before this change, for a profile p with max_execution_time = 10 CONST SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = 999; SET profile = 'p', max_execution_time = DEFAULT; ``` ### The fix A new `SettingsConstraints::checkCanReset` validates a reset request, reached through `Context::checkSettingsConstraintsForDefaults` from both `InterpreterSetQuery` entry points, the Arrow Flight reset branch, and the analyzer: * For a built-in setting the compiled-in default is checked as the new value, via the new `Settings::getDefaultValue`, so min/max, `CONST`, tier and source restrictions all apply. Resetting a setting that already holds its default stays allowed, including under `readonly = 1`, because the constraint checker skips a change equal to the current value. * A custom setting has no compiled-in default - resetting it erases it - so only its writability is checked. This matters: erasing a `CONST` custom setting that a row policy reads through `getSetting` is exactly how the reported isolation boundary was broken. `buildSelectExpression` also no longer ignores a nested `SETTINGS name = DEFAULT`, which was previously a silent no-op; it is now checked and applied as a reset. It is applied to the subquery's context only and is not recorded on the `QueryNode`, so it stays invisible to the consumers that read a subquery's settings off the query tree - as it was when the clause was dropped outright. That limitation is documented at the call site and tracked in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115415. For the `profile` case, `InterpreterSetQuery` now checks the rest of the statement against the constraints the profile installs. That requires the profile to have been applied first, so the checking runs on a scratch copy of the context and nothing is applied to the real one until all of it passes: a rejected statement leaves the session alone rather than applying the profile and dropping its own tail. The changes are then applied in one call with the original list, so the order in which they take effect - and therefore which assignment wins - is unchanged. ### Behaviour change A `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view - the default for `CREATE VIEW` - whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails. This restores the behaviour of the legacy interpreter, which has always checked that clause. An administrator can keep such a view working with `SQL SECURITY DEFINER`, because `getSQLSecurityOverriddenContext` switches to the definer, whose constraints then apply. Note the limit of that workaround: it copies the invoker's changed setting *values* while switching the user, so a `CONST`/`MIN`/`MAX` constraint does not travel and the view works, but a `readonly = 1` value does travel and the inner clause is rejected even under `DEFINER`. A `readonly` user reading a view whose inner query sets a setting therefore has no workaround other than removing the clause from the view. ### Testing `05019_settings_constraints_reset_and_nested` covers, in a `CONST`-constrained session: a rejected `SET x = DEFAULT`; a no-op reset of an already-default setting still being allowed; a `CONST` custom setting resisting erasure; a nested `SETTINGS` clause rejected in a subquery, in a CTE, and in the `= DEFAULT` form; an unconstrained nested clause still working; and a `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` view still reading while its `INVOKER` equivalent is rejected. It also pins down that a `SETTINGS` clause written after a nested `UNION` or `INTERSECT` is rejected: the parser attaches such a clause to one of the member `SELECT`s rather than to the compound query, so it is covered by the same check, whichever member it lands on. `05021_settings_constraints_set_profile_in_same_query` covers the `profile` case: an explicit value and a reset after the `profile` change both rejected against the profile's constraints, the profile left unapplied by a rejected statement, an assignment before the `profile` change still allowed, the profile's constraints in force afterwards, and an unconstrained setting after the change still applying. `05020_settings_constraints_readonly_user` covers a user under a `readonly = 1 CONST` profile: `SET readonly = DEFAULT` and `SET max_memory_usage = DEFAULT` both rejected, the session still readonly afterwards, and a nested `SETTINGS` clause unable to lift the user's row filter. One existing test needed a fix. `04102_hash_join_stress_test` used `SETTINGS max_joined_block_rows = 100` inside a subquery; the setting is called `max_joined_block_size_rows`. The misspelling went unnoticed because `Settings` accepts custom settings, so `Settings::set` stores an unrecognised name instead of rejecting it, and the `SQL_`/`custom_` prefix validation lives in `AccessControl::checkSettingNameIsAllowed`, reached only from `SettingsConstraints::checkImpl`. The same clause on a top-level query has always been rejected with `UNKNOWN_SETTING`; only the nested form escaped. The name is now spelled correctly. The Arrow Flight reset branch is not covered by a test: there is no functional-test harness for the Arrow Flight server, and the change there is the same three lines as its sibling value-assignment branch. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Critical Bug Fix (crash, data loss, RBAC) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a settings-constraint bypass. A `SETTINGS` clause inside a subquery, a CTE or a view's inner query, `SET <name> = DEFAULT`, and a setting assigned or reset after a `profile` change in the same `SET` statement, now all enforce settings constraints, so none of them can be used to leave readonly mode or to override a `CONST`, `MIN` or `MAX` constraint. Note that a `SQL SECURITY INVOKER` view whose inner query carries a `SETTINGS` clause the invoking user is not allowed to set now fails, matching the behaviour of the old analyzer; use `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` for such a view. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115397&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115397](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115397+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Enforce allow_non_metadata_alters on the mutation path, and document what it blocks
signal.text:
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115058 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `allow_non_metadata_alters = 0` now also rejects the `ALTER` commands that reach a `MergeTree` table as explicit mutations: `UPDATE`, `DELETE WHERE`, the five `MATERIALIZE` forms, `APPLY DELETED MASK`, `APPLY PATCHES` and `REWRITE PARTS`. Previously the check only saw the commands represented by the schema-alter path, so these rewrote parts anyway. `DELETE FROM` and `UPDATE` stay permitted, including `ON CLUSTER`. The setting description now lists what is refused, and that the check is `MergeTree`-only. ### Description The setting was only read in `MergeTreeData::checkAlterIsPossible`. The commands listed above go into a `MutationCommands` segment, which calls `checkMutationIsPossible`, whose `Settings` parameter `MergeTreeData` declared unused. The fix names it and rejects when `hasNonEmptyMutationCommands()` holds, the predicate that already decides whether the mutation runs, so guard and execution cannot drift. Plain `DELETE FROM` needed care: under the default `lightweight_delete_mode` it synthesizes `ALTER TABLE ... UPDATE _row_exists = 0`, which the storage cannot tell from the user-written form. Exempting by shape would reopen the hole, so the synthesizing interpreter grants it on a private context. `StorageWindowView::cleanup()` is the only other such call site in `src/`. A setting cannot carry that provenance across nodes: the worker re-clamps shipped settings against its own profile. So `DELETE FROM ... ON CLUSTER` now dispatches the `DELETE` itself, as `InterpreterUpdateQuery` does. Two consequences: - `DDLWorker` now leader-routes `ASTDeleteQuery`, so a replicated shard runs it once, not once per replica. This also covers a multi-shard `Replicated` database, which is reached by a plain `DELETE` rather than by `ON CLUSTER`: it replicates the `DELETE` at database level, and `ON CLUSTER` against it is rejected as a non-initial query both before and after this PR. Mid-upgrade an old and a new worker can both execute one entry, which duplicates the mutation and converges; the two closest precedents also shipped ungated. - `InterpreterDeleteQuery` now inlines SQL user-defined functions, as the interpreters it used to re-enter did. That store is not replicated by default, so an unexpanded body either failed with `UNKNOWN_FUNCTION` on the other hosts or, if defined differently there, silently deleted different rows there. Refusals happen only where the setting is 0, but the two bullets above apply at any value of it, including the default. @PedroTadim, the compatibility question is open if you prefer the docs half.
Validation, allow_non_metadata_alters = 0 on a debug build Three binaries: base, the guard without the caller exemption, and the fix. | Statement | base | guard only | fix | |---|---|---|---| | the mutation commands listed above | OK | 524 | 524 | | user-written `ALTER ... UPDATE _row_exists = 0`, local and `ON CLUSTER` | OK | 524 | 524 | | `DELETE FROM` (default mode) | OK | 524 | OK | | `DELETE FROM ... ON CLUSTER`, profile constrains the setting to 0 | OK | 524 | OK | | `DELETE FROM` (`lightweight_update` mode) | OK | OK | OK | | lightweight `UPDATE ... SET` | OK | OK | OK | | `DROP COLUMN` of an `ALIAS`, `ADD COLUMN`, `COMMENT COLUMN`, `MODIFY SETTING` | OK | OK | OK | | the alters already refused before this change | 524 | 524 | 524 | | every refused statement again under `= 1` | OK | OK | OK | 524 is `ALTER_OF_COLUMN_IS_FORBIDDEN`, the code the existing alter-path guard already throws. `DELETE FROM` is the only cell where the middle column differs from the fix, so the relaxation is exactly one statement wide. `01413_allow_non_metadata_alters` is extended with these cases and fails without the fix; each new expected-error line was justified against the base binary first, where all of them succeed. The clustered cases need a settings profile, which a stateless test cannot set, so they live in `test_allow_non_metadata_alters_on_cluster` (11 arms). Two assert a single mutation entry per shard, one for a `ReplicatedMergeTree` table reached by `ON CLUSTER`, one for a multi-shard `Replicated` database reached by a plain `DELETE`; both fail on the base binary with 2 entries. `lightweight_deletes_sync` is 2 and the DDL output mode is `THROW`, so that read happens after every host finished, with no polling or sleep. Two define a function on one host only, and differently on each host: without the inlining they fail with `UNKNOWN_FUNCTION` and with divergent surviving keys respectively.

signal.title: Add clickhouse-proxy application mode
signal.text: Implements a new application mode in the `clickhouse` binary, named `proxy`. The proxy accepts connections over end-user ClickHouse protocols, finds the upstream backend based on configurable rules (hostname from TLS SNI or HTTP header, user name, database name, and — for HTTP — query type), and forwards the traffic to it. It is built on the `silk` fiber framework so that many concurrent connections are handled with low RAM usage. Start it with `clickhouse proxy --config-file proxy_config.xml`; a fully commented example config is in `programs/proxy/proxy_config.xml`, and the feature is documented at `docs/en/operations/clickhouse-proxy.md`. **What it does** - Protocol frontends for HTTP(S), native TCP, MySQL, PostgreSQL, transparent TLS-by-SNI, and opaque TCP streams. It handles only end-user protocols (not Keeper or inter-server replication). The user name and database are parsed from the first packets where the protocol allows it (HTTP headers/params/Basic auth, native `Hello`, PostgreSQL `StartupMessage`, HTTP query type). MySQL is server-speaks-first with in-band TLS, so it is forwarded transparently and routed by peer address or the default pool. - TLS routing options: terminate and re-encrypt (the proxy and each backend hold their own certificates), terminate only (unwrap: TLS to clients, plaintext to backends), and transparent (route by SNI without decrypting). Optional ACME certificate provisioning, as in `clickhouse-server`. - Multi-criteria routing rules matching host / user / database / query type / protocol, by exact value or regular expression; regexp captures can be substituted into a backend address template (e.g. route users `ch-<tenant>` to per-tenant backends). - Pools with pluggable load balancing (`random`, `round_robin`, `least_connections`, `lowest_latency`, `least_resources`) behind a common interface; a pool may list several backends for load balancing. - Session stickiness by `session_id` (from the HTTP URL) or by peer address, using a consistent (rendezvous) hash of the backends. - Backend health monitoring (connect latency, consecutive failures) and optional CPU/memory polling with per-backend credentials, feeding the `least_resources` strategy; a JSON status endpoint, `/ping`, and static pages are served by the proxy itself. - An abstract routing table exposing hooks (unknown route, no backends available, first time a user or database is seen) that run a shell command — for example to provision a backend on demand and wait for it to become available. Validated end to end against a live server: HTTP `/ping`, static pages, the status endpoint, GET/POST forwarding, the no-backend error paths, native protocol round-trips, and clean shutdown. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk/pull/120 (the `splice` operation this proxy relies on, sent to `silk` upstream) ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new `proxy` mode to the `clickhouse` binary: a lightweight, protocol-aware proxy that routes end-user connections (HTTP, native, MySQL, PostgreSQL, TLS-by-SNI, and raw TCP) to backend servers based on a configurable routing table, with TLS termination/passthrough, load balancing, health checks, and session stickiness. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110105&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110105](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110105+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Undo non-transactional removal marks when `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit` fails
signal.text: `MergeTreeData::Transaction::commit` marks covered parts as removed before the `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE` that moves them to `Outdated`, because that marking can fail: a concurrent transaction may hold the removal lock, and storing `txn_version.txt` can fail on I/O. For a non-transactional commit nothing undid the marks that had already been written (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97211 fixed only the dangling lock part, not the marks), so those parts stayed `Active` with `removal_tid = Tx::NonTransactionalTID` and `removal_csn = Tx::NonTransactionalCSN`. After https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/92141 the lock is released inline and that lock cleanup became obsolete, yet the vector https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/97211 introduced to collect the parts was still filled and never read. Such a part is inconsistent in several ways: * it is invisible to every transactional read while non-transactional reads still return its rows; * `TRUNCATE` skips it silently from then on; * `canBeRemoved` short-circuits to true for a non-transactional removal, so the part may be deleted as soon as anything moves it to `Outdated`, ignoring `old_parts_lifetime`; * if the part carries `txn_version.txt`, i.e. it was created or removed by a transaction, the inconsistency is persisted, survives a restart, and the part is then loaded as removed. The failure is reachable because `MergeTreeTransaction::rollback` restores the parts of a rolled-back removal to `Active` and only resets and unlocks their removal TID in a second loop, without holding the parts lock in between. A non-transactional `TRUNCATE` or `DROP PARTITION` covering such a part gets `SERIALIZATION_ERROR` in the middle of the loop, after earlier parts have already been marked. Track the covered parts that were marked and reset `removal_tid` and `removal_csn` for them if the loop throws. Only the non-transactional branch needs this: for transactions `MergeTreeTransaction::rollback` already resets and unlocks. The undo is best effort — every failure is logged per part, and the number of parts left inconsistent is appended to the propagated exception together with a pointer to `system.parts`. The second commit removes the `getActivePartsToReplace` call that was repeated inside `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE`. The parts lock is held for the whole of `commit`, and parts in `precommitted_parts` never cover each other, so the values computed before the scope stay valid and are now reused. That also removes a termination path, since `getActivePartsToReplace` throws `LOGICAL_ERROR` for intersecting or duplicate parts and any exception inside `NOEXCEPT_SCOPE` reaches `std::terminate`. Two failpoints and two tests cover the two ways the marking loop can fail: `04838_truncate_and_drop_part_transaction_rollback_race` freezes a transaction rollback between restoring the parts and unlocking their removal TID, then checks that a concurrent `TRUNCATE` fails with `SERIALIZATION_ERROR` and leaves no part marked as removed; `04839_fail_to_remove_covered_part_in_the_middle_of_the_list` injects a failure after the first covered part of a merge has been marked. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a case where a failed non-transactional `TRUNCATE`, `DROP PARTITION` or merge left covered parts `Active` but marked as removed. Such parts were invisible to transactional reads while non-transactional reads still returned their rows, were silently skipped by later `TRUNCATE` queries, could be deleted ignoring `old_parts_lifetime`, and for parts carrying `txn_version.txt` the inconsistency survived a restart. This was only reachable when transaction were enabled. signal.title: Add server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread`
signal.text: Each thread accumulates up to `max_untracked_memory` (4 MiB by default) of allocations before reporting them to the server-wide `MemoryTracker`. With many threads, this unreported memory can sum to a large amount, causing the server's tracked memory usage to under-count actual consumption and leading to OOM. This PR introduces a server-level setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) and speculatively charges this amount to the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. The global tracked memory becomes a tighter upper bound on actual consumption when `max_untracked_memory` for those workers does not exceed this setting; operators that permit a larger per-query value must raise the server setting accordingly. The reservation is charged on the server-wide (total) tracker only — deliberately not through the query's tracker chain. Query-level accounting feeds heuristics that compare memory deltas against byte thresholds (conversion of aggregation hash tables to two-level via `group_by_two_level_threshold_bytes`, spill-to-disk decisions), and phantom reservations of `num_threads * 4 MiB` trip those thresholds immediately: an earlier revision of this PR that charged the query tracker showed consistent slowdowns of GROUP BY queries in performance tests for exactly this reason. The reservation itself does not alter query-level or user-level accounting (`max_memory_usage`, `memory_usage` in `system.processes`); however, every pipeline worker flushes its pending real allocation reports before releasing its outermost reservation, so those counters and memory-based heuristics can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. The speculative reservation uses the throwing path of the memory tracker, so when it would exceed the server memory limit the corresponding job is treated as failed with `MEMORY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` — the same behavior as if the job itself had exceeded the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a new server setting `additional_memory_tracking_per_thread` (default 4 MiB) which speculatively reserves this amount on the server-wide `MemoryTracker` for each worker thread of a `PipelineExecutor`, including query, merge, and mutation pipelines. When it is at least the workers' `max_untracked_memory`, it makes server-wide tracked memory a tighter upper bound on actual consumption and reduces the risk of OOM with many concurrent pipeline workers. The reservation does not alter query-level or user-level accounting, but workers flush pending real allocation reports before releasing their outermost reservation, so those counters can become visible sooner while a worker yields, downscales, or completes. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - signal.title: Prometheus HTTP API: implement /api/v1/metadata
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/57545 ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Experimental Feature** ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **Adds Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` support for `TimeSeries` tables.** ### Description This adds the Prometheus `/api/v1/metadata` endpoint backed by the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table. ### Why this matters - **Prometheus-compatible tools** use `/api/v1/metadata` to discover **metric types, help text, and units**. - Without this endpoint, clients need separate configuration or lose this metadata when using ClickHouse as a Prometheus-compatible endpoint. - This keeps the `Metrics` target of a `TimeSeries` table as the **source of truth** for that metadata. Supported parameters: - `metric` filters the response to one metric family. - `limit` limits the number of metric families. - `limit_per_metric` limits the metadata objects returned for each family. Other details: - Metadata objects are unique. Entries returned for each family are sorted. - `limit=0` returns no metric families. - Zero and negative `limit_per_metric` values mean no per-family limit. - Positive `limit_per_metric` values bound the number of unique metadata objects returned for each family. The selected subset is not specified. - `FINAL` is used whenever the Metrics target supports it, including wrapped targets. - Metadata parameters stay endpoint-local and are not treated as ClickHouse settings. - The generated query uses the normal query pipeline and is recorded in `query_log`. - Access to the configured `TimeSeries` table and related table functions is checked. - The endpoint works with dedicated handlers and the combined `/api/v1` handler. ### Tests Added integration coverage for: - unique metadata across multiple parts. - stable results after `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL`. - JSON escaping for quotes, backslashes, newlines, tabs, and Unicode. - metric filtering and both limit parameters. - invalid limit values. - high-cardinality metadata with per-family limits. - primary-key filtering. - wrapped `FINAL` targets. - aliases and `prefer_column_name_to_alias`. - query logging. - endpoint and table-function access control. - unknown endpoint handling. - GET/HEAD and unsupported-method handling. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Documentation was added to the Prometheus protocols page. signal.title: Improve canceling queries in nested expression functions in FilterTransform
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103705 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Improve canceling queries by `KILL QUERY` and Ctrl+C in `clickhouse-client` while a long-running function is evaluated in a filter expression: `FilterTransform` (`WHERE`, including the `FilterSortedStreamByRange` path) and `TotalsHavingTransform` (`HAVING` with `WITH TOTALS`) now forward cancellation into nested expression functions. This supersedes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/103705 by @rvasin (Roman Vasin), whose commits are preserved here — all credit for the feature goes to them. The original branch is in a fork with maintainer edits disabled, so the merge conflicts with `master` and the remaining review feedback could not be pushed there. On top of the original PR, this PR: - Merges `master` and resolves the conflicts (`FailPoint.cpp` failpoint list, `FilterTransform.cpp` includes). - Addresses the two unresolved review threads (the AI review "Request changes" verdict): - `FilterSortedStreamByRange` holds a private `FilterTransform` and calls its `transform` directly, but the pipeline cancels only the outer processor. Now `FilterSortedStreamByRange::onCancel` forwards the cancellation into the inner transform, so `cancelExecution` reaches functions of range-filter predicates from `PartsSplitter`. - `TotalsHavingTransform` evaluated the `HAVING` expression without a cancellation callback, so a long-running function in `HAVING` remained uninterruptible. It now mirrors `FilterTransform`: `onCancel` cancels function execution, `expression->execute` gets a `check_cancelled` callback, and the transform returns before the totals/filter bookkeeping when cancelled. - Adds a test `04658_kill_query_having_totals_pause` with a new `totals_having_transform_pause` failpoint, mirroring `04612_kill_query_filter_pause`. - Adds immediate pre-evaluation cancellation guards in `FilterTransform` and `TotalsHavingTransform`, with `04905_kill_query_cancelled_before_expression` covering the already-dispatched-task race. - Addresses the latest review thread: `ConvertingTransform::onCancel` now forwards cancellation into functions executing target-side conversion/default expressions, with `04909_kill_query_converting_transform_wasm` covering a cancelled `INSERT` through a `DEFAULT` WASM expression. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112705&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112705](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112705+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.text: Experimental support for storing the Keeper changelog directly on object storage (S3) instead of (or in addition to) a local disk, gated behind the coordination setting `s3_experimental_changelog`. signal.title: Push join key filters into MergeTree index during recursive CTE evaluation
signal.text: When a recursive CTE joins against a `MergeTree` table, each recursion step previously scanned the entire table, because the join condition (e.g. `ON e.from_id = t.current_id`) was not pushed into `MergeTree`'s key condition. This change analyzes the recursive query's join tree to find equi-join conditions between the CTE working table and real tables. Before each step it reads the join-key values from the working table and injects them as an `IN (...)` predicate directly into the `WHERE` clause of each recursive `QueryNode` that joins against the CTE (the original `WHERE`/`HAVING`/`QUALIFY` clauses are snapshotted at construction and restored after each step, so nothing accumulates across steps). The planner then lowers this predicate into `ReadFromMergeTree`'s key condition. The injected set is bounded by the new setting `recursive_cte_max_in_filter_cardinality`, and injection fails closed to a plain scan whenever it could otherwise change results — when the generated set would exceed `max_rows_in_set`/`max_bytes_in_set`, cannot be materialized under `max_memory_usage`, or the `IN` predicate cannot be resolved for the join-key type. Parallel replicas are disabled for the recursive step queries to avoid stale cached `GLOBAL JOIN` tables returning incorrect results; the forcing mode `allow_experimental_parallel_reading_from_replicas = 2` raises `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` for the recursive part rather than silently downgrading. For a table with ~1M rows and 10 recursion steps, `read_rows` drops from ~10M to ~120. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/75026 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `WITH RECURSIVE` queries that use `ON` or comma equi-joins against `MergeTree` tables can now use the primary key index, reducing the number of rows read per recursion step. The optimization is controlled by the new setting `recursive_cte_max_in_filter_cardinality`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) No separate documentation page is needed — this is a transparent performance improvement. The only user-visible addition is the setting `recursive_cte_max_in_filter_cardinality`, which is documented at the source level in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`. <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches recursive CTE execution and query settings, and dynamically injects `additional_table_filters`, which could affect correctness/performance for some JOIN patterns despite being scoped to recursive steps. > > **Overview** > Improves recursive CTE performance by detecting equi-join conditions between the CTE working table and real tables, then **pushing join-key values into `additional_table_filters`** (built as `IN (...)` predicates) on each recursive step so MergeTree reads can use the primary-key index; user-provided `additional_table_filters` are merged rather than overwritten. > > Also **disables parallel replicas** for recursive CTE step queries to avoid incorrect results from reused cached GLOBAL JOIN tables, and adds a stateless test (`03924_recursive_cte_join_index`) asserting both correct output and low `read_rows` for explicit `INNER JOIN` and comma-join forms. > > <sup>Written by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/dashboard?tab=bugbot) for commit 37f26180bfa2189247b6862712551c7ecc41ed18. This will update automatically on new commits.
