signal.title: Fix quadratic gzip/zlib streaming decompression of single-block streams
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/114045 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/108074 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114054 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix `O(n^2)` decompression of gzip/zlib/deflate streams whose single DEFLATE block spans the whole stream, the shape zlib-ng produces at compression level 1 (the default of the official .NET SDK): a 24 MiB gzip HTTP body that took 11 s to ingest in 26.7 now takes 0.12 s, identical to a multi-block body, with memory bounded by the buffer size instead of the block size. ### Details The root cause: the streaming decompressor added to `contrib/libdeflate` kept its resume checkpoint only at DEFLATE block boundaries. On input exhaustion or output-buffer overflow it rolled back to the start of the current block, so for a stream that is one giant block, every socket refill re-decoded the block from its beginning — quadratic time — and the whole block's output had to be buffered before any byte was exposed — unbounded memory. The work happens in `copyDataImpl` while assembling the query, before the query starts, so it was invisible in `system.processes` and `query_duration_ms`. The fix (https://github.com/ClickHouse/libdeflate/pull/6, vendored by this PR in `contrib/libdeflate`) re-takes the checkpoint at every symbol boundary in the generic decode loop, plus two new decompressor fields (`in_block`, `block_is_final`) that let a resumed call jump straight back into symbol decoding — the litlen/offset decode tables already persist in the decompressor between calls. The fastloop is untouched: suspensions can only trigger from the generic loop, which always runs between the fastloop and input exhaustion. A suspension now loses at most one partially decoded symbol, so decompression is linear-time with bounded memory regardless of block structure. `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer` needed no logic changes, only comment updates: its "grow the output buffer" path is now reachable only when a single match (≤ 258 bytes) or stored block (≤ 64 KiB) exceeds the free output region. Verification: - Standalone harness: 5000+ randomized round-trips (zlib streams at all levels with random flush points; crafted static- and dynamic-Huffman single-block streams with matches reaching the full 32 KiB window; input chunking down to 1 byte; random output regions), zlib inflate as decode oracle, one-shot decoder as cross-check, and a progress assertion on every suspension. - End-to-end with the issue's reproducer shape (24 MiB single-block gzip body, `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`, local release build): **11.25 s before → 0.12 s after**, now identical to a multi-block body of the same content (0.12 s). Verified the vendored zlib-ng really emits this shape: at level 1 it produces 1 block for a 4 MiB input (stock zlib: 80 blocks). - No throughput regression on normal multi-block streams: 685 → 697 MB/s on a 256 MB zlib-level-6 stream. New tests: - `LibdeflateSingleBlock.StreamingConsumesInputWithinBlock` pins the linearity contract (a suspension inside a Huffman block leaves at most a few bytes unconsumed). Against the pre-fix library it fails immediately, with 35 MB left unconsumed on a 32 MiB single-block stream. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.RoundTripFromZlibNgLevelOneLarge` decodes a large stream produced by the vendored zlib-ng at level 1 — the real-encoder shape of the issue. - `LibdeflateInflateTest.SingleDeflateBlockSpanningWholeMember` decodes crafted single-block gzip/zlib members through `LibdeflateInflatingReadBuffer`. - `04836_http_gzip_single_deflate_block` ingests a crafted single-block gzip body over HTTP with chunked transfer encoding, end to end. Because the pre-fix decoder is correct, just quadratic, the assertion is on time: the body is one 36 MB block and the request is capped at 15 s. Ingest time for a single-block body of a given size, release build, `master`'s `contrib/libdeflate` vs this branch's: 10 MB - 1.8 s vs 0.05 s; 20 MB - 6.9 s; 40 MB - 27.3 s vs 0.20 s; 48 MB - 39.1 s vs 0.25 s. So the limit sits 2.6x below the pre-fix time and 60x above the fixed one, and the clean quadratic growth means the pre-fix margin does not depend on the machine speed. The payload is 120 lines of 400 KB so that line parsing and the `MergeTree` write do not dominate. Note: `Bugfix validation (unit tests)` reports `ERROR` (inconclusive, non-blocking) here for a structural reason: the fix itself lives in `contrib/libdeflate`, and the job cannot populate its merge-base "before" worktree at the merge-base submodule revision, so it refuses to build a before-binary that would validate the wrong submodule code. The functional test above is what validates the fix. Note: this PR and the revert #114054 are alternatives on master — if the revert merges first, this branch will be updated to re-apply the integration together with the fix; if this merges first, the revert can be closed (the 26.7 backport of the revert can proceed independently). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114059&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114059](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114059+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: SYSTEM RELOAD/UNLOAD DICTIONARY ON CLUSTER ignores the initiator's current database and silently targets `default`
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse CI monitoring (@groeneai). ### Describe what's wrong `SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY <bare-name> ON CLUSTER <c>` and `SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY <bare-name> ON CLUSTER <c>` do not resolve the dictionary name against the initiator's current database before the statement is put on the DDL queue. The bare name is serialized as-is, so every worker re-resolves it against its own current database, which for a query arriving over the DDL queue is `default`. Consequence: run from database `mydb`, the command silently reloads/unloads `default.d` instead of `mydb.d`, and it returns success. If `default.d` does not exist the command is a no-op; if it does exist, an unrelated dictionary is reloaded. There is no error either way, so the operator has no signal that the wrong dictionary was touched. Filed at the request of @Manerone in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111756, which fixes part of this. See "Additional context" for what that PR covers and what remains. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Version: master `26.8.1.1` (commit `c462bd70270441b71070b4c5417a32e33cac0bab`), debug build. No non-default settings. Single node is enough. The server needs `<distributed_ddl>`, a keeper, and a cluster containing itself: ```xml <clickhouse> <distributed_ddl><path>/clickhouse/task_queue/ddl</path></distributed_ddl> <remote_servers> <one_node><shard><replica><host>127.0.0.1</host><port>9000</port></replica></shard></one_node> </remote_servers> </clickhouse> ``` ```sql CREATE DATABASE mydb; -- the dictionary the user means CREATE OR REPLACE DICTIONARY mydb.d (k UInt64, v String) PRIMARY KEY k SOURCE(NULL()) LAYOUT(FLAT()) LIFETIME(0); -- a same-named decoy in `default` CREATE OR REPLACE DICTIONARY default.d (k UInt64, v String) PRIMARY KEY k SOURCE(NULL()) LAYOUT(FLAT()) LIFETIME(0); SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY mydb.d; SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY default.d; USE mydb; SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY d ON CLUSTER one_node; SELECT database, name, status FROM system.dictionaries WHERE name = 'd' ORDER BY database; ``` ### Expected behavior `mydb.d` is `LOADED`, `default.d` stays `NOT_LOADED` -- the same target the non-`ON CLUSTER` form picks. ### Actual result ``` after ON CLUSTER default d LOADED after ON CLUSTER mydb d NOT_LOADED ``` Control, same session, same server, `ON CLUSTER` dropped: ``` after local (control) default d NOT_LOADED after local (control) mydb d LOADED ``` The statement returned success in the failing case. The entry serialized into Keeper carries the unqualified name: ``` query: SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY ON CLUSTER one_node d ``` `SYSTEM UNLOAD DICTIONARY ... ON CLUSTER` behaves the same way. ### Additional context Code path on master (`a1ae499e22944d8`): * `InterpreterSystemQuery::execute` returns inside the `if (!query.cluster.empty())` branch (`src/Interpreters/InterpreterSystemQuery.cpp:361-366`) **before** the `RELOAD_DICTIONARY` / `UNLOAD_DICTIONARY` canonicalization block at `:378-382`, so on the `ON CLUSTER` path no qualification happens at all. * The worker-side rewrite does not supply it either: `ASTSystemQuery::getRewrittenASTWithoutOnCluster` (`src/Parsers/ASTSystemQuery.h:278-281`) calls `removeOnCluster` (`src/Parsers/ASTQueryWithOnCluster.h:48-57`), which injects `params.default_database`. `DDLTask.cpp:507` sets that from `address_in_cluster.default_database`, i.e. the cluster address's `<default_database>`, not the initiator's current database. PR #111756 by @Manerone moves the qualification ahead of the `ON CLUSTER` dispatch and fixes the case above. I verified that empirically: with only its `InterpreterSystemQuery.cpp` hunk applied to `a1ae499e22944d8` (build id `a9c961304b95de468e98629a04ada7c56003c136`), an `ON CLUSTER` command issued from a node that is itself in the cluster and hosts `mydb.d` leaves `mydb.d LOADED` and `default.d NOT_LOADED`. One case is still open with that patch applied, which is why the PR was left unmerged. `ExternalDictionariesLoader::qualifyDictionaryNameWithDatabase` (`src/Interpreters/ExternalDictionariesLoader.cpp:211-232`) only fills in `.database` when the calling server can resolve the name itself (`has(resolved_name)`). So a coordinator or gateway node that enqueues the DDL without hosting the dictionary leaves the name bare and each worker falls back to `default` again. Measured on a two-node setup, both nodes running the patched binary: node A is the initiator and is **not** a member of cluster `c_workers` and hosts no dictionaries; node B is the only cluster member and hosts both `mydb.d` and `default.d`. ``` -- on node A, in database mydb: SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY d ON CLUSTER c_workers; -- returns success -- observed on node B: default d LOADED mydb d NOT_LOADED ``` Keeper entry: `query: SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY ON CLUSTER c_workers d`. The precondition is confirmed on node A: `USE mydb; SYSTEM RELOAD DICTIONARY d` throws `Code: 36. DB::Exception: Dictionary (\`d\`) not found. (BAD_ARGUMENTS)` and `system.dictionaries` there is empty, so the `has()` check takes the leave-bare path. Fixing this seems to need the initiator's current database propagated independently of whether the initiator can resolve the dictionary locally. That has one wrinkle worth deciding explicitly: for a bare name, local execution resolves an XML dictionary ahead of a same-named dictionary in the current database, so unconditionally qualifying would change which one a bare `ON CLUSTER` name selects on workers that host an XML dictionary of that name.

signal.title: Re-land: make Ctrl+C terminate the output of a result set in the client promptly
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/22426 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106430 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107845 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107828 ### Description This re-lands #106430 ("Make Ctrl+C terminate the output of a result set in the client promptly"), which was reverted by #107845, and folds in the data-race fix from the (now closed) #107828 so the feature can land safely this time. Why it was reverted: `BuzzHouse (amd_tsan)` reported a ThreadSanitizer data race on master (STID 5296-4b74) on the client's persistent stdout buffer (`std_out`, an `AutoCanceledWriteBuffer<WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor>`). The interruptible-output feature installed a cancellation hook on `std_out` at the start of `processOrdinaryQuery` and cleared it via `SCOPE_EXIT({ std_out->setCancellationHook({}); })` at the end of the same scope. When the result set is written with parallel formatting, `ParallelFormattingOutputFormat` runs a background collector thread that writes through `std_out` and reads its `cancellation_hook` in `WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor::nextImpl`. On the normal end-of-stream path the collector is joined by `output_format->finalize` before the scope guard runs, so the clear is safe; but on paths that leave `processOrdinaryQuery` by an exception without first finalizing the output (a `NetException`, or a `LocalFormatError` rethrown from `receiveResult`), the scope guard cleared the hook while the collector thread was still alive and reading it — a data race on the `std::function`. The fix (from #107828): the hook is cleared in `resetOutput` right after `output_format.reset()`, which destroys the parallel formatter and joins its collector thread, so the mutation is single-threaded with respect to `std_out`'s hook. The hook is also re-pointed for the teardown flushes that follow: on normal completion the interrupt handler is still armed and is honored, so a fresh Ctrl+C keeps interrupting a flush to a slow or stuck stdout; on exception paths the handler is already stopped (its `cancelled` is then unconditionally true), so the genuine cancellation flag is used instead to avoid discarding already-produced output. `resetOutput` runs on every exit path and at the start of the next query, so `std_out` (which outlives a single query) never carries a stale hook into the next query. The pager and `INTO OUTFILE ... AND STDOUT` buffers are per-query and destroyed in `resetOutput` after the collector join, so they were never affected. The change is split into two commits: the first reapplies #106430 verbatim (a revert of the revert #107845); the second folds in the #107828 fix, confined to `src/Client/ClientBase.cpp`. The low-level `WriteBufferFromFileDescriptor` (used server-wide on a hot single-threaded write path) is unchanged by the fix. Revert that motivated this: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/107845 TSAN report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=73e97deb9abbc3258e75d297aabfc3fbe7c3ca5e&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_tsan%29 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Pressing Ctrl+C in `clickhouse-client`/`clickhouse-local` now promptly stops printing a large result set, even when the output is being written to a slow or stuck destination such as a slow terminal. Previously the first Ctrl+C could appear to have no effect. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108078&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108078](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108078+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix AI functions embedding counters behavior on error
signal.text: `aiEmbed` and `aiSimilarity` under-report provider usage in `system.query_log` when a request fails: with the default `ai_function_throw_on_error = 1` the exception row shows `AIAPICalls = 0` and `AIInputTokens = 0`, although the provider was called and billed. Flipping only that setting records the call: | `ai_function_throw_on_error` | `AIAPICalls` | `AIRowsSkipped` | |---|---:|---:| | `1` (default) | 0 | 0 | | `0` | 1 | 1 | Same query and endpoint, with `ai_function_max_retries = 0` so exactly one attempt is made. **Cause.** `embedTexts` accumulates the counters in a local `EmbeddingResult` and returns it by value. When a failed request rethrows, `return` is never reached: the local is destroyed while unwinding and the caller's `embedding_result` is never constructed, so the caller's `ProfileEvents::increment` calls are both skipped and left with nothing to read. That defeats the intent stated at the accumulation site, which counts `api_calls` *before* issuing the request so that failed calls are still counted. **Fix.** `embedTexts` now reports `AIAPICalls` and `AIInputTokens` itself, from a `SCOPE_EXIT` guard, so the normal and throwing exits both publish them. They are plain locals rather than fields of `EmbeddingResult`, so no caller can count them twice. Callers keep their own row counters, which mean different things: texts for `aiEmbed`, pairs of texts for `aiSimilarity`. **Not covered.** Row counters are still dropped when the query throws. It delivered no rows, and preserving them would need `embedTexts` to take an out-parameter in both callers. **Tests.** Three integration tests, each verified to fail with the source reverted to `master`: one per caller for `AIAPICalls`, plus one driving the quota-exceeded throw so a batch succeeds first and `AIInputTokens` is non-zero. The failed-request tests cannot cover `AIInputTokens`, since there the first request fails and no tokens are consumed. The same defect on the text-generation path is fixed in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830, which is what introduced a throwing path there. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111830 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `aiEmbed` and `aiSimilarity` reporting zero `AIAPICalls` in `system.query_log` when a provider request failed, and losing `AIInputTokens` already consumed by earlier successful batches. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114905&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114905](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114905+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject a bare carriage return in HTTP header names and values
signal.text:
`HTTPHeaderFilter::checkAndNormalizeHeaders` rejected an embedded line feed (`
`) in HTTP header names and values, but not a bare carriage return (``). A lone `` also terminates a header line, so a value such as `tokenX-Injected: evil` could still smuggle a second header into an outgoing request (request/response splitting). This rejects `` alongside `
`, for both header names and values, in the shared filter. This covers the callers that route header names/values through `HTTPHeaderFilter` — the SQL-facing paths where headers are supplied per query: the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, S3/Web configuration, and the DataLake/REST catalogs. Outbound HTTP clients that build headers without this filter (for example the AI providers and the BigQuery client, whose header values come from named collections, OAuth tokens, or DDL configuration) are not affected by this change; enforcing the same invariant at the shared HTTP send path for those clients is left to a separate follow-up. Deferred from #110313 to keep that pull request focused on refactoring. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110313 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Reject a bare carriage return (``), in addition to a line feed (`
`), in HTTP header names and values that pass through the HTTP header filter. This closes an HTTP header injection (request/response splitting) gap for features that pass user-provided headers, such as the `url` table function and engine, HTTP dictionaries, and data lake catalogs.

signal.title: Do not hold the DDL guard during TRUNCATE
signal.text: `TRUNCATE TABLE` held the table's DDL guard while removing data, and truncate can wait for running merges or for other replicas to process `DROP_RANGE`. Any DDL on that name — including background threads that need it — was blocked for that whole time. Release the guard before `IStorage::truncate` for databases with UUIDs, matching `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`, which never took it. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TRUNCATE TABLE` no longer blocks concurrent `DROP`, `RENAME` and other DDL queries on the same table while the data is being removed. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114672&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114672](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114672+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: CSVWithNames and CSVWithNamesAndTypes Incorrectly exports NULL Tuple as single column but defines multiple columns
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse/pg_chdb ### Describe what's wrong In 26.7 (but not 26.5), exporting values for a `Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))` column breaks the value up into multiple columns, but when the value is `NULL`, only one of the columns is populated. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes ### How to reproduce Using `clickhouse client --allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1`: ``` CREATE TABLE boxes ( id Int32 PRIMARY KEY, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point)) ); INSERT INTO boxes VALUES (1, NULL); INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('/tmp/geos-tmp.csv', 'CSVWithNames', 'id Int32, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))') SELECT * FROM boxes SETTINGS allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert=1 SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/geos-tmp.csv', 'CSVWithNames', 'id Int32, box Nullable(Tuple(high Point, low Point))') SETTINGS allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1, engine_file_truncate_on_insert=1 ``` ### Expected behavior As seen in 26.5: ``` ┌─id─┬─box──┐ 1. │ 1 │ ᴺᵁᴸᴸ │ └────┴──────┘ ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace In 26.7: ``` Received exception: Code: 27. DB::Exception: Cannot parse input: expected ',' before: '\n': (at row 1) : Row 1: Column 0, name: id, type: Int32, parsed text: "1" Column 1, name: <SKIPPED COLUMN>, type: Nothing, parsed text: "<BACKSLASH>N" ERROR: Line feed found where delimiter (,) is expected. It's like your file has less columns than expected. And if your file has the right number of columns, maybe it has unescaped quotes in values. : (in file/uri /tmp/geos-tmp.csv): While executing ParallelParsingBlockInputFormat: While executing File. (CANNOT_PARSE_INPUT_ASSERTION_FAILED) ``` ### Related issues and pull requests _No response_ ### Additional context The content of `gens-tmp.csv` on 26.5 is: ```csv "id","box" 1,\N ``` But on 26.7 it's: ```csv "id","box.high.1","box.high.2","box.low.1","box.low.2" 1,\N ``` Not sure why the tuple was converted to multiple columns on export, but `NULL` is not properly mapped to that pattern.

signal.title: Keep one output port per shard when a JOIN side reads nothing
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115057 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109393 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`Join is supported only for pipelines with one output port`) for a `full_sorting_merge` JOIN with `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges` enabled when one of the two sides is pruned to no parts at all - by the primary key, by column statistics, or because the table is empty. ### Description A JOIN sharded by primary-key ranges pairs the shards of its two sides positionally, so both sides have to produce exactly one output port per layer. `optimizeJoinByShards` builds the layers from the parts of all the sources at once and hands every source the same number of them, and `ReadFromMergeTree::readByLayers` keeps the port of an empty layer occupied by substituting a `NullSource` for it. That invariant did not hold for a source that reads nothing at all: `ReadFromMergeTree::initializePipeline` replaced the whole side with a single `NullSource` before it ever reached the layers. A side pruned to zero parts therefore arrived at the JOIN with one port while the other side kept its layers, the stream counts disagreed, `JoinStep` stopped using sharding, and the `YShaped` pipeline it went to instead accepts only a single port per side: ``` Logical error: 'Join is supported only for pipelines with one output port, got 1 and 2' ``` The fix emits one `NullSource` per layer, so the number of ports stays what the plan says it is. The layers are only ever set by `optimizeJoinByShards` (gated by `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges`, off by default) and are ignored for a read coordinated across parallel replicas, so for every other query the pipeline is unchanged. The comment at the `JoinStep` fallback claimed that the regular pipeline handles diverging stream counts. That is true for `joinPipelinesRightLeft` (hash) but not for the merge-join path, and it is what made the missing invariant look intentional, so it is corrected as well. This replaces the approach in #109393, which merged the diverging streams back together inside `joinPipelinesYShaped`; @vdimir asked there for the invariant to be fixed at its source instead, which is what this pull request does. The throw in `joinPipelinesYShaped` is left in place. Reproducer (the second query is the shape from the CI report - the sharded side keeps its layers while the other side is pruned away): ```sql CREATE TABLE t_l (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 128; CREATE TABLE t_r (k UInt64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k SETTINGS index_granularity = 128; INSERT INTO t_l SELECT number FROM numbers(1000); INSERT INTO t_r SELECT number FROM numbers(1000); SET query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges = 1, join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge', max_threads = 4; SELECT count() FROM t_l AS l JOIN (SELECT * FROM t_r WHERE k > 1000000) AS r ON l.k = r.k; SELECT count() FROM (SELECT * FROM t_l WHERE k > 1000000) AS l LEFT JOIN t_r AS r ON l.k = r.k; ``` ### How the CI report maps onto this The failing test in the report is `03447_analyzer_correlated_subqueries_tpc_h` (TPC-H Q2), run by the settings randomizer with `query_plan_join_shard_by_pk_ranges = 1` and `join_algorithm = 'full_sorting_merge'`. Replaying that query with the report's own settings, `EXPLAIN PLAN indexes=1` shows the sharded join with one side gone: ``` Join (JOIN YShaped) part ⋈ partsupp Join conditions: p_partkey = ps_partkey Sharding: [(p_partkey = ps_partkey)] ├── ReadFromMergeTree (part) Parts: 0 | Granules: 0 <- pruned by the statistics on p_size └── ReadFromMergeTree (partsupp) Parts: 1 | Granules: 1 ``` `part` is pruned to `Parts: 0` and collapses to a single port; `partsupp` keeps one port per layer. CI report this starts from: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=172d9bf947f5081ddd3288073fe0cf6be664b924&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28arm_debug%29 The stack is one of the most frequent stress and AST-fuzzer failures at the moment: 57 hits of this exact `STID 4488-4e11` since 2026-05-27 (5 of them on master), plus 21 more of the two sibling stacks `4488-4590` and `4488-4a91`. ### Verification - The reproducer above, the one from #115057, and the new test `05019_join_shard_by_pk_ranges_pruned_side` all abort on a master binary (`got 4 and 1`) and pass with the fix. - The new test also compares the sharded result against `join_algorithm = 'hash'` with `count()` plus a `cityHash64` checksum for the `LEFT`/`RIGHT` cases, where every row of the surviving side reaches the output. This covers the semantics of the padded pipeline, not only the disappearance of the exception. - TPC-H Q2 from `03447_analyzer_correlated_subqueries_tpc_h` with the report's full settings passes. - All 1061 local stateless tests matching `join`, and the primary-key-sharding tests (`03357`, `03668`, `03774`, `04065`, `04251`, `04517`, `04655`, `04812`), pass. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115352&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115352](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115352+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1724` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix segfault when a subquery scopes `distributed_plan_execute_locally`
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110084 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes a segfault and a `LOGICAL_ERROR` (`No host found for exchange stream final_result__0_0`) when a subquery sets `distributed_plan_execute_locally` in its own `SETTINGS` clause under `make_distributed_plan`. The distributed plan and the code executing it read the setting from two different contexts and could disagree, so the initiator built a self-contradictory pipeline. ### Description `QueryPlan::convertToDistributed` decides whether a `make_distributed_plan` query runs in-process or is dispatched to workers, but that decision was read from two different settings objects: `QueryPlan.cpp` used `optimization_settings` (the interpreter's context), while `createExchangeLookup` and `createDistributedQueryExecutor` re-read `distributed_plan_execute_locally` from `CurrentThread::tryGetQueryContext()`. A subquery with its own `SETTINGS` clause gets a fresh context the planner uses and the outer interpreter never sees, so the two sides can disagree. One query produced both failures: - the plan built no `TaskToHostMap` (it saw local) while the executor factory chose the remote executor (it saw non-local), whose constructor dereferences that null pointer: a segfault, present in release builds; - the plan left the exchange stream hosts empty while the lookup was built for streaming exchanges, so resolving `final_result__0_0` threw `LOGICAL_ERROR`. The fix decides once, where the decision already lives. `createExchangeLookup` takes the mode as a parameter, and `createDistributedQueryExecutor` derives it from `task_to_host_map == nullptr` instead of re-reading the setting, so the remote executor can no longer be selected with a null map. `doExecuteTask` threads the mode through: `true` from the local executor, `false` from the stateless worker. No wire format, default, or setting changes. Found in CI: five failures over ninety days across three unrelated pull requests and two check types (`Stress test`, `AST fuzzer`), no master hits, since the setting is experimental and off by default. No carrier touches this code. Example report: [Stress test (amd_debug) on #110084](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110084&sha=58929adaa0cb4921dad56606d5c4a06df5cd4bd1&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_debug%29). A deterministic repro segfaults on master 5 of 5 runs and returns the correct result with the fix. The new test covers both directions plus a control, and reverting either half of the fix independently reddens it on a different failure mode. `#86353` conflicts textually in `DistributedPlanExecutor.cpp` but does not fix this: it keeps both ambient reads. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113422&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113422](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113422+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1725` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Perf: bulk copy dense values in timeSeriesFromGrid
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - **Performance Improvement** ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): **`timeSeriesFromGrid` bulk-copies values for dense rows.** ## What changed - Add a **dense-row fast path** to `timeSeriesFromGrid`. - Use **one `insertRangeFrom` call** for dense values. - Remove repeated **per-sample `insertFrom` calls** on that path. - Use ClickHouse’s existing **`memoryIsZero()` null-map helper** for nullable rows. - Keep the **existing sample-by-sample path** for rows containing NULLs. - Keep **timestamp generation** unchanged. - Keep **row ordering and result offsets** unchanged. - Add **mixed dense and sparse multi-row coverage**. - Add a **dense nullable row after a sparse row** to cover a nonzero nested-array offset. - Add a **dense negative-timestamp case**. - Add an **all-NULL case** for the sparse fallback. ## Why this is safe - **Input length validation is unchanged.** Every row still needs exactly `num_steps` values. - **Non-nullable rows are always dense**, so they can use the range copy directly. - **Nullable rows check only their row slice** of the null map before taking the bulk path. - Rows with **any NULL stay on the existing path**, including sparse and all-NULL rows. - For nullable values, the fast path copies the already-unwrapped **nested `T` column into the non-nullable result `T` column**. - The optimization changes only **how dense values are copied**. - **Timestamps, NULL filtering, row order, and offsets keep the existing behavior.** ## Benchmark Focused `timeSeriesFromGrid` benchmark on Apple arm64 with **Release/O3 binaries**. The baseline and patch used the same remaining build objects and differed only in `timeSeriesRange.cpp` (`std::none_of` versus `memoryIsZero`). Each case ran **10 identical queries in one `clickhouse local --multiquery` process**, with `max_threads = 1`, 4,096 grid points, 10,000 input rows, and `arraySum` over the returned values so the value payload was consumed. Times below are total wall time for the 10 queries. | Workload | Baseline | Patch | Change | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | Non-nullable dense | 2.98 s | 2.51 s | **15.8% faster** | | Nullable dense | 2.24 s | 2.17 s | **3.1% faster** | | One NULL at first position | 3.49 s | 3.47 s | **flat** | | One NULL at final position | 3.55 s | 3.55 s | **flat** | | 10% NULL | 3.78 s | 3.80 s | **0.5% slower** | | 50% NULL | 2.66 s | 2.66 s | **flat** | A sample-width sweep at **256, 1,024, 4,096, and 16,384 points** showed the same shape. The sparse nullable cases stayed within normal run-to-run noise, including the late-NULL case. ## Tests - Add **dense and sparse rows in the same function call** to `03254_timeseries_range`. - Add a **sparse-first, dense-second** row pair to exercise `values_base_offset != 0`. - Cover **dense values**. - Cover **sparse values**. - Cover **nullable values**. - Cover **all-NULL values**. - Cover **dense negative timestamps**. - Compile the changed translation unit with **Ninja**. - Run **direct output checks** for mixed, offset, all-NULL, sparse, nullable, and negative-timestamp inputs. - Run **`git diff --check`**.

signal.title: Support the NetCDF format
signal.text: Adds support for the [NetCDF](https://www.unidata.ucar.edu/software/netcdf/) format, a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays that is the standard way climate, weather, oceanographic and other scientific data is distributed. There is a lot of public data in it (ERA5, CMIP, NOAA, Copernicus), and until now the only way to query it with ClickHouse was to convert it first. Reading is supported for the three "classic" versions of the format: CDF-1, CDF-2 (64-bit offset) and CDF-5 (64-bit data), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. The files are parsed directly, so there is no new dependency. A NetCDF-4 file, which is an HDF5 file with a different data model on top, is recognized and reported with a message that says how to convert it. **Data model.** Every variable of a file becomes a column, and the rows enumerate the Cartesian product of all the dimensions that the variables use; a variable that does not use some of them is repeated along them. The `to_dataframe` method of `xarray` produces a table with the same columns and the same set of rows, though possibly in a different order: `to_dataframe` puts the dimensions in alphabetical order by default, while ClickHouse keeps the order of the dimensions of the variables. So a file with the dimensions `time`, `lat`, `lon` and the variables `time(time)`, `lat(lat)`, `lon(lon)`, `temperature(time, lat, lon)` reads as a table with four columns and `time * lat * lon` rows. The classic format has no string type, so a `char` variable is read as a String whose length is the last dimension of the variable, when that dimension serves only as the length of the strings; a dimension that anything else in the file uses as a real axis stays in the row space, and such a `char` variable is read as one character per row. Only the variables that a query needs are read, the number of rows comes from the header (so `count()` does not read any data), and an input that cannot be seeked is read into memory instead. **Writing.** Every column becomes a variable over a single dimension named `row`, so a file written by ClickHouse is read back with the same column names and the same rows; the types come back as the closest types of the classic format (a `FixedString` as a `String`, an `Enum` or a `LowCardinality` column as the type it wraps, dates and times as plain numbers, a `Nullable` column as its base type unless read with `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null`). The version of the format is chosen automatically: CDF-5 when a column needs a type that only CDF-5 has or takes more than 4 GiB, CDF-2 otherwise. A `Nullable` column is written with the `_FillValue` attribute, and a column with dates or times gets the `units` attribute of the CF conventions, so `xarray` decodes it back into timestamps. **Settings.** `input_format_netcdf_fill_value_as_null` reads the values equal to the `_FillValue` (or `missing_value`) attribute of a variable as NULL, which is how the CF conventions mark missing data such as sea surface temperature over land. `input_format_netcdf_add_dimension_columns` adds a column with the index along every dimension that has no coordinate variable of the same name, for the files that have none. **Testing.** The test files in `tests/queries/0_stateless/data_netcdf` were written by the netCDF C library, not by this code. Beyond the two functional tests, during development the reader was compared value by value against an independent reference implementation for all three format versions, the output was checked by opening it with the netCDF C library for every supported type family, and 321 truncated and bit-flipped files were fed to the reader — all of them either parsed or failed with a clean error, with no crashes. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Support the `NetCDF` format for both reading and writing. It is a self-describing binary format for multidimensional arrays, widely used for climate, weather and other scientific data. Reading supports all three classic versions of the format (CDF-1, CDF-2 and CDF-5), and writing produces CDF-2 or CDF-5, whichever the data needs. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111932&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111932](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111932+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Assign merges for all partitions at once for OPTIMIZE FINAL
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/46770 For a non-replicated `MergeTree` table, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` without an explicit partition used to process partitions one by one: it selected and ran the merge for one partition, waited for it to finish, and only then moved on to the next one. On a table with many partitions this serialized all the work and only ever showed a single merge in `system.merges`. Now the per-partition merges are assigned and executed in parallel, so all partitions are merged at once. The degree of parallelism is bounded by the configured `background_pool_size` and reserves only currently available merge-executor capacity. This mirrors how `StorageReplicatedMergeTree::optimize` already assigns a merge per partition and then waits for all of them. Notes: - Tables inside an explicit transaction keep the sequential path, because parallel merges would otherwise share a single transaction object that is not made for concurrent use. - The wait for already-running merges inside `selectPartsToMerge` (the `OPTIMIZE FINAL` path) is now scoped to the current partition: merges in other partitions cannot prevent selecting all the parts of this one, and waiting for them would needlessly serialize the parallel assignment. Verified on a local build: on a table with 8 partitions, `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` now runs 8 merges concurrently (observed via `system.merges`) instead of one at a time, and every partition is still correctly merged into a single part (checked for `MergeTree`, `OPTIMIZE ... FINAL DEDUPLICATE`, and `ReplacingMergeTree`, plus the `optimize_skip_merged_partitions` / `optimize_throw_if_noop` no-op paths and two concurrent `OPTIMIZE FINAL` queries). ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on a non-replicated `MergeTree` table now assigns and runs the merges for all partitions at once instead of processing them one partition at a time. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109004&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109004](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109004+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Avoid copying data for the NONE compression codec when writing
signal.text: Avoid copying data for the `NONE` compression codec when writing. For `CODEC(NONE)` the compressed block on disk is byte-identical to the input, so the payload does not need to be copied between the compressor's working buffer and the output buffer. When a `CompressedWriteBuffer` exclusively owns its output buffer, the working buffer is now pointed directly into the output buffer (reserving room for the checksum and header in front of the data), so the caller writes the uncompressed data straight to where it will be flushed; `nextImpl` only fills in the header and checksum in place, with no payload copy. The header is written by a new `ICompressionCodec::writeHeader` helper factored out of `compress`. When the output buffer is too small, the writer falls back to the previous owned-buffer copy path. This is the same zero-copy buffer-aliasing technique that `HashingWriteBuffer` already uses. The zero-copy path (`out_buffer_is_exclusive`) is enabled only where the compressor is the sole, sequential writer of its output buffer: the wide-part column data streams, the primary-index stream, and the temporary-data buffer. It is intentionally left off where the output buffer is shared and written interleaved — the per-column streams of compact parts (which share one `plain_hashing`) and the network protocol buffer (interleaved with raw packet framing) — because there the reserved window could be overwritten by another writer. It is also left off for the marks streams of wide and compact parts: their `marks_file` has a small fixed-size buffer (4096 bytes), so the direct path would clamp `NONE`-coded mark blocks to it instead of the configured `marks_compress_block_size`; the regression test `04539_marks_compression_codec_none_block_size` covers this. Note: for `NONE`, compressed block sizes become bounded by the output buffer size, so the on-disk byte layout can differ slightly from before (an occasional shorter block at buffer boundaries). This is deterministic and does not affect reads. The read side already decompresses `NONE` data directly into the destination column via `readBig`, so no change is needed there. ### Performance evidence Measured with two `clickhouse` binaries built from the same base commit, differing only by this PR (cherry-picked onto the same parent), so the comparison isolates exactly this change. Isolated write-path microbenchmark — 4 GiB through a `CompressedWriteBuffer` with the `NONE` codec into a discarding sink (no disk), 1 MiB blocks and output buffer, toggling only `out_buffer_is_exclusive`: | `out_buffer_is_exclusive` | throughput | |---|---| | `false` (old copy path) | ~8.5–9.2 GB/s | | `true` (zero-copy path) | ~13.6–14.0 GB/s | | **speedup** | **~1.5–1.6x** | End-to-end `INSERT` of 8 wide `String CODEC(NONE)` columns (3M rows, single insert thread, no dedup/squashing/sparse, merges stopped; baseline = exact parent commit; median of interleaved reps): **2.96s → 2.62s (~1.13x, ~13% faster)**. The end-to-end gain is below the disk-free microbenchmark because disk I/O and data generation (equal in both binaries) dominate the rest of the insert. A focused performance test, `tests/performance/codec_none_read.xml`, is added. It scans `CODEC(NONE)` columns, so in the PR-vs-master comparison the table is filled by each side's own write path (old vs new block layout) and then read by the identical read code. This guards against a read regression from the slightly changed `NONE` block layout, and tracks `NONE` read throughput in general (relevant for incompressible data such as vector embeddings). Measured read time is unchanged before/after (~0.62s vs ~0.61s for 100M rows, single thread), confirming the write-path change is read-neutral. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Avoid an extra data copy when writing columns and temporary data compressed with the `NONE` codec by writing the data directly into the output buffer. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108096&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108096](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108096+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: [ClickHouse-58380] Implement Retries in distributed queries when server stopped during queries
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Add settings `distributed_query_retries` and `distributed_query_retry_interval_ms` (disabled by default): when enabled, a query to a `Distributed` table or to the `remote` table function is retried after a network error (`NETWORK_ERROR`, `SOCKET_TIMEOUT`, `ATTEMPT_TO_READ_AFTER_EOF`, e.g. when the remote server is stopped while the query is running). The query is retried on another available replica and only if no result data has been received from the remote server yet, so the result never contains duplicated rows. Queries executed with parallel replicas and cluster function tasks are not retried. While a retry is still possible, the progress reported by the remote server is deferred until the first block of result data (or the completion of the query), so the work replayed by a retry is not double-counted in read limits and quotas. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!--- The settings documentation is autogenerated from the setting descriptions in `src/Core/Settings.cpp`. --> Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/58380 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=66791&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/66791](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F66791+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add retry policy to Remote Query Executor to be able to retry failed leaf queries
signal.text: This is a continuation of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/71059, including addressing feedback kindly provided in reviews from @devcrafter . I don't have permission to push to the original branch and it's significantly out of date, so I've started a new one here. As ClickHouse clusters scale and you begin to have multiple shards with many replicas, the probability of 1 of those nodes saturated, busy or not in a condition to serve queries increases. This can often mean that a Distributed query say across dozens of shards, might fail just because of a single node. This means all the work and resources we've used on other shards is effectively thrown away, and we return an error to the client which can choose to retry the whole query if that want to. This is quite wasteful, and can often lead to cascading values if clusters are busy. This commit adds a new setting: `distributed_shard_retry_count` which defaults to 0 to effectively turn retries off for backwards compatible behaviour. If this setting is > 0 and a leaf node in a distributed query returns an error, we will retry the query on a different leaf node. Co-authored-by: Christian Cendres Co-authored-by: Anton Kozlov ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add the ability retry certain errors in distributed queries ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) - Parameters: If the feature being added takes arguments, options or is influenced by settings, please list them below with a brief explanation. distributed_shard_retry_count - the number of times a distributed query should be retried on a leaf node on the event it hits a retryable error.

signal.title: Keep the SeaweedFS mini admin gRPC port out of the ephemeral range
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109368 --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109368 Related: https://github.com/seaweedfs/seaweedfs/issues/10838 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... ### Description `test_database_iceberg_seaweedfs_catalog` can fail in fixture setup with a `Connection refused` reading as "the catalog never started" ([report](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109368&sha=4443610796f2ef985ff5615a261456a7ea4155ea&name_0=PR&name_1=Integration%20tests%20%28amd_tsan%2C%205%2F6%29), tagged `retry_ok`). It did start: it answered 200 on all 314 polls; the refusal is the last poll, after the container exited 255. Its log shows why. ``` E mini.go:1583 Admin server error: failed to listen on port 33646: bind: address already in use F mini.go:1598 Admin server readiness check failed ... after 240 attempts ``` `weed mini` derives the admin gRPC port as `admin.port + 10000` = 33646, inside the Linux ephemeral range (floor 32768), so one of mini's own startup dials can take it as a source port before admin binds it. It is the only derived gRPC port above the floor; the other four land in 18333..19340. The failure hides itself: `glog.Fatalf` skips `defer close(allServicesReady)`, and the call creating `-tableBucket=analytics` runs only after `<-allServicesReady`. S3 and Iceberg keep answering 200 while `analytics` is never created, so `"analytics" in buckets` never becomes true and a longer wait cannot help. `-admin.port=12646` derives 22646: below the floor, and below the 22768 cap SeaweedFS derives for this same problem in its own test port allocator (seaweedfs/seaweedfs#10209, which left the `mini` default alone). That default is 23646 on 4.41, 4.42 and master, so an image bump does not help; it is filed upstream. Raising `ip_local_port_range` via `sysctls`, as the Kafka composes do, would work too, but for every dial mini makes. It reaches users too: the SeaweedFS catalog guide and connector page both document `mini` on `image: latest`, so the bucket each tells the reader to use never appears. Both are pinned here; the guide's locale copies are left to the translation workflow. Validated with `docker run --sysctl net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range="33646 33646"`: unpinned reproduces the CI log verbatim, pinned creates the bucket, a default-range control is green. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115512&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115512](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115512+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Use the primary key index for first-tuple-element conditions and `pointInEllipses`
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54805 Follow-up to #112956, which taught `KeyCondition` to use the primary key index for `pointInPolygon(coord, [...])` with a `Point` key column. This PR closes the remaining gaps of the same shape: 1. **Conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column** (`coord.1 < 100`, `tupleElement(coord, 1) = 5`, or access by element name for named tuples) now use the primary key index. Tuple values are ordered lexicographically, so the first element is a non-strictly monotonic function of the tuple; it is analyzed through the regular monotonic-functions chain (`FunctionFirstTupleElementOfKey`), so composed chains such as `coord.1 + 1 <= N` and `NOT` also work. Other elements are not monotonic w.r.t. the tuple order and remain unanalyzed. 2. **`pointInEllipses(x, y, x0, y0, a, b, ...)`** over key columns now uses the primary key (and minmax) index. The analysis stores the union bounding box of the ellipses as a rectangle ring and reuses the existing `pointInPolygon` evaluation unchanged, in both the regular and the lightweight analysis paths. The box follows the function's exact semantics: an ellipse with a non-positive or `NaN` parameter matches no point (the function's own bounding-box check never passes for it); if all ellipses are empty, the condition folds to `ALWAYS_FALSE`; a non-finite box declines the analysis. The atom only ever reports `{maybe, maybe}` or `{no match, maybe}`, so `NOT pointInEllipses` stays correct. 3. **`pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), ...)` and `pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, ...)`** — the point written as the two elements of one tuple-typed key column — resolve to the single-key-column form from #112956, deriving the point's bounding box from the range of the tuple key column. Previously this natural rewrite silently disabled the index. ```sql CREATE TABLE points (coord Point) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY coord; INSERT INTO points SELECT (number, number) FROM numbers(100000); SELECT count() FROM points WHERE coord.1 <= 25000; -- Before: 100000 rows read (full scan). After: 26/100 granules. SELECT count() FROM points WHERE pointInEllipses(coord.1, coord.2, 0., 0., 5000., 5000.); -- Before: full scan. After: 6/100 granules. ``` Note: the reference outputs of the two new tests were computed analytically (counts from the data distribution, granule counts from `index_granularity = 1000`); if CI reports a formatting difference in the `EXPLAIN` lines, I will update the references from the CI output. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Use the primary key index for conditions on the first element of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `coord.1 < 100` for a table ordered by a `Point` column), for `pointInEllipses` over key columns, and for `pointInPolygon`/`pointInEllipses` with the point written as the two elements of a tuple-typed key column (e.g. `pointInPolygon((coord.1, coord.2), [...])`). Follow-up to [#112956](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112956). 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115482&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115482](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115482+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Validate IN tuple/subquery column count mismatch in analyzer
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/74442 The analyzer (`resolveFunction`) now validates that the number of elements on the left side of `IN` matches the number of columns in the right-side subquery. Previously, constant folding could optimize away the `IN` expression and silently hide the mismatch: for example, `(1, 1) IN (SELECT 1)` wrapped in a subquery with a constant-false outer `WHERE` succeeded silently. Now it correctly throws `NUMBER_OF_COLUMNS_DOESNT_MATCH` during analysis. A single `Tuple` column on the right side is still accepted, since `FunctionIn` compares the whole left-side value against it; `LowCardinality` and `Nullable` wrappers are unwrapped before the check. Covered by the new test `03380_in_tuple_subquery_column_count`, including the original reproducer from the issue. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Detect column count mismatch between a tuple and a subquery in the `IN` clause during analysis, preventing constant folding from silently hiding the error. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=97540&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/97540](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F97540+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Support the Vortex file format
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87327 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/74 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added support for reading and writing the [Vortex](https://github.com/vortex-data/vortex) columnar file format (the `Vortex` input and output format). This closes [#87327](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87327). ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes The implementation uses the Rust `vortex` crate (v0.83.0) through a new C FFI crate `rust/workspace/vortex` (`_ch_rust_vortex`), following the same pattern as `prql` and `polyglot`. Data crosses the FFI boundary through the Arrow C Data Interface and is converted with the same `ArrowColumnToCHColumn`/`CHColumnToArrowColumn` code as the `Arrow` format. IO is delegated back to ClickHouse through callbacks: reads go through ClickHouse's own read buffers (range reads for seekable inputs, whole-file buffering otherwise), and the produced file is streamed into the output buffer. The library spawns no threads of its own: a scan is split into tasks that ClickHouse runs on its own thread pools (`max_parsing_threads` for decoding, `max_download_threads` for reads), writing is driven on the calling thread, and Rust panics are caught at the FFI boundary and turned into exceptions. Features: - Reading with projection pushdown: only the columns used by the query are read from the file. - Parallel reading (merged from https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 by @m7kss1): the file is split into row ranges that are read, filtered, and decoded concurrently; nearby segment reads are coalesced into one request. Chunks are returned as soon as they are decoded, so the row order is not guaranteed unless `input_format_vortex_preserve_order` is set. - Schema inference and `count()`-only queries answered from file metadata without reading data. - Writing with the library's default adaptive compression (BtrBlocks-style cascading encodings + zstd), including a valid empty file for empty results. - Graceful errors on malformed and truncated files (fuzzer-friendly: no aborts, Rust panics become exceptions). Limitations (documented in `docs/reference/formats/Vortex.mdx`): - `Map`, `Int128`/`UInt128`/`Int256`/`UInt256`, `IPv6`, and `Interval` columns cannot be written (no corresponding Vortex type). - `String` and `FixedString` are written as Vortex `Binary` (ClickHouse strings are arbitrary bytes, while Vortex requires `Utf8` to be valid UTF-8). - The format is disabled in MSan builds: the MSan-instrumented library (with origin tracking) is so large that linking `unit_tests_dbms` overflows the 2 GiB `R_X86_64_PC32` relocation range (same approach as `wasmtime` and `delta-kernel-rs`). - Writing is single-threaded in this first version: the adaptive compressor samples many encodings per column, so writes are slower than `Parquet` — parallelism can be added later. Reading is parallel since https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115096 was merged into this PR: on ClickBench, reads went from geomean ~26.8x slower than `Parquet` to ~1.2x, winning 9 of 43 queries (see the [benchmark results](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112950#issuecomment-5337908877)). Filter pushdown (added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114373, `input_format_vortex_filter_push_down`, on by default) reduces the rows decoded by selective queries; whole segments are not yet pruned by statistics, so the most selective queries are still 1.5-5.5x slower than `Parquet`, which skips pages via min/max statistics. The 127 new vendored Rust crates are added in https://github.com/ClickHouse/rust_vendor/pull/74 (the `contrib/rust_vendor` submodule is bumped to that branch). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112950&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112950](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112950+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: [RFC] Text index: columnar front coding and `dictionary_block_encoding` parameter
signal.text: This RFC proposes two changes to the text index dictionary: 1. A new parameter `dictionary_block_encoding`, which names the token layout of a dictionary block. It replaces the boolean `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression`. 2. A new layout `columnar_frontcoding`. It stores the same data as front coding, but keeps the per-token integers in two bit-packed columns. It is smaller and decodes faster. The two are independent. The parameter is useful on its own, and the layout could ship under the old boolean. Together they also leave room for further layouts later. ## Background The text index dictionary lives in `.dct`. It is split into blocks of `dictionary_block_size` tokens (512 by default). Tokens inside a block are sorted. Two facts about `.dct` shape this proposal. - **It is already compressed.** Each dictionary block starts a new compressed block, so a lookup decompresses only one block. The codec comes from `default_compression_codec`, then the server `<compression>` config, then the built-in `LZ4`. Nobody has to ask for it. - **The format is self-describing.** Each block starts with a `tokens_format` varint. `deserializeTokens` reads it and picks the decoder. So one table can hold parts with different formats, and a merge can read them all. Today the index parameter `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression` picks between two formats: `0` for raw tokens, `1` for front coding. Front coding is a *token encoding*. It runs before the codec, not instead of it. With default settings the dictionary is front coded, then `LZ4` compressed. ## Motivation Front coding stores two varints per token: the length of the prefix shared with the previous token, and the length of the suffix. The suffix bytes follow. This costs space. A prefix length needs about 5 bits, but a varint spends 8. Tokens are sorted, so suffixes are short, often one or two bytes. The two varints can be bigger than the data they describe. This costs decode time too. `deserializeTokensFrontCoding` does two dependent varint reads per token inside the reconstruction loop. The loop also calls `resize_exact`, because the total size is not known in advance. Both costs grow when tokens are short. With `ngrams(6)`, sorted tokens share 5 characters with the previous token, so the suffix is one byte. The varints are twice the payload. ## New parameter: `dictionary_block_encoding` The current parameter is a boolean, so it cannot name a third layout. Replace it with names: | `dictionary_block_encoding` | `tokens_format` | Meaning | |-------------------------|-----------------|---------| | `none` | `0` | Raw tokens | | `frontcoding` | `1` | Front coding, today's default | | `columnar_frontcoding` | `2` | New layout, below | A matching setting `text_index_dictionary_block_encoding` sets the table default, like the other `text_index_*` settings. The index argument wins over the table setting. `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression` stays accepted. See Compatibility. ## New layout: `columnar_frontcoding` Keep front coding, but move the two integers out of the byte stream. A block stores all prefix lengths, then all suffix lengths, then all suffix bytes. Current layout (`tokens_format = 1`): ``` varint tokens_format varint num_tokens varint first_token_size bytes first_token varint prefix_length \ varint suffix_size | repeated per token bytes suffix / ``` Proposed layout (`tokens_format = 2`): ``` varint tokens_format varint num_tokens varint first_token_size bytes first_token varint prefix_length_width -- bits per value, 0 if all values are 0 varint suffix_size_width -- bits per value bits prefix_length[n-1] -- bit-packed column bits suffix_size[n-1] -- bit-packed column bytes all suffixes ``` The token infos after the tokens do not change. ### Example Four sorted tokens: `token1`, `token10`, `token11`, `token2`. | Token | Prefix length | Suffix | |-----------|---------------|--------| | `token1` | - | - | | `token10` | 6 | `0` | | `token11` | 6 | `1` | | `token2` | 5 | `2` | Today, interleaved: ``` 6 "token1" | 6 1 "0" | 6 1 "1" | 5 1 "2" ``` Proposed, three regions: ``` 6 "token1" | widths: 3 1 | prefix: 6 6 5 | suffix: 1 1 1 | bytes: "0" "1" "2" ``` The prefix column needs 3 bits per value, because the largest value is 6. The suffix column needs 1 bit. So one token costs 4 bits instead of two varints. For a full block of 512 tokens: | Layout | Bytes for the integers | |--------|------------------------| | Front coding | 512 × 2 varints ≈ 1024 | | Columnar front coding | 512 × 4 bits + 2 width bytes ≈ 258 | ### Why it decodes faster - Each column holds one kind of value, so a per-block bit width beats a varint per value. - Both columns are unpacked in bulk first. The reconstruction loop then does two `memcpy` per token and no varint decoding. - The total size is known before reconstruction starts, so the output column is sized once. ## Measurements Background merges were stopped, so all configurations get the same part layout. Sizes are summed over active parts only. Decode is a full dictionary scan with `use_text_index_dictionary_cache = 0`, minimum of 7 runs. Parts are unmerged and each holds its own dictionary, so read the ratios, not the absolute numbers. Token layout alone, with `default_compression_codec = 'NONE'`: | Dataset | `frontcoding` | `columnar_frontcoding` | Size | Decode | |---------|---------------|------------------------|------|--------| | `text_log`, 50M rows, `splitByNonAlpha` | 119.3 MB / 262 ms | 111.4 MB / 250 ms | **−6.7%** | **−4.6%** | | hackernews, 8M rows, `splitByNonAlpha` | 135.8 MB / 391 ms | 128.6 MB / 373 ms | **−5.3%** | **−4.6%** | | `text_log`, 10M rows, `ngrams(5)` | 54.2 MB / 138 ms | 48.7 MB / 133 ms | **−10.2%** | **−3.6%** | | `text_log`, 10M rows, `ngrams(6)` | 142.2 MB / 380 ms | 124.0 MB / 363 ms | **−12.8%** | **−4.5%** | The size gain grows as tokens get shorter, as the layout predicts. The decode gain is about 4.5% everywhere. With the inherited codec on top, which is what would ship: | Configuration | `.dct` | Decode | |---------------|--------|--------| | `frontcoding` + `LZ4`, today | 107.2 MB | 312 ms | | `columnar_frontcoding` + `LZ4` | 103.4 MB (**−3.5%**) | 292 ms (**−6.4%**) | **The size gain depends on the data once a codec runs on top.** Bit-packing removes redundancy the codec used to find: a varint column repeats a lot, a bit-packed column does not. On a synthetic dictionary of `token0 … token99999`, `columnar_frontcoding` + `LZ4` was **0.25% larger**. On `text_log` it was 3.5% smaller. The decode gain does not depend on the codec. Write cost is not measurable. Build time is dominated by tokenization and posting lists. It varied by about 1% with no ordering that followed the layout. ## Configuration ```sql -- per index INDEX idx doc TYPE text(tokenizer = 'splitByNonAlpha', dictionary_block_encoding = 'columnar_frontcoding') -- per table, for text indexes that do not set the argument SETTINGS text_index_dictionary_block_encoding = 'columnar_frontcoding' ``` The table setting applies to new parts only. Existing parts keep their layout. To see what a part uses: ```sql SELECT DISTINCT part_name, dictionary_compression FROM mergeTreeTextIndex(currentDatabase(), tab, idx); ``` `dictionary_compression` gains a `columnar_front_coded` value, next to `raw` and `front_coded`. The numeric enum values do not change. ## Compatibility ### The old parameter keeps working `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression` is stored in the `CREATE TABLE` text of existing tables. ATTACH parses index arguments again, and an unknown argument throws `Unexpected text index arguments`. Removing it would stop those tables from starting. So it stays as a deprecated alias: | Deprecated | New equivalent | |------------|----------------| | `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression = 0` | `dictionary_block_encoding = 'none'` | | `dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression = 1` | `dictionary_block_encoding = 'frontcoding'` | `0` must mean "raw tokens that still inherit the part codec". That is what `none` means here. Mapping `0` to "raw tokens, no compression" would make every affected dictionary larger after an upgrade. Precedence: - Both arguments in one index definition: error. They set the same thing. ```sql -- error INDEX idx doc TYPE text(tokenizer = 'splitByNonAlpha', dictionary_block_encoding = 'frontcoding', dictionary_block_frontcoding_compression = 1) ``` - Both settings on one table: `text_index_dictionary_block_encoding` wins if set explicitly, otherwise the old setting is used. Settings come from several config layers, so both being set is not always a mistake. - An index argument always wins over a table setting. ### Reading old parts Nothing to do. Each block stores its own `tokens_format`. ### Old servers reading new parts This is the only real risk. A server that does not know `tokens_format = 2` fails with `CORRUPTED_DATA: Unknown tokens serialization format (2)`. It affects a downgrade after an upgrade, and a mixed-version cluster where an old replica fetches a new part. Being self-describing does not help, because the reader has never heard of the format. Plan: 1. Add the parameter with default `frontcoding`, so nothing changes on upgrade. 2. Change the default to `columnar_frontcoding` in a later release. Record it in `SettingsChangesHistory.cpp` so `compatibility` restores the old value, and add a changelog note about downgrades. ### Merges A merge reads source parts with different layouts and writes the output in the currently configured layout. This works because the format is per block. The merge path must resolve the layout the same way the insert path does. Otherwise a merge can silently rewrite `columnar_frontcoding` back to `frontcoding`, and no error is raised. So a test should assert the layout of the merged part, not only the query results. ## Follow-up Front coding has one more cost. A token can only be decoded after the token before it. So to read one token, the whole block must be decoded. Example: `hasToken(doc, 'clickhouse')` needs one dictionary block. That block holds 512 tokens. All 512 are decoded. Then a binary search picks the one token that was needed. Restart points would fix this. Every 32 tokens, store the full token instead of a prefix length. A lookup then decodes 32 tokens instead of 512. The measurements above do not show this. They are full dictionary scans, which decode every token anyway. A point lookup should gain much more than 4.5%. Restart points would also help SIMD. Today each token waits for the token before it, so the decode loop cannot be vectorized.
