signal.title: Web terminal: do not connect before the host page supplies the credentials
signal.text: A `/webterminal` page embedded in a host page - `play.html`, or the ClickHouse Cloud console - is loaded without credentials in its URL and receives them from the host page over `postMessage`, on the iframe's `load` event. It nevertheless opened a connection of its own at startup, before that message could arrive, so every embedded terminal authenticated twice: first with an empty password, which can only succeed for a passwordless user, and then, a moment later, with the credentials from the host page, after the first WebSocket had been closed and replaced. The visible symptom is `Connecting...` printed twice - `attemptConnect` announces every attempt, and whether the first line is erased before the second is printed depends on timing. Behind it are a wasted WebSocket, a guaranteed-failing authentication, and, for a passwordless user, an established session that gets torn down right away. The page now waits for the credentials instead of connecting on its own. A host page that never sends them - it does not implement the protocol, or its origin is not trusted - would leave a terminal that neither connects nor prompts, so the page says that it is waiting and Enter hands the login over to the interactive prompt; credentials arriving after that no longer hijack what the user is typing. The pages opened as a normal tab, or with a `user` URL parameter, keep connecting immediately. The wait became a state of the page's own state machine, which makes the `waitingForCredentials` and `initialAutoAuth` flags, and the `ws.onclose` branch they served, unnecessary. The new `tests/integration/test_webterminal_startup` follows the existing `test_play_reconcile_startup`: it fetches `/webterminal` from a real server and runs the page's real script in a Node `vm` with a stubbed terminal and `WebSocket`, then drives each flow and asserts which connections were opened and what was displayed. Against this branch all 34 checks pass; against `master` 23 fail, including `announces the attempt exactly once -- actual: 2`. It also pins the paths that must keep connecting immediately, the prompt after a rejected password, and that credentials from an untrusted origin, from a trusted host over plain HTTP, or from a window that is not the parent are ignored - the wait is now the only way into an embedded session, so a hole in either check would hand the terminal to a foreign page. Reported by a user of clickhouse.new, where the console drives the terminal through exactly this embedded flow. signal.title: Retry the release-branch version-bump push onto origin's advanced tip
signal.text: The deferred patch version bump is pushed to the release branch as the last release step. The branch is already re-synced to origin's tip before the push, but a backport landing in the window between that re-sync and the push still rejects it as non-fast-forward. `Git.push` gains an optional `rebase_retries` (with `git_prefix` for the committer identity): on a non-fast-forward rejection it fetches the branch, rebases the local commits onto its new tip, and retries. The first push runs outside the loop and each retry rebases first, so `rebase_retries=N` performs N real retries. The version-bump push passes `rebase_retries=5`, so `patch+1` lands on top of the backport without discarding it. `VERSION_GITHASH` stays the released commit and rebase replays the bump commit unchanged, so the tweak baseline is preserved. `Git.push` also runs its first push verbosely (the command logs the parameters and its output diagnoses a rejection), and on a dry run it now runs `git push --dry-run` — contacting the remote and reporting what would happen without updating any ref — instead of skipping the push. Adds `test_bump_retries_onto_advanced_branch_tip` (the only non-dry push test) and a `_setup_bare_origin` helper so the dry-run tests exercise the real `git push --dry-run` against a local bare origin. The version-bump correctness fix and the `prepare` decision refactor landed separately in #114472; this is the push-retry hardening on top. ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113834&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113834](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113834+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1722` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Offer the `/`-commands of the client, and name them when misspelled
signal.text: Typing `/` at the beginning of the input now shows the client's own commands (`/clear`, `/help`, `/man`) as as-you-type hints, and typing more of a name narrows the list down. `Tab` completes the command being typed, which is also how they are completed when the instant hints are disabled (`--hints 0`, `--highlight 0`, `--disable_suggestion`). Until now these commands could only be found in the documentation; now the prompt itself lists them. A mistake in the name of a command is reported as such, with the commands it may have meant, instead of being parsed as SQL and reported as a syntax error at the `/`: ``` :) /hepl Exception on client: Code: 36. DB::Exception: Unknown command `/hepl`. Maybe you meant: ['/help']. Type `/` at the beginning of the line to see all the commands. (BAD_ARGUMENTS) ``` An argument given to a command that takes none (`/clear now`) is reported the same way. Batch `clickhouse-client` still parses such input as the SQL it is, exactly like it already does for `help` and `clear`; `clickhouse-local` reports it like the interactive client. The commands come from a single list, `clientSlashCommands`, shared by the hints, the completion and the diagnostics. An offered command replaces the whole typed prefix including the `/`, which `replxx` counts as a word break character and would otherwise leave in place. The offer is off for `keeper-client` and `clickhouse-disks`: they reuse the same line reader, and a leading `/` is the beginning of a path there. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/114043 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): The `/`-commands of the client (`/help`, `/man`, `/clear`) are now offered by the line editor: typing `/` at the beginning of the input lists them as hints, and `Tab` completes the command being typed. A mistake in the name of a command is reported with the similar commands suggested, instead of being parsed as SQL. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115039&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115039](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115039+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Introduce `system.iceberg_files` table
signal.text: ### Background Currently ClickHouse provides `system.iceberg_history` (src/Storages/System) for snapshot history and `system.iceberg_metadata_log` for low-level debug logging of metadata parsing. However, there is no structured, queryable view of the data files that make up an Iceberg table's current snapshot. Spark exposes `table.files / table.data_files` (https://iceberg.apache.org/docs/latest/spark-queries/#files) metadata tables that allow users to inspect the table's physical layout. This is valuable for: - Diagnosing performance issues (e.g. too many small files, skewed partitions) - Understanding table structure without external tooling - Monitoring partition-level file/row counts `system.iceberg_metadata_log` contains similar information but as raw JSON/Avro blobs, is per-query (not a stable view of the table state), and requires explicit opt-in via `iceberg_metadata_log_level`. ### Implementation notes Proposed schema ``` database String table String snapshot_id Int64 content Enum8('DATA' = 0, 'POSITION_DELETE' = 1, 'EQUALITY_DELETE' = 2) file_path String file_format String record_count Int64 file_size_in_bytes Int64 partition String schema_id Int32 sequence_number Int64 sort_order_id Nullable(Int32) null_value_counts Map(Int32, Int64) column_sizes Map(Int32, Int64) value_counts Map(Int32, Int64) equality_ids Nullable(Array(Int32)) ``` - Follow the existing `StorageSystemIcebergHistory` pattern: iterate all Iceberg tables, read metadata, fill columns. - Most fields already exist in `ManifestFileEntry`. Two fields — `record_count` and `file_size_in_bytes` are present in the Avro manifest schema (field-ids 103 and 104) but currently not stored in ManifestFileEntry and need to be added. - The partition column should contain a human-readable serialization of `ManifestFileEntry::partition_key_value`. Example ```sql CREATE TABLE iceberg_db.events ( event_date Date, user_id UInt64, event_type String ) ENGINE = IcebergS3('http://s3:9000/warehouse/events', ...) PARTITION BY event_date SETTINGS iceberg_format_version = 2; After a simple insert: INSERT INTO iceberg_db.events VALUES ('2025-01-01', 1, 'click'), ('2025-01-01', 2, 'view'), ('2025-01-02', 3, 'click'); SELECT database, table, content, file_path, file_format, record_count, file_size_in_bytes, partition, sequence_number FROM system.iceberg_files WHERE database = 'iceberg_db' AND table = 'events'; ┌─database───┬─table──┬─content─┬─file_path──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─file_format─┬─record_count─┬─file_size_in_bytes─┬─partition──────┬─sequence_number─┐ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-01/00000-0-....-00001.parquet │ PARQUET │ 2 │ 847 │ {2025-01-01} │ 1 │ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-02/00000-0-....-00002.parquet │ PARQUET │ 1 │ 631 │ {2025-01-02} │ 1 │ └────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────┘ After a second insert (two snapshots, three data files): INSERT INTO iceberg_db.events VALUES ('2025-01-01', 4, 'purchase'); ┌─database───┬─table──┬─content─┬─file_path──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─file_format─┬─record_count─┬─file_size_in_bytes─┬─partition──────┬─sequence_number─┐ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-01/00000-0-....-00001.parquet │ PARQUET │ 2 │ 847 │ {2025-01-01} │ 1 │ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-02/00000-0-....-00002.parquet │ PARQUET │ 1 │ 631 │ {2025-01-02} │ 1 │ │ iceberg_db │ events │ DATA │ warehouse/events/data/event_date=2025-01-01/00000-1-....-00001.parquet │ PARQUET │ 1 │ 620 │ {2025-01-01} │ 2 │ └────────────┴────────┴─────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┴────────────────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────┘ ``` <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Resolved by: #104415 - Merged into: `26.6.1.614` (included in `26.6` and later) - Backported to: `26.5.8.4` <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Parquet fails to write Nullable(Tuple) correctly
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe the unexpected behaviour When writing a Nullable(Tuple(...)) column (including the geo aliases, Nullable(Point), Nullable(Ring) element types, Array(Nullable(Point))) to Parquet, the tuple's own null map is discarded: the schema written is a required group with nullable leaves, so Nullable(Point) comes out as Tuple(1 Nullable(Float64), 2 Nullable(Float64)). Reading the file back with the original schema fails with Code: 53 ... Requested type of column p doesn't match parquet schema: parquet type is Tuple, requested type is Nullable(Point) (TYPE_MISMATCH); reading with schema inference turns NULL row into (NULL,NULL) Parquet can express this (an optional group), and Arrow, ArrowStream, & ORC all round-trip correctly. `output_format_parquet_use_custom_encoder` 1 and 0 produce the same schema. ### How to reproduce Repro on 26.6.1.431: ``` -- clickhouse local --allow_experimental_nullable_tuple_type=1 INSERT INTO FUNCTION file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet, 'p Nullable(Point)') SELECT * FROM values('p Nullable(Point)', (1,2), (NULL)); DESCRIBE file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet); -- p Tuple(`1` Nullable(Float64), `2` Nullable(Float64)) SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet, 'p Nullable(Point)'); -- Code: 53. DB::Exception: ... parquet type is Tuple, requested type is Nullable(Point). (TYPE_MISMATCH) SELECT * FROM file('/tmp/np.parquet', Parquet); -- (1,2) then (NULL,NULL), NULL row lost ``` Same for `Nullable(Tuple(a UInt8, b String))` & `Array(Nullable(Point))` ### Expected behavior round trip preserves NULL ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_ ### Additional context _No response_

signal.title: Uncompressed Keeper snapshots are written as 0-byte files; node cannot restart
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong **With `compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format=false`, every snapshot Keeper writes to a local disk is 0 bytes although it logs `Created persistent snapshot N`. On the next restart Keeper dies with `Failure to load from latest snapshot ... Cannot read all data. Bytes read: 0 ... Manual intervention is necessary for recovery. Problematic snapshot can be removed but it will lead to data loss (CORRUPTED_DATA)`.** - **Root cause:** In the non-zstd branch the file buffer is wrapped BY REFERENCE (`std::make_unique<CompressedWriteBuffer>(*writer)`), so finalizing `compressed_writer` (:903) only pushes bytes into `writer`'s in-memory buffer; `compressed_writer->sync()` (:906) is the base no-op for that class and `writer.reset()` (:910) destroys the file buffer without `finalize`/`next`, discarding everything. The zstd branch passes ownership (`wrapWriteBufferWithCompressionMethod(std::move(writer), ...)`), so finalize/sync propagate — which is why only the uncompressed path is broken. <details> <summary>Analysis details (evidence, affected locations, impact)</summary> **Why we believe this is a bug:** `KeeperStateMachine::create_snapshot` -> `writeSnapshotToDisk` -> `KeeperSnapshotManager::writeSnapshotFile` (KeeperStateMachine.cpp:1027, local-disk branch) -> KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:896. **Affected locations:** - [`src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:896`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/ac58c4e749468/src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp#L896) — non-owning CompressedWriteBuffer over the file write buffer - [`src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:910`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/ac58c4e749468/src/Coordination/KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp#L910) — writer.reset() without finalize/sync - [`src/Coordination/KeeperStateMachine.cpp:1027`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/ac58c4e749468/src/Coordination/KeeperStateMachine.cpp#L1027) — local-disk snapshots go through writeSnapshotFile **Impact:** Any Keeper/ClickHouse deployment with `compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format=false` silently writes empty snapshots. The node refuses to start after any restart and recovery requires deleting the snapshot, which ClickHouse's own message describes as data loss; a leader also has nothing usable to send to a recovering follower. </details> ### Does it reproduce on most recent release? Yes — confirmed on current `master` (commit `ac58c4e749468`). ### How to reproduce ```python import pytest import helpers.keeper_utils as keeper_utils from helpers.cluster import ClickHouseCluster cluster = ClickHouseCluster(__file__) node_zstd = cluster.add_instance( "node_zstd", main_configs=["configs/keeper_zstd.xml"], stay_alive=True, with_remote_database_disk=False ) node_plain = cluster.add_instance( "node_plain", main_configs=["configs/keeper_plain.xml"], stay_alive=True, with_remote_database_disk=False ) SNAPSHOT_DIR = "/var/lib/clickhouse/coordination/snapshots" @pytest.fixture(scope="module") -- def started_cluster(): -- try: cluster.start() yield cluster -- finally: cluster.shutdown() @pytest.mark.parametrize("node_name", ["node_zstd", "node_plain"]) -- def test_snapshot_survives_restart(started_cluster, node_name): node = cluster.instances[node_name] keeper_utils.wait_until_connected(cluster, node) zk = keeper_utils.get_fake_zk(cluster, node.name) zk.create("/test_uncompressed_snapshot", b"somedata") idx = keeper_utils.send_4lw_cmd(cluster, node, cmd="csnp").strip() node.wait_for_log_line(f"Created persistent snapshot {idx} with path") sizes = node.exec_in_container(["bash", "-c", f"stat -c '%n %s' {SNAPSHOT_DIR}/snapshot_*"]).strip() print(f"{node_name} SNAPSHOT_FILES: {sizes}") node.restart_clickhouse() keeper_utils.wait_until_connected(cluster, node) zk = keeper_utils.get_fake_zk(cluster, node.name) assert zk.get("/test_uncompressed_snapshot")[0] == b"somedata" # configs/keeper_zstd.xml and configs/keeper_plain.xml are identical single-node keeper # configs (tcp_port 9181, server_id 1, local log/snapshot paths, four_letter_word_white_list *), -- # except that keeper_plain.xml adds inside <coordination_settings>: # <compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format>false</compress_snapshots_with_zstd_format> ``` ### Expected behavior ``` Both parameterizations pass: the snapshot file is non-empty for both settings and the node restarts and still serves /test_uncompressed_snapshot. ``` ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` node_zstd SNAPSHOT_FILES: /var/lib/clickhouse/coordination/snapshots/snapshot_13_ebe6b90817820fc1.bin.zstd 440 -> PASSED node_plain SNAPSHOT_FILES: /var/lib/clickhouse/coordination/snapshots/snapshot_15_4d88ed92c255dd85.bin 0 -> FAILED (Exception: Cannot start ClickHouse, see additional info in logs) node_plain clickhouse-server.err.log: 2026.08.19 01:42:55.320161 <Error> void DB::KeeperDispatch ``` <details> <summary>Suggested fix</summary> Finalize and sync the underlying file buffer in the non-zstd branch, e.g. after `compressed_writer->finalize()` add `writer->finalize(); writer->sync();` (or give the LZ4 branch ownership of `writer` the way the zstd branch does). </details> <details> <summary>Additional context</summary> **Open risks:** - The same non-owning wrap exists at KeeperSnapshotManager.cpp:687 (`serializeSnapshotToBuffer`), but there the sink is `WriteBufferFromNuraftBuffer` whose `getBuffer()` finalizes, so that path is correct. Found during automated review of [PR #111715](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111715). Severity P1 · Finding `h_pr111715_001` </details> cc @al13n321 @antonio2368 (from #111715)

signal.title: Add Decimal-returning pow(Decimal)
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse ### Use case It would be useful to provide a precision-preserving variant of `pow()` that returned a Decimal value for Decimal arguments. ### Describe the solution you'd like The current [pow function](https://clickhouse.com/docs/reference/functions/regular-functions/math-functions#pow) returns Float64, even when its argument is a Decimal. This leads to loss of precision. Consider this example (CH v26.7.2): ``` SELECT pow(1.2345678901234567, CAST(2, 'Decimal')) ┌─pow(1.234567⋯'Decimal'))─┐ 1. │ 1.5241578753238834 │ └──────────────────────────┘ ``` Compare to the use of numeric arguments in Postgres (which perfectly preserve precision): ``` david=# select pow(1.234567890123456789, 2::numeric); pow ---------------------- 1.524157875323883675 ``` ### Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ### Additional context ClickHouse/pg_clickhouse#339

signal.title: Fix AI SQL generation failing on prompts that need several schema lookups
signal.text: AI SQL generation (`??`) failed on any prompt needing more than one schema lookup: the bundled `ai-sdk-cpp` rebuilt every step's request from the initial options, so the model lost all earlier tool results and kept re-requesting the same schemas until the step limit — and the client then prepopulated the model's explanatory text as if it were the generated query, claiming success. Observed output (result previews trimmed): ``` :) ?? query all nodes for their partitions with most active parts (only show one row per node, ...) • Starting AI SQL generation with schema discovery... ───────────────────────────────────────────────── 🔧 Calling: list_databases [toolu_01...] ✓ list_databases completed 🔧 Calling: list_tables_in_database [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system"} ✓ list_tables_in_database completed 🔧 Calling: get_schema_for_table [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system","table":"parts"} ✓ get_schema_for_table completed 🔧 Calling: get_schema_for_table [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system","table":"clusters"} ✓ get_schema_for_table completed 🔧 Calling: get_schema_for_table [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system","table":"parts"} ✓ get_schema_for_table completed 🔧 Calling: get_schema_for_table [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system","table":"clusters"} ✓ get_schema_for_table completed 🔧 Calling: get_schema_for_table [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system","table":"parts"} ✓ get_schema_for_table completed 🔧 Calling: get_schema_for_table [toolu_01...] └─ Args: {"database":"system","table":"clusters"} ✓ get_schema_for_table completed ───────────────────────────────────────────────── • ⚠️ No SQL query was generated: the schema exploration step limit was reached (ai.max_steps = 10) ``` (The honest final status line is itself part of this PR — previously this run ended with `✨ SQL query generated successfully!` and the model's explanatory prose prepopulated at the prompt.) Update `ai-sdk-cpp` to the upstream fix (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ai-sdk-cpp/pull/40). On the client side: extract the query from the last `<sql>` block and treat a response without the tags as "no query generated"; report when the step limit was reached (naming `ai.max_steps`); show the model's text when it answered with prose. Also raise the default `ai.max_steps` from 5 to 10: the [client documentation](https://clickhouse.com/docs/concepts/features/interfaces/client) has always stated the default is `10`, and 5 was too small in practice — the final answer consumes a step too, so exploring even two tables could exhaust the limit. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Fixed AI SQL generation (`??` in `clickhouse-client`) failing on prompts that require several schema lookups: the model lost earlier tool results between steps and re-requested the same schemas until the step limit was reached. The client now reports honestly when no query was generated, and the default `ai.max_steps` matches the documented value of 10.

signal.title: Fix DPsub join reordering silently dropping single-table ON-clause filters
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111898 The `dpsub` join-order algorithm silently dropped single-table filter and constant predicates that live in a `JOIN ... ON` clause (e.g. `t1.value = 'x'`), returning extra rows. `greedy` uses a different placement path and was unaffected. The predicates are placed in `collectJoinEdgesMask`. Two placement conditions there each silently dropped such a predicate: - `two_relations` required the whole join step to be exactly two relations, so the predicate was dropped whenever its relation was introduced against an already-multi-relation subplan (e.g. `t1` at the top of `t1 JOIN (t2 JOIN t3)`). - `fromLeft() || fromRight() || fromNone()` dropped the predicate for any single-table filter on a relation whose id is >= 2, because `fromLeft`/`fromRight` test relation ids 0 and 1 specifically (they describe the two inputs of a binary join step, not "references a single relation"). The predicate is now attached at the join that introduces its relation (the split whose one side is exactly that relation), and pure constants at the earliest two-relation join. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `dpsub` join-order optimization (`query_plan_optimize_join_order_algorithm = 'dpsub'`) silently dropping single-table filter conditions from a `JOIN ... ON` clause, which could return extra rows. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114629&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114629](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114629+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Split the new-release-branch and patch release flows into separate jobs
signal.text: Follow-up to #113834 addressing https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113834#discussion_r3757704220: the single `release_job.py` entangled `create_new_release`, `is_branch_release`, and `release_type == "patch"` across one step sequence. The "new" (cut a release branch) and "patch" flows share almost nothing, so they are fully separated — into two job files **and** two dispatch workflows. - `ci/jobs/release_branch_job.py` + `ci/workflows/create_release_branch.py` (`CreateReleaseBranch`) — the "new" flow only: fetch history, configure git auth, prepare, push tag, push the new branch, open the master version-bump PR, merge. Its only inputs are `ref` and `dry-run`; it has no `release_type` branching, no `create_new_release`, no `only-repo`/`only-docker`, and no Docker/R2/GPG setup — so its credential cleanup only removes the env script. - `ci/jobs/release_job.py` + `ci/workflows/create_release.py` (`CreateRelease`) — the "patch" flow only. The `type` input is gone and every previous `release_type == "patch"` guard is now unconditional; `auto_releases.yml` no longer passes `type: patch` (it only ever released patches). `create_release.py` loses its argparse CLI: both orchestrators (and the tests) call its release actions as functions directly (`prepare_release_info`, `push_release_tag`, ..., `merge_prs`, `post_status`). The two job files drop argparse too — their parameters only ever arrive as workflow inputs, read via praktika `Info`. `update_contributors` uses `os.path.relpath` so the embedded "autogenerated by" path no longer requires the module to live under cwd. `create_release.yml` / `create_release_branch.yml` were regenerated via `praktika yaml`. Validated with workflow dry-runs: the new-branch flow is green end-to-end; the patch flow reaches the inherently non-hermetic package download (S3 404 for a synthetic version, same as before the refactor). Stacked on #113834 (based on its branch, not `master`). Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113834 ### Changelog category (leave one): - CI Fix or Improvement (changelog entry is not required)

signal.title: Fix wrong results of the partial aggregation strategy in distributed query plans
signal.text: The partial+merge aggregation strategy of `make_distributed_plan` rewrites a final aggregation into a partial `AggregatingStep` plus a memory-efficient `MergingAggregatedStep`. The memory-efficient merge consumes each input as a stream of two-level buckets in ascending order, but the rewrite kept `should_produce_results_in_order_of_bucket_number = false` on the partial step, so its multi-stream output was combined into the single exchange stream in arbitrary order. When a bucket arrived after the merge had already emitted it, the merge emitted it a second time: duplicated `GROUP BY` keys with split aggregate states (for ClickBench Q08, a wrong `COUNT(DISTINCT UserID)`). The fix, one commit each: - Make the row count estimation look through `LogicalExchangeStep`. The `#if CLICKHOUSE_CLOUD` guard around it was needed when the exchange steps existed only in the private repo; since they are in the public repo, the guard only made every aggregation over a distributed read fall back to the Shuffle strategy in non-cloud builds (and masked this bug there). - Validate the bucket delivery order in `GroupingAggregatedTransform`: an unannounced late bucket now fails with a `LOGICAL_ERROR` exception instead of silently duplicating groups. - Wait for delayed buckets in `GroupingAggregatedTransform` when the consumer needs the output in bucket order, and release the announcements of finished inputs. Covered by a gtest. - Build the partial step with `should_produce_results_in_order_of_bucket_number = true` when the merge is memory-efficient (`AggregatingStep::cloneAsPartial`). The partial aggregation then produces a single bucket-ordered stream per worker, the same contract the classic distributed path establishes on shards. signal.title: Add MergeTree settings `max_table_size_rows`, `max_table_size_bytes_compressed`, `max_table_size_bytes_uncompressed`
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115063 Adds three new `MergeTree`-level settings that limit the total size of a table, for multi-tenant, temporary, and demo services: - `max_table_size_rows` — the maximum total number of rows in active data parts; - `max_table_size_bytes_compressed` — the maximum total size on disk across all active and inactive data parts; - `max_table_size_bytes_uncompressed` — the same for uncompressed bytes. The limits are checked against the current table size at the beginning of `INSERT` and when new data parts are committed to the working set; on exceeding a limit, the query fails with the new `TABLE_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` error. Inserts done by materialized views (including refreshable ones) and async insert flushes are checked as well, since they go through the same sinks and part commits. The check also triggers on committing the results of background merges and mutations, so a mutation (e.g. an `UPDATE` increasing the table size) will be repeated without finishing while the table exceeds the limit, which is intended. The check is skipped on replicated fetches and on the execution of replication log entries that add data already accepted by another replica (`ATTACH_PART`, `REPLACE_RANGE`), which permits a race condition when parallel inserts into multiple replicas overdraft the limit. Committing empty data parts is always allowed, so the data can be removed from a table that exceeds the limits, e.g. with `TRUNCATE` or `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PARTITION`. The limit on the number of rows is counted only for active data parts, while the limits on the number of bytes are counted across all active and inactive data parts, because their purpose is to limit disk usage (inactive parts are removed in the background, so the observed size can decrease over time). ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add `MergeTree` settings `max_table_size_rows`, `max_table_size_bytes_compressed`, and `max_table_size_bytes_uncompressed` that limit the total size of a table. The limits are checked at the beginning of `INSERT` and when new data parts are committed (including the results of background merges and mutations), but not on replicated fetches. This closes [#115063](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115063). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115069&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115069](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115069+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Do not execute an IN subquery during statistics part pruning
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107619 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113904 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `LOGICAL_ERROR` "Not-ready Set is passed as the second argument for function `globalNullIn`" and the loss of the query's real error message, which could happen when statistics part pruning speculatively executed an `IN`/`GLOBAL IN` subquery during index analysis and that subquery failed. ### Description Related: #107619 (one carrier). Reported on #113904. Statistics part pruning runs before primary-key analysis and builds its own `KeyCondition` per part. That constructor walks the predicate and, for an IN-family atom, called `buildOrderedSetInplace`, which **executes the subquery**. For `GLOBAL IN` an external table exists, so the plan-preserving clone is skipped and the plan is consumed by `std::move(source)`. When that speculative subquery failed, the per-part best-effort handler in `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor` swallowed the exception at debug level, leaving the set permanently unbuilt, so `FunctionIn` aborted with `Not-ready Set` and the real error was lost. In the cited CI run the discarded error was `Code: 181 ILLEGAL_FINAL`. Part pruning is analysis-only, so it now declines an `IN` atom whose set is not already built, via a `require_ready_sets` flag on `KeyCondition::BuildInfo` passed only by `StatisticsPartPruner`. Same rule `tryRewriteInTruthyCondition` already applies in this file. **Cost.** Pruning is preserved where no execution is needed: literal `IN` lists and subquery sets already built earlier, notably when the `IN` column is in the primary key. Primary-key, partition, minmax and skip-index analysis are untouched (the flag defaults to false). What remains: `IN (subquery)` on a *non-key* column with statistics no longer prunes, the one case whose alternative is the defect itself. The per-part handler is deliberately unchanged: narrowing it by error code would redden `02707_skip_index_with_in.sql:25`, and the protected region runs an arbitrary user subquery, so no code identifies a statistics failure. Complementary to #102192 and #102308, which target the silent-stop case: #102308 restores only in the not-created branch, so an exception still escapes with `source` moved from. New test `04852_statistics_part_pruning_no_subquery_execution` asserts the pruning outcome in the declined case and both preserved cases. Fails on unpatched master, passes with the fix, 100/100 green; `02707`, `04209_statistics_*`, `02864_statistics_*` and `03788_statistics_part_pruning*` unchanged. Fixes the statistics-pruning carrier, not all of #107619. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114121&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114121](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114121+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1713` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend
signal.text: Fix wrong intDiv/divide monotonicity for a constant dividend Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106136 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes silently missing rows when a query filters on `intDiv(constant, key)` or `divide(constant, key)`. Primary-key and partition analysis reports the wrong direction of monotonicity for a constant divided by a key column, so matching granules are pruned away and the query returns fewer rows with no error. Also fixes `intDiv` with an unsigned constant dividend whose high bit is set, stops claiming monotonicity when a `Decimal` operand makes the division compute in the decimal's native width, and stops key analysis from raising `Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long` for a valid query that divides an `IPv4`/`IPv6` constant by a key column. ### Description `FunctionBinaryArithmetic::getMonotonicityForRange` reports the direction of `c / x` incorrectly in its `const / variable` branch, so `KeyCondition::applyMonotonicFunctionsChainToRange` inverts the transformed range exactly when it must not, the range matches no granule, and matching rows are dropped with no error and exit code 0. Reproduced at completely default settings (no `SETTINGS` clause), 20000-row `Int32`-keyed MergeTree: ```sql SELECT count() FROM t WHERE intDiv(toInt32(-1000000), a) >= 11; -- keyed MergeTree: 0 ENGINE = Memory oracle: 10909 ``` #### Root cause For `f(x) = c / x` on an interval excluding 0, `d/dx (c/x) = -c/x²`, whose sign is `-sign(c)` for every `x != 0` — the `x²` denominator is positive on both sides of 0. So the direction is governed by `sign(c)` alone and is the *same* on the negative and the positive branch; only the values differ. The code instead treated the two arms as needing opposite polarity, which is the intuition that `1/x` "flips" across the branches. It does not: it is monotone on each branch separately, which is exactly why the strict range-sign guards are there. The two arms are now one return with a single `!is_constant_positive`, and the strict guards are kept verbatim. Fixing only that is not sufficient, and on its own would be *worse* than the current code for one shape. Three further defects live in the same branch: * **Unsigned constant dividend.** `intDiv` casts the dividend through `make_signed_t` whenever either operand is a signed integer (`DivisionUtils.h`), so an unsigned constant whose high bit is set divides as negative — `intDiv(toUInt8(200), x)` is `intDiv(toInt8(-56), x)` — while the raw `Field` still compares as positive. The boundary is `2^(8 * width - 1)` of the dividend's own width (verified for 8/16/32/64/128/256-bit dividends; the divisor width is irrelevant). This is reachable with no cast at all, because the literal `200` is `UInt8`. On a *negative* range the un-negated arm is accidentally correct for this shape, so adding the missing `!` alone would turn a correct answer into a wrong one. A new `intDivConstDividendReinterpretsNegative` helper corrects the effective sign; it deliberately does not reuse the existing `intDivConstReinterpretsNegative`, whose width early-out has the opposite polarity here. * **`Decimal` operand.** With a `Decimal` on either operand and no `Float` operand, the division computes in the decimal's native width (`DecimalBinaryOperation` casts both operands to `NativeResultType` and substitutes the integral operation even for `divide`). The divisor is then truncated, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), x)` is periodic in `x` with period `2^32` and not even monotonic. Nothing is claimed for that combination, mirroring the rejection the sibling `variable / constant` branch already performs. A `Decimal`/`Float` pair is exempt: it is converted to `Float64` before the operation, never truncates, and is itself a carrier of the direction defect, so those shapes are fixed rather than rejected. The rejection is deliberately keyed on the operand types and not on the constant's value, so it also covers a *zero* dividend and therefore runs ahead of the `constant == 0` fast path. That ordering is load-bearing: the truncation moves where the quotient is defined, so a range that strictly excludes 0 can still contain a point where the function is undefined, which is exactly what the zero-constant guard assumes away. With `Decimal32` the divisor truncates to `Int32`, so `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), key)` over an `Int64` key range around `2^32` raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`; letting the zero guard win would claim monotonicity, prune the raising row away, and return a silent answer instead. Pinned by `c5iv`. * **Non-numeric operand (pre-existing exception on a valid query).** `IPv4`/`IPv6` are substituted with `UInt32`/`UInt128`, so their declared width does not describe the arithmetic, and their raw `Field` cannot be compared with a numeric zero. Two existing comparisons against zero therefore raise `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD "Cannot compare DB::IPv4 with long"` during key analysis today: one in the single-value fast path (reached when a granule's min equals its max) and one in the zero-constant guard (reached otherwise). Both roles are affected — `intDiv(toIPv4('192.168.0.1'), numeric_key)` and `intDiv(1, ipv4_key)` — and one of them fires even when the key range spans 0. A numeric gate hoisted above the fast path removes both; after it each query returns the correct rows with no pruning. Placing the gate inside the `const / variable` block would cover only the second site, which the new test pins at two granularities. Scope note: "both roles" here means the IP value as the dividend constant and as the key column, both with the constant on the left. The mirror shape, an IP constant as the *divisor* (`intDiv(numeric_key, toIPv4(...))`), still raises the same exception, as do `plus`/`minus`/`multiply` with an `IPv4`/`IPv6` operand. Both are pre-existing (measured byte-identical on `origin/master`) and are tracked separately rather than widened into this PR, since a correct fix for them also has to touch the `multiply` arm and the shared fast path. #### Behaviour changes to be aware of * **Two pre-existing key-analysis exceptions disappear.** As above, a non-numeric operand now reports non-monotonic instead of raising, so the query succeeds unpruned. This is a scope extension beyond "fix the direction", included because those same comparisons against zero are the mechanism being corrected and an exception on a valid query is a bug either way. * **Pruning is lost for `Decimal` shapes with no `Float` operand.** Measured with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1`: | shape | before | after | |---|---|---| | `Decimal32(0)` key, `intDiv(toInt32(-1000), a) = -25`, positive range | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 4/4` | | `UInt64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(1000, 0), a) = 250` | `Granules: 2/4` | `Granules: 3/4` | | `Int64` key, `intDiv(toDecimal32(0, 0), a) = 5`, range around `2^32` | `Granules: 0/2` | `Granules: 2/2` | The first two queries return the same rows before and after — the index simply stops filtering. The third is the zero-dividend case: it must stop pruning, because the pruned plan silently returned `0` for a query that correctly raises `ILLEGAL_DIVISION`. This mirrors the decision already shipped for the `variable / constant` branch, where the same truncation applies. `Decimal`/`Float` pairs keep pruning and are additionally fixed. No committed reference in the repository changes. * **Everything else keeps pruning.** Strictly-positive ranges with a signed constant, both-unsigned operands, `Float` divisors, and unsigned key ranges crossing the divisor's own `2^(8W-1)` are all unaffected. That last group is worth naming: the *values* jump across the wrap while the *order* is preserved, which satisfies the non-strict definition of `Monotonicity`, so rejecting them would delete pruning that is correct today. The new test pins them, with plan-level assertions. #### Testing `04651_intdiv_const_variable_monotonicity` and its three siblings `..._decimal_float`, `..._controls` and `..._ip` compare a keyed MergeTree against an identical `ENGINE = Memory` table on the same data, so each of their 86 count rows prints `1` when index-based pruning agrees with the full-scan ground truth. The probes are split by family across four files, sharing one case numbering, so that no single file outgrows the CI per-test time limit: the cost is fixture DDL for the 26 tables of the (type, range, granularity) matrix, which cannot be trimmed without dropping coverage. Together they cover both range signs for both functions and both constant signs, unsigned dividends at several widths, `Decimal` in either role plus the `Decimal`/`Float` exemption, `Float64`/`LowCardinality`/`Nullable` keys, ranges that span zero or have zero as an endpoint, the unsigned wrap shapes, and the `IPv4`/`IPv6` cases at two granularities. Twelve further rows assert with `EXPLAIN indexes = 1` that the surviving shapes still prune (so the fix cannot silently degrade into "no pruning at all") and that the zero-dividend `Decimal` shape stops pruning — 98 asserted rows in total. On a master-HEAD binary the tests fail: 34 rows print `0` and `..._ip` aborts with `Code: 169 BAD_TYPE_OF_FIELD`. On this branch they pass, including 50/50 runs with randomized settings. Each of the four edits was mutation-tested individually — reverting the negation, the sign correction, the `Decimal` rejection, the `Float` exemption, the numeric gate, the gate's hoisted position and its role restriction each make specific named rows fail. `index_granularity` decides whether the range handed to `getMonotonicityForRange` is strictly negative, strictly positive or spans zero, so it is pinned per DDL and the test carries `no-random-merge-tree-settings` with that reason stated inline in each of the four files. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112156&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112156](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112156+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1714` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Preserve unchanged TOAST values in MaterializedPostgreSQL
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/83517 Preserve PostgreSQL columns encoded as unchanged TOAST references in `MaterializedPostgreSQL` replication instead of replacing them with default values. The consumer resolves the previous value from an earlier row in the same replication buffer when possible. Otherwise, it reads the current row from the nested `ReplacingMergeTree` by replica identity, batching key lookups to avoid a query per value. The old replica identity tuple is used when an update changes the key. An unchanged TOAST value in a replica identity column is rejected because the replication message does not contain a value that could identify the row. The integration test covers a regular update, multiple updates of the same row in one PostgreSQL transaction, and a replica identity change. The user-facing documentation is updated for both `MaterializedPostgreSQL` engines. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `MaterializedPostgreSQL` now preserves unchanged PostgreSQL `TOAST` values during updates instead of replacing them with default values. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=111552&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/111552](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F111552+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` accepted with session `allow_statistics = 1` but executed with the server default — permanently stuck mutation when the profile disables statistics
signal.text: ### Describe what's wrong `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` is **validated with the submitting session's `allow_statistics` value, but executed with the server-default value**. When a server profile sets `allow_statistics = 0` and a session enables it per-query (`SETTINGS allow_statistics = 1` — the same session-level opt-in that `ADD STATISTICS` honors), the mutation is accepted and then fails forever in the background: - `mutations_sync = 1` returns `Code: 341 UNFINISHED` wrapping `Code: 80. DB::Exception: Alter table with statistics is disabled. Turn on allow_statistics.`; - without `mutations_sync` the statement returns success and the mutation sits in `system.mutations` with `is_done = 0`, retrying the same failure indefinitely, wedging the table's mutation queue until a manual `KILL MUTATION`. The behavior is also internally inconsistent: - `ADD STATISTICS` under the same session opt-in succeeds (metadata change honors the session value); - background **merges materialize the declared statistics regardless of the gate** (measured: `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` on the same server writes the `TDigest` statistics while the explicit mutation verb is refused). So the only affected path is the explicit `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` mutation, and it fails at execution time after passing validation at submission time. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — master 26.8.1.1673 (official build). ### How to reproduce Server profile disables statistics (`users.xml`): ```xml <clickhouse> <profiles><default><allow_statistics>0</allow_statistics></default></profiles> </clickhouse> ``` Then: ```sql CREATE TABLE gt (k UInt64, a Int64) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY k; INSERT INTO gt SELECT number, number FROM numbers(100); ALTER TABLE gt ADD STATISTICS a TYPE tdigest SETTINGS allow_statistics = 1; -- OK ALTER TABLE gt MATERIALIZE STATISTICS a SETTINGS allow_statistics = 1, mutations_sync = 1; -- Code: 341. DB::Exception: Exception happened during execution of mutation 'mutation_2.txt' -- with part 'all_1_1_0' reason: 'Code: 80. DB::Exception: Alter table with statistics is -- disabled. Turn on allow_statistics. (INCORRECT_QUERY)' SELECT mutation_id, is_done, latest_fail_reason FROM system.mutations WHERE table = 'gt'; -- mutation_2.txt 0 Code: 80. DB::Exception: Alter table with statistics is disabled. ... -- (retries forever; KILL MUTATION is the only way out) ``` Required settings: only the profile-level `allow_statistics = 0` plus the session-level `= 1`; everything else is defaults. ### Expected behavior Either of: - validate at submission and reject the `MATERIALIZE STATISTICS` immediately when the effective execution context will refuse it (fail fast, no stuck mutation), or - execute the mutation under the value the submitting session was authorized with (the way merges already materialize declared statistics irrespective of the gate). A statement that is accepted but can never complete, and that blocks the table's mutation queue until a manual `KILL MUTATION`, is the worst of both. ### Additional context Found by an automatic optimizer-testing framework (differential testing of optimizer settings, query plans, and equivalent rewrites).

signal.title: Parts written by an INSERT concurrent with DROP PROJECTION keep the dropped projection; after any mutation CHECK TABLE permanently fails with UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Describe what's wrong An `INSERT` that is still running when `ALTER TABLE ... DROP PROJECTION` commits keeps using its metadata snapshot from query start, so the parts it writes after the drop still materialize the dropped projection (`.proj` directory on disk and an entry in the part's `checksums.txt`). Nothing ever reconciles those parts: the drop's cleanup mutation was created before their block numbers, so it never rewrites them, and every later ordinary mutation hardlinks the orphaned `.proj` directory into the new mutated part. Beyond the false alarm, merges are blocked wherever affected and clean parts coexist in one partition: merge assignment refuses ranges whose parts have differing projection sets, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE ... FINAL` and `OPTIMIZE ... PARTITION` permanently fail with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE` (`Parts have different projection sets: {} in '...'`), and the partition can never merge down. In that mixed state nothing non-destructive heals it: `DETACH PARTITION` + `ATTACH PARTITION` re-attaches the part still carrying the orphaned `.proj` (renumbered, still failing `CHECK`), `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR PROJECTION <dropped name> IN PARTITION` completes without removing the directories, and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. `OPTIMIZE FINAL` heals only the uniform case where every part in the partition carries the same orphaned projection set (they merge together and the merge drops the unknown projection). The lasting symptom appears as soon as any mutation rewrites such a part: `CHECK TABLE` permanently fails for the mutated part with `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` (`Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj`), although every data file is intact and all rows are readable. The un-mutated ancestor part passes `CHECK TABLE` (it is covered by the unknown-projection tolerance), so the table degrades from "checks clean" to "permanently reports broken parts" at the first mutation, which for an operator is a corruption alarm that never clears. On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the background part-check thread (`ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix`) logs the same `Part has broken projections` for the part, on every replica that has it. The unknown-projection tolerance in `checkDataPart` (added for parts that legitimately carry a projection dropped while they were detached) removes the unknown `.proj` entries from the in-memory checksums and sets `is_broken_projection` with a comment saying the caller can then handle it gracefully — but the entries are not erased from `projections_on_disk`, so the `require_checksums && !projections_on_disk.empty()` branch right below throws `UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART` anyway (`src/Storages/MergeTree/checkDataPart.cpp`, "Found unexpected projection directories"). A mutated part takes the `require_checksums` path, which is why the throw fires exactly for the mutation descendants. ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes. Reproduces on 26.8.1.1708 (official master build) and on 26.4.1.1, so it is long-standing, and on both `MergeTree` and `ReplicatedMergeTree` (2-replica cluster: `CHECK TABLE` returns 0 on both replicas). ### How to reproduce Against any running server (the race window is the INSERT's runtime, ~5 s here, so the interleaving is reliable): ```bash clickhouse-client -q "CREATE TABLE t (id UInt64, val UInt64, part UInt8) ENGINE = MergeTree PARTITION BY part ORDER BY id" clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t ADD PROJECTION p1 (SELECT part, sum(val) GROUP BY part)" # slow INSERT: the metadata snapshot is taken at query start clickhouse-client -q "INSERT INTO t SELECT number, sleepEachRow(0.05)*0 + number, 0 FROM numbers(100) SETTINGS max_block_size=10, min_insert_block_size_rows=10, max_insert_threads=1" & sleep 1.5 # DROP PROJECTION commits while the INSERT is still running clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t DROP PROJECTION p1" wait # any ordinary mutation over the affected parts clickhouse-client -q "ALTER TABLE t UPDATE val = val + 1 WHERE id < 50 SETTINGS mutations_sync=2" clickhouse-client -q "SELECT count() FROM t" # 100 - data is fine clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=1" # 0 clickhouse-client -q "CHECK TABLE t SETTINGS check_query_single_value_result=0" | grep $'\t0\t' ``` The same end state is reached with asynchronous mutations (`mutations_sync=0`); the synchronous form above is only for determinism. In this repro all parts of the partition carry the orphaned projection, so `OPTIMIZE TABLE t FINAL` merges them and heals the check. When the partition mixes affected and clean parts (one more concurrent INSERT after the drop is enough), `OPTIMIZE` fails with `Code: 388` `CANNOT_ASSIGN_OPTIMIZE: Parts have different projection sets` and only `DROP PARTITION` clears the state. It survives server restarts. ### Expected behavior Either the INSERT does not materialize a projection that was dropped before its parts were committed, or parts that legitimately carry a since-dropped projection keep passing `CHECK TABLE` after mutations, matching the graceful-handling intent already present in `checkDataPart` for the un-mutated case. A part whose data files are all intact must not be reported broken forever, and its presence must not permanently block merge assignment in its partition. ### Error message and/or stacktrace ``` 0_8_8_0_12 0 Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) (version 26.8.1.1708 (official build)) ``` On `ReplicatedMergeTree` the same error surfaces through the background part check: ``` Part `0_7_7_0_11` has broken projections. It will be ignored. Broken projections info: Code: 227. DB::Exception: Found unexpected projection directories: p1.proj. (UNEXPECTED_FILE_IN_DATA_PART) 5. DB::checkDataPart(...) 7. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartImpl(String const&, bool) 8. DB::ReplicatedMergeTreePartCheckThread::checkPartAndFix(String const&, std::optional<long>*, bool) 9. DB::StorageReplicatedMergeTree::checkDataNext(std::shared_ptr<DB::IStorage::DataValidationTasksBase>&) ``` ### Additional context Related but distinct from #100413: that issue covers a fetch-side flavor where `checksums.txt` references a `.proj` directory that was never transferred (`NO_FILE_IN_DATA_PART`). Here no detach, attach or fetch is involved — an `INSERT` racing `DROP PROJECTION` plus one mutation is enough, and the direction is inverted: the `.proj` directory exists on disk but is unknown to the table metadata.

signal.title: Columns Cache
signal.text: Implement the deserialized columns cache that keeps columns in memory. In comparison to the uncompressed cache, this saves time on deserialization and copying. Closes #82335. The cache identifies entries by table UUID, so it is only active for tables in databases that assign UUIDs (`Atomic` and `Replicated`); tables in `Ordinary` databases are silently excluded. The feature is gated behind the `EXPERIMENTAL` settings `use_columns_cache`, `enable_reads_from_columns_cache`, and `enable_writes_to_columns_cache`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Implement an experimental columns cache that keeps deserialized columns in memory for `MergeTree` tables. signal.title: Nullable(Array) stages 1-2: type foundation and collision-free substream names
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115394 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104816 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/105192 Stages 1 and 2 of the staged `Nullable(Array(T))` implementation described in the RFC, ClickHouse/ClickHouse#115394. Internal machinery only: **the type is still unreachable from any query**, and there is no user-visible change. `DataTypeFactory` continues to reject the string `Nullable(Array(UInt8))`, so this cannot be reached through DDL, a table function's column list, or any function that takes a type by name. That boundary is itself pinned by a test, so opening it in a later stage is a deliberate change to a failing assertion rather than something that can drift in unnoticed. The two stages ship together because Stage 1 alone has no production caller — `makeNullableAllowingArray` would land exercised only by unit tests. Stage 2 is the first thing that uses it. They are separate commits. ### Stage 1: the type-level foundation `DataTypeArray::canBeInsideNullable` keeps returning `false`, permanently. That predicate is consulted in 105 places across 75 files, and each encodes an assumption about which types can be wrapped. Leaving its meaning untouched means no existing code path can begin producing `Nullable(Array(...))` on its own; only code that explicitly opts in can. `makeNullableAllowingArray` is that opt-in and it is the only door — the constructor it uses is private, reachable through a single friend declaration. `ColumnNullable` admits a nested `ColumnArray` by an explicit exception to its own invariant, for the same reason. The cost is that `canBeInsideNullable` now answers `false` for a type that can in fact sit inside `Nullable`. Two consequences are pinned by tests so they are deliberate rather than discovered later: `makeNullable` rejects an array, and `makeNullableSafe` silently returns the array unwrapped instead of throwing. The second is how a `Nullable(Array)` could be quietly degraded to `Array`; the sites where that matters are audited in a later stage. ### Stage 2: collision-free substream names `Nullable` appends `.null` to a stream name and `Array` appends `.size0`, `.size1` and so on, while array *elements* contribute no component at all. A `Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))` column would write two different null maps to the same file. A second, structured naming scheme inserts an explicit `.array` component when descending into array elements, and is selected per column from the type as stored in the part: ```text Nullable(Array(UInt32)) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.nested Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))) -> c.null c.size0 c.array.null c.array.nested Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32)))) -> c.size0 c.array.null c.array.array.size0 c.array.array.nested.null c.array.array.nested Array(Nullable(UInt32)) -> c.size0 c.null c (unchanged) ``` Types legal today keep byte-identical names, so existing parts stay readable with no migration and no format version bump. ### Testing Expectations are derived from real `enumerateStreams` walks rather than hand-built substream paths. That distinction turned out to matter: `SerializationNullable` emits its null-map substream and pops it before recursing, so a path such as `[NullMap, NullableElements, ArraySizes]` never occurs. The real path is `[NullableElements, ArraySizes]`, and the naming code branches on whether a null map precedes the final substream. Expectations written against constructed paths can be entirely self-consistent and still disagree with what is written to disk. The criteria are stated as properties over a corpus rather than as spot checks: - **No existing stream name changes.** Asserted as a proof rather than a sample: for 28 currently-legal types the structured scheme is never selected, neither by type nor by any enumerated path. If it is never reached then the legacy naming code is the only code that runs, and this change does not modify it. - **Typed and untyped callers agree** for every legal type, so a column cannot be written under one set of names and read under another. - **All names distinct** for thirteen shapes placing `Nullable(Array)` inside arrays, tuples, maps and variants — including their substream cache keys and their prefix/suffix substreams. - **Subcolumn reads resolve to files the writer produced.** 31 unit tests across the three suites; the full `unit_tests_dbms` suite is green at 22732 passed, 0 failed. ### Two things worth a reviewer's attention **The substream-to-name mapping existed in three places** — `getNameForSubstreamPath`, a full copy, and a partial per-element copy — and the full copy had already drifted: it was missing `MapBucketIndexes`, so a bucketed `Map` holding a `Nullable(Array)` would have lost that name component and could have written two streams under one file name. Both copies are gone, replaced by `ISerialization::getLegacyNameForSubstreamPath`. **The naming scheme cannot be decided from the substream path alone.** The path `[ArrayElements, NullMap]` must name `c.null` for `Array(Nullable(UInt32))` and `c.array.null` for `Array(Nullable(Array(Nullable(UInt32))))`. The column type is load-bearing, and a caller that does not supply one cannot be answered correctly. Where the path proves a type was needed — `NullableElements` above an array substream can only come from a `Nullable` directly over an `Array` — resolving a name without one now raises `LOGICAL_ERROR` rather than quietly returning a legacy name no writer produced. A test asserts this guard never fires for any currently-legal type. Ensuring every MergeTree caller passes the type is an explicit obligation for the next stage. ### Attribution The design and a substantial amount of the code originate in ClickHouse/ClickHouse#104816 by @zhanglistar, which was closed in favour of this staged implementation. Both commits carry a `Co-authored-by` trailer. The blocker analysis that shaped the design is @Avogar's, and the resolutions to it are @alexey-milovidov's. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115464&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115464](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115464+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Detect when tables behind a query have changed
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/108713 Adds a way to detect when the data behind a query has changed, and uses it to make the query cache consistent and to skip unnecessary refreshes of materialized views. A new virtual method `getModificationHash` on `IStorage` returns an optional `UInt128` that changes whenever the data behind the table changes (similar to an HTTP ETag). It is not a hash of the data and the way it is computed is engine-specific. It returns `NULL` when the engine cannot give a usable value, so callers fail closed. Implemented for engines that can expose a loop-free (no-ABA) value - one that never returns to an earlier value across a change-and-change-back (an `A -> B -> A` transition): - `MergeTree` family: the block-number ranges of the active data parts, their content checksums, the table structure/key metadata, a per-lifetime counter that advances on every active-part-set change (so a drop that restores an identical part set does not reproduce an earlier hash), and a per-lifetime metadata version that advances on every metadata change (so a metadata `ALTER` and back does not either). Changes on insert, merge, mutation, `ALTER`. - `Memory`: identity of the current set of blocks plus the row count and a monotonic version. - `Log`, `TinyLog`, `StripeLog`: total rows and bytes plus structure and a monotonic version. - `Merge` and `Distributed`: combine the hashes of the underlying tables (`Distributed` asks each shard through `system.tables`), folding each table's identity (database, name, UUID) so two different tables with the same hash are distinguished; they fail closed if any underlying table does. - `View` and `MaterializedView` are looked through: a view hashes the tables behind its stored `SELECT` (plus its own UUID, columns, and security metadata), a materialized view hashes its target table. They fail closed for parameterized views and in databases without table UUIDs (`Ordinary`), where incarnations of a re-created view cannot be told apart. `URL` and object storage (`S3`, ...) trust the resource's strong (non-weak) `ETag` when one is exposed, and fail closed (report `NULL`) otherwise - for glob/failover patterns, a weak or absent `ETag`, or an unreachable source. The `ETag` is loop-free for content (the same `ETag` denotes the same content), but unlike the engines above there is no monotonic version to fold, so an `A -> B -> A` rewrite back to byte-identical content within a single query's read window can in principle repeat it. That residual is narrow and both consumers below are opt-in, so we keep these engines in the feature rather than drop them. `File` fails closed: its only change signals are size and modification time, both weak. It is exposed as a lazily-computed `modification_hash` column in `system.tables`, and used for two features: - New setting `query_cache_use_only_when_data_was_not_changed`: when enabled, the combined modification hash of the tables referenced by a query is folded into the query cache key, so a cached result is reused only while none of those tables changed. If consistency cannot be guaranteed (e.g. a query calling a non-deterministic function, whose result can change while every referenced table is unchanged; a table function; a `File` table; a `URL`/object-storage table without a strong `ETag`; an object-storage read pruned by a `_path`/`_file`/Hive-partition filter, where the consumed subset cannot be compared with the full listing; a query inside a transaction, which reads the transaction's snapshot while the hash samples the live table state; or a referenced table with an active row policy for the current user, which changes what the user reads while every referenced table is unchanged - row policies existing only on remote shard servers of a `Distributed` table cannot be seen and remain part of the best-effort window), the query cache is bypassed for that query. - `REFRESH ... IF CHANGED` for refreshable materialized views: a scheduled refresh is skipped when none of the tables the view reads from changed since the last refresh that rebuilt the view (e.g. `REFRESH EVERY 1 MINUTE IF CHANGED`). It always rebuilds when a source table cannot prove it is unchanged. The `clickhouse` binary was built and all new tests pass locally, including a functional check that `Distributed.modification_hash` changes when a remote table changes and that `IF CHANGED` skips refreshes while the source is unchanged. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a `modification_hash` column to `system.tables` that changes whenever the data behind a table changes. Based on it, added a setting `query_cache_use_only_when_data_was_not_changed` to make the query cache consistent (a cached result is reused only while the referenced tables are unchanged) and a `REFRESH ... IF CHANGED` option for refreshable materialized views to skip refreshes when the source data did not change. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108721&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108721](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108721+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add the `logsql` dialect: LogsQL, the query language of VictoriaLogs
signal.text: <!--- A technical comment, you are free to remove or leave it as it is when PR is created The following categories are used in the next scripts, update them accordingly utils/changelog/changelog.py tests/ci/cancel_and_rerun_workflow_lambda/app.py --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): Added an experimental `logsql` dialect: LogsQL, the log query language of VictoriaLogs, can now be used to query ClickHouse tables with logs. Enable it with `SET allow_experimental_logsql_dialect = 1, logsql_table = '<table>', dialect = 'logsql'` (plus `logsql_database`, `logsql_time_column`, and `logsql_message_column` as needed). LogsQL queries are translated at parse time into ordinary `SELECT` queries, so text filters expect `String`-backed log columns, while the `math` pipe applies raw arithmetic and needs numeric operand columns (`String` field values are not coerced to numbers). Documentation entry for user-facing changes. - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) Implementation notes: - Nearly the whole language is supported: the filters (words, phrases, prefixes, `field:value`, `:=`, `~`, comparisons, `range`, `in` with subqueries, `contains_any`/`contains_all` with subqueries, `seq`, `len_range`, `string_range`, `ipv4_range`, `ipv6_range`, `pattern_match*`, `contains_common_case`/`equals_common_case`, `json_array_contains_any`, `i()`, full `_time:` filters with `day_range`/`week_range`, `_stream:{...}` selectors), and the pipes `fields`, `delete`, `copy`, `rename`, `limit`, `offset`, `sort`/`first`/`last` (including `rank` and `partition by`), `stats` (with `by`-buckets, per-function `if`, `switch`, `rate`), `where`, `uniq`, `top`, `math`, `extract`, `extract_regexp`, `format`, `unpack_json`, `unpack_logfmt`, `join`, `union`, `unroll`, `running_stats`, `total_stats`, `len`, `hash`, `coalesce`, `decolorize`, `split`, `unpack_words`, `time_add`, `sample`, `generate_sequence`, `field_values`, `json_array_len`, `json_array_concat`, `replace`, `replace_regexp`, `pack_json`, `pack_logfmt`. On typed (non-`String`) columns, filters that emit string functions fail with a type error instead of applying VictoriaLogs' schemaless per-value matching. The numeric stats functions (`sum`, `avg`, `median`, `quantile`, `stddev`, `rate_sum`) parse the numeric value out of every field value and skip the values that are not numbers, like VictoriaLogs, which computes its stats in `float64`; a numeric column is therefore aggregated with `Float64` precision and not exactly. - The dialect is modeled on the existing `kusto`/`prql`/`promql`/`polyglot` dialects: a parser under `src/Parsers/LogsQL/` builds a ClickHouse `ASTSelectQuery` directly, so all downstream machinery (analyzer, distributed queries, query log) works as usual. Relational pipes map to real SQL constructs: `join` to `LEFT`/`INNER JOIN ... USING`, `union` to `UNION ALL`, `running_stats`/`total_stats` and the `rank`/`partition by` clauses to window functions. - The lexer and the grammar mirror the reference implementation in VictoriaLogs (`lib/logstorage` of `VictoriaMetrics/VictoriaLogs`, Apache 2.0), including Go-style string literals, compound tokens (`foo-bar.com:123/x`), comments with `#`, and the exact filter/pipe syntax. The test queries are reused from the VictoriaLogs parser tests: 675 of its 878 valid parser-test queries run end-to-end against a ClickHouse table, and 605 of its 612 invalid queries are rejected. - The implicit table is configured by the `logsql_database`/`logsql_table` settings (like `promql_database`/`promql_table`). The special fields `_time` and `_msg` are mapped to columns via `logsql_time_column`/`logsql_message_column`, so real tables (e.g. `system.text_log` with `event_time`/`message`) can be queried after setting those. - Word and phrase filters translate to `hasToken`/`match` with token boundaries, so tables with `tokenbf_v1` indexes on the message column benefit from index analysis. - Documented deviations from VictoriaLogs: word boundaries follow ClickHouse tokenization (ASCII alphanumerics; VictoriaLogs also treats `_` and non-ASCII letters as word characters); numeric comparison filters parse `String` field values per row (rows with non-numeric values do not match) and compare typed numeric columns exactly, but the per-row parsing of field values understands plain numeric text only (decimal integers, floats, scientific notation, `inf`/`nan`) - LogsQL-only spellings such as `10KiB`, `1h`, `0x10`, or `1_000` are supported in query literals but are treated as non-numeric when stored in a field value, whereas VictoriaLogs parses them there too; equality with a non-numeric value compares with the native column type instead of VictoriaLogs' string semantics; `count(field)` counts non-NULL values instead of non-empty strings; `pattern_match*` placeholders are approximated with regular expressions (VictoriaLogs uses a greedy matcher with extra boundary rules); `seq()` matches substrings in order without word-boundary checks. - The only constructs that remain `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` (with clear errors naming the construct) are the ones with no ClickHouse meaning: VictoriaLogs storage introspection (`block_stats`, `blocks_count`, `query_stats`, `value_type`, `histogram` buckets, `set_stream_fields`, `stream_context`), features that require the dynamic set of fields of a schemaless store (`facets`, `field_names`, wildcard field selectors like `foo*:filter`, stats over all fields like `sum(*)`, `unpack_json` without a `fields` list), `unpack_syslog` (a stateful wall-clock-dependent parser), and `collapse_nums` (its number-boundary rules require lookaround which RE2 lacks). <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=113207&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/113207](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F113207+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
