signal.title: Aggregation pushdown below JOIN in the Cascades optimizer
signal.text: ## Motivation Queries like `SELECT count() FROM t1 LEFT JOIN t2 ON t1.key = t2.key GROUP BY t1.key` aggregate after the join, although most of the aggregation work can be done on one join input before the join. When the pushed side has few distinct group keys, aggregating first shrinks the join input dramatically. This is the classic *eager aggregation* transformation (Yan & Larson, VLDB 1995). It is not always a win — with nearly-unique group keys the extra aggregation is pure overhead — so it is implemented as a cost-based alternative in the Cascades optimizer: the memo keeps both plans and the cost model picks. ## What is implemented A new transformation rule `AggregationPushdown` with two variants: - **Partial pushdown**: a partial aggregation (`final = false`) below one join input, and a `MergingAggregated` step above the join. The pushed side's group keys are extended with every column of that side referenced by the join condition and residual filter, which makes all rows within a partial group indistinguishable to the join — the join then filters or duplicates whole groups uniformly, and merging `m` duplicated copies of a state equals processing the underlying rows `m` times. This is semantically exact, including for `ALL` joins with fan-out, and requires no uniqueness knowledge. - **Full pushdown**: when every `GROUP BY` key belongs to the pushed side, the join-condition columns are a subset of the `GROUP BY` keys, and the strictness rules out duplication (`ANY`/`SEMI`/`ANTI` with the join kind matching the pushed side), the aggregation stays final below the join and no merge is needed. When legal, it strictly dominates the partial variant and is emitted instead of it. The legality matrix was derived from the hash-join implementation and independently re-verified during review. Notably, `ANY INNER JOIN` is excluded from the matrix entirely: it emits at most one row per join *key* (`setUsedOnce`), not per probe row, so pushing aggregation below it would change results. The correctness test contains a tripwire scenario against future wrong enablement. Safety rules encoded in the rule (each bails out and leaves the classic plan): the pushed side must never be null/default-extended by the join (an unmatched preserved row would otherwise carry an empty aggregate state and silently contribute nothing); global aggregation (`GROUP BY ()`) is excluded (an empty join output must still produce one row); all aggregate arguments must resolve to the pushed side; `join_use_nulls`/`USING` type-changing joins, grouping sets, `overflow_row`, `max_rows_to_group_by`, in-order aggregation, and name collisions between the two sides are all rejected. Supporting changes: - `MergingAggregatedStep` gets an opt-in `allowInputWithoutAggregatedChunkInfo` mode (join output chunks carry no `AggregatedChunkInfo`, and special column representations must be materialized before merging). The `only_merge` aggregator consumes keys and states positionally, so the rebuilt join projects keys first, then state columns. - **Wire format**: the new mode is serialized as flag bit 64 of `MergingAggregatedStep`, gated behind query plan serialization version 9 (bumped from 8). On a mixed-version cluster the plan fails at plan time with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED` (naming `SET cascades_aggregation_pushdown = 0` as the escape hatch) instead of a remote runtime error. Note that the version bump also excludes version-8 replicas from parallel-replicas distributed plans, per the documented design of `DBMS_QUERY_PLAN_SERIALIZATION_VERSION`. - `AggregatingStep::rebaseOntoInput` re-bases an aggregation onto a new input with a different key set; new memo helpers build the three-level (partial) and two-level (full) alternatives. The rule is gated by the new `EXPERIMENTAL` setting `cascades_aggregation_pushdown` (default on) and takes effect only together with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` and `make_distributed_plan = 1`. ## Testing - `04926_cascades_aggregation_pushdown`: EXPLAIN plan shapes for both variants and both sides, stat-hint steering in both directions, guard negatives (`FULL`, `ASOF`, `INNER ANY`, `join_use_nulls`, grouping sets, global aggregation, mixed-side aggregate arguments), executed queries with hand-verified values (including fan-out multiplicity and mixed equi+residual conditions), and a 3-join task-budget sanity check. - `04927_cascades_aggregation_pushdown_correctness`: 22+ scenarios, each executed with the optimizer on and off with identical results (fan-out duplication, unmatched rows, multi-key and expression join keys, residual conditions, `count`/`sum`/`min`/`avg`/`uniqExact`/`countIf`, keys from both sides, `SEMI`/`ANTI`/`ANY`, keys-only `GROUP BY`, empty inputs, full-pushdown cases), plus plan-shape canaries proving the pushed plans actually fire for the test's tables. - The full `*cascades*` and `*merging_aggregated*` stateless test sets pass locally on a test-config server. One pre-existing test (`04330_cascades_activation_gating`) pins the new setting off in one case whose own assertion (about subplan broadcasting) would otherwise be made vacuous by the new, cheaper plan. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added aggregation pushdown below `JOIN` (eager aggregation) to the experimental Cascades optimizer as a cost-based alternative: a partial aggregation is performed on one join input before the join and merged above it, or, when the join provably neither duplicates nor null-extends the aggregated side and the join keys are a subset of the `GROUP BY` keys, the aggregation is pushed below the join entirely. Controlled by the new setting `cascades_aggregation_pushdown` (enabled by default; takes effect only with `enable_cascades_optimizer = 1` and `make_distributed_plan = 1`). --- 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115354&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115354](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115354+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: When a Refreshable MaterializedView fails to delete tmp tables, it keeps creating more tmp tables until the server runs out of disk
signal.text: ### Company or project name _No response_ ### Describe the unexpected behaviour I created a large materialized view with 1-day refresh. The server ran out of disk space the next week. When I got the server back online, table bytes showed 1 `tmp.inner_id.123` table and 7 `_tmp_replace_xyz` tables, all for the same MV. The entry in `system.view_refreshes` showed this: ``` exception: Code: 359. DB::Exception: Table or Partition in <db.table> was not dropped. Reason: 1. Size (65.89 GB) is greater than max_[table/partition]_size_to_drop (50.00 GB) 2. File '/var/lib/clickhouse/flags/force_drop_table' intended to force DROP doesn't exist How to fix this: 1. Either increase (or set to zero) max_[table/partition]_size_to_drop in server config 2. Either pass a bigger (or set to zero) max_[table/partition]_size_to_drop through query settings 3. Either create forcing file /var/lib/clickhouse/flags/force_drop_table and make sure that ClickHouse has write permission for it. signal.title: Skip writing all-default columns during MergeTree INSERT
signal.text: ## Summary During MergeTree INSERT, columns whose values are entirely type-defaults (e.g., all zeros for `UInt64`, all empty strings for `String`, all `NULL`s for `Nullable`) are detected and excluded from the part's column list before constructing `MergedBlockOutputStream`. This avoids writing unnecessary `.bin` files (Wide parts) or data streams (Compact parts), saving disk space for sparse-update workloads where most columns in each INSERT are left at their type's default. The optimization is opt-in via the MergeTree setting `skip_empty_columns_on_insert` (off by default). It additionally requires `serialization_info_version` to be set to `with_missing_columns` (the format version that records frozen defaults for missing columns), so that a cluster pinned to a lower version for compatibility never writes parts that older servers cannot read. The block itself is passed intact to the writer, so skip indices, projections, primary index, and min-max index are all computed from the full data. Reading a part that lacks a column fills it with type-defaults automatically — the same mechanism used by `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN` on existing parts. To keep reads stable, a structured `missing_columns` array is recorded in the part's `serialization.json` (a new `WITH_MISSING_COLUMNS` serialization-info version). Each entry carries the column name and a `type_default` marker. On read, `fillMissingColumns` consults this marker and fills a missing column with its type-default even if the column later gains a new `DEFAULT` expression, so that a subsequent `ALTER MODIFY COLUMN ... DEFAULT` does not retroactively change the values that were actually inserted. The marker is propagated through merges, mutations, and on-the-fly `ALTER RENAME COLUMN`, so the inserted type-defaults survive part-lifecycle operations. The `MissingColumnInfo` struct also reserves a `DefaultKind::Expression` variant for future use (issue #92475: `ALTER MODIFY DEFAULT` freezes old expression into parts). This PR only writes `type_default` markers; reading an `expression` marker throws `CORRUPTED_DATA` to fail closed until Phase 2 implements expression evaluation. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/4968, https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/92475 **On-disk format (`serialization.json`):** ```json { "missing_columns": [ { "name": "b", "default": "type_default" } ], "version": 2 } ``` **Changes:** - Add MergeTree setting `skip_empty_columns_on_insert` (default `false`). - Add `IColumn::hasOnlyTypeDefaults` with optimized overrides for `ColumnVector`/`ColumnDecimal` (`memoryIsZero`), `ColumnString`/`ColumnArray` (zero offsets), `ColumnNullable` (all-`1` null map), `ColumnSparse` (no stored non-default values), and `ColumnTuple` (delegates to sub-columns). - Filter all-default columns in `MergeTreeDataWriter::writeTempPartImpl` (`skipEmptyColumnsOnInsert`). Columns with a `DEFAULT`/`MATERIALIZED`/`ALIAS` expression are never skipped. A column is skipped only when `IDataType::getDefault()` coincides with the column's zero representation (`isDefaultAt(0)` on a column filled via `getDefault()`), which correctly excludes types like `Date32` (type-default 1900-01-01 ≠ memory-zero) and `Enum` (first declared value ≠ 0). Patch parts are excluded, and at least one physical column is always kept. - Gate the optimization on `serialization_info_version >= with_missing_columns`. The populating step is authoritative about the part format version, so `SerializationInfoByName::getVersion` never silently upgrades a part past the configured value (which would make older servers reject it during a rolling upgrade). - Record the missing columns in `serialization.json` via `SerializationInfoByName` (new `WITH_MISSING_COLUMNS` version). Only `type_default` markers are written; `expression` markers are rejected on read until Phase 2. The list is written in sorted order so that identical parts produce identical checksums on different replicas. - Propagate the missing-columns marker through the part lifecycle: through merges (`MergeTask`, for columns that end up absent from the merged part), through mutations (`MutateTask::getColumnsForNewDataPart`, including renames of missing columns), through compact-part renames (`splitAndModifyMutationCommands`), and through on-the-fly `ALTER RENAME COLUMN` on read (`IMergeTreeReader::fillMissingColumns` translates the requested name back through `alter_conversions`). - Add a stateless test with 46 cases covering: basic skip; all-default keeps one column; merges (horizontal and vertical); mutation; `Nullable`; key columns; `DEFAULT` expression not skipped; `Array`; `Tuple`; `ColumnSparse` source; compact parts; `LowCardinality`; stable values across `ALTER ... DEFAULT`; a non-zero-default `Enum`; marker across mutation/merge/rename after `ALTER DEFAULT`; version gate; DETACH/ATTACH TABLE; DETACH/ATTACH PARTITION; BACKUP/RESTORE; FREEZE; CHECK TABLE; MATERIALIZE COLUMN; CLEAR COLUMN; lightweight DELETE; chained mutations; INSERT SELECT; REPLACE PARTITION; ATTACH PARTITION FROM; ALTER ADD/DROP COLUMN; projections; FixedString; Map; mixed parts merge; Date/DateTime; pre-ADD-COLUMN + skip merge; type-changing mutation; compact-part rename+mutation; Date32 regression. - Add an integration test (`test_skip_empty_columns`) with 6 cases: replicated consistency; merge marker propagation across replicas; mixed-version version gate; backward-compat fallback for old parts; restart durability; REPLACE PARTITION across replicated tables. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree INSERT can now skip writing columns whose values are entirely type-defaults (zeros, empty strings, `NULL`s), saving disk space for sparse-update workloads. Enabled by the MergeTree setting `skip_empty_columns_on_insert` together with `serialization_info_version = 'with_missing_columns'`. Missing columns carry frozen defaults in `serialization.json`, so a later `ALTER MODIFY COLUMN ... DEFAULT` does not retroactively change the inserted values. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is not required (bug fix, no new user-facing feature) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=98472&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/98472](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F98472+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Add query plan cache for SELECT queries
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add experimental query plan cache. When `allow_experimental_query_plan_cache = 1` and `enable_query_plan_cache = 1`, eligible single-table `SELECT` queries reuse a previously built `QueryPlan` and skip parsing/analysis/planning on subsequent identical executions. Per-table metadata version, row policy expression, user identity, and active roles all participate in the cache key, so schema/RBAC/policy changes invalidate transparently. `SYSTEM DROP QUERY PLAN CACHE` clears the cache; metrics and events surface as `QueryPlanCacheBytes`, `QueryPlanCacheEntries`, `QueryPlanCacheHits`, `QueryPlanCacheMisses`. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) ### Description This PR introduces an experimental **Query Plan Cache** for eligible `SELECT` queries. Unlike the [Query Cache](https://clickhouse.com/docs/operations/query-cache) which caches query *results*, the Query Plan Cache caches the *plan* — every cache hit still executes the query and reads up-to-date data, so it is transactionally consistent. Two-stage design so cached plans survive table snapshot rotations: - **Universalize** (write side): every storage-bound step (`ReadFromMergeTree`, …) is replaced with a storage-agnostic `ReadFromTableStep` carrying only `StorageID` + selected columns. Storage-specific state (parts, marks, prewhere actions) is stripped before serialization. - **Materialize** (read side): on a cache hit, the universalized plan is deserialized and `resolveStorages` rebinds each `ReadFromTableStep` to the current storage snapshot, restoring an executable `QueryPlan`. #### Cache key - 128-bit hash of the normalized query AST - 64-bit hash of planner-affecting session settings (resource limits, output formatting, logging are excluded — see `isSettingIgnoredInQueryPlanCache`; `extremes` / `max_rows_to_sort` / `max_bytes_to_sort` are intentionally NOT excluded because they are baked into `SortingStep` / `ExtremesStep`) - Table metadata version (or schema content hash for non-replicated tables) plus storage UUID — Atomic-DB `DROP+CREATE` of the same name no longer collides - Row policy expression hash, user identity, and sorted current role IDs #### Eligibility (all must hold) - Single-table `SELECT` (no JOIN / UNION / cross-table subqueries), local non-system non-view storage - `enable_analyzer = 1` (default) and `enable_parallel_replicas = 0` - No non-deterministic functions, no subqueries #### Safety on cache hit - `SELECT` access is re-checked on every hit (column-level when applicable). Permission revocation surfaces as `ACCESS_DENIED` and propagates rather than silently re-planning. - Fallback to normal planning is restricted to `INCORRECT_DATA` / `UNKNOWN_TABLE` (stale or corrupt entries); other exceptions including `LOGICAL_ERROR`, `QUERY_WAS_CANCELLED`, OOM are rethrown. - Per-user byte accounting (`query_plan_cache_size_in_bytes_quota`) is maintained incrementally via the `CacheBase` eviction hook — `O(1)` admission, no full LRU scan on every insert. #### Relation to plan-v3 / #97261 This PR builds on top of `QueryPlan::serialize` / `deserialize` (already used for parallel replicas). The `universalizePlan` / `materializePlan` helpers add the *storage-independent* layer needed for caching across snapshots. They do not replace plan-v3 serialization; they are complementary and both will continue to evolve. Cross-link: RFC #93812, plan-v3 part 2 #97261. #### Files of interest - `src/Interpreters/Cache/QueryPlanCache.{h,cpp}` — LRU/SLRU cache, key, per-user quota - `src/Interpreters/Cache/QueryPlanCacheUtils.{h,cpp}` — eligibility, key construction, on-hit access check - `src/Interpreters/{universalize,materialize}Plan.{h,cpp}` — pre-serialization / post-deserialization passes - `src/Interpreters/executeQuery.cpp` — admission/serve path with code-based fallback discrimination - `docs/en/operations/query-plan-cache.md` — user-facing documentation <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Introduces a new cross-query cache that injects serialized plans into `executeQuery`, touching planning/execution, access checks, and query plan serialization; while gated behind an experimental setting, cache-key/invalidations and plan materialization could cause subtle correctness or security regressions if wrong. > > **Overview** > Adds an *experimental* query plan cache for eligible `SELECT` queries that reuses a previously built `QueryPlan` to skip repeated planning, with new settings (`allow_experimental_query_plan_cache`, per-user `query_plan_cache_size_in_bytes_quota`) and server config knobs (`query_plan_cache.*`). > > Integrates the cache into `executeQuery` by building a cache key (AST + semantic settings hash + table schema version/hash + user/roles + row-policy hash), rejecting nondeterministic queries/subqueries/system tables/views/remote tables, revalidating `SELECT` access on cache hits, and serializing/universalizing plans on misses for storage. > > Extends query plan serialization to pass version through step (de)serialization, updates `ReadFromTableStep` to persist explicit `PREWHERE`, adds new metrics/events and `SYSTEM DROP QUERY PLAN CACHE` privilege/command, and includes unit/integration/stateless tests covering hits/misses, invalidation, ACL revocation, and runtime config reload behavior. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 3d2780c2545b1a942b46935dfb47764e2fbd8534. Bugbot is set up for automated code reviews on this repo. Configure [here](https://www.cursor.com/dashboard/bugbot).</sup> <!-- /CURSOR_SUMMARY --> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=99309&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/99309](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F99309+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Hash the type-derived parameter in the ALP, FPC and GCD codecs
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `ALP`, `FPC` and `GCD` omitting their type-derived parameter from the codec hash. In a Compact part the writer shares one compressed stream per distinct codec hash, so two columns of different value width under the same codec collided and shared one codec object carrying the wrong width. This rejected valid inserts with `CANNOT_COMPRESS` when the widths disagreed, and otherwise compressed one of the columns worse than it should have. ### Description Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/113940 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/113798 `MergeTreeDataPartWriterCompact::addStreams` keys compressed-stream reuse on `codec->getHash()` with no key-equality fallback, so a hash collision is an object-identity collision. Three codecs resolve a parameter from the column type, keep it out of the codec description AST, and hash only that AST, so two columns of different width shared one codec object and the loser of the race got the other's width: - `ALP` and `FPC` derive `float_width`. With `Float64` declared first the shared codec carries `float_width = 8`, a `Float32` granule is not a multiple of 8, and `ALP` throws `Code: 270 ... data size 404 is not aligned to 8 (CANNOT_COMPRESS)`. A mixed-width `Tuple(Float64, Float32) CODEC(ALP)` reaches the same throw, since the codec is resolved per substream. `FPC` ceil-divides instead of throwing, so its half is ratio-only: measured +10.0%. - `GCD` derives `gcd_bytes_size`, so the divisor width depended on declaration order and the ratio suffered. Data round-trips either way, because the width is in the GCD block header. Added on review request so the class stays revertable as one change; #113798 fixes the same `updateHash` for its own `is_signed_type` and goes forward independently. The fix adds the missing field to each hash, matching `SZ3`, `DoubleDelta`, `Gorilla`, `T64` and `Delta`, which already hash their type-derived width. Wide parts were never affected: one stream per column. Two consequences worth noting. Codec hashes also gate `can_substitute_codec_arguments`, a whole-codec flag, so `Tuple(Float32, Float64) CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` now shows as `CODEC(FPC, LZ4)` rather than `CODEC(FPC(12), LZ4)`; `Delta` and `Gorilla` already behave this way, same-width tuples still resolve, and a bare `CODEC(FPC)` still means level 12. No format change: each codec records the parameter in its own block header, so existing parts stay readable both ways. <details> <summary>Validation</summary> Debug build, base `f9dd35fa7f57bbd8ec97be53c15acd82848a98f1`. signal.title: Query result cache on disk
signal.text: On-disk configuration for query result cache is provided in addition to the already existing in-memory configuration. When data is written to the cache, it will be written to both of them (write-through). When data is searched inside the cache, it is searched in memory first, then on disk. If the data is found on disk, it will be also put in memory. On-disk cache has independent configurations of max size, max elements and max element size. ``` <query_cache> <max_size_in_bytes>1073741824</max_size_in_bytes> <max_entries>1024</max_entries> <max_entry_size_in_bytes>1048576</max_entry_size_in_bytes> <max_entry_size_in_rows>30000000</max_entry_size_in_rows> <on_disk> <max_size_in_bytes>2147483648</max_size_in_bytes> <max_entries>2048</max_entries> <max_entry_size_in_bytes>2097152</max_entry_size_in_bytes> <max_entry_size_in_rows>60000000</max_entry_size_in_rows> </on_disk> </query_cache> ``` The data is stored in subdirectory `query_cache/` relative to the base directory (`<path>...</path>` in the server configuration). For each query result, a file is created, with the AST tree hash as file name. To support future changes of the persistence format, a file `query_cache/format_version.txt` stores the version of the data, e.g. `1`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added an optional on-disk tier for the query result cache. The on-disk cache has its own `max_size_in_bytes`, `max_entries`, `max_entry_size_in_bytes`, and `max_entry_size_in_rows` limits, configured under `<query_cache><on_disk>` in the server configuration. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [ ] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features)

signal.text: Reworks the `diff-review` skill in `.claude/skills/diff-review` — the local in-browser diff review that Claude Code serves before a commit or a PR. signal.title: Make storage key and skip-index expression types independent of type-affecting session settings
signal.text: <!-- Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109181 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a `Bad cast` logical error (for example `Bad cast from ColumnVector<UInt32> to ColumnDecimal<DateTime64>`) that broke the next `INSERT` or mutation on a `MergeTree` table whose `ORDER BY`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `PARTITION BY` or skip index uses a function whose result type depends on a session setting (`enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions`, `cast_keep_nullable`, `function_date_trunc_return_type_behavior`, `geo_distance_returns_float64_on_float64_arguments`, `function_json_value_return_type_allow_nullable`, `least_greatest_legacy_null_behavior`, `h3togeo_lon_lat_result_order`, `allow_lossy_numeric_supertype`, `use_variant_as_common_type`), after any metadata-changing `ALTER` ran with that setting at a different value. Key and skip-index expression types are now resolved against the server settings baseline, so they stay consistent with the data the storage writes. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109181 ### Description A `MergeTree` key or skip-index expression's result type must not depend on the transient session settings that happen to be set when someone (re)builds the metadata. Several settings change the result type of a key expression, for example `enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions` (`toStartOf*`/`toMonday`/... on `Date32`/`DateTime64` return `DateTime64`/`Date32` instead of `DateTime`/`Date`) and `cast_keep_nullable` (`CAST` and `to<T>OrDefault` over a `Nullable` argument return `Nullable(T)` instead of `T`). `KeyDescription::data_types` is recomputed with whatever context runs `CREATE`/`ALTER`, so running any metadata-changing `ALTER` (even `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COMMENT`) with such a setting flipped changes the in-memory key type. The storage keeps producing the key column through `getCombinedIndicesExpression`, which analyzes the same AST with the storage's own context, so the produced column type diverges from the serializer's expected type and the primary-index writer aborts with `Bad cast ...` on the next `INSERT` or mutation, leaving the table broken until the server reloads its metadata. Reproducer from the issue (aborts in debug/sanitizer builds, throws in release): ```sql CREATE TABLE t0 (c1 Date, c2 DateTime64) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY (toStartOfTenMinutes(c2)); SET enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions = 1; INSERT INTO TABLE t0 (c2, c1) VALUES ('2118-08-18 18:05:25', '1998-10-21'); ALTER TABLE t0 CLEAR COLUMN c1; ``` The same divergence through `cast_keep_nullable`, which is how `MasterCI` `BuzzHouse (amd_debug)` hits it (STID 3520-704a, `Bad cast from type DB::ColumnVector<unsigned long> to DB::ColumnNullable`, report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?REF=master&sha=d5011f599b4c9c13bf17baaf58e53d84fd09eac3&name_0=MasterCI&name_1=BuzzHouse%20%28amd_debug%29). `toUInt64OrDefault` is a `FunctionCastOrDefault`, so its return type follows `cast_keep_nullable`; BuzzHouse reaches the metadata recompute through `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY COLUMN ... MODIFY SETTING` and needs `allow_nullable_key = 1`, which its fuzzer server config sets: ```sql SET cast_keep_nullable = 0; CREATE TABLE t (a Int32, b Nullable(Int32)) ENGINE = MergeTree() ORDER BY (a, toUInt64OrDefault(b)) SETTINGS allow_nullable_key = 1; ALTER TABLE t MODIFY COLUMN a MODIFY SETTING max_compress_block_size = 16 SETTINGS cast_keep_nullable = 1; INSERT INTO t VALUES (2, 2); ``` Fix: analyze key and skip-index expressions in a context where every enumerated type-affecting setting is pinned to the server settings baseline (the global default/system profile, including any `compatibility`), via the new `createKeyExpressionContext` used by `KeyDescription::getKeyFromAST`, `IndexDescription::initExpressionInfo`, `IndicesDescription::getSingleExpressionForIndices` and `getCombinedIndicesExpression`. The key type then does not depend on the session that (re)builds the metadata, and it matches what a fresh metadata reload resolves, because the reload path already runs under that same baseline. The explicit `toStartOf*Extended` function family (#108002) is the supported way to define an intentionally extended key. Keys whose expression is re-analyzed in the query context at read time must not be canonicalized, otherwise validation would accept a configuration the runtime filter then breaks. `KeyDescription::getKeyFromAST` therefore takes a `canonicalize_key_types` flag, set to false for the sampling key (its read-time filter is built in `MergeTreeDataSelectExecutor`), for the `parallel_replicas_custom_key` validator, and for object-storage hive-style partitioning (the partition value is a path string produced and parsed back under the query context, not a persisted binary key file). Note for reviewers on compatibility: a table declared with e.g. `ORDER BY toStartOfTenMinutes(dt64)` under `enable_extended_results_for_datetime_functions = 1` never had a persistable `DateTime64` key anyway (the type reverts to `DateTime` on restart, and the on-disk primary index is always written with the baseline type), so this makes an already-inconsistent state consistent rather than removing a working configuration. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109196&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109196](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109196+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix inconsistent results with filter push-down over `ANY INNER JOIN`
signal.text: `ANY INNER JOIN` returns an arbitrary match per left row, so filtering the right table before the join can change which row is matched: a predicate that would have rejected the original match may accept the replacement, thus resulting in outputs inconsistent with evaluating the join and the filter in order, observable within one query as the added test shows. Block push-down of such predicates to the right side only. The left side is preserved and its rows are probed independently, so dropping some of them cannot change the match taken for the others. Predicates over the equi-join keys are still pushed to both sides, since every row of a match set shares the key value. 01655_plan_optimizations test changes only in the operand order of an equi-key push-down: those conjuncts now reach the right stream through the equivalent-columns path rather than the direct one. Fixes https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/79189 ### Changelog category: - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry: Fix inconsistent results when a filter on a non-key column of the right table was pushed down below an ANY INNER JOIN. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114313&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114313](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114313+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> <!-- ch-version-info:start --> ### Version info - Merged into: `26.8.1.1708` (included in `26.8` and later) <!-- ch-version-info:end -->

signal.title: Look up the SSH key and support ssh-agent in clickhouse-client
signal.text: `--ssh-key-file` can now be specified without a value. In that case the key is looked up the same way as `ssh` does it: - the identity files configured for this host in `~/.ssh/config` and in `/etc/ssh/ssh_config`; - the default identity files, such as `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`; - the keys held by the `ssh-agent`. A key held by the `ssh-agent` is preferred, because it does not need a passphrase. It is also used when `--ssh-key-file` names a key file that the agent holds - an encrypted key that was added with `ssh-add` no longer asks for the passphrase. Signing with the agent is implemented in `SSHAgent`, a small client of the agent protocol, which produces the same `SSHSIG` signature as `SSHKey::signString` does for a local key (for RSA keys it asks the agent for `rsa-sha2-256`, because agents sign with SHA-1 by default and the server rejects that). The client reports the key it has chosen: ``` $ clickhouse-client --user abcuser --ssh-key-file Using the SSH key 'the key of abcuser' from the ssh-agent. ``` Two related changes of the existing behavior: the passphrase is now asked only if the key file is really encrypted (before, `--ssh-key-file` always asked for it), and the message about a key that cannot be imported now names the file. Tests: a new stateless test `04908_ssh_key_file_lookup` covers the default identity file, an `ed25519` key from the `ssh-agent`, and an `ssh-rsa` key from the `ssh-agent` with an empty `~/.ssh`. The existing `test_ssh_keys_authentication` integration tests pass. ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `clickhouse-client` accepts `--ssh-key-file` without a value: the key is looked up the same way as `ssh` does it - the identity files configured for the host in `~/.ssh/config`, the default identity files, such as `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`, and the keys held by the `ssh-agent`. Authentication with a key held by the `ssh-agent` is now supported, and it does not need a passphrase. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115072&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115072](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115072+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: --> Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/libssh/pull/15

signal.title: Silk fibers integration
signal.text: Splits the silk runtime integration out of https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111275, so that it can be reviewed on its own. This adds the plumbing that lets ClickHouse run work on [silk](https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk) fibers, without yet putting any subsystem on them. - `Silk::initializeFiberScheduler` / `Silk::destroyFiberScheduler`, called by the server when the `enable_silk_runtime` server setting is enabled. The fiber stack size is configurable through the `silk.fiber_stack_size` configuration key (320 KiB by default, which leaves enough room for OpenSSL handshakes). - `FiberLocal` - fiber-local storage. A fiber can migrate between operating-system threads, so it must not observe another fiber's `thread_local` state; the values of the registered slots are swapped in and out on every fiber switch instead. `current_thread` (`ThreadStatus`), the OpenTelemetry tracing context, and the memory-tracker and exception blockers are moved to it. - The silk thread-local-storage sanitizer: an LLVM pass in `utils/silk-thread-local-storage-sanitizer` that instruments every `thread_local` access and aborts when a fiber touches raw thread-local storage. Without it, a variable that was not migrated to `FiberLocal` produces silent corruption rather than a diagnostic. It is enabled in the debug and ASan CI builds. - `Silk::ConnectionPool` and `Silk::streamSocketFactory` - a `Connection` pool and a socket factory that suspend the calling fiber instead of blocking the operating-system thread. `PoolBase` and `ConnectionPool` are templated on the lock and the condition variable to make that possible, and `ConnectionPool` stays an alias of the `std::mutex` instantiation, so the existing call sites are unchanged. - Memory that the runtime maps outside the C++ heap - fiber stacks and `io_uring` rings - is charged to `total_memory_tracker` through silk's mmap accounting hooks. - The low-level silk runtime counters are exported to `system.asynchronous_metrics` under a `Silk` prefix. - `Common/Fiber.h` and `Common/FiberStack.h` are renamed to `Common/StackfulCoroutine.h` and `Common/CoroutineStack.h`. They implement the boost-context coroutines used by `AsyncTaskExecutor`, which are unrelated to silk fibers, and having two different things called "fiber" in the same codebase is confusing. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/111275 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added experimental support for the [silk](https://github.com/ClickHouse/silk) fiber runtime, enabled with the `enable_silk_runtime` server setting. When it is enabled, the server initializes the silk fiber scheduler at startup, so that subsystems supporting it can run their jobs on fibers instead of occupying an operating-system thread while waiting for I/O. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112667&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112667](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112667+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Break symlink loops in StorageFile glob expansion
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/106676 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `Too many levels of symbolic links` errors and duplicate or missing rows when the `file()` table function expands a recursive glob (`**`) over a directory tree containing a symlink to an ancestor directory. Such a walk is now pruned per (directory, remaining pattern) frame, and matches are deduplicated by resolved parent directory, so a symlinked ancestor neither loops nor yields a file twice while a symlink to a file is still reported under its own name. ### Description Recursive glob expansion in `listFilesWithRegexpMatchingImpl` did not protect against directory symlinks that target an ancestor. `fs::directory_iterator` does not follow symlinks for iteration, but `directory_entry::is_directory` does, so the recursion descended a loop until the kernel hit `ELOOP` and surfaced a raw `std::filesystem::filesystem_error: Too many levels of symbolic links` (`STD_EXCEPTION`). The depth cap added in #106676 does not catch this because the kernel error fires first. The walk now enters each frame at most once, where a frame is the canonical directory together with the pattern still to be matched there. That pair is the whole state of the walk, so a frame repeating it can only redo what another frame already did, whether that is an enclosing frame (a cycle) or a finished sibling (an alias). Keying on the directory alone is wrong, because `**` matches zero levels: the re-application enters the current directory with a shorter suffix while the enclosing frame is still there, and directory-only keying dropped it, so `file('root/*/**/top.txt')` with `root/x/back -> ..` returned 0 rows instead of 1. Because a `**` walk can now reach one file through two frames, its match deduplication resolves the parent directory of each match; lexical forms do not resolve symlinks. The final component is deliberately left as written, so a symlink to a file and its target stay two rows, which is what the pattern selected. This is scoped to `**` expansions, since a finite glob can also name one file twice through two ancestor aliases sharing a filename, and master reports both. Deduplication only filters results, so it cannot stop the walk re-descending; a dense graph of aliased directories previously returned 109600 rows for eight real files, and now returns 8. `04325_test_storage_file_glob_symlink_loop` covers the loop, aliasing, finite-glob and write-refusal shapes above; each assertion is mutation-tested. <details> <summary>Canonicalization cost on large symlink-free trees</summary> Deduplicating by canonical path needs the canonical parent of each match. Every entry one invocation emits shares that parent, so a glob suffix resolves once per directory rather than once per file. A purely finite glob resolves nothing. Counting `readlink` against master: | pattern, tree | master | here | rows | |---|---|---|---| | `**/*.tsv`, 20 000 files in one directory | 26 | 34 | 20 000 | | `**/*.tsv`, 10 000 files in 100 dirs at depth 3 | 26 | 1 702 | 10 000 | | `**/file.txt`, 251 files in 500 dirs | 4 033 | 7 038 | 251 | A literal suffix costs more: the globstar frame resolves its directory, then applies the suffix in a fresh call that resolves the match's own parent, which for a multi-component suffix is a deeper directory. Both are bounded by directories walked, not by rows. Latency on the 10 000-file tree is 329 ms against 417 ms. Pruning cost on dense alias graphs, where every one of N sibling directories links to every other and none links to an ancestor: | aliases | frames remembered while descending only | frames remembered once walked | |---|---|---| | 6 | 0.46 s | 0.10 s | | 8 | 30.2 s | 0.10 s | | 10 | over 700 s | 0.11 s | </details> <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=106697&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/106697](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F106697+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Hash the AST members that `getTreeHash` did not see
signal.text: Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/110833 This is the `getTreeHash` part of #110833, split off because it stands on its own: it fixes wrong results that have nothing to do with that pull request's motivation (comparing stored table definitions). Only the `src/Parsers` changes were taken; the `sameAST` helper and the metadata comparison stay in #110833. `IAST::getTreeHash` identifies an AST subtree, and several callers use it as the identity of an expression or of a query: `Context::executeTableFunction` caches the result of a table function under it, `ExecuteScalarSubqueriesVisitor` caches the value of a scalar subquery, `ActionsVisitor` keys prepared sets, `ComparisonGraph` and `WhereConstraintsOptimizer` decide whether two expressions are the same one. The default implementation hashes only `getID` and `children`, so anything a node keeps outside `children` is invisible to it, and a number of nodes keep meaningful state there. Two ASTs that mean different things then get the same hash, and a caller that treats the hash as an identity silently substitutes one for the other. For example, on `master`: ```sql SELECT (SELECT count() FROM view(SELECT 1 AS x UNION ALL SELECT 1)) AS union_all, (SELECT count() FROM view(SELECT 1 AS x UNION DISTINCT SELECT 1)) AS union_distinct ``` ``` ┌─union_all─┬─union_distinct─┐ 1. │ 2 │ 2 │ └───────────┴────────────────┘ ``` The second `view` returns `2` instead of `1`: `union_mode` is not a child of `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery` and was not hashed, so the two calls got the same cache key. The same happens for `INTERSECT` against `EXCEPT`, for `LIMIT 2` against `OFFSET 2` (the same literal in a different role), for `WITH FILL ... TO 5` against `WITH FILL ... STEP 5`, for a window frame bounded from below against one bounded from above, and for `APPLY(quantile(0.1))` against `APPLY(quantile(0.9))`. This change hashes the members that are part of an element's meaning and are not children: * `ASTSelectQuery`, `ASTProjectionSelectQuery`, `ASTOrderByElement` - the role each child plays (`WHERE` against `HAVING`, the limit against the offset, the `WITH FILL` upper bound against the step), which is recorded only in `positions`. `ASTSelectQuery::group_by_with_grouping_sets` was missing as well. * `ASTSelectWithUnionQuery` - `union_mode` and `list_of_modes`; `ASTSelectIntersectExceptQuery` - `final_operator`. * `ASTWindowDefinition` - the frame and the parent window name; `ASTWindowListElement` - the name the window is bound to. * `ASTWithElement` - the name the CTE is bound to, `MATERIALIZED`, and the column aliases. * `ASTQueryWithOutput` - the `INTO OUTFILE` modifiers; `ASTQueryWithTableAndOutput` - `TEMPORARY` and an explicit `UUID`. * `ASTSetQuery` - `is_standalone`, the settings reset with `= DEFAULT`, the query parameters, and the node's own identity, which this override skipped altogether. * `ASTTTLElement` - the mode, the destination, the `GROUP BY` key and assignments, and the recompression codec. * `ASTIndexDeclaration`, `ASTConstraintDeclaration`, `ASTProjectionDeclaration` - the declared name (and the index granularity, and `CHECK` against `ASSUME`). * `ASTCollation` - the collation name; `ASTStreamSettings` - the cursor tree and the watermark column and idle timeout. Follow-up fixes in the same area, found by the debug build's format+parse round-trip check and by review: * A per-column `PRIMARY KEY` is normalized by `ParserCreateQuery` into the storage definition, but `primary_key_specifier` stayed `true` on the column declarations while formatting never printed it, so once the flag was hashed, such a `CREATE` no longer round-tripped format+parse to the same tree hash and the debug build reported the `Inconsistent AST formatting` logical error. The parser now clears the flag when its meaning is transferred; where it does survive - `ALTER TABLE ... ADD/MODIFY COLUMN` - formatting now prints `PRIMARY KEY` instead of silently dropping it. * `ParserQueryWithOutput` canonicalizes the output-option children to the end of `children`, and most parsers add the database/table children first, but several `clone` implementations rebuilt them in a different order, so a clone of `CHECK TABLE t FORMAT JSONEachRow` or `SHOW CREATE TABLE t INTO OUTFILE 'x'` hashed differently than the original. The clones now rebuild `children` in the parser's order. Along the way: `ASTDropQuery::clone` and `ASTUndropQuery::clone` did not clear the copied `children` (the clone kept the source's children and appended the cloned ones on top), `ASTOptimizeQuery::clone` pushed `deduplicate_by_columns` into `children` while the parser keeps it member-only, and `ASTCheckTableQuery::partition`, `ASTWatchQuery::limit_length`, and the `where_expression` / `limit_length` of `SHOW COLUMNS` / `SHOW INDEXES` were left shared with the source instead of being cloned. * The `static_assert`s pinning the size of the AST nodes are checked only on 64-bit targets: the wasm32 parser build has a different layout. Two more fixes in the same area: * `ASTColumnsApplyTransformer` reached its non-child `parameters` and `lambda` through `updateTreeHashImpl` rather than `updateTreeHash`, which stops at the node itself and never descends into it, so the `0.5` of `APPLY(quantile(0.5))` was not hashed. * `ASTWithAlias` hashed the alias without its length, so the alias ran into whatever the node writes next and `foo` followed by `Identifier_bar` produced the same byte stream as the alias `bar` on `Identifier_foo`. `ASTCollation::readJSON` and `ASTWithElement::readJSON` put a member into `children` that neither the parser nor `clone` puts there, so an AST restored from JSON had a shape - and a hash - that no parsed AST has, and `clone` of it dropped the child again. They now reproduce the parser's shape. `ASTTTLElement::clone` left the recompression codec shared with the source, which the new unit test surfaced. New tests: `04836_tree_hash_ast_identity` covers the wrong results above, and `gtest_tree_hash_completeness` covers the members that no pair of queries can differ in on their own, by editing the JSON serialization of the AST, plus the JSON round-trip shape. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fix wrong results for a query that calls the same table function twice with arguments that differ only in a part of the query that was not taken into account by the AST hash, such as `UNION ALL` against `UNION DISTINCT`, `INTERSECT` against `EXCEPT`, `LIMIT` against `OFFSET`, or the bounds of a window frame. The second call reused the result of the first one. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=114171&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/114171](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F114171+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Perf: Optimize PromQL and for exact groups
signal.text: ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): PromQL `and` expressions with an exact group key skip redundant matching stages. ## What changed - add a fast path for the PromQL set operator `and` - use it when both inputs already match on the original `group` column - join the unique left and right `VECTOR_GRID` inputs directly - keep the left-hand values and filter them by right-side sample presence - keep `on(...)`, non-empty `ignoring(...)`, `on()`, and other transformed matching keys on the existing general path - add exact-output coverage for grouped `and` expressions - cover empty `ignoring()` when both inputs already have exact groups - add a performance fixture with an exact-group query and an `and on(instance)` control ## Why this is safe `VECTOR_GRID` guarantees one row per `group`. The fast path is enabled only when the matching rules leave the original `group` column unchanged on both sides, so the join key is already unique and exact. The exact-group path removes the right-side per-group count aggregation and the transformed-key join. It returns the left value only when the corresponding right value is present, which is the existing `and` masking behavior. `on(...)`, non-empty `ignoring(...)`, and other cases that transform the matching key keep the current general lowering. Empty `ignoring()` is treated like default matching when both inputs already have exact groups. ## Benchmark Ran `tests/performance/promql_set_operators_and.xml` on Apple Silicon with the Release build from this PR. - 8,000 series - 4,000 matching groups - 300 samples per series - 7 measured runs per query on each of two local server instances The table shows the average of the two per-server medians. Both queries are equivalent for this fixture. The default query uses the new exact-group fast path. The `and on(instance)` query keeps the existing generic implementation. | Query | Median | | --- | ---: | | exact-group `and` | 130.2 ms | | equivalent `and on(instance)` query | 139.8 ms | The exact-group query took 130.2 ms versus 139.8 ms for the existing implementation, which is 6.9% faster in this test. ## Tests - add grouped exact-output coverage for `and` - add exact-output coverage for empty `ignoring()` - keep the existing ungrouped and transformed-key `and` coverage - compile the changed translation unit with the ClickHouse warning set and `-Werror` Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/115219 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115374&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115374](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115374+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Measure CLI tools startup time in CI
signal.text: - Add a `CLI startup benchmark` job that spawns `clickhouse local` and `clickhouse client` and compares CPU time and minor page faults against the latest master build. - Gate on minor page faults at 1.05x and on CPU time at 1.15x, since faults count work done rather than time taken and so barely move on a shared runner. - Attach the `system` and `information_schema` tables in `clickhouse local` on first access rather than at startup, keeping `system.one` eager because every `FROM`-less query resolves it during analysis. - Stop resolving the UTC time zone in `TimezoneMixin`, so that naming a `DateTime` type no longer builds a lookup table nothing reads; the serializations that do need it hold their own. - Resolve the client hostname in `ClientInfo` on first use instead of through a blocking `getaddrinfo` on every invocation. - Set a system table's comment before attaching it, instead of copying its whole `StorageInMemoryMetadata` twice. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Speed up `clickhouse local` startup: system tables and `information_schema` are now attached on first access, naming a `DateTime` type no longer builds an unused UTC lookup table, and the client hostname is resolved only when it is actually reported instead of on every invocation.

signal.title: TimeSeries: optional TTL'd recent samples table preferred by PromQL for short time ranges
signal.text: On a large `TimeSeries` table the most frequent queries — alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards — pay primary-key analysis over the whole multi-billion-row samples table and read one full granule per series: on a 71.4B-sample corpus a bare instant selector takes 0.85 s cold to return a few hundred points. When the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a fourth target table (`RECENT SAMPLES`) mimicking the samples table, plus an inner materialized view `.inner_id.recentsamplesmv.<uuid>` copying `id`, `timestamp`, `value` into it on every insert. The recent table adds `PARTITION BY` from `recent_samples_partition_by` (default `toDate(timestamp)`), `TTL toDateTime(timestamp) + toIntervalSecond(<ttl>)` with `ttl_only_drop_parts = 1`, and `recent_samples_index_granularity` (default 8192). PromQL selector reads (`prometheusQuery`, `prometheusQueryRange`, the HTTP API, remote read) prefer it whenever the selector's whole range fits in the TTL window (`min_time >= now() - TTL`) — safe because `ttl_only_drop_parts` drops a part only when all its rows have expired. The preference can be disabled with the new query setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. Off by default; not supported in `Replicated` databases yet (the inner materialized view would get a different UUID on every replica). Measured on a 71.4B-sample / 30-day / 413k-series corpus (40 PromQL queries, cold geomean vs the same binary without the feature): rules 5x (bare selector 0.85 s → 0.03 s, alert 1.9 s → 0.20 s), 30m dashboards 3.5-4.3x, 6h 1.4x, 24h 1.1x, overall 1.6-1.7x; results value-identical to 1e-15. A TTL of ~3 days is the sweet spot: it covers the intraday horizon including `offset 24h` panels at +10% disk, and avoids the regression seen with a 10d TTL, where 7d-range queries switch to the recent table and get 15% slower than on the single sorted part. Hourly partitioning is a wash overall and multiplies part count 24x, so day partitioning is the default. The cost is ingest: a fresh remote-write load of 1.3B samples slows from 324 s to 455-475 s (−30% throughput) — hence opt-in; a dedicated batched sink instead of the generic materialized-view chain is a possible follow-up. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Experimental Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): `TimeSeries` tables can now keep a "recent samples" table: when the new engine setting `recent_samples_ttl_seconds` is non-zero, the engine creates a TTL'd copy of the samples table (partitioned by `recent_samples_partition_by`, by day by default) fed by an inner materialized view, and PromQL queries whose time range fits in the TTL window automatically read from it, making alert/recording rules and short-range dashboards several times faster on large tables. The preference can be disabled with the new query-level setting `time_series_prefer_recent_samples_table`. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115441&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115441](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115441+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reject WITH FILL bounds that do not fit the ORDER BY column type
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109454 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/109216 --> `WITH FILL FROM`/`TO` values are converted to a type wide enough for the arithmetic - `Int64` for every integer column type - while the generated values are written into a column of the column's own type, which truncates whatever does not fit its range. A truncated value wraps around, so the filled stream stops being monotonic while the query plan keeps claiming that it is still sorted by the fill columns. `DISTINCT` in order relies on that claim and reads the stream as a sequence of sorted runs, so it deduplicates within wrong ranges: ```sql SELECT count() FROM (SELECT DISTINCT x, s FROM (SELECT toUInt8(5) AS x, 'Hello' AS s ORDER BY x ASC WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 1025)); ``` returns `1024` instead of `257` in a release build, because `WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 1025` over a `UInt8` column generates `1..255, 0, 1..255, 0, ...`. In a debug or sanitizer build the same query aborts in `DistinctSortedStreamTransform` with `Equal values are not contiguous within the range assumed to be sorted`, which is what the AST fuzzer hit: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109454&sha=b0030d87c1f4e4b31d2766c17286e42492a2da94&name_0=PR&name_1=AST%20fuzzer%20%28amd_msan%29 https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/109454 The fuzzer query is unrelated to that pull request; the abort reproduces on `master`: ```sql SELECT DISTINCT x, isZeroOrNull(materialize(true)), s FROM ( SELECT 5 AS x, 'Hello' AS s ORDER BY x ASC NULLS LAST WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 10 INTERPOLATE (`s` AS concat(s, 'A')) LIMIT 1048576 UNION ALL SELECT 5 AS x, 'Hello' AS s ORDER BY x ASC NULLS LAST WITH FILL FROM 1 TO 1025 INTERPOLATE (`s` AS concatAssumeInjective(s, 'A')) LIMIT 1048576 ) ORDER BY s ASC; ``` ### Fix Reject `FROM`/`TO` values that cannot be represented in the type of the `ORDER BY` column with `INVALID_WITH_FILL_EXPRESSION`, next to the existing check that rejects negative bounds for an unsigned column type. This matches how the equivalent `Date`/`DateTime` bound mismatch is already rejected (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/30421). `TO` is an exclusive bound, so it may still be outside of the range as long as the values that filling actually generates fit: `WITH FILL FROM 0 TO 256` over a `UInt8` column keeps generating `0..255`, and so does `WITH FILL FROM 0 TO 257 STEP 3`, which stops at `255`. The last generated value is known up front only when `FROM` and a plain numeric `STEP` are given. Without `FROM` the sequence is anchored at a data value, so which values are generated is known only at execution time: `WITH FILL TO 257 STEP 3` over a `UInt8` column stops at `254` when the data ends at `11` but reaches `256` when it ends at `13`. Still, whenever filling generates anything at all, its last value lands within one step before `TO`, so such a bound is rejected only when even the value one whole step away from `TO` (clamped towards zero, so that anchors close enough to `TO` to generate nothing keep being accepted) does not fit the column type - that is, only when filling provably wraps for every possible anchor. An `INTERVAL` step performs its calendar arithmetic in the column's own native type, so unlike a plain numeric step it wraps around within the column domain and can never reach a `TO` outside of it: filling would generate wrapped-around values forever (it does on current master, e.g. `SELECT toDate(0) AS d ORDER BY d ASC WITH FILL FROM toDate(0) TO 70000 STEP INTERVAL 100 YEAR` never terminates). Such a `TO` is therefore rejected regardless of `FROM` - but only when it is out of range in the fill direction. A `TO` out of range against the fill direction (e.g. `ORDER BY d DESC WITH FILL TO 70000 STEP INTERVAL -1 YEAR` over a `Date` column) is a guaranteed no-op instead: every possible anchor is already past it, filling never takes a single step, and the bound is accepted - the same clamp towards zero as in the numeric case. `STALENESS`, which is allowed only without `FROM`, replaces `TO` as the effective bound whenever it comes first, so the sequence can stop arbitrarily far below `TO` and such a `TO` is not checked either. Float and Decimal bounds are not checked: they saturate instead of wrapping, and a `Float64` bound is generally inexact in a `Float32` column, so requiring exact representability there would reject ordinary queries. On top of the storage range, the calendar arithmetic of an `INTERVAL` step clamps at the boundaries of the representable calendar - the `[0000-01-01, 9999-12-31]` window of `DateLUTImpl`, taken in the local civil calendar of the column's time zone, so for `DateTime64` the boundary in raw ticks shifts by the UTC offset (the last reachable second of a `DateTime64(0, 'Etc/GMT-14')` column is `253402250399`, not the UTC `253402300799`) - and for `Date32` and `DateTime64` that window is strictly narrower than the storage type. A `TO` beyond the calendar boundary in the fill direction fits the storage type but can never be reached: the filling keeps generating the clamped boundary value forever (it does on current master, e.g. `SELECT toDate32('9999-12-31') AS d ORDER BY d ASC WITH FILL TO 3000000 STEP INTERVAL 1 YEAR` never terminates). Such a `TO` is rejected against the calendar limits, scale-aware for `DateTime64`. For `Date` the calendar clamp coincides with the `UInt16` storage boundary, and `DateTime` wraps within `UInt32`, where any in-range `TO` stays reachable from some anchor, so the storage check covers those two. Beyond reachability, for `Date32` and `DateTime64` the values between the calendar boundary and the boundary of the storage type are invalid in themselves: no conversion produces them (they all clamp at the calendar boundary), yet a `FROM` bound in that gap is materialized into the column as is and serialized as the clamped boundary date - a spurious duplicate of the genuine boundary value next to it (e.g. `SELECT d FROM (SELECT toDate32('2000-01-01') AS d ORDER BY d ASC WITH FILL FROM -719529 TO -719528 STEP INTERVAL 1 YEAR)` on current master returns a `0000-01-01` row holding the day number `-719529`, which is not `0000-01-01`). The representability check therefore tests bounds of these two types against the calendar window (in the local civil calendar of the column's time zone for `DateTime64`), not just the storage range: an out-of-calendar `FROM` is rejected for any kind of step - like a `FROM` out of the storage range already is - and a numeric-step `TO` is rejected when the last value generated under it provably lands in the gap, under the same rules as the storage range. The last-generated-value computation covers the `Decimal64`-carried `DateTime64` bounds as well as the `Int64`-carried types: a numeric step over `DateTime64` advances raw ticks of the column's scale, and ticks beyond the calendar do not wrap but are equally invalid (they all serialize as the clamped boundary date). Finally, the calendar clamp makes an `INTERVAL` step able to stagnate: adding the interval to a value whose result would leave the calendar returns the value unchanged, so the sequence can stop advancing strictly below a perfectly representable `TO` and never terminate (e.g. `WITH FILL FROM toDateTime64('9999-06-01 00:00:00', 0, 'UTC') TO toDateTime64('9999-12-31 00:00:00', 0, 'UTC') STEP INTERVAL 1 YEAR` hangs on current master). With an explicit `FROM` the whole sequence is known up front - `FillingRow::next` advances it by one application of the step function at a time - so it is walked at construction time with the same step function, under a bounded budget (65536 steps), and rejected when it provably stagnates before reaching `TO`. The walk mirrors the runtime step exactly, so it can never misjudge a terminating sequence; a fill whose stagnation lies beyond the budget (a fine-grained step over a huge span) is accepted as before. The same walk rejects a step that turns back instead of stagnating: the calendar arithmetic is performed in the storage type of the column, so a step whose result would leave that type wraps around (e.g. `WITH FILL FROM toDateTime('2106-01-01 00:00:00', 'UTC') TO 4294967295 STEP INTERVAL 100 YEAR` jumps from 2106 back to 2069 and keeps cycling below `TO` forever on current master). The value such a step wrapped from is above the type maximum, hence above `TO`, so the sequence has already overshot the bound and every value generated from there on is spurious - out of order and past the `TO` the query asked for - whether or not the wrapped-around walk happens to land beyond `TO` later on and terminate. For data-dependent paths whose effective bound comes from the next input row or `STALENESS`, `FillingRow::next` checks every generated step at runtime. A step that does not advance in the sorting direction now throws `INVALID_WITH_FILL_EXPRESSION`, preventing both wrapped rows and non-terminating fills. The stateless test covers the `Int64` between-rows overflow case. ### Changelog category Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry Reject `WITH FILL` bounds and steps that would wrap, generate non-monotonic output, or never terminate. ### Documentation entry - [x] Documentation is not required. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112650&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112650](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112650+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Reload a persisted `url()` table with the storage its creation selected
signal.text: <!-- Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/104437 --> ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed a server that refuses to start after a table was created with `CREATE TABLE ... AS url('http://host/**/', ...)` while `allow_experimental_url_wildcard_from_index_pages` was enabled. Loading such a table's metadata re-evaluated the experimental check and failed with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`, aborting startup. ### Description Reported by @ bacek on #104437, where `Stress test (amd_tsan)` failed with `Cannot start clickhouse-server` after a fuzzer created `url('/**/', JSONEachRow, 'x int')`. No fuzzer is needed: enable the setting, create such a table, restart with the default. Root cause is one defaulted parameter. `ITableFunction::execute` declares `bool is_insert_query = false`; `CREATE ... AS url(...)` passes `true` explicitly (`InterpreterCreateQuery.cpp:2403`), while metadata replay (`DatabaseOnDisk.cpp:117`) passes nothing. `TableFunctionURL::getStorage` computes `use_web_wildcard = !is_insert_query && ...`, so the two take opposite branches for the same stored table: creation builds a plain `StorageURL` and never reaches the experimental check, replay builds `StorageObjectStorage` and does. The check is dead at creation and live only on replay, and metadata loading rethrows. The fix treats a definition arriving with stored columns as a persisted one being replayed, so it resolves to the storage creation selected. The check is not suppressed, it becomes unreachable because the correct branch is taken. Suppressing it would instead enable index-page expansion with the setting disabled and give the table a read-only storage. `ENGINE = URL` was already fixed this way in 64abbdd31d85b15 ("Gate `URL` wildcard experiment check to creation"). Behaviour change: a persisted glob `url()` table that today rebuilds as `StorageObjectStorage` after a restart now rebuilds as the `StorageURL` its creation built. Both carriers are covered by the one change and both are tested: explicit structure, and `structure = 'auto'` via `StorageTableFunctionProxy` (the surface of an earlier `test_url_wildcard_schema_inference` failure). `urlCluster` cannot persist a table. The creation-time check in `getActualTableStructure` is deliberately untouched, since a columns-less `CREATE` reaches it before `execute`. Querying `url()` directly still requires the setting. Out of scope: the check stays dead at creation, so `CREATE` with a glob still succeeds with the setting off. `ytsaurus()` has the same problem by another mechanism. CI report: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=104437&sha=bee15ffc5ec3d2a9b5479bd1fbc197ac6458eebc&name_0=PR&name_1=Stress%20test%20%28amd_tsan%29 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=115095&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/115095](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F115095+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Improve the performance of `MODIFY TTL`
signal.text: `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` currently rewrites every part of the table, which on a large table means reading and writing all of its data just to change when rows expire. Very often the new TTL is the old one shifted in time - the retention period is extended or shortened, e.g. `create_time + INTERVAL 300 DAY` becomes `create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY`. In that case every row's expiry time moves by the same constant number of seconds, so the parts do not have to be rewritten at all: it is enough to shift the expiry timestamps ClickHouse already stores per part. This pull request adds that fast path, and the result for the user is that such a `MODIFY TTL` completes almost instantly instead of taking minutes or hours: ```sql CREATE TABLE test_fast_ttl (`id` UInt32, `name` String, `create_time` DateTime) ENGINE = MergeTree ORDER BY id TTL create_time + toIntervalDay(300); INSERT INTO test_fast_ttl SELECT number, 'AAA', date_sub(day, 100, now()) from numbers(100000000); -- Before ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 25.564 sec. -- After ALTER TABLE test_fast_ttl MODIFY TTL create_time + INTERVAL 10 DAY; -- 0 rows in set. Elapsed: 0.046 sec. ``` There is nothing to enable and no new syntax: the optimization is applied automatically inside the `MATERIALIZE TTL` mutation that `MODIFY TTL` already produces, and a plain `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from it as well. The observable result is exactly the same as before - the same rows expire and the parts end up with the same TTL bounds - only the work is avoided. Per part, the mutation now does one of the following: - the part is fully expired under the new TTL - it is replaced with an empty part; - no row of the part is expired yet - the part is cloned (its data files hardlinked) and only its stored TTL bounds are shifted; - otherwise - the part is rewritten exactly as before. The fast path is only taken when it is provably equivalent to the rewrite. It requires that the unconditional rows TTL (`TTL <expr>`) is the only TTL of the table, and that the old and the new TTL are the same date/time column shifted by constant fixed-length intervals, so that `new_ttl(row) - old_ttl(row)` is one constant for every row. Calendar `MONTH`/`YEAR` intervals, `DAY`/`WEEK` intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, and row-dependent expressions are all rejected. The proof is redone for each part against the TTL expression (and time zone) that the part's stored timestamps were actually computed under, so a part that lags the table metadata, or was written by an older server, falls back to the regular rewrite rather than being shifted unsoundly. The same applies to the boundary cases of the stored timestamps themselves: a part containing a row whose TTL timestamp is exactly `1970-01-01 00:00:00` UTC (which ClickHouse treats as "no TTL"), a shift that would move some timestamp onto that value, and a part whose stored TTL is already fully expired (which the regular rewrite drops wholesale, even when the new TTL is longer) all take the regular rewrite. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes to CHANGELOG.md): `ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY TTL` no longer rewrites the table's data when the new TTL is the old one shifted by a constant amount of time (the same date/time column plus fixed-length intervals), which is the common case of extending or shortening the retention period. Fully expired parts are replaced with empty ones and the rest are cloned with only their stored TTL metadata shifted, which makes such an `ALTER` nearly instant. Cases where the shift is not provably constant - calendar month/year intervals, day/week intervals in a time zone with daylight saving time, or row-dependent TTL expressions - fall back to the regular rewrite. `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE TTL` benefits from the same optimization. <!--- Directly edit documentation source files in the "docs" folder with the same pull-request as code changes or Add a user-readable short description of the changes that should be added to docs.clickhouse.com below. signal.title: Respect max_http_get_redirects setting in HTTPDictionarySource
signal.text: ### What this PR does `HTTPDictionarySource` did not call `withRedirects` on its HTTP request builder, so HTTP dictionary sources rejected every redirect with `TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS` even when `max_http_get_redirects` was set to a non-zero value. This made it impossible to create dictionaries from HTTP(S) URLs that redirect (e.g. pre-signed object-storage URLs), while the `url` table function and other HTTP sources already follow redirects. This adds `.withRedirects(context->getSettingsRef()[Setting::max_http_get_redirects])` to all four request paths (`loadAll`, `loadUpdatedAll`, `loadIds`, `loadKeys`), matching the pattern already used in `StorageURL`. The `max_http_get_redirects` value is taken from the dictionary's `SETTINGS` clause; the default of `0` keeps the previous (redirect-rejecting) behavior, so this is not backward incompatible. A new stateless test `04498_http_dictionary_max_redirects` starts a local HTTP server that issues a `302` redirect and verifies that the dictionary refuses to follow it when `max_http_get_redirects = 0` (`TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS`) and loads successfully when redirects are allowed. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/90521 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes): HTTP dictionary sources (`SOURCE(HTTP(...))`) now respect the `max_http_get_redirects` setting, so dictionaries can be created from URLs that redirect. Previously such dictionaries always failed with `TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS`. - [ ] Documentation is written (no docs needed for this change) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=101768&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/101768](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F101768+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->
