signal.title: Apply `SORT + LIMIT` before `ARRAY JOIN`
signal.text: ## Use case ```sql SELECT payload FROM t ARRAY JOIN arr ORDER BY ts LIMIT 10; ``` With an average array size `k`, the `ORDER BY` currently sorts `rows(t) * k` rows, although the sort key does not depend on the array at all. The same holds for `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY`: the truncation happens above the expansion, so the expansion is performed for rows that are immediately discarded. The plan is: ``` Limit(10) Sorting(ts, limit=10) Expression ArrayJoin(arr) ReadFromMergeTree ``` The `ARRAY JOIN` is already *below* the sort, so the fix is a reorder, not a push-down of a new step. Note that this is not about avoiding column replication — that is largely solved already. `enable_lazy_columns_replication` defaults to `true` (`src/Core/Settings.cpp:6641`), the joined element column *is* the array's nested column (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:280`, `getDataPtr`), all other columns are only index-wrapped (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:288-292`), and `transformColumnsWithSharedIndex` (`ColumnReplicated.cpp:784`) transforms the shared index once per block. What remains is that the sort itself processes `k` times more rows than it has to. ## Why the reorder is sound `ArrayJoinResultIterator::next` walks input rows in order and takes elements from the nested column in order. So every input row expands into a **contiguous run** of output rows, and the runs preserve input order. Therefore, if every input row produces at least one output row, the first `n` output rows come from the first `k <= n` input rows, and a plain row-count limit of `n` may be evaluated below the `ARRAY JOIN`. The only counterexample is an input row that produces zero output rows: an empty array under an inner `ARRAY JOIN`. `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` is immune, because `emptyArrayToSingle` in the iterator constructor already guarantees at least one element. This means **no weighted limit is needed for correctness** — an emptiness guard is enough. The same reasoning is already written down for the `arrayJoin`-in-expression form in `liftUpFunctions.cpp:96-103`, where the reorder is currently refused only when a `LIMIT` is present. ## Proposed implementation ### 1. Emptiness guard below an inner `ArrayJoinStep` Insert `Filter(length(c) > 0)`. This removes exactly the rows the `ARRAY JOIN` removes itself, so it is a valid rewrite on its own, independent of any limit — a small first commit with a trivial correctness argument. - `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` — no guard needed. - inner, aligned — `length(c1) > 0` for any one joined column; `hasEqualOffsets` (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:277`) enforces equal sizes anyway. - inner, unaligned — `greatest(length(c1), ..., length(cn)) > 0`, because `arrayResize` pads every array to the maximum size. - `Map` columns — `length(m)` is defined and is the right function here. - Constant arrays — the guard const-folds away. - Several chained `ARRAY JOIN`s — one guard per step (the multiplicities multiply). - Use `length(arr) > 0`, not `arr.size0 > 0`: `optimize_functions_to_subcolumns` is a query-tree pass and cannot rewrite a filter created by the plan optimizer. The subcolumn form is only needed by the follow-up issue below. ### 2. Teach `ArrayJoinStep` that it preserves order `getTraits` sets `preserves_sorting = false` (`ArrayJoinStep.cpp:26`), so `applyOrder` drops all sortedness across the step. Contiguous runs mean order *is* preserved for every sort prefix that does not touch the joined columns, so the flat bool should become a prefix rule in `applyOrder.cpp`: keep the prefix up to the first joined column. Trap: a joined column keeps its **name** across the step — `ArrayJoinAction::prepare` replaces the column in place and only the type changes. So the rule must exclude joined columns by name; checking that a sort key is present in the input header is not sufficient. `buildSortingDAG` already performs exactly this removal (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:313-318`). ### 3. Move `Sorting` below `ArrayJoin` Swap the two steps and keep `limit = n` unchanged. This is the change that matters: an `n * k`-row top-N becomes an `n`-row top-N. - Precondition: no sort key is a joined column (by name, see above), and all sort keys are present in the step's input header. - First version: `SortingStep::Type::Full`, `!hasPartitions()`, no `limit_by` hint. - Only cross the `ArrayJoinStep` itself and `ExpressionStep`s that preserve order and cardinality (no `arrayJoin` inside). A `FilterStep` between the sort and the `ARRAY JOIN` blocks the move, since the guard cannot account for it. - Pass ordering: `tryExecuteFunctionsAfterSorting` normally lifts the intervening `Expression` above the sort first, so run after it and match a direct child. ### 4. Move `Limit` below `ArrayJoin` `ArrayJoinStep` fails the `preserves_number_of_rows` check in `tryPushDownLimit` (`limitPushDown.cpp:136`), so the case without `ORDER BY` needs an explicit branch that inserts the guard and swaps the steps. Expected payoff on its own is modest — roughly one block of expansion, because `LimitTransform` already finishes the pipeline and `ArrayJoinResultIterator` is `max_block_size`-windowed (`ArrayJoinAction.cpp:222-233`). Its real value is that it makes the follow-up issue (deferring the array read) possible. There is no offset work to do: `LimitStep::getLimitForSorting` already returns `limit + offset` (`LimitStep.h:29`), and the planner sets `partial_sorting_limit = limit_length + limit_offset` (`Planner.cpp:525`). ### 5. Optional follow-up: exact weighted limit Instead of the guard, the sort could keep rows until the prefix sum of `length(arr)` reaches `n`, which prunes harder (`n / avg_size` rows instead of `n`) and needs no filter. The cost is that `limit` is a scalar threaded through `PartialSortingTransform` (the `limit - 1`-th row threshold, `PartialSortingTransform.cpp:152-160`), `MergeSorter`, the remerge heuristic `limit * 2 < sum_rows_in_blocks` (`MergeSortingTransform.cpp:210-214`), `MergedData`, and `TopKThresholdTracker`. This is a sharpening, not a prerequisite; it should be driven by performance tests. ## Read-in-order interaction `buildSortingDAG` zeroes the limit when it sees a `FilterStep` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:297-298`), so the guard blocks the read-in-order limit hint. This is not a regression: the hint is *already* zero for inner `ARRAY JOIN` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp:309-310`), and `LEFT ARRAY JOIN` keeps it because it needs no guard. Recovering it for the inner case is what the weighted limit above would buy. `optimizePrimaryKeyConditionAndLimit` walks through `FilterStep`, so that path is unaffected. ## Scope limits This issue covers only the `ARRAY JOIN` clause form, that is, a real `ArrayJoinStep`. The `arrayJoin` function form lives inside `ActionsDAG` and is invisible to plan passes; extracting it into an `ArrayJoinStep` is tracked separately and would unblock roughly twenty `hasArrayJoin` bail-outs at once. ## Test plan - Correctness matrix: inner / `LEFT`, aligned / unaligned, several joined arrays, `Map`, empty arrays, all arrays empty, `Nullable`, constant arrays, `LIMIT` with `OFFSET`, `LIMIT WITH TIES` (must be refused), `LIMIT BY` between the steps, `ORDER BY` mentioning a joined column (must be refused), chained `ARRAY JOIN`s. - `EXPLAIN` plan shape tests, plus plan-serialization tests for the new step shape. - Check that `rows_before_limit_at_least` and `exact_rows_before_limit` are unchanged. - `tests/performance/` case with a large average array size and a small `LIMIT`. - Each stage behind its own setting, default off, flipped in a later commit.

signal.title: Support arrayElement and arraySlice for QBit
signal.text: arrayElement(qbit, n) (and the qbit[n] operator) reconstructs the n-th vector element at the full precision of the QBit element type, reading only the bit planes of the stride group that contains the element. Out-of-range indices follow the Array semantics: default value for arrayElement, NULL for arrayElementOrNull, negative indices count from the end. arraySlice(qbit, offset[, length]) returns a QBit over the selected dimensions (projection to a subset of dimensions). The offset and length must be constants because the dimension of a QBit is part of its type. A slice aligned to stride-group boundaries keeps the stride and reuses the stored bit-plane streams without copying; an octet-aligned slice is a pure byte move; any other slice repacks the bits, reading only the planes of the stride groups it overlaps. Possible follow-up: an analyzer pass (similar to DistanceTransposedPartialReadsPass) could rewrite these functions to read only the needed bit-plane subcolumns from disk, extending the "only needed strides" guarantee from the in-memory execution down to storage I/O. Closes #109942 ### Changelog category - New Feature ### Changelog entry Functions `arrayElement` (the `vec[n]` operator) and `arraySlice` now work for the `QBit` data type: `qbit[n]` returns the n-th vector element at full precision, and `arraySlice(qbit, offset, length)` returns a projection to a subset of dimensions. Both read only the bit planes of the stride groups they need, and slices aligned to stride-group boundaries reuse the stored streams without copying. This closes #109942. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=109953&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/109953](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F109953+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Cross-compile ClickHouse for Windows
signal.text: Draft. Cross-compiles `clickhouse.exe` for `x86_64-w64-windows-gnu` (mingw-w64 + clang + lld → a native PE, no emulation layer and no MSVC licence). The goal is `clickhouse-client` and `clickhouse-local` running natively on Windows. **State: it links, it has never been run.** The development host is aarch64 and its Wine has no x86-on-ARM emulator, so everything here is compiled and linked but not executed. That is the next step and needs an x86-64 Windows machine. ``` programs/clickhouse.exe: PE32+ executable for MS Windows 6.00 (console), x86-64 520 MB · imports ADVAPI32, IPHLPAPI, KERNEL32, USER32, WS2_32, dbghelp, msvcrt ``` Every import ships with Windows, so the binary is a single self-contained file. Linux builds and links `clickhouse` unchanged after every commit in the branch. CI builds `clickhouse` for Windows on every pull request, so the port cannot silently regress. ## What is here The runtime (libc++/libc++abi/libunwind with SEH, compiler-rt builtins), 117 contribs behind a self-maintaining CI gate, all of Poco — whose Windows layer had been deleted from this fork and is restored from upstream 1.9.3 — every library under `src`, and `programs`. Roughly 900 of the changed lines are one mechanical class: `std::filesystem::path` used where a `String` is wanted, which compiles on POSIX through an implicit conversion that does not exist on Windows. Implemented natively rather than stubbed, because a client needs them: terminal size and console encoding, raw console mode and keystroke reading, Ctrl+C and Ctrl+Break, socket liveness, `statvfs` via `GetDiskFreeSpaceEx`, file mapping, `pread`, per-thread CPU time, `setThreadName`, `isLocalAddress`, `readpassphrase`, and a `WakeupFd` built on a loopback socket pair (a Windows pipe cannot be waited on alongside sockets). Compiled out with the reason recorded at each site, all server-side or POSIX-only: the sampling profiler and signal handlers (Windows reports faults through SEH), `ThreadFuzzer`, the `fork`-based watchdog, `ShellCommand` and everything built on it, the pseudo-terminal features, and the `su`/`docker-init`/`install` tools. ## Known gaps - Not executed, as above. - `-g0` on Windows: a PE image cannot exceed 4 GiB and the DWARF alone is several times that, and PE has no `.gnu_debuglink` equivalent to carry it separately. A crash symbolizes to module and offset, not file and line. - No `Epoll` backend, so nothing that polls sockets through it works yet. - Local syslog, archives (`libarchive` needs a hand-written Windows `config.h`), conditional writes to the local object storage (they need `flock` on a directory and sub-second modification times), and the web terminal report `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`. `docs/en/development/build-cross-windows.md` has the build instructions and a per-subsystem inventory of what remains. Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112185 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/112767 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Build/Testing/Packaging Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added a cross-compilation target for Windows (`x86_64-w64-windows-gnu`), producing a native `clickhouse.exe`. The build is not yet tested at runtime. ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=112824&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/112824](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F112824+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: TTL CLEAR INDEX for MergeTree parts
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/107804 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/78714 TTL CLEAR INDEX lets a MergeTree table keep secondary indexes for recent parts while dropping the physical index files from old parts. I recommend reviewing commit-by-commit. The motivating case is Observability log storage. For log tables, the raw data is not always the dominant cost. Text indexes can be very large, and most queries only touch recent data. We want to keep the index where it helps and stop paying for it on old parts that are rarely searched. Example syntax: ```sql TTL timestamp + INTERVAL 7 DAY CLEAR INDEX message_text ``` This follows the existing meaning of `ALTER TABLE ... CLEAR INDEX`: remove the per-part index files, but keep the index definition in table metadata. Queries remain correct. Parts without the index just fall back to scanning. ## What this changes The patch adds a new table TTL action, `CLEAR INDEX`, and stores its per-part min/max TTL info in `ttl.txt` as `index_clear_ttl`. When a part is fully past the TTL for a target index, future maintenance may remove that index’s files from the part. If the table later reads that part, the secondary index reader already handles missing index files and simply does not use that index for that part. The patch also adds system table visibility: ```text system.parts.index_clear_ttl_info.{index_name,expression,min,max} ``` ## Merge behavior There are two cases. First, normal merges apply the TTL policy to their output. If a merge output is fully past the `CLEAR INDEX` TTL, the merge should not retain the target index files. This is important for late-arriving data: a tiny old insert should not cause a merge that rebuilds a huge old text index. Second, there is a dedicated TTL maintenance merge type: `MergeType::TTLClearIndex`. This is used for the case where a single old part has expired index files and does not otherwise need a merge. The first implementation is intentionally conservative: it selects one source part and produces one replacement part. Dedicated `TTLClearIndex` selection obeys the normal full-part merge byte and row limits. This keeps cleanup conservative when preserving the part would require copying unchanged files rather than hardlinking them. For eligible full-storage parts, the implementation uses a fast path: hardlink or copy unchanged files, omit the expired index files, rewrite checksums and metadata, and publish the replacement part. Projection directories are copied wholesale because the row set is unchanged. This avoids reading and rewriting the raw data. If the fast path is not safe, the code falls back to the normal rewrite path. The fallback may rewrite the part, but it still must not retain expired index files in the final output. Parts with incomplete TTL metadata are not selected for dedicated cleanup; `MATERIALIZE TTL` or an ordinary merge must first recalculate the current TTL rules. The fast path currently opts out for cases like packed part storage, UUID parts, legacy parts without metadata-version files, metadata version mismatches, patch parts, part-format changes, and projection subdirectories it cannot copy as-is. On remote or zero-copy storage, it copies unchanged files instead of hardlinking them. It handles packed skip-index archives by excluding dirty `skp_idx.packed` files from the hardlink/copy set and rewriting the archive for surviving packed entries. ## Rollout safety `TTLClearIndex` is a new merge type, and merge types are serialized in replicated MergeTree log entries. Older replicas would not understand a new merge type. For that reason, generation is gated by a setting: ```sql enable_ttl_clear_index_merge_type_generation ``` The default is off. The binary can parse and execute `TTLClearIndex`, but a server will not write that merge type to the replicated log unless the setting is enabled. The intended rollout is: 1. deploy code everywhere; 2. once every replica that can read the log understands `TTLClearIndex`, enable generation; 3. later we can consider changing the default. With the gate off, replicas will not schedule dedicated `TTLClearIndex` maintenance work. Regular merges can still apply the clear-index TTL to their outputs, which is safe because missing per-part index files are already supported. ## Interaction with `SYSTEM STOP TTL MERGES` `CLEAR INDEX` is a TTL effect, so it respects the TTL merge blocker. If TTL merges are already stopped before a regular merge starts, the merge continues without applying clear-index TTL effects. If TTL merges are stopped after a merge has already decided to apply clear-index TTL effects, the merge is cancelled, matching existing TTL-delete behavior. ## Validation and edge cases covered The tests cover: - invalid target index names - per-part `index_clear_ttl_info` in `system.parts`, including the target index name - minmax index clearing - text index clearing - the late tiny insert case, where an old cleared part later merges with a small old part - adding `CLEAR INDEX` TTL to a table that already has old indexed data - TTL dependency recalculation after mutating a column used by the TTL expression - replicated execution with embedded Keeper - generation off vs generation on ## Things deliberately left conservative The fast path is narrow on purpose. Physically unsupported parts use the regular fallback, while parts with incomplete TTL metadata wait for recalculation. We can broaden the fast path later once we are comfortable with storage-specific details. The generation gate is also conservative. It is there to make rolling upgrades safe, not to disable all `CLEAR INDEX` TTL behavior. Possible follow-ups: - share more code with the existing `ALTER ... CLEAR INDEX` mutation path - add more schema-evolution tests around dropping or changing target indexes - add more direct instrumentation around which files were hardlinked vs copied in the fast path ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): MergeTree tables now support `TTL ... CLEAR INDEX index_name`, which clears secondary index files from parts once all rows in the part are past the TTL. This can help to manage the lifecycle of large indexes on older data, to conserve disk space. <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=108069&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/108069](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F108069+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

This allows expressions such as `*`, `COLUMNS('...')`, `COLUMNS(a, b)`, `EXCEPT`, `APPLY`, and `REPLACE` to be expanded before expression validation and execution. ~~The change also adds `namedTuple` function to make matcher-expanded named tuple expressions ergonomic in tests and user queries.~~ The tests cover these use cases, direct and indirect cyclic default-expression dependency detection, and nested matcher expansion. ### Changelog category: - New Feature ### Changelog entry: - Support column matchers such as `*` and `COLUMNS` in column default value expressions, `DEFAULT`, `ALIAS`, `MATERIALIZED`, and `EPHEMERAL` expressions, and in data skipping index expressions. ### Note ~~About the newly added `namedTuple` function: I read the previous discussions in [1], [2], and [3], and my impression is that the existing `enable_named_columns_in_function_tuple` setting is not very discoverable. Please let me know if this direction is not desirable.~~ [1] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/63524 [2] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54921 [3] https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/54881 <!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY --> --- > [!NOTE] > **Medium Risk** > Touches core expression/DDL validation paths (defaults, aliases, ALTER, mutations, skip indexes), which can affect query planning and error behavior if matcher expansion or cycle detection is incorrect. > > **Overview** > Enables column matchers (e.g. `*`, `COLUMNS(...)` plus `EXCEPT`/`APPLY`/`REPLACE`) inside column `DEFAULT`/`MATERIALIZED`/`ALIAS`/`EPHEMERAL` expressions by expanding matchers before validation/execution, honoring `asterisk_include_*` settings and rejecting qualified matchers. > > Updates DDL/default validation, alias expansion, read-order optimization, merge/SELECT paths, and mutation/materialize flows to use a shared `cloneAndExpandColumnDefaultExpression` helper and adds cycle detection that accounts for matcher-expanded dependencies. > > Extends skip index parsing/analysis to normalize matcher and alias usage (including cyclic-alias detection) before `TreeRewriter` analysis, and adds docs + comprehensive stateless tests covering matcher expansion, errors, and ALTER/mutation/index scenarios. > > <sup>Reviewed by [Cursor Bugbot](https://cursor.com/bugbot) for commit 48ab80fd074599c63f967f624435e0a2e7f166ed. signal.title: Support bearer-token authentication in BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP
signal.text: `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP` had no way to authenticate with a bearer token: callers spliced an `Authorization: Bearer` entry into the header list themselves and had to remember not to pass HTTP Basic credentials at the same time, because both occupy the same header. `create` now takes the credential directly, in three overloads: Basic credentials, a bearer token, or both — with a non-empty token taking precedence, so the either/or rule lives in one place instead of in every caller. `create` also appends the bearer header to a local copy of the header list rather than mutating the builder, so a builder can be reused without carrying over a stale token. Every bearer-token call site of the class is migrated to the new overloads: - `HTTPBasedCatalogUtils` and `UnityCatalog`: built the header by hand and passed never-used HTTP Basic credentials alongside; now call `create` with the token. - `RestCatalog`, `OneLakeCatalog`, `BigLakeCatalog`: `getAuthHeaders` now returns an `AuthHeaders` (a bearer token plus extra headers). The bearer goes to `create`; only genuine extra headers (a user-supplied `auth_header`, `x-goog-user-project`, `User-Agent`) stay in the header list. `OneLakeCatalog`'s pre-obtained token also moved from a spliced header to the bearer. - `PaimonRestCatalog`: the `bearer` token provider (the `dlf` request-signing branch keeps its own signed headers). Out of scope — different transport (plain Poco requests or S3-client headers), not `BuilderRWBufferFromHTTP`: `OpenAIProvider`, `CloudJWTProvider`, ArrowFlight `AuthMiddleware`, GCS `diskSettings`. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Not for changelog (changelog entry is not required) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): ... <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=110313&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/110313](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F110313+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Hybrid SQL-standard short-name fallback for subquery columns
signal.text: This is a hybrid solution: it preserves ClickHouse's current projection-naming behavior exactly as-is, and additionally lets the outer query refer to a subquery / CTE projection column by its short name, the way the SQL standard and every other major engine (PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server) do. Both ways of addressing the column work in parallel. In ClickHouse today, the reproducer from #87022 fails: ```sql WITH t1 AS (SELECT 1 AS f1, 2 AS f2), t2 AS (SELECT 1 AS f1, 5 AS f2), t3 AS (SELECT b.f1, b.f2 FROM t1 AS a JOIN t2 AS b ON a.f1 = b.f1) SELECT * FROM t3 WHERE f1 = 1; -- => Unknown expression identifier `f1` ... (UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER) ``` The CTE's projection column is named `b.f1` (the analyzer keeps the full dotted form), so `WHERE f1 = 1` cannot resolve. Workarounds users have to fall back to today are `` WHERE `b.f1` = 1 `` or `SELECT b.f1 AS f1` — both surprising. The standard says the implicit column name is just `f1` (the rightmost component). This PR adds a new opt-in compatibility setting: - `analyzer_enable_short_column_names_from_subquery` (default `false`). When on, the outer query can refer to the column by either name: - canonical name `b.f1` (existing behavior, unchanged), - short name `f1` (new), - via outer alias + short name: `t3.f1` (new). The fallback is strictly additive: - The canonical projection name stays the same — `DESCRIBE`, `SELECT *`, result-set headers, and the wire protocol are byte-identical. - The short name is registered for a projection `.` only when (a) the short name is unique among sibling projections, and (b) it does not collide with any other column's canonical name. An explicit alias of the same short name always wins canonical resolution. - The short-name map is empty unless the setting is on, so the default-off path is a single `unordered_map::empty()` check on the cold miss path of identifier resolution. Scope limitation: the short-name fallback does NOT apply while resolving `JOIN USING` column lists. A USING list matches keys by `ColumnNode::getColumnName`, which still returns the canonical (dotted) name for a short-name-resolved column, so allowing the fallback there would make `USING` accept mismatched left/right names and silently fail to merge them. The fallback is suppressed in USING context — `JOIN ... USING (f1)` against a side that only exposes `f1` via this fallback raises `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` exactly as on master. Use an explicit `AS f1` alias or the canonical dotted name for that form. The same fix closes the related issues #66133 (subquery on the right side of a JOIN) and #94858 (3-way self-join inside a CTE). #94558 was closed by upstream changes already and is kept as a `Related:` reference (its CROSS JOIN shape is also handled by the new fallback). Implementation lives entirely inside the analyzer: - `AnalysisTableExpressionData` gains a per-table-expression `short_name_to_column_node` map plus `tryGetShortNameColumnNode` / `canBindShortName` accessors. - `QueryAnalyzer::initializeTableExpressionData` populates it for `QueryNode` / `UnionNode` table expressions when the setting is on, and also for `TableNode`s that represent materialized CTEs (the `WITH ... AS MATERIALIZED` rewrite path). - `IdentifierResolver::tryResolveIdentifierFromStorage` consults it after the existing canonical / subcolumn / Nested-prefix lookups miss. - `IdentifierResolver::tryResolveIdentifierFromJoinTree` wraps the join-tree walk in a two-pass: pass 1 disables short-name so any canonical / Nested-prefix match anywhere in the tree wins; pass 2 retries with the fallback enabled only when pass 1 found nothing. Pass 1's `UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER` throw (which preserves master's "alias-prefix miss kills sibling resolution" semantics) is caught at the join-tree level and converted into a pass-2 retry; the `JOIN USING` push/pop in `tryResolveIdentifierFromJoin` is wrapped in `SCOPE_EXIT` so the catch can't leave a dangling pointer on `scope.join_using_columns`. - `resolveJoin` disables the fallback for the duration of `JOIN USING` identifier resolution, via the same `SCOPE_EXIT`-guarded flag. - A new test, `04339_short_column_names_from_subquery.{sql,reference}`, covers all the issue reproducers, the additive guarantees, the materialized-CTE path, the conflict / ambiguity matrix, cross-join Nested-prefix precedence, alias-qualified short-name lookup vs sibling literal columns, the `JOIN USING` exclusion, and the exception-safe push/pop path for `scope.join_using_columns`. For each open issue it closes, there are now symmetric default-off (`serverError UNKNOWN_IDENTIFIER`) and setting-on (succeeds and returns the expected row) assertions. Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/87022 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/66133 Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/94858 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/94558 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Add the opt-in setting `analyzer_enable_short_column_names_from_subquery` (default `false`). When enabled, an outer query may refer to a subquery / CTE / materialized-CTE projection column whose canonical name is an unaliased qualified identifier like `b.f1` either by its dotted canonical name (existing behavior) or by its SQL-standard short name `f1`. The canonical name keeps working in every case; the short name is purely additive and is registered only when unambiguous and non-colliding. The fallback does not apply while resolving `JOIN USING` column lists — use an explicit `AS` alias or the canonical dotted name for that form.

signal.title: Iceberg: refresh the trusted table UUID on a reused metadata object
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/115124 Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/99981 `Iceberg` metadata file *content* is cached in `IcebergMetadataFilesCache` under a key that includes the table's `table-uuid`. The UUID is in that key precisely to tell apart two different tables that occupy the same storage path at different times. It was captured once, when the `IcebergMetadata` object was first opened, and never refreshed: `IcebergMetadata::supportsUpdate` returns `true` while there was no `IDataLakeMetadata::update` override, so `DataLakeConfiguration::update` called the base no-op and the persistent components were never rebuilt. As a result the UUID failed in exactly the case it exists for. If an external writer drops and recreates the table at the same root with a new `table-uuid` and restarts the metadata numbering, a reused `IcebergMetadata` object probes the old key and is served the **previous** table's `metadata.json`, i.e. the previous schema and snapshot. ### The change The trusted UUID now lives in `Iceberg::TrustedTableUuid`, a `SharedMutex`-guarded cell shared by every copy of `PersistentTableComponents` describing the same table, so that struct's "thread-safe or immutable" contract still holds and a refresh is observed by all copies. All read and write call sites go through the new `PersistentTableComponents::getTableUuid` accessor. `IcebergMetadata::update` selects the current metadata file and, when the selected version does **not** strictly advance past the last validated one, re-reads that file's own `table-uuid` bypassing the UUID-keyed content cache. An Iceberg writer appending new metadata files advances the version strictly, so the extra read is skipped on the ordinary path and the cache behaves as before; a table recreated in place restarts the numbering and is caught. When the UUID does change, the latest-version cells under the previous UUID and under the table path are dropped — the content cells keyed by the previous UUID become unreachable once the trusted UUID moves, so ordinary eviction is enough for those. ### Trade-offs, stated explicitly - **A legitimate writer can move the version non-monotonically.** `iceberg_recent_metadata_file_by_last_updated_ms_field` selects by `last-updated-ms` and can pick a lower version, and snapshot expiry or rollback tooling can too. The gate is conservative in the safe direction: those cases only pay one extra uncached `metadata.json` read and still return correct data. - **A replacement can advance the version.** If a recreated table's writer happens to start at a version higher than the last validated one, the gate does not fire and the stale key is still used. Closing that would require revalidating on every `update`, which disables the metadata content cache on essentially every read. This is a bounded improvement, not a complete guarantee. - **Cost for a table whose version does not advance.** One extra uncached `metadata.json` `GET` per `update`. With the default `iceberg_metadata_staleness_ms = 0` the `metadata/` directory is listed on every query anyway, so this is a small marginal cost on top of work already being done. - `format_version` and `table_location` are still the values observed when the table was opened, and are not refreshed by `update`. That was already true before this change. ### Testing - `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/tests/gtest_iceberg_trusted_table_uuid.cpp` pins the revalidation gate and the thread-safe accessor. Built and run locally: 6/6 pass, and the 142 tests matching `*Iceberg*:*DataLake*:*ObjectStorage*` still pass. - `tests/integration/test_storage_iceberg_no_spark/test_table_replaced_in_place.py` reproduces the reported behaviour end to end: it warms the content cache, relocates a second, independently created Iceberg table's metadata onto the first table's root (leaving the first incarnation's data files in place, so a stale read returns the previous rows rather than raising), and asserts the new rows are returned. It also asserts the same with `use_iceberg_metadata_files_cache = 0` as a control. **This integration test has not been executed.** The development environment here has no ClickHouse server binary for Linux and cannot run the integration harness, so the test is unverified and relies on CI. The gtest results above were produced locally on a Debug macOS build. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixed `Iceberg` tables serving a previous table's metadata from `IcebergMetadataFilesCache` when an external writer dropped and recreated the table at the same storage path. The `table-uuid` used as the metadata cache key is now refreshed instead of being pinned to the value observed when the table was opened.

signal.title: Support `UNIQUE` predicate that tests for no duplicate rows in a subquery
signal.text: Implement the SQL standard `UNIQUE` predicate that returns true when all rows in a subquery are distinct and false when duplicates exist. Empty subqueries return true (vacuously unique). The implementation follows the same pattern as `EXISTS`: - Parser: `UniqueLayer` class parses `UNIQUE(subquery)` syntax - Analyzer: rewrites to `SELECT count() = uniqExact(*) FROM (subquery)` - Analyzer: correlated subqueries are rejected with a clear `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` error; the old analyzer rejects `UNIQUE` with a clear error as well Closes #99609 ### Changelog category (leave one): - New Feature ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Added `UNIQUE(subquery)` predicate that returns true when all rows in the subquery are distinct. It behaves according to the SQL standard: duplicates yield false, empty subqueries yield true. Closes #99609 ### Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is written (mandatory for new features) <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=99877&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/99877](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F99877+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Paimon incremental read: a Keeper watermark left ahead of the warehouse (e.g. after restore) silently and permanently skips committed data
signal.text: ## Describe what's wrong A Paimon table read with incremental reads enabled (`paimon_incremental_read = 1`, which keeps a consumed-snapshot watermark in Keeper at `<paimon_keeper_path>/committed_snapshot`) can **silently and permanently skip durably-committed data** if the Keeper watermark is ever left ahead of the warehouse's latest snapshot id — for example after the Paimon warehouse is restored from an older backup, or is rolled back / truncated by another engine, while the ClickHouse Keeper cursor is not correspondingly reset. `PaimonMetadata::collectIncrementalDataFiles` resolves the resume point by comparing the Keeper watermark to the warehouse's current latest snapshot id, and treats "watermark `>=` latest" as an unconditional no-new-data case: ```cpp else if (*committed_snapshot_id >= state->snapshot_id) // PaimonMetadata.cpp:825 { LOG_DEBUG(log, "Snapshot {} already processed (committed={}), no new data", // :828 state->snapshot_id, *committed_snapshot_id); return {}; // :830 } ``` There is no read-repair and no error on this path — it returns an empty file list at `LOG_DEBUG`. So every snapshot the writer commits after the restore whose id is `<=` the stale watermark is never delivered to any consumer, with no exception and no user-visible log. Snapshots committed *above* the stale watermark resume normally, which makes the loss a silent hole rather than a total stall. The table-identity guard `validateTableIdentity` does not catch this: it re-reads schema-0 `timeMillis`, which is unchanged by a byte-copy restore, so the guard passes and the stale watermark is trusted. This is distinct from the *documented* At-Most-Once loss (`PaimonStreamState.h:35-37`), which concerns the window between advancing the watermark and finishing consumption *within a single poll*; here durably-committed data that no consumer ever received is dropped at resume time. This surface is behind the experimental setting `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine` (default off). ## Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on `26.8.1.1`; the code on current `master` is identical (`PaimonMetadata.cpp:825-830`). ## How to reproduce Requires the experimental Paimon engine and a Paimon warehouse (e.g. written with `pypaimon`), read via `PaimonLocal` with incremental reads and a Keeper cursor: 1. Create a warehouse with snapshots 1..3 (300 distinct rows) under the server's `user_files/`. Back up the warehouse directory at the snapshot-1 point. 2. `CREATE TABLE pt (...) ENGINE = PaimonLocal('<table_path>') SETTINGS paimon_incremental_read = 1, paimon_keeper_path = '/paimon/cursor', paimon_replica_name = 'r1'` with `allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine = 1`. 3. Poll `SELECT ... FROM pt` incrementally — all 300 rows are delivered and the Keeper watermark reaches 3. 4. Restore the warehouse directory from the snapshot-1 backup (schema unchanged). Have the Paimon writer append two new snapshots of new, distinct rows — these become snapshots 2 and 3 again (ids `<=` the stale watermark 3). 5. Poll again (and once more): **zero of the new rows are returned, no error is raised**, and the Keeper watermark stays 3. 6. Append one further snapshot (snapshot 4, id `>` 3): only snapshot 4's rows are returned — confirming the consumer is alive and the loss is confined to the snapshots at id `<=` the stale watermark. Controls that isolate the cause: reading the same restored-and-re-appended warehouse under a **fresh** `paimon_keeper_path` delivers all the new rows (so the warehouse content is intact and readable); and without the restore, appending snapshots above the watermark delivers normally. ## Expected behavior When the committed watermark is ahead of the warehouse's latest snapshot id (the warehouse has moved backwards relative to the cursor), ClickHouse should detect the disagreement and either fail loudly or reset the cursor to the warehouse state, rather than silently returning no data and permanently skipping every subsequent commit at id `<=` the stale watermark. ## Error message and/or stacktrace None — the defining property is that the skip is silent (only a `LOG_DEBUG` "no new data" line).
signal.author: zlareb1

signal.title: Paimon incremental read: the unfenced processing_lock lets a second consumer silently duplicate acknowledged rows after a session expiry
signal.text: ## Describe what's wrong The Paimon incremental-read stream state (`allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine`) coordinates competing consumers that share one `paimon_keeper_path` with an ephemeral `processing_lock` znode. That lock has **no fencing**, so if the lock is lost while a consumer is mid-read (the usual cause being a Keeper session expiry that auto-removes the holder's ephemeral node), a second consumer acquires the freed lock and re-reads the same committed snapshot range. Both consumers then deliver the same committed data — an at-least-once **duplicate of already-acknowledged rows, with no error logged anywhere**. The `processing_lock` exists precisely to make the read/commit critical section mutually exclusive, so this defeats its only purpose. The unfenced-ness is visible in three places in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/PaimonStreamState.cpp` (line numbers on `master`): 1. Acquire writes the owner's `replica_name` into the lock node but it is **never read back** anywhere — the value is dead (`acquireProcessingLock`, lines 70–90): ```cpp keeper->create(processing_lock_path, replica_name, zkutil::CreateMode::Ephemeral); ``` 2. Release is an **unconditional** `tryRemove(path, -1)` whose return code is discarded, so it deletes whatever node is at the path — including an ephemeral created by a *different* session (`removeProcessingLock`, lines 269–274): ```cpp keeper->tryRemove(processing_lock_path, -1); ``` 3. The watermark advance is a **blind** `makeSetRequest(..., -1)` in its own standalone `tryMulti` with no check op on the lock and no monotonicity guard, so it succeeds regardless of whether the caller still holds the lock or whether another consumer moved the watermark underneath it (`setCommittedSnapshot`, lines 214–238): ```cpp ops.emplace_back(zkutil::makeSetRequest(committed_path, toString(snapshot_id), -1)); ``` For contrast, the sibling `is_active` node in the *same file* is fenced correctly — it reads the node back with its `Stat` and removes it version-checked (`tryGet(is_active_path, existing_identifier, &stat)` then `tryRemove(is_active_path, stat.version)`, lines ~159 and ~165) — so applying the same discipline to `processing_lock` is clearly feasible. Note this is distinct from the documented "at-most-once" window (a *loss* on crash between watermark advance and delivery): the issue here is a **duplicate with no crash**, produced by a routine session expiry, which an at-most-once contract does not permit. ## Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes, reproduces on current `master`. The Paimon storage engine is experimental (`allow_experimental_paimon_storage_engine`, default off). ## How to reproduce Two ClickHouse instances (two Keeper sessions), each with a Paimon incremental-read table over the **same** warehouse and the **same** `paimon_keeper_path`: ```sql -- on both servers CREATE TABLE c (id Int64, v String) ENGINE = PaimonLocal('/warehouse/db.db/t1') SETTINGS paimon_incremental_read = 1, paimon_keeper_path = '/paimon/stream', paimon_replica_name = 'ra'; -- 'rb' on the second server ``` 1. Commit snapshot 1 to the warehouse; consumer A drains it, so `committed_snapshot` = 1. 2. Commit snapshots 2 and 3 (ids above the watermark). 3. Consumer A starts an incremental read: it acquires `processing_lock`, reads `committed_snapshot` (still 1), and plans the read of snapshots 2–3. 4. Consumer A's Keeper session expires (network blip / GC pause / Keeper failover exceeding `session_timeout_ms`). A's ephemeral `processing_lock` is auto-removed, but A's in-flight read continues (its server process is alive; the ZooKeeper client reconnects on a fresh session). 5. Consumer B polls: it acquires the now-free `processing_lock`, reads `committed_snapshot` (still 1, because A has not advanced it yet), and delivers snapshots 2–3. 6. Consumer A finishes: its blind `setCommittedSnapshot(3)` succeeds (version `-1`), and A also delivers snapshots 2–3. Both consumers have now delivered snapshots 2–3 — the same committed rows twice, with no error. The window in step 3–4 is deterministically reproducible by pausing A's `setCommittedSnapshot` multi to Keeper and deleting the `processing_lock` znode during the pause (which is exactly what a session expiry does to the ephemeral), then letting B poll and finally releasing A. ## Expected behavior Each committed snapshot is delivered to at most one consumer. A consumer that lost its `processing_lock` (session expiry, or the node otherwise gone) must not silently commit over another consumer's progress: the watermark advance and the lock release should be fenced by lock ownership (e.g. a version/session check, as `is_active` already does) so that a stale holder fails loudly instead of duplicating acknowledged data. ## Error message and/or stacktrace None — this is the problem. No exception is thrown and nothing is logged; the duplication is silent. ## Additional context The three call sites above are all in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Paimon/PaimonStreamState.cpp`.

signal.title: Native protocol: send String columns with a size stream
signal.text: ### Company or project name chconn ### Use case In the Native protocol, `String` columns are sent as `varint(size) + bytes` for every row. A client has to decode this row by row: read one varint, copy one value, repeat. The client also can not preallocate the buffer, because it does not know the total data size before reading all rows. For string-heavy queries this is the most expensive part of reading data in a client. I am the author of [chconn](https://github.com/vahid-sohrabloo/chconn) (Go client, native protocol) and in profiles of string-heavy SELECTs this decode loop dominates the client CPU time. On the storage side this problem is already solved. Since 25.10 there is `MergeTreeStringSerializationVersion::WITH_SIZE_STREAM` (default since 25.11): String columns in MergeTree parts are stored as a sizes substream (UInt64 per row) plus a data substream. But the Native protocol still always uses `SINGLE_STREAM`. `NativeWriter` and `NativeReader` build their `SerializationInfo` with `SerializationInfoSettings::enableAllSupportedSerializations()`, and this function keeps `string_serialization_version = SINGLE_STREAM`. The comment on this function already says: "Additional serialization versions can be added here in the future" — this proposal is exactly that. ### Describe the solution you'd like Add a new protocol revision, same pattern as `DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_V2_DYNAMIC_AND_JSON_SERIALIZATION`: ``` DBMS_MIN_REVISION_WITH_STRING_WITH_SIZE_STREAM_SERIALIZATION = 54487 ``` When both sides are on this revision or higher: - `NativeWriter` builds the `SerializationInfo` with `string_serialization_version = WITH_SIZE_STREAM` and `propagate_types_serialization_versions_to_nested_types = true`. So all Strings use the new format, also inside `Array` / `Nullable` / `Map` / `Tuple` / `Variant` / `JSON`. This reuses the same serialization trees that MergeTree uses since 26.3, no new format code is needed. - `NativeReader` enables the same versions based on the peer revision. So the server can also accept this format on INSERT, and `clickhouse-client` supports it automatically (same code). In a Native block all substreams go into one buffer, so for a plain String column the layout is: ``` N x UInt64 sizes (little-endian) | all string data concatenated (no per-row prefixes) ``` A client on the new revision reads `8*N` bytes, sums the sizes (so it can allocate the exact buffer size), and then reads the whole data with one bulk read. No per-row parsing, no reallocation. Clients keep both decoders and select by the negotiated revision, like it already works for LowCardinality, custom serializations and Dynamic/JSON V2. Old clients and old servers are not affected at all. INSERT works in both directions: a client on the new revision must also send Strings in this format, because the server reader selects the serialization from the peer revision. So inserts get faster too, but a client has to implement both read and write. ### Describe alternatives you've considered _No response_ ### Additional context I made a small prototype on master (12 lines, writer side only, gated by a setting just to test) and implemented the client side in chconn. Client-side decode benchmark (same data, both formats, Go): | workload | varint | size-stream | speedup | |---|---|---|---| | 1M strings, len 20 | 35 ms, 4 allocs | 8.9 ms, 0 allocs | ~4.0x | | 1M strings, len 0-60 | 41 ms, 4 allocs | 9.3 ms, 0 allocs | ~4.4x | | 100k strings, len 200 | 7.1 ms | 3.1 ms | ~2.3x | End to end (patched master 26.7.1.1, localhost TCP, `SELECT s FROM bench_strings`, 5M rows, avg length 29.5, MergeTree, same server and table, only the wire format is different): | | wall time | rows/s | |---|---|---| | varint | 152-158 ms | ~32M | | size-stream | **39 ms** | **~128M** | I verified the results are byte-identical between both formats. One note: the new format sends more bytes for short strings (8-byte sizes instead of 1-byte varints, about +35 MB for these 5M rows) and it is still ~4x faster on localhost. With LZ4/ZSTD compression the size bytes are mostly zeros and compress very well, so on a real network it should also win. The nested types come almost for free from `propagate_types_serialization_versions_to_nested_types`, but the transport needs round-trip tests for all of them (Array, Nullable, Map, Variant, JSON...). If there is interest I can prepare a PR (writer + reader + revision constant + tests).

signal.title: Allow interactive queries finish in the background
signal.text: **Use case** A user can run an interactive session with long-running INSERT SELECT. If the session is interrupted, the query is typically canceled (after an exception about connection loss in an attempt to send progress or read a network packet from a user). But it is sad if the query was running for a long time. **Describe the solution you'd like** If a query is not expected to return any result to the user (such as SELECT) and does not require any data from the user (such as INSERT without SELECT), we can catch exceptions related to a network connection with the user, stop sending the progress packets and waiting for the incoming packets (such as cancellation), and continue normally. The user can reconnect and then observe the progress in `SHOW PROCESSLIST`. **Additional context** The current behavior (query termination on connection loss) is also good. signal.title: Vectorize `least`/`greatest` for Nullable and 3+ numeric arguments, and `clamp` for numeric arguments
signal.text: Functions `least` and `greatest` have a fast vectorized implementation only for exactly two non-Nullable numeric arguments. Nullable arguments, or three and more arguments, fall back to a generic per-row `compareAt`/`insertFrom` loop that is 3–5× slower, although the operation is just an element-wise min/max over column buffers. This PR adds a vectorized min/max fold to `FunctionLeastGreatestGeneric` for numeric (possibly Nullable) arguments of any arity. The arguments are already cast to the common supertype, so type promotion is unchanged; for Nullable arguments the result null map is the AND of the input null maps and a NULL operand loses against any non-NULL one — exactly the existing semantics (`least(NULL, x) = x`, NULL only when all arguments are NULL), including NaN ordering. Non-numeric types keep using the generic loop. The same treatment is applied to `clamp`, which used the same generic per-row `compareAt`/`insertFrom` loop for all types: numeric arguments now go through a branch-free vector loop replicating the `compareAt` semantics with `nan_direction_hint = 1` (NaN compares greater than any number), with the per-row `min > max` validation hoisted into a separate pass. NULLs do not reach the fast path because `clamp` uses the default implementation for NULLs. Clamping 50M `UInt64` rows drops from ~0.48 s to ~0.07 s (6.9×), 50M `Float64` rows from ~0.55 s to ~0.14 s (4.1×). Single-thread benchmark on a 100M-row table, `Nullable(UInt32)` columns `a`, `b` (~9–14% NULLs), plain `UInt32` columns `an`, `bn`: | query | master | this PR | speedup | |---|---|---|---| | `least(a, b)` | 1.35 s | 0.37 s | 3.7× | | `least(a, bn)` | 1.19 s | 0.36 s | 3.3× | | `least(an, bn, an)` | 0.94 s | 0.25 s | 3.8× | | `least(an, bn, an, bn)` | 1.20 s | 0.29 s | 4.1× | | `greatest(a, b, a, b)` | 2.11 s | 0.61 s | 3.5× | | `least(an, bn)` (existing fast path) | 0.22 s | 0.20 s | unchanged | Results were verified identical to the previous implementation on the 100M-row table and on a randomized matrix of all numeric type pairs/triples/quads with all nullability combinations, including NaN/Inf values, the legacy NULL behavior setting, and non-numeric types. ### Changelog category (leave one): - Performance Improvement ### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Vectorize functions `least` and `greatest` for `Nullable` numeric arguments and for three or more numeric arguments, and function `clamp` for numeric arguments. These cases were previously evaluated row-by-row and are now 3–7 times faster.

signal.title: Refuse to materialize columns used in sort key expressions
signal.text: Changelog category: Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) Changelog entry: Fixed `ALTER TABLE ... MATERIALIZE COLUMN` for `MergeTree` tables: materializing a column required by a key expression (sorting key, partition key, projection sorting key, or the engine sign/version column) — directly or via a dependent `MATERIALIZED` column — is now refused instead of silently corrupting the sort order / partition assignment of existing parts. Dependent skip indices, projections, statistics and TTL bounds that read a recomputed column are rebuilt instead of being hardlinked with stale values. Documentation entry for user-facing changes - [x] Documentation is not required (bug fix) ## What this PR does `ALTER TABLE MATERIALIZE COLUMN c2` was allowed when `c2` appeared inside a sort key expression like `ORDER BY metroHash64(c1, c2)`, but was correctly blocked for direct sort keys like `ORDER BY c2`. Materializing such a column recalculates its values (e.g., `MATERIALIZED now()` produces new timestamps), which invalidates the sort order of existing data parts. Subsequent merges or deletes then fail with: ``` Logical error: 'Sort order of blocks violated for column number 2' ``` ### Root cause The original check only consulted `getSortingKeyColumns()`, which returns the top-level column names in `ORDER BY`. For function-based keys like `ORDER BY metroHash64(c1, c2)`, the column names are `metroHash64(c1, c2)` — not `c1` or `c2`. So the check missed columns used as arguments to sort key functions. ### Fix `MATERIALIZE COLUMN` now mirrors the protections `UPDATE` already has, refusing the command (with `CANNOT_UPDATE_COLUMN`) when the materialized column — or a stored `MATERIALIZED` column computed from it (one level, matching `UPDATE`) — is required to evaluate: - the table sorting key expression (`getColumnsRequiredForSortingKey`, subcolumn-aware); - the partition key expression; - a projection's sorting key expression; - the engine merge-semantic column (`CollapsingMergeTree` sign / `ReplacingMergeTree` version). When the command is allowed, a dependent stored `MATERIALIZED` column is recomputed in an extra mutation stage, and any skip index / projection / statistics / TTL expression that reads a rewritten column is fed into the mutation stream so the derived object is rebuilt instead of hardlinked with stale values. ## Test plan - [x] Stateless test `04046_materialize_column_sort_key_expr.sql` covering: direct sort key column, sort-key function expression, subcolumn-parent sort key, projection sorting key, partition key (and subcolumn-parent partition key), skip-index/projection/statistics rebuild, dependent `MATERIALIZED` columns (recompute and key-feeding refusal), TTL recalculation, and the engine sign/version columns. A column not used in any key still materializes successfully (no over-rejection). - [ ] CI (full test suite) Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/93139 <!-- CI automatic block start :ci_links: --> --- Workflow [[PR](https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/json.html?PR=99647&sha=latest&name_0=PR)] Sync PR [[sync-upstream/pr/99647](https://github.com/search?q=head%3Async-upstream%2Fpr%2F99647+org%3AClickHouse+type%3Apr&type=pullrequests)] <!-- CI automatic block end :ci_links: -->

signal.title: Fix serialize_query_plan=1 requiring shard tables to exist on the initiator
signal.text: Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/111893 ### Changelog category (leave one): - Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release) ### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md): Fixes `serialize_query_plan = 1` failing with `UNKNOWN_DATABASE`/`UNKNOWN_TABLE` when a shard's table doesn't need to exist in the initiator's own catalog -- e.g. `remote('host:port', 'db', 'table')` where `db` only exists on the remote target, or a `Distributed` table relying on a per-shard `default_database` in the cluster config. Both cases now work the same under `serialize_query_plan = 0` and `= 1`. --- ### Problem `serialize_query_plan = 1` builds each shard's query plan on the initiator (to serialize and ship it), instead of shipping query text for the shard to resolve itself. `createLocalPlan` did this by constructing a fresh `InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer` from the raw query AST, which requires every referenced table to resolve in the initiator's own `DatabaseCatalog`. Two real cases where that's not true: 1. `remote('host:port', 'db', 'table')` where `db` only exists on the remote target, not the initiator. 2. A `Distributed` table declared with an empty database, relying on a per-shard `<default_database>` in the cluster config to fill it in at query time -- each shard's actual database (e.g. `shard_1`) may not exist on the initiator either. ### Fix `SelectStreamFactory::createForShardImpl` already receives an already-resolved `query_tree` (from the outer/initiator-level analysis) that it never threaded into `createLocalPlan`. Added an optional `query_tree` parameter; when present, `createLocalPlan` constructs `InterpreterSelectQueryAnalyzer` from the tree directly (no query tree passes applied) instead of re-resolving from the AST, avoiding local catalog lookup entirely for case 1. For case 2, the reused tree carries the empty-database placeholder baked into its `StorageDummy` from before any per-shard information was available. Added `fillInDefaultDatabaseForEmptyDatabaseTables`, which walks the tree and rebuilds a corrected `StorageDummy` using the shard's `default_database` -- the same pattern `replaceStorageInQueryTree` already uses elsewhere, but correcting the database on an existing table node instead of substituting a whole new storage. Also had to guard the existing `Context::setCurrentDatabase(default_database)` call (which asserts the database exists in the initiator's own catalog) to only run on the AST-based fallback path -- it was firing unconditionally and rejecting valid per-shard databases before the tree-based path even got a chance to run. ### Testing - Verified live against two real, separate ClickHouse server processes on different ports (not a self-referencing single-node trick) for case 1, and a genuine 2-shard cluster (real `shard_0`/`shard_1` databases on two separate server processes) for case 2. Both `serialize_query_plan = 0` and `= 1` now return byte-identical row content. - Confirmed no regression against a normal `Distributed` table with a real, fully-declared database. - Confirmed an unrelated fix in the same general code area (`ActionsDAG::serialize`-adjacent, from a separate PR) still works correctly after this change. - Added `tests/queries/0_stateless/04928_serialize_query_plan_per_shard_default_database.sql` covering case 2, using the stock `test_cluster_two_shards_different_databases` cluster already defined in the test config. - Case 1 needs a genuinely separate server process (a different catalog), which the single-server `0_stateless` harness can't express -- not covered by an automated test in this PR, verified manually instead as described above. Happy to add an integration test if that's preferred. Please review, happy to make changes if needed.

signal.title: Keeper: parent `Stat` fields `cversion` and `pzxid` differ from ZooKeeper
signal.text: ### Company or project name gmonit.ru ### Describe what's wrong Two fields of a parent node's `Stat` behave differently in ClickHouse Keeper than in ZooKeeper, and the two differences go in opposite directions: * **`cversion` changes more often than in ZooKeeper** — Keeper bumps a parent's `cversion` on every `setData` of a direct child. * **`pzxid` changes less often than in ZooKeeper** — Keeper does not update a parent's `pzxid` when a child is removed. **What I'm asking:** whether both are intentional. I don't have an opinion on which behaviour is correct and I'm not proposing a change — the rest of this issue is just the evidence. The two concrete questions are at the bottom. Measured with the same Java client (3.9.5) against Keeper 26.8.1.1431 and 26.3.9.8, and against `zookeeper:3.9` as a reference. Both Keeper versions behave identically. Operations on a **direct child** of the observed parent: | Operation on child | ZK `cversion` | Keeper `cversion` | ZK `pzxid` | Keeper `pzxid` | |--------------------------|---------------|-------------------|------------|----------------| | `create` | +1 | +1 | bumped | bumped | | `delete` | +1 | +1 | bumped | **not bumped** | | `setData` | unchanged | **+1** | unchanged | unchanged | | anything on a grandchild | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | unchanged | `numChildren` matches ZooKeeper in all cases. On Keeper I also checked `setACL` on a child (leaves the parent untouched) and an ephemeral child expiring with its session (`cversion` +1, `pzxid` not bumped); I did not run those two against ZooKeeper, so they are out of the comparison. The difference is confined to the stat: the parent's `cversion` bump does not fire a child watch, so `NodeChildrenChanged` is not emitted on `setData` of a child. ### Where this comes from **`cversion`** — the `Set` handler increments the parent's counter after updating the node itself: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L882-L890 ZooKeeper stores the *number of creates* and converts it to the *number of changes* when the stat is handed to a client, so deletes are accounted for without a second counter and `setData` cannot contribute: https://github.com/apache/zookeeper/blob/7af463e0fd5097930f52864911b224d8b9e6a485/zookeeper-server/src/main/java/org/apache/zookeeper/server/DataNode.java#L155-L164 ```java // when we do the Cversion we need to translate from the count of the creates // to the count of the changes (v3 semantics) // for every create there is a delete except for the children still present to.setCversion(stat.getCversion() * 2 - numChildren); ``` **`pzxid`** — in the `Remove` handler the update is guarded by `restored_from_zookeeper_log`, so it happens only while replaying a log imported from ZooKeeper, not on ordinary deletes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L534-L536 ZooKeeper updates it on every delete (`DataTree.deleteNode`). ### Why the combination matters Taken together, no single field answers ZooKeeper's "did the child set change?" question on Keeper: `cversion` reports changes that did not touch the child set, `pzxid` misses removals, and `numChildren` cannot see one child being replaced by another. Only the pair `(pzxid, numChildren)` is equivalent. ClickHouse itself reads `cversion` with ZooKeeper semantics in three places, which is expected since the same code also runs against real ZooKeeper: * [`DatabaseReplicated.cpp#L454`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Databases/DatabaseReplicated.cpp#L454) and [`#L476`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Databases/DatabaseReplicated.cpp#L476) — reads the replica list, re-reads the stat of `/replicas`, and retries if `cversion` changed, throwing `ALL_CONNECTION_TRIES_FAILED: Cannot get consistent cluster snapshot` after `max_retries = 10`. On Keeper a `setData` on any `/replicas/<host>` node counts as a change even though the set of replicas did not change. * [`ClusterDiscovery.cpp#L319`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Interpreters/ClusterDiscovery.cpp#L319) — uses `cversion` as the version of the shard list. * [`NamedCollectionsMetadataStorage.cpp#L274`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Common/NamedCollections/NamedCollectionsMetadataStorage.cpp#L274) — detects that the collection list changed. I have not seen a failure from any of these; they are listed because they show the direction of the effect — extra work rather than missed updates. ### Migrating from ZooKeeper 1. **Client code.** Code that reads `cversion` to mean "children were added or removed" becomes more sensitive on Keeper; code that reads `pzxid` for the same purpose becomes less sensitive and misses deletions without any error. 2. **Snapshot conversion.** `clickhouse-keeper-converter` reads `cversion` from the ZooKeeper snapshot as-is ([`ZooKeeperDataReader.cpp#L132`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/ZooKeeperDataReader.cpp#L132)), but a ZooKeeper snapshot stores the internal value (the create count), not what clients were served. For a node that had children deleted, `cversion` therefore drops after conversion relative to what ZooKeeper reported. The same field seeds the sequential counter later in the same loop ([L146](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/ZooKeeperDataReader.cpp#L146)), so the two uses are coupled. The txn-log half of the conversion works on the stored counter rather than the served one. `Remove` increments `cversion` unconditionally ([L593](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L593)), including while replaying a `DeleteTxn`, whereas ZooKeeper leaves the stored counter untouched on a delete — the +1 a client sees there is produced by the `2C − N` translation at read time. In practice the drift is bounded: a replayed `CreateTxn` carries `parent_cversion` and the Create handler snaps to it ([L356-L359](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Coordination/KeeperStorageImpl.cpp#L356-L359)), so only deletes after a parent's last create leave a lasting difference. <details> <summary>Why the existing tests do not surface the difference</summary> * [`test_keeper_back_to_back/test.py#L173`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_back_to_back/test.py#L173) — `assert_eq_stats` does compare `cversion` between real ZooKeeper and Keeper, and [`test_stats`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_back_to_back/test.py#L182) does call `set`. But `set` is applied to the node whose stat is then compared, so the *parent* (`/`) is never inspected and the difference falls outside the assertion. * [`test_keeper_session/test.py#L286`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_session/test.py#L286) — `test_create2_tree_parent_stats` only creates children, so `setData` on a child is never exercised; it also asserts the parent's `cversion` with `>=` rather than `==` ([L308](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_session/test.py#L308)), so it would not fail even if it were. * [`test_keeper_zookeeper_converter/test.py#L292`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_zookeeper_converter/test.py#L292) — compares `cversion` after conversion. The pre-snapshot deletions in these tests are all of children of `/`, and `compare_states` skips `/` and `/zookeeper` by design ([L350](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_zookeeper_converter/test.py#L350), commented "both paths have strange stats"). For the nodes whose stats are compared no children had been deleted, so `2C − N` reduces to `C` and the conversion difference is invisible. * [`test_keeper_znode_time/test.py#L51`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/tests/integration/test_keeper_znode_time/test.py#L51) also asserts `cversion` equality, but between two Keeper nodes rather than against ZooKeeper, so it cannot catch this either. * There are no unit tests covering `cversion` in `src/Coordination/tests/`. </details> ### Does it reproduce on the most recent release? Yes — reproduced on 26.8.1.1431 and on 26.3.9.8. ### How to reproduce Create a parent, then create / modify / delete children under it, reading the parent's stat after each step. Any ZooKeeper client will do. **`cversion`.** Create one child, then write to it five times — Keeper: ``` after create /s1/a cversion=1 pzxid=41508 numChildren=1 after 5x setData /s1/a cversion=6 pzxid=41508 numChildren=1 ``` `zookeeper:3.9`, the same first two steps, then continued through a grandchild and the deletes: ``` create /t1/a cversion=1 pzxid=9 numChildren=1 5x setData /t1/a cversion=1 pzxid=9 numChildren=1 create grandchild /t1/a/deep cversion=1 pzxid=9 numChildren=1 delete grandchild and /t1/a cversion=2 pzxid=17 numChildren=0 ``` (The last step deletes two nodes but `cversion` moves by one, since only `/t1/a` is a direct child of the observed parent.) **`pzxid`.** Create two children, write to one, delete both — Keeper: ``` baseline cversion=0 pzxid=41646 numChildren=0 create a cversion=1 pzxid=41647 numChildren=1 create b cversion=2 pzxid=41648 numChildren=2 setData a cversion=3 pzxid=41648 numChildren=2 delete a cversion=4 pzxid=41648 numChildren=1 delete b cversion=5 pzxid=41648 numChildren=0 ``` `pzxid` stops moving after the last `create`, while in the ZooKeeper run above it advances from 9 to 17 on the deletes. ### Expected behavior Two questions, per the note at the top: * Is the `Set` handler incrementing the parent's `cversion` deliberate? The same increment is present in v22.3 ([`KeeperStorage.cpp#L613`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/v22.3.20.29-lts/src/Coordination/KeeperStorage.cpp#L613), inside `KeeperStorageSetRequestProcessor`) and survived the later storage refactorings, and the in-process `TestKeeper` used by ClickHouse's own tests does the same thing ([`TestKeeper.cpp#L554`](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/4c1d9c8ad564ef2d7aa4c6ecfc7bf9b141219194/src/Common/ZooKeeper/TestKeeper.cpp#L554)), so it doesn't look accidental. * Is the `restored_from_zookeeper_log` guard on the `pzxid` update in `Remove` intentional? If both are intentional, documenting them alongside the other known ZooKeeper compatibility gaps (#59489) would help — `cversion` on Keeper answers a different question than on ZooKeeper ("did anything about my direct children change, including their data"), and that is useful to know either way. If they are not, one thing worth weighing first: `cversion` participates in the node digest, digests travel in the Raft log, and a mismatch is fatal (`std::terminate` in `assertDigest`), so changing the computed value needs care across a rolling upgrade of a live quorum, not just a `KEEPER_CURRENT_DIGEST_VERSION` bump. ### Error message and/or stacktrace _No response_

signal.title: Add a TOLERANCE clause to ASOF JOIN
signal.text: ### Company or project name ClickHouse ### Use case `ASOF JOIN` currently matches each left row with the most recent right row at or before the left timestamp, with no way to cap how far back that match may reach. We would like an optional `TOLERANCE` clause that bounds the maximum time gap between the left key and the matched right key, so that only "recent enough" matches are returned and stale rows are excluded. This is a common requirement in time-series and financial analytics (for example transaction cost analysis, quote-to-trade enrichment, and sensor/state enrichment), where a match that is technically the latest available but minutes or hours old is misleading. **Current behavior** For a trade joined to the prevailing quote: ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time ``` If the nearest preceding quote for a given trade is very old, `ASOF JOIN` still returns it. There is no built-in way to say "only match if the quote is within N units of the trade". ### Describe the solution you'd like An optional `TOLERANCE` clause on `ASOF JOIN` that accepts an interval (or numeric) value and restricts matches to those where the difference between the left and matched right key is within the given bound. Suggested syntax (open to alternatives): ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF LEFT JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time TOLERANCE INTERVAL 10 SECOND ``` **Semantics**: a left row at `t.time` matches a right row at `q.time` only if both hold: - `q.time <= t.time` (existing ASOF inequality) - `t.time - q.time <= tolerance` When no right row is within tolerance, the behavior should follow the join type: `ASOF LEFT JOIN` returns the left row with NULL/default right columns, `ASOF JOIN` (inner) drops the row. ### Describe alternatives you've considered The gap can be filtered after the join: ```sql SELECT t.time, t.symbol, t.price, q.bid, q.ask FROM trades AS t ASOF JOIN quotes AS q ON t.symbol = q.symbol AND t.time >= q.time WHERE t.time - q.time <= INTERVAL 1 SECOND ``` This is correct but can be slower than necessary. The join still scans backward to find a match that the `WHERE` clause then discards. With a native tolerance, the backward scan can stop as soon as a right row is older than the left row by more than the tolerance, since no earlier row can qualify. For an `ASOF LEFT JOIN`, a post-join WHERE instead removes the entire result row, breaking `LEFT JOIN` semantics. ### Additional context This capability is well established, which gives a clear reference for expected semantics.
